title: How to replace the hard disk used as hostPath storage for elasticsearch in Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform without losing data?
issue: We have configured OCP to use hostPath storage for elasticsearch as per [documentation](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/3.11/install_config/aggregate_logging.html#aggregated-logging-hostPath-Elasticsearch).
Now we are running out of disk space on the hard disk that is being used for the hostPath storage for elasticsearch.
The disk is not a LVM Logical Volume and thus can't be expanded.
How can we replace the disk that is currently being used to store elasticsearch data without losing log data?
resolution: Please follow the below steps in order to replace the hard disk used as hostPath storage for elasticsearch. * First, verify that the elasticsearch cluster is in the "green" state: $ oc exec-n-c elasticsearch-- health * Make sure that the file system mounted on "/elasticsearch/persistent" is not over 80% allocated. Should this be the case, please manually remove unused indices: $ for pod in $(oc get po-n-l component=es-o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do echo $pod; oc exec $pod-n-c elasticsearch-- df-h /elasticsearch/persistent; done * Prevent shard balancing before purposely bringing down nodes: $ oc exec-n-c elasticsearch-- \ curl-s \--cacert /etc/elasticsearch/secret/admin-ca \--cert /etc/elasticsearch/secret/admin-cert \--key /etc/elasticsearch/secret/admin-key \-XPUT 'https://localhost:9200/_cluster/settings' \-d '{"transient": {"cluster.routing.allocation.enable": "none"}}' Complete the following steps for each DeploymentConfig. Make sure to double check the elasticsearch cluster state before proceeding with the next one. * Take note of the node(s) on which the Pod(s) are scheduled on. Those should be static when using [hostPath](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/3.11/install_config/aggregate_logging.html#aggregated-logging-hostPath-Elasticsearch). $ oc-n get pods-o wide * Scale DeploymentConfig to zero replicas and verify that the pod was terminated: $ oc-n scale dc--replicas=0 $ oc-n get pods-o wide * Drain the node on which the pod was scheduled on: $ oc adm drain--ignore-daemonsets=true--delete-local-data=true * Adjust the storage configuration to your needs. For example, you can perform any of the following: Expand the volume Copy the data from the old volume to a new, larger volume using rsync; then update Elasticsearch to point to the new volume instead: $ oc edit dc... volumes:- name: site-data VOLUME_DATA- Note: when using persistent volumes (instead of host path), if using a volume with a new name, you might need to adjust the `volumeMounts` section of the DC as well, to point to the new volume name * Roll out the latest version $ oc rollout latest * Scale the logging-es DCs back up: $ oc-n scale dc--replicas=1 $ oc-n get pods-o wide * It may be required to re-enable shard balancing $ oc exec-c elasticsearch-- \ curl-s \--cacert /etc/elasticsearch/secret/admin-ca \--cert /etc/elasticsearch/secret/admin-cert \--key /etc/elasticsearch/secret/admin-key \-XPUT 'https://localhost:9200/_cluster/settings' \-d '{"transient": {"cluster.routing.allocation.enable": "all"}}'

title: APIcast logs [alert] message - worker_connections are not enough
issue: - APIcast logs message: 2020/01/16 10:16:54 [alert] 29#29: 16192 worker_connections are not enough- What are recommendations for hits/sec to APIcast and needed CPUS/RAM? For example- 200 hits/s-> 4 cores?- 500 hits/s-> 8 cores?- 1000 hits/s-> 16 cores?
resolution: worker_connections is the maximum number of connections that can be opened by each APIcast worker thread. APIcast is by default sets this limit to 16192. This represents all the connections- connection with proxied servers, clients. The log message indicates that APIcast is unable to open connections. The worker_connections includes all the connections from APIcast- proxied servers, clients, 3scale backend. In case 3scale backend is the cause of this message, then 3scale needs to be scaled. Scaling 3scale to handle API requests upon a number of things- request/second: sustained and peak rate- request size- Memory of nodes- No of cpus per node. There is currently no sizing document. However, following are some of the guidelines that can be followed for sizing and can be used to see if the above issues can be resolved.- [Hardware requirements](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_3scale_api_management/2.7/html-single/installing_3scale/index#system-requirements-for-installing-threescale-on-openshift) describes recommendations for hardware for deploying 3scale on OpenShift. It also recommends to test and configure the environment for your specific needs.- [Scaling Up 3scale](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_3scale_api_management/2.7/html-single/operating_3scale/index#scaling_up_3scale_on_premise) describes guidelines for scaling 3scale.- [Scaling Up Performance](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_3scale_api_management/2.7/html-single/operating_3scale/index#scaling_up_performance) describes the tuning of parameters such as [APICAST_WORKERS](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_3scale_api_management/2.7/html-single/administering_the_api_gateway/index#workers), PUMA_WORKERS, UNICORN_WORKERS.- [3scale Batcher Policy](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_3scale_api_management/2.7/html-single/administering_the_api_gateway/index#batcher) caches authorization status and batches usage reports reducing the number of requests to the 3scale backend but with reduced accuracy of rate limits. This may be useful for high-throughout API. For further guidance, please contact Solution Architect or Red Hat Consulting. TBD- confirm if this should be here. Open Issue: * What should PUMA_WORKERS be set to? It looks like it should be number of cores or adjusted depending upon usage and not the default value of 16- See [THREESCALE-4259-comment](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/THREESCALE-4259https://issues.redhat.com/browse/THREESCALE-4259?focusedCommentId=13952827&page=com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.issuetabpanels%3Acomment-tabpanel#comment-13952827)
root_cause: No sizing document although documentation has some guidelines related to scaling.

[ALERT] 170/095408 (13581): Error(s) found in configuration file: /var/lib/haproxy/conf/haproxy.config [ALERT] 170/095408 (13581): Fatal errors found in configuration. ~~~

title: Imagestreams references are showing IPs instead of "docker-registry.default.svc" in OpenShift
issue: Imagestreams resolve to the internal registry IP, rather than the hostname on s2i builds after upgrading the cluster. Example: ~~~ $ oc describe is app-example Name: app-example Namespace: app-namespace [...] Tags: 1 1.0 tagged from app-namespace/buildah-base@sha256:8b4e78a88359d8b477e6d946bba34b655a562a10fe9c89a096f873fa2f6d36b1
172.30.1.100:5000/app-namespace/buildah-base@sha256:cf97cfc9d2c9bb4f9da5785a35692a8e0818fe1c43018981dcec909dbe2b42bb About a minute ago ~~~
resolution: 1. Check file `/etc/origin/master/master-config.yaml` in all master nodes and make sure these lines are present: ~~~ imagePolicyConfig: internalRegistryHostname: docker-registry.default.svc:5000 ~~~ 2. Add the following environment variables to the `docker-registry` deployment configuration: ~~~- name: REGISTRY_OPENSHIFT_SERVER_ADDR value: docker-registry.default.svc:5000- name: OPENSHIFT_DEFAULT_REGISTRY value: docker-registry.default.svc:5000 ~~~ Using the CLI, this could be done with: ~~~ $ oc project default $ oc set env dc docker-registry REGISTRY_OPENSHIFT_SERVER_ADDR=docker-registry.default.svc:5000 OPENSHIFT_DEFAULT_REGISTRY=docker-registry.default.svc:5000 ~~~ 3. Wait for the new `docker-registry` pods to deploy, test an s2i build and check if the imagestream has the correct tag.
root_cause: Proper environment variables were missing from the `docker-registry` deployment config that could cause tagging to use the internal registry's IP rather than the hostname.

title: How to configure path-based routing with additional remote APIcast instances in different domains
issue: What problem/issue/behavior are you having trouble with? What do you expect to see? We are trying to configure additional APIcast deployments per the instructions at https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_3scale_api_management/2.4/html/infrastructure/onpremises-installation#connect_apicast_from_an_openshift_cluster_outside_an_openshift_cluster_containing_3scale. We are using path-based routing. The problem we're seeing is that the APIcast base URLs for staging and production are necessarily on the cluster domain where APIcast is running, but APIcast itself updates its service configurations from another cluster where those base URLs match. So the remote APIcast running on another Openshift cluster will never have services configured for that cluster. For example 3scale AMP runs on an Openshift cluster with domain one.com with APIcast routed on one.com (api.staging.one.com, api.production.one.com). A remote APIcast runs on an Openshift cluster two.com with routes on two.com (api.staging.two.com, api.production.two.com). The two.com APIcast will fetch service configurations that have base URLs of api.staging.one.com and api.production.one.com but only received traffic on api.staging.two.com and api.production.two.com and never match any service to a request. Where are you experiencing the behavior? What environment? Development cluster What information can you provide around timeframes and the business impact? This is an effort to provide a more stable platform with > 1 point of failure.

title: Understanding Node Exporter Server Metrics in Grafana dashboard in Openshift
issue: What do the values `active`, `commit`, `apps`, `cache` mean in Grafana dashboard for server metrics?
resolution: The `active`, `commit`, `apps`, `cache` metrics in Grafana pertain to the memory metrics offered by the [Node Exporter Server Metrics dashboard](https://grafana.com/grafana/dashboards/405). To elaborate the meaning of each metric, refer below details: [Active](https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/master/examples/grafana/node-exporter-full-dashboard.json#L2399-L2404)- Memory that has been used more recently and usually not reclaimed unless absolutely necessary. [Committed](https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/master/examples/grafana/node-exporter-full-dashboard.json#L2507-L2512)- Amount of memory presently allocated on the system. [Apps](https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/master/examples/grafana/node-exporter-full-dashboard.json#L1794-L1800)- Memory used by user-space application. [Cache](https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/master/examples/grafana/node-exporter-full-dashboard.json#L1829-L1835)- Parked file data (file content) cache.

title: Renew the expired custom certificates for the web console
issue: - When any oc command is executed, it returns the following error. ~~~ $ oc login-us***

The server is using an invalid certificate: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid You can bypass the certificate check, but any data you send to the server could be intercepted by others. ~~~
resolution: - The method to renew the expired custom certificates of the web console is the same as that of configuring it.- The named certificate can be easily renewed by getting the new certificate with the same CN (Common Name) from the same CA which signed the earlier certificate.- Then place the certificate and key file at the same path with the same name on all master nodes as to that of already configured named certificates in the "servingInfo:" namedCertificates section inside master-config.yaml file. Copying the new certificate and key file will override the old ones. ~~~ servingInfo: bindAddress: 0.0.0.0:443 bindNetwork: tcp4 certFile: master.server.crt clientCA: ca.crt keyFile: master.server.key maxRequestsInFlight: 500 requestTimeoutSeconds: 3600 namedCertificates:- certFile: ayush.crt keyFile: ayush.key names:- "xyz.redhat.com" ~~~- Certificate and key files are required to be placed on the same path with the same name so that there will be no need to edit the master-config.yaml file.- After doing all the steps, restart API and controllers.- For OCP 3.5.x ~~~ # systemctl restart atomic-openshift-master-api atomic-openshift-master-controllers ~~~- For OCP 3.11.x ~~~ # /usr/local/bin/master-restart api # /usr/local/bin/master-restart controllers ~~~
root_cause: - Custom certificates for the web console get expired.

title: LDAP Result Code 200 "Network Error": x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
issue: - Unable to login with LDAP users.- Certificate error in API logs when trying to login with LDAP users. ~~~ E0219 12:27:08.921765 1 login.go:166] Error authenticating "demo" with provider "ldap": LDAP Result Code 200 "Network Error": x509: certificate signed by unknown authority E0219 12:27:20.208598 1 login.go:166] Error authenticating "demo" with provider "ldap": LDAP Result Code 200 "Network Error": x509: certificate signed by unknown authority ~~~
resolution: - The `/etc/origin/master/master-config.yaml` file on all master nodes must contain the same CA certificate inside the respective identity provider section which issued the LDAP server certificate. ~~~ oauthConfig: identityProviders:- name: ldap challenge: true login: true mappingMethod: claim provider: apiVersion: v1 kind: LDAPPasswordIdentityProvider attributes: id:- dn email:- mail name:- givenName preferredUsername:- uid bindDN: uid=demo,ou=user,dc=ldap,dc=redhat,dc=com bindPassword: demopass ca: /etc/origin/master/ldap-ca.crt <----------- insecure: false url: ldaps://ldap.server.com:389/uid=demo,ou=user,dc=ldap,dc=redhat,dc=com?uid ~~~- The CA certificate must be present in `/etc/origin/master/` directory and the `absolute` path to the certificate should be specified in the `master-config.yaml` file such as `/etc/origin/master/ldap-ca.crt`.- If in case the LDAP server certificate is signed by an intermediate CA certificate, then the certificate file specified in `/etc/origin/master/master-config.yaml` for the LDAP identity provider must contain the root CA and intermediate CA certificate's content. ~~~ # cat /etc/origin/master/ldap-ca.crt-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIICwDCCAaigAwIBAgIBATANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQsFADARMQ8wDQYDVQQDEwZyb290-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ZdxL33rn/Qro0GrMWebCZz5l93+2mWJt6hYDL6PLqsWvVYgW-----END CERTIFICATE----------BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIC6jCCAdKgAwIBAgIBATANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQsFADAmMSQwIgYDVQQDDBtvcGVu-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- IebIKzo9mHaBsVeIQ1WUaBWXdFwMOaWqadTAL6n3-----END CERTIFICATE----- ~~~- It can be verified whether the CA certificate specified in `master-config.yaml` file is the correct CA which signed the LDAP server certificate.- First, obtain the certificate which is being served by the LDAP server. ~~~ # openssl s_client-connect ldap.server.com:389-showcerts CONNECTED(00000003) depth=1 CN = ldapCA verify return:1 depth=0 CN = ldap.server.com verify return:1--- Certificate chain 0 s:/CN=ldap.server.com i:/CN=ldapCA-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIC2zCCAcOgAwIBAgIUZ4dolOYRfqaTnxI5SHeMCH8BcuIwDQYJKoZIhvcNAQEL---------------------------------------------------------------- DFtU8gBINeG8HKh+oF9m-----END CERTIFICATE-------- Server certificate subject=/CN=ldap.server.com issuer=/CN=ldapCA--- Acceptable client certificate CA names /CN=ldapCA ~~~- A new certificate file should be created such as `ldap-server.crt` containing the certificate content starting from `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----` to `-----END CERTIFICATE-----` obtained from the output of the previous command.- The LDAP server certificate can be verified by executing the following command. ~~~ # openssl verify-CAfile /etc/origin/master/ldap-ca.crt /home/user/ldap-server.crt /home/user/ldap-server.crt: OK ~~~
root_cause: - The CA certificate specified inside the `/etc/origin/master/master-config.yaml` for the LDAP identity provided was not correct.

title: Cloudguard Dome9 support / compatibility with OpenShift
issue: - We would like to know if Cloudguard Dome9 is supported under OpenShift
resolution: CloudGuard Dome9 is a cloud security posture management solution for cloud environments such as Amazon AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform. It provides network security policy management and automation for cloud environments across providers, regions and accounts. The agent is not currently supported under OpenShift Container Platform 3.x. With regards to OpenShift Container Platform 4.x, since Red Hat does not own the software, the recommendation is to contact the third party vendor, for additional information related to it.
root_cause: - The Dome9 agent can be deployed on Kubernetes v1.12 and later, and supports Helm v3.0 and later, while OpenShift Container Platform latest 3.x version is based on Kubernetes v1.11.

title: CodeReady Workspaces (air-gapped) fails to pull image

title: Red Hat OpenShift 4 IPI installation on OpenStack fails with error "ignition ... GET error ... x509: certificate signed by unknown authority"
issue: OpenStack endpoints use a custom PKI or self signed certificate

Ignition reports (OpenShift 4.2) ~~~ [80558.038518] ignition[666]: GET error: Get https://openstack-controller.example.intern:13808/v1/AUTH_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx/xxxx-xxxx/bootstrap.ign?temp_url_sig=xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx&temp_url_expires=xxxxxxxxxxxx: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority ~~~

Ignition reports (OpenShift 4.3) ~~~ [31.816448] ignition[1112]: GET error: Get https://openstack-controller.example.intern:13808/v1/AUTH_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx/xxxx-xxxx/abcabc152514abcbabc: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority ~~~
resolution: - Use Red Hat OpenShift 4.3.2 and later AND- Configure swift endpoints to include all intermediate certificates if you use a custom PKI
root_cause: If the Red Hat OpenStack cluster has been configured to use either a private certificate authority (custom PKI) or uses self signed certificates for the public endpoints like swift, the openshift-installer does not support this up until the 4.3.2 release. Red Hat OpenShift 4.3.2, 4.4 and later support a private certificate authority by reading out the "cacert" setting in OpenStack's clouds.yaml file and using this as the trust source for retrieving ignition files. ~~~ # ~/.config/openstack/clouds.yaml clouds: openstack: auth: auth_url:..... cacert: /home/stack/ssl/ca.crt.pem # <-- read by the installer and added to ignition region_name: "regionOne" interface: "public" identity_api_version: 3 ~~~ The rootCA certificate of the custom PKI used by OpenStack must be the first certificate in the file referenced by "cacert". Also a single CA must be added here, as only a single entry will be added to the ignition file as of now. The system wide ca trust bundle should not be referenced here, as this will also break the installer as the ignition size passed in via user-data will then exceed 64Kb in size, which is not possible on OpenStack. If the Red Hat OpenStack cluster uses a custom PKI with a trust chain using intermediate or signing sub-CA's (e.g. myRootCA-> mySubCA [-> mySigningSubSubCA]-> serverCert), which is a typical setup, the verification of the trust chain requires, that OpenStack is configured to return all required intermediate CA's as well as the endpoint's server certificate. Note: Red Hat engineering is currently working on adding support to add multiple CA certificates to the ignition process, however in a properly configured OpenStack cluster with endpoints serving all server and intermediate certs, this is usually not required. Please contact [Red Hat Support](https://access.redhat.com/support/contact/technicalSupport) for further updates.

title: 'rook-ceph-detect-version-XXX' pod is stuck in 'Pending' state during the automatic upgrade from OCS 4.2.1 to 4.2.2.
issue: `rook-ceph-detect-version-XXX` pod is stuck in `Pending` state during the automatic upgrade from OCS 4.2.1 to 4.2.2 and the upgrade doesn't starts.

`rook-ceph-detect-version-XXX`, `csi-cephfsplugin-provisioner-XXX`, `csi-rbdplugin-provisioner-XXX`, `noobaa-core-0` and `rook-ceph-drain-canary` pods are stuck in `Pending` state after autmatic upgrade is triggered for OCS.

OCS pods are stuck in `Pending` state, with messages in `Events`: Events: Type Reason Age From Message------------------------- Warning FailedScheduling default-scheduler 0/15 nodes are available: 12 node(s) didn't match node selector, 3 node(s) had taints that the pod didn't tolerate.
root_cause: * The message **3 node(s) had taints that the pod didn't tolerate**, in the `Events` denotes that few nodes, which matched `node-selector` were tainted and thus pods cannot be scheduled on the node. * Confirm that no additional taint other than the allowed one **(node.ocs.openshift.io/storage=true:NoSchedule)** is added to the OCS nodes. * Having the following taints, would restrict the OCS pods from getting scheduled as OCS doesn't have tolerations against the taint `node.ncs.openshift.io/storage=true:NoSchedule` Taints: node.ncs.openshift.io/storage=true:NoSchedule node.ocs.openshift.io/storage=true:NoSchedule

title: OpenShift Service Signing CA expired (OpenShift 4)
issue: - Applications talking between services within OpenShift all suddenly stopped being able to communicate with TLS errors.
resolution: You need to follow the documented process for [manually rotate service ca service serving certificate](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/latest/authentication/certificates/service-serving-certificate.html#manually-rotate-service-ca_service-serving-certificate) to correct this issue. It will renew your Service Signing CA for 1 year. You are also encouraged to Update to [4.3.5]() or [4.2.22]() so that product enhancements can automate this CA rotation for you.
root_cause: When OpenShift GA'ed not all CA's within the cluster had a mechanism or controller monitoring them, thus CA's with a shorter lifespan (such as the Service Signing CA) run the risk of expiring and impacting application using certificate issues by this feature. Red Hat since corrected this issue by adding a controller to automate the rotation of the CA certificates, however one assumption that functionality has it that pods are restarted at least once a year (this happens naturally with OCP 4 upgrades due to node reboots). This pod restart is needed so that pods not dynamically loading in secrete data from Kubernetes can pick up newly issues (renewed) certificates for the services they represent.

title: Error "Action not allowed with tested creds" when installing AWS UPI OpenShift 4
issue: - The environment has a policy that limits access by IP address. So that the AWS key could only be used by our IP addresses. The policy does not allow for a null IP. ~~~ WARNING Action not allowed with tested creds action="ec2:AllocateAddress" WARNING Action not allowed with tested creds action="ec2:AssociateAddress" WARNING Action not allowed with tested creds action="ec2:AssociateDhcpOptions" ~~~
root_cause: The policy was missing input required to evaluate the `policy aws:SourceIP` or `aws:SourceVPC`. These are global values that are set during execution. They were not set when OpenShift called Policy Simulator API. The accounts do work in the real runtime environment.

title: Why is the error "The target exists, contains other items, or is in use" popping up when removing a device using the Heketi CLI?

Can not remove device XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX at this time. ~~~

title: How to enable multicast communication over the interface with additional network added via multus?
issue: Enabled the additional network for by implementing Multus (IPVLAN) CNI and provided additional static IP Address to the Pod with the relevant netmask and Gateway (Note that this address is from the range that can receive multicast).
Checked the connectivity to this second IP address by pinging it from another machines from the same network and from machine from other networks (routing) as well- successfully.
Checked the stand alone machine with the same network as the Pod's second network for ability to receive multicast streaming- it receiving streaming successfully.
Checked the pod for ability to receive multicast streaming- it not receiving streaming.
resolution: * In the IPVLAN CNI definitions both networks- "Multicast Group master network" and "Multicast source network" for static routin as destination("dst") like shown below; ~~~ additionalNetworks:- name: testipvlan namespace: test-multicast rawCNIConfig: '{"cniVersion": "0.3.1", "type": "ipvlan", "master": "eno1", "mode": "l2", "ipam": {"type": "host-local", "ranges": [[{"subnet": "x.y.z.0/24", "rangeStart": "x.y.z.154/24", "rangeEnd": "x.y.z.154", "gateway": "x.y.z.254"}]], "routes": [{"dst": "a.b.c.11/32"}, {"dst": "f.0.0.0/8"}]}}' type: Raw ~~~

title: Pod and SDN issues during upgrades in OCP 3.X
issue: During the upgrade process pods can be removed from the network and left in an IDLE state with no network connection. Customer has been running an upgrade of OCP 3.10 to 3.11.X. After this upgrade it was discovered that pods are having network problems. There were no OVS flows created for this pod. On investigation it was discovered that this pod vethXXX interface did not show when running: ~~~ ovs-ofctl-O OpenFlow13 dump-ports-desc br0 ~~~ When running the upgrade the SDN/OVS pods must be restarted, and at the same time the bridge was recreated. So for some reason some pods vethXXX interfaces were added back but some pods were not.

title: How does openshift 4 upgrade the OS?
issue: Large Openshift setup is done in a restricted environment with a very limited and low bandwidth internet. How do upgrade would perform with low bandwidth? Will it choke up the bandwidth as all nodes will go for an upgrade?
resolution: - By default, it doesn't upgrade all the nodes at a time. It would be just one node at a time. See the [maxUnavailable](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.3/updating/updating-cluster-between-minor.html) option.- With respect to bandwidth, it doesn't download large files. See more info about [OS Upgrades](https://github.com/openshift/machine-config-operator/blob/master/docs/OSUpgrades.md)

title: After restarting, scc settings of some pods changed to anyuid
issue: - Pods are unable to start after restart.- SCC for a pod is changed to `anyuid` after pod restart.
resolution: Verify whether `cluster-admin` role was added to the `serviceaccount` and remove it.
root_cause: Cluster role` cluster-admin` was added to the pod's serviceaccount. `cluster-admin` role causes pod to use `anyuid` scc.

xyz: ok=397 changed=169 unreachable=0 failed=1 localhost: ok=32 changed=2 unreachable=0 failed=0 INSTALLER STATUS **************************************************************

resolution: Adding below Parameter in azure.conf file. ~~~ useInstanceMetadata: true ~~~

The reason behind this is, that it will reduce the number of API calls made by OpenShift Container Platform- Node. Since there is a limit of how many API calls can be made per unit time per service principal this will improve the reliability of the cloud controller. This Parameter will enable the Azure Instance Metadata Service to provide information about currently running virtual machine instances and that information can be used to manage and configure your virtual machines. Information provided includes the SKU, network configuration, and upcoming maintenance events.

title: OpenShift router pods stuck in "Pending" state when using multiple "region" labels for infrastructure nodes
issue: - Trying to scale a router pod to several replicas- e.g. 6- on different nodes. Four of the nodes have the label set region=region1 and two have the label set region=region2. Depending on how the pods are started either two or four pod instances do not start, but stay in "Pending".- Router deployment hangs in "Pending" state with error message "No nodes are available that match all of the following predicates:: CheckServiceAffinity (xx), Insufficient pods (x), MatchNodeSelector (xx), PodFitsHostPorts (x)."
resolution: - If the OpenShift scheduler is configured with a serviceAffinity as a "predicate" in scheduler.json- make sure all nodes the pods are supposed to run on have the same label for the labels specified in serviceAffinity- Use the same "region" label for all infrastructure nodes that are supposed to run the router- Use multiple router deployments via sharding if you need to have region specific infrastructure nodes- Use a single "region" label for all infrastructure nodes
root_cause: Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 3.x is configured to contain two default affinity ("serviceAffinity") and anti-affinity rules ("serviceAntiAffinity") in scheduler.json as a default: ~~~ # File /etc/origin/master/scheduler.json {"apiVersion": "v1", "kind": "Policy", "predicates": [... {"argument": {"serviceAffinity": {"labels": ["region"]}}, "name": "Region"}],... "priorities": [... {"argument": {"serviceAntiAffinity": {"label": "zone"}}, "name": "Zone", "weight": 2}]} ~~~ The serviceAffinity rule defined makes sure that all pods that service the same (kubernetes) service are always scheduled on nodes that have the same set of labels for all labels defined in "serviceAffinity". This is independent of the actual nodeSelector for the deploymentconfig of the pods, which may be based on a totally different label. The node labels of the node, where the first pod of the deployment is scheduled upon determines which region labels required. Example: If the first pod of a deployment is scheduled on a node with a region label of "region=region1", all pods must be scheduled on nodes with the region label "region=region1", even if the nodeSelector is based on another label.

title: How to use GPUs with Device Plugin in OpenShift 3.11
resolution: NVIDIA drivers for RHEL must be installed on the host as a prerequisite for using GPUs with OpenShift. Let’s prepare the host by installing NVIDIA drivers and NVIDIA container enablement. The following procedures will make containerized GPU workloads possible in OpenShift, leveraging the Device Plugin feature in OpenShift 3.10. ### Prerequisites for IBM POWER architecture Before installing the NVIDIA components on POWER, the udev Memory Auto-Onlining Rule must be disabled for the CUDA driver to function properly. To disable it, follow these steps. If x86_64 is in use, skip this prerequisite. Copy the /lib/udev/rules.d/40-redhat.rules file to the directory for user overridden rules. ~~~ # cp /lib/udev/rules.d/40-redhat.rules /etc/udev/rules.d/ ~~~ Edit the /etc/udev/rules.d/40-redhat.rules file. ~~~ # vim /etc/udev/rules.d/40-redhat.rules ~~~ Comment out the "# Memory hotadd request" section (about 7 lines), optionally delete the first line of the file, since the file was copied to a directory where it cannot be overwritten. Restart the system for the changes to take effect. ~~~ # reboot ~~~ ### NVIDIA Driver Installation NVIDIA drivers are compiled from source. The build process requires the kernel-devel package to be installed. ~~~ $ sudo yum-y install kernel-devel-`uname-r` ~~~ The nvidia-driver package requires DKMS package. DKMS is not supported or packaged by Red Hat. Work is underway to remove the NVIDIA driver requirement on DKMS for Red Hat distributions. DKMS can be installed from the EPEL repository. First install the epel repository. ~~~ $ sudo yum install-y https://dl.fedoraproject.org/pub/epel/epel-release-latest-7.noarch.rpm ~~~ The newest NVIDIA drivers are located in the following repository. ~~~ $ sudo yum install-y https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/rhel7/x86_64/cuda-repo-rhel7-10.0.130-1.x86_64.rpm ~~~ Auxiliary tools and libraries are contained in the following packages. This will also install the nvidia-kmod package, which includes the NVIDIA kernel modules. ~~~ $ sudo yum-y install nvidia-driver nvidia-driver-cuda nvidia-modprobe ~~~ Remove the nouveau kernel module, (otherwise the nvidia kernel module will not load). The installation of the NVIDIA driver package will blacklist the driver in the kernel command line (nouveau.modeset=0 rd.driver.blacklist=nouveau video=vesa:off), so that the nouveau driver will not be loaded on subsequent reboots. ~~~ $ sudo modprobe-r nouveau ~~~ Load the NVIDIA and the unified memory kernel modules. ~~~ $ sudo nvidia-modprobe && nvidia-modprobe-u ~~~ Verify the installation and the drivers are working. Extracting the name of the GPU can later be used to label the node in OpenShift. ~~~ $ nvidia-smi--query-gpu=gpu_name--format=csv,noheader--id=0 | sed-e 's/ /-/g' Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB ~~~ ### Adding the nvidia-container-runtime-hook The version of docker shipped by Red Hat includes support for OCI runtime hooks. Because of this, we only need to install the nvidia-container-runtime-hook package. On other distributions of docker, additional steps may be necessary. See NVIDIA’s documentation for more information. The next step is to install libnvidia-container and the nvidia-container-runtime repository. ~~~ $ curl-s-L https://nvidia.github.io/nvidia-container-runtime/centos7/nvidia-container-runtime.repo | tee /etc/yum.repos.d/nvidia-container-runtime.repo ~~~ The next step will install an OCI prestart hook. The prestart hook is responsible for making NVIDIA libraries and binaries available in a container (by bind-mounting them in from the host). Without the hook, users would have to include libraries and binaries into each and every container image that might use a GPU. Hooks simplify management of container images by ensuring only a single copy of libraries and binaries are required. The prestart hook is triggered by the presence of certain environment variables in the container: NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITES=compute,utility. ~~~ $ sudo yum-y install nvidia-container-runtime-hook ~~~ This package will install also the config/activation files for docker/podman/cri-o. Beware that the hook json in the package will only work with cri-o > = 1.12 for crio-1.11 use the following json file: ~~~ $ cat < <'EOF' > > /usr/share/containers/oci/hooks.d/oci-nvidia-hook.json {"hasbindmounts": true, "hook": "/usr/bin/nvidia-container-runtime-hook", "stage": ["prestart"]} EOF ~~~ Additionally, the default hooks dir for crio is /etc/containers/oci/hooks.d/, so ensure that the above file is copied there as well if the cluster is using crio. ### Adding the SELinux policy module To run NVIDIA containers contained and not privileged, we have to install an SELinux policy tailored for running CUDA GPU workloads. The policy creates a new SELinux type (nvidia_container_t) with which the container will be running. Furthermore, we can drop all capabilities and prevent privilege escalation. See the invocation below to have a glimpse how to start a NVIDIA container. First install the SELinux policy module on all GPU worker nodes: ~~~ # wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zvonkok/origin-ci-gpu/master/selinux/nvidia-container.pp # semodule-i nvidia-container.pp ~~~ ### Check and restore the labels on the node The new SELinux policy heavily relies on the correct labeling of the host. Therefore we have to make sure that the files that are needed have the correct SELinux label. Restorecon all files that the prestart hook will need ~~~ $ sudo nvidia-container-cli-k list | restorecon-v-f- ~~~ Restorecon all accessed devices ~~~ # restorecon-Rv /dev ~~~ Restorecon all files that the DevicePlugin will need ~~~ # restorecon-Rv /var/lib/kubelet 0 ~~~ Everything is now set up for running a GPU-enabled container. ### Verify SELinux and prestart hook functionality To verify correct operation of driver and container enablement, try running a cuda-vector-add container. We can run the container with docker or podman. ~~~ $ sudo podman run--user 1000:1000--security-opt=no-new-privileges--cap-drop=ALL \--security-opt label=type:nvidia_container_t \ docker.io/mirrorgooglecontainers/cuda-vector-add:v0.1 $ sudo docker run--user 1000:1000--security-opt=no-new-privileges--cap-drop=ALL \--security-opt label=type:nvidia_container_t \ docker.io/mirrorgooglecontainers/cuda-vector-add:v0.1 ~~~ If the test passes, the drivers, hooks and the container runtime are functioning correctly and we can move on to configuring OpenShift. ### OpenShift 3.11 with the GPU Device Plugin After successful installation of OpenShift 3.11, the first step is to install the NVIDIA Device Plugin. To schedule the Device Plugin on nodes that include GPUs, label the node as follows: ~~~ $ oc label node openshift.com/gpu-accelerator=true node " " labeled ~~~ This label will be used in the next step. ### Deploy the NVIDIA Device Plugin Daemonset The next step is to deploy the NVIDIA Device Plugin Note that the NVIDIA Device Plugin (and more generally, any hardware manufacturer’s plugin) is supported by the vendor, and is not shipped or supported by Red Hat. Clone the following repository, there are several yaml files for future use. ~~~ $ git clone https://github.com/redhat-performance/openshift-psap.git $ cd openshift-psap/blog/gpu/device-plugin ~~~ Here is an example daemonset (device-plugin/nvidia-device-plugin.yml) which will use the label we created in the last step so that the plugin pods will only run where GPU hardware is available. Now create the NVIDIA Device Plugin daemonset. ~~~ $ oc create-f nvidia-device-plugin.yml ~~~ Lets verify the correct execution of the Device Plugin. You can see there is only one running, since only one node was labeled in the previous step. ~~~ $ oc get pods-n kube-system NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset-s9ngg 1/1 Running 0 1m ~~~ Once the pod is running, let’s have a look at the logs. ~~~ $ oc logs nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset-7tvb6-n kube-system 2018/07/12 12:29:38 Loading NVML 2018/07/12 12:29:38 Fetching devices. 2018/07/12 12:29:38 Starting FS watcher. 2018/07/12 12:29:38 Starting OS watcher. 2018/07/12 12:29:38 Starting to serve on /var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins/nvidia.sock 2018/07/12 12:29:38 Registered device plugin with Kubelet ~~~ At this point the node itself will advertise the nvidia.com/gpu extended resource in it’s capacity: ~~~ $ oc describe node | egrep 'Capacity|Allocatable|gpu' Capacity: nvidia.com/gpu: 2 Allocatable: nvidia.com/gpu: 2 ~~~ Nodes that do not have GPUs installed will not advertise GPU capacity. ### Deploy a pod that requires a GPU Let’s run a GPU-enabled container on the cluster. We can use the cuda-vector-add image that was used in the Host Preparation step. Use the following file (device-plugin/cuda-vector-add.yaml) as a pod description for running the cuda-vector-add image in OpenShift. Note the last line requests one NVIDIA GPU from OpenShift. The OpenShift scheduler will see this and schedule the pod to a node that has a free GPU. Once the pod create request arrives at a node, the Kubelet will coordinate with the Device Plugin to start the pod with a GPU resource. First create a project that will group all of our GPU work. ~~~ $ oc new-project nvidia ~~~ The next step is to create and start the pod. ~~~ $ oc create-f cuda-vector-add.yaml ~~~ After a couple of seconds the container finishes. ~~~ $ oc get pods NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE cuda-vector-add 0/1 Completed 0 3s nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset-s9ngg 1/1 Running 0 9m ~~~ Let’s have a look at the logs for any errors. We are looking for Test PASSED in the pod logs. ~~~ $ oc logs cuda-vector-add [Vector addition of 50000 elements] Copy input data from the host memory to the CUDA device CUDA kernel launch with 196 blocks of 256 threads Copy output data from the CUDA device to the host memory Test PASSED Done ~~~ This output is the same as when we ran the container directly using podman or docker. If you see a permission denied error, check to see that you have the correct SELinux label.

title: Configure SSL cert for full stack application
issue: - Routes having `self-signed` certificates.- Frontend pod is not able to communicate with the backend pod.
resolution: - The routes for frontend and backend pod uses `self-signed certificates`. Frontend pod uses the backend route as it's API URL to serve the requests i.e. the backend route for retrieving the data or any other operation based on the request.- As the backend route is used as an API, it doesn't give any warning on the browser tab like `Your connection is not private` due to which the certificate can't be accepted manually on the browser and frontend is not able to establish a connection with backend.- This issue can be resolved either by manually accepting the certificates of both the routes for the first time so these certs will become trusted or else configure the route certificates which are signed by the `trusted CA`.
root_cause: Web browser marks a certificate insecure if it is self-signed or signed by an unknown CA.

title: How to use tcpdump or other system-level commands inside OpenShift v3 pod using CRI-O?
issue: - Need to do packet capture (tcpdump) from inside an OpenShift Pod using CRI-O.- Can you use commands in a container via nsenter to capture information with tools that are not built into the pod?- How to run iperf and other Linux tools that are not in the container's built-in command list- How to run commands (tcpdump, ping, etc.) from inside an OpenShift pod's network namespace
resolution: *If you are using OpenShift 3, please see [How to use tcpdump inside OpenShift v3 Pod](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/3480421)* We can make use of nsenter on the node where the pods are hosted:- Login to node where pod is hosted.- Identify Container ID (series of numbers and letters) of the pod sandbox container using *crictl* ~~~ # cid=$(crictl ps | grep) # pid=$(crictl inspect $cid--output yaml | grep 'pid:' | awk '{print $2}') ~~~ Start the tcpdump in the container's network namespace using. Make sure to replace ethX with the relevant interface (e.g. eth0, lo, etc): ~~~ # nsenter-n-t $pid-- tcpdump-s 0-n-i ethX-w /tmp/$HOSTNAME_$(date +\%Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S).pcap # ls /tmp/*.pcap ~~~ *See this page for more details on using the tcpdump command: [How to capture network packets with tcpdump](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/8787)* The command (or the shell) started in the step above will run inside pod's network namespace, i.e. it will see pod's networking (instead of host's). Example- Example steps to perform packet capture on a pod named ruby-ex-1-2bdp8: ~~~ # oc get pods-o wide-n test NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE IP NODE ruby-ex-1-2bdp8 1/1 Running 0 1d 10.130.0.8 node-0 # cid = crictl ps | awk ' /ruby-ex-1-2bdp8/ {print $1} ' # echo $cid # pid=$(crictl inspect $cid--output yaml | grep 'pid:' | awk '{print $2}') # echo $pid # nsenter-n-t $pid-- tcpdump-s 0-n-i any-w /host/tmp/$HOSTNAME_$(date +\%Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S).pcap ~~~- From another terminal: ~~~ # oc-n test rsh ruby-ex-1-2bdp8 # curl http://localhost:8080 <-- This HTTP request will appear in the packet capture started above. ~~~
root_cause: - Container runtimes use many mechanisms to isolate processes running inside containers from the host and other containers. One of them is network namespaces, which make each container believe that the available network stack (interfaces, connections...) is different.- By applying this solution, the networking tool will be run inside the network namespace of the pod, so it will see the same networking stack as the pod, but it won't be isolated in any other way (it still sees the filesystem of the node instead of the one of the container, you are still root user with no additional SELinux or capabilities restrictions...).

title: AWS conditional policy support for aws:SourceIP and aws:SourceVPC
issue: - Security policy requires that IAM User accounts with access keys be restricted to IP addresses and VPCs that are owned by the company so they are not used from unauthorized locations. The OpenShift Credentials Operator and the openshift-install command need to pass either the `aws:SourceIP` value if run outside of a VPC or `aws:SourceVPC` value if on a VPC to provide the same environment information of the execution environment so policies based on these values evaluate correctly.
root_cause: - Internal feature request has been raised with our engineering team. Contact [Red Hat Support](https://access.redhat.com/support/contact/technicalSupport/) for more information on feature request.

title: TCP performance issues and stalls when using kernel-3.10.0-957.21.3.el7 or any kernel with TCP SACK PANIC CVE fixes
issue: - After updating to a kernel which includes the fix for TCP SACK Panic [CVE-2019-11478](https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/tcpsack), TCP connections stall or time out.
resolution: **Errata for this issue are still outstanding for some minor releases. If you do not find an errata for your release then please open a case with Red Hat Technical Support.** Please update to one of the following package versions or higher to resolve this issue:- The below errata include the following two patches:- [tcp: refine memory limit test in tcp_fragment()](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=b6653b3629e5b88202be3c9abc44713973f5c4b4)- [tcp: be more careful in tcp_fragment()](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=b617158dc096709d8600c53b6052144d12b89fab) **Release** | **Errata** | **Package version**-----|-----|----- RHEL 8.1 | [RHSA-2019:3517](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:3517) | kernel-4.18.0-147.el8 RHEL 8.1 RT | [RHSA-2019:3309](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:3309) | kernel-rt-4.18.0-147.rt24.93.el8 RHEL 8.0 | [RHSA-2020:0204](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2020:0204) | kernel-4.18.0-80.15.1.el8_0 RHEL 7.8 | [RHSA-2020:1016](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2020:1016) | kernel-3.10.0-1127.el7 RHEL 7.7.z | [RHSA-2019:2600](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:2600) | kernel-3.10.0-1062.1.1.el7 RHEL 7.6 EUS | [RHSA-2019:2837](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:2837) | kernel-3.10.0-957.35.1.el7 RHEL 7.5 EUS | [RHSA-2019:2975](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:2975) | kernel-3.10.0-862.43.1.el7 RHEL 7.4 EUS | [RHSA-2019:2696](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:2696) | kernel-3.10.0-693.58.1.el7 RHEL 7.3 AUS | [RHSA-2019:2900](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:2900) | kernel-3.10.0-514.69.1.el7 RHEL 7.2 AUS | [RHSA-2019:2899](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:2899) | kernel-3.10.0-327.82.1.el7 RHEL 6.10.z | [RHSA-2019:2736](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:2736) | kernel-2.6.32-754.22.1.el6 RHEL 6.6 AUS | [RHSA-2019:2869](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:2869) | kernel-2.6.32-504.81.2.el6 RHEL 6.5 AUS | [RHSA-2019:2695](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:2695) | kernel-2.6.32-431.96.1.el6 MRG 2 | [RHSA-2019:2730](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:2730) | kernel-rt-3.10.0-693.58.1.rt56.652.el6rt---- The below errata include only [tcp: refine memory limit test in tcp_fragment()](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=b6653b3629e5b88202be3c9abc44713973f5c4b4) fix. They do **not** include [tcp: be more careful in tcp_fragment()](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=b617158dc096709d8600c53b6052144d12b89fab).- The below errata will resolve the issue for most users but it is possible the TCP stalls may still occur. In that case an errata from the above list is required. **Release** | **Errata** | **Package version**-----|-----|----- RHEL 7.7 | [RHSA-2019:2029](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:2029) | kernel-3.10.0-1062.el7 RHEL 7.6 EUS | [RHBA-2019:2397](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHBA-2019:2397) | kernel-3.10.0-957.27.4.el7 RHEL 7.5 EUS | [RHSA-2019:2566](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2019:2566) | kernel-3.10.0-862.41.1.el7---- Please refer to the below **Diagnostic Steps** portion of this article for a list of affected kernels.- As a workaround, do one of the following:- Ensure the sysctls `net.ipv4.tcp_wmem` and `net.core.wmem_max` are not set too conservatively.- If an application uses the `SO_SNDBUF` socket option, increase the size of the allocation. How this is done depends on the application.- Use the latest available kernel package for your release which does not contain fixes for CVE-2019-11477, CVE-2019-11478 & CVE-2019-11479. If this option is chosen, be sure to apply one of the CVE mitigations for under the **Resolve** tab here: [TCP SACK PANIC- Kernel vulnerabilities- CVE-2019-11477, CVE-2019-11478 & CVE-2019-11479](https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/tcpsack)
root_cause: - It has been discovered that the fix for CVE-2019-11478 can cause a performance regression.- The commit which addresses CVE-2019-11478 but introduces the performance regression is [tcp: tcp_fragment() should apply sane memory limits](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=f070ef2ac66716357066b683fb0baf55f8191a2e)- Upstream has a fix for the regression introduced by `tcp: tcp_fragment() should apply sane memory limits`. The fix is in [tcp: refine memory limit test in tcp_fragment()](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=b6653b3629e5b88202be3c9abc44713973f5c4b4)- Applications can be affected by this problem under any of the following conditions:- The application uses the `setsockopt()` system call and sets a small `SO_SNDBUF` value.- The application does not set `SO_SNDBUF` and the system `sysctl` parameter `net.ipv4.tcp_wmem` third value is small.- There is a second followup commit to the original CVE-2019-11478 commit: [tcp: be more careful in tcp_fragment()](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=b617158dc096709d8600c53b6052144d12b89fab). Under certain lossy conditions a connection may still stall regardless of buffer size.

title: How to add worker node to OpenShift 4 cluster running on vShphere
issue: - How to add a worker node to an already running OpenShift 4 cluster deployed using VMware vSphere?
resolution: - Adding a new worker node to a running OCP 4 cluster deployed over VMware vSphere will require manual VM provisioning as this is a [UPI deployment](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/openshift_container_platform/4.1/html/installing/installing-on-vsphere#installation-infrastructure-user-infra_installing-vsphere).- The process of adding a RHCOS VM is explained in this [document](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.1/installing/installing_vsphere/installing-vsphere.html#installation-vsphere-machines_installing-vsphere).- This solution aims to have a step by step guide to add new worker nodes to a running OCP 4 over vSphere. # **Prerequisites**:- Add the new node`VM` MAC address to `DHCP` server with the require IP address prior to powering it on.- Add The new node `VM` hostname should to the `DNS` server prior to powering it on.- **If required**, add the new node's hostname/IP to your loadbalancer. # Steps: 1. Prepare worker ignition file: **Situation A**: If the OCP 4 cluster is running for less than 24 hours, the initial worker ignition file `worker.ign` can still be used: ~~~ # ls append-bootstrap.64 append-bootstrap.ign auth bootstrap.ign master.64 master.ign metadata.json worker.64 <---- base64 representation of the initial ignition file created for worker nodes worker.ign <---- initial ignition file created for worker nodes ~~~ **Situation B**: If the OCP 4 cluster is running for more than 24 hours, the initial worker ignition file `worker.ign` CANNOT be used and it is required to create a new one:- Switch to the installation directory: ~~~ # cd ~~~- Backup initial worker ignition files `if exists`: ~~~ # cp worker.ign worker.ign.bkp # cp worker.64 worker.64.bkp ~~~- Retrieve currently used certificate for internal cluster communication: ~~~ # openssl s_client-connect api-int.${domain}:22623-showcerts <---- replace ${domain} variable with your cluster domain Example: # openssl s_client-connect api-int.example.com:22623-showcerts ~~~- Copy certificate block: ~~~ # openssl s_client-connect api-int.example.com:22623-showcerts..... Certificate chain 0 s:/CN=api-int.example.com i:/OU=openshift/CN=root-ca-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- <---- start copying from here MIIDezCCAmOgAwIBAgIIG8GsPc6z6L4wDQYJKoZIhvcNAQELBQAwJjESMBAGA1UE CxMJb3BlbnNoaWZ0MRAwDgYDVQQDEwdyb290LWNhMB4XDTIwMDMxOTA4MzcxN1oX DTMwMDMxNzA4MzcxOVowNTEzMDEGA1UEAxMqYXBpLWludC5zaGlmdDQubGFiLnVw.... K2NZft6JgbSlzw/9GYMCGEhBq3mhMnvRKjFt4kn5IfVjgOW0DWWXrRreGFRFO2Nz 7C9zqpyPL/L0rENKlmrEh7p1pK14clwYT5O56uffHg==-----END CERTIFICATE----- <---- End here..... Server certificate..... ~~~- Paste the copied certificate to a file: ~~~ # cat api-init.cert-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- <---- start copying from here MIIDezCCAmOgAwIBAgIIG8GsPc6z6L4wDQYJKoZIhvcNAQELBQAwJjESMBAGA1UE CxMJb3BlbnNoaWZ0MRAwDgYDVQQDEwdyb290LWNhMB4XDTIwMDMxOTA4MzcxN1oX DTMwMDMxNzA4MzcxOVowNTEzMDEGA1UEAxMqYXBpLWludC5zaGlmdDQubGFiLnVw.... K2NZft6JgbSlzw/9GYMCGEhBq3mhMnvRKjFt4kn5IfVjgOW0DWWXrRreGFRFO2Nz 7C9zqpyPL/L0rENKlmrEh7p1pK14clwYT5O56uffHg==-----END CERTIFICATE----- ~~~- Edit `worker.ign` file: ~~~ # vim worker.ign ~~~- Replace ` ` part with the new certificate that is copied from `init.cert` file ~~~ {"ignition":{"config":{"append":[{"source":"https://api-int.shift4.lab.upshift.rdu2.redhat.com:22623/config/worker","verification":{}}]},"security":{"tls":{"certificateAuthorities":[{"source":"data:text/plain;charset=utf-8;base64, ","verification":{}}]}},"timeouts":{},"version":"2.2.0"},"networkd":{},"passwd":{},"storage":{},"systemd":{}} ~~~- Convert the worker Ignition config file to Base64 encoding: ~~~ # base64-w0./worker.ign >./worker.64 ~~~ 2. Download Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS- vSphere image from the [Product Downloads](https://access.redhat.com/downloads/content/290). ~~~ Notes:- For any micro version of OCP 4.2.x there is only one Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS- vSphere base image that can be used: rhcos-4.2.0-x86_64-vmware.ova- Same rule applies for OCP 4.1.x, OCP 4.2.x, OCP 4.3.x,...etc ~~~ 3. Create a new worker node `VM` from vSphere client:- Go to the clusters datacenter and directory in vSphere client- From the `Hosts and Clusters` tab, right-click your cluster’s name and click `Deploy OVF Template`.- On the `Select an OVF` tab, specify the name of the `RHCOS OVA` file that you downloaded.- On the `Select a name and folder` tab, set a `Virtual machine name`, click the name of your vSphere cluster, and select the correct folder if required.- On the `Select a compute resource` tab, click the name of your vSphere cluster.- **Optional**: On the `Select storage` tab, customize the storage options.- On the `Select storage` tab, configure the storage options for your VM:- Select `Thin Provision`.- Select the datastore that you specified in your `install-config.yaml` file that was generated while deploying the COP4 cluster.- On the `Select network` tab, specify the network that you configured for the cluster, if available.- Finish creating the `VM` and **don't** start it.- On the `Configure` tab of the VM, expand `Settings` and select `vApp options`:- Scroll down and under `Properties` apply the configurations:- Click `Edit Configuration`, and on the `Configuration Parameters` window, click `Add Configuration Params`. Define the following parameter names and values:- `guestinfo.ignition.config.data`: Paste the contents of the base64-encoded Ignition config file `worker.64`.- `guestinfo.ignition.config.data.encoding`: Specify `base64`.- `disk.EnableUUID`: Specify `TRUE`.- Save and boot up the `VM` 4. Monitor the `VM` booting tasks till it shows the login prompt with the correct hostname 5. Login to OCP4 vluster and approve the CSRs of the newly added node **if required**: ~~~ # oc get csr NAME AGE REQUESTOR CONDITION csr-8b2br 15m system:serviceaccount:openshift-machine-config-operator:node-bootstrapper Pending csr-c57lv 5m26s system:node:newnode.example.com Pending # oc adm certificate approve ~~~ 6. Make sure the newly added node is showing up and running properly: ~~~ # oc get node ~~~ # References: [Creating Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS) machines in vSphere](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.1/installing/installing_vsphere/installing-vsphere.html#installation-vsphere-machines_installing-vsphere) [Adding worker nodes to the OCP 4 UPI cluster existing 24+ hours](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/4799921) [How to add OpenShift 4 RHCOS Worker Nodes in UPI](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/4246261)

title: API server request latency spiking randomly, rendering parts of the cluster unusable until a control plane restart
issue: - It takes a long time for `oc` commands to complete. Sometimes the command fails with the following error: $ time oc whoami Error from server (Timeout): the server was unable to return a response in the time allotted, but may still be processing the request (get users.user.opens real 1m0.331s user 0m0.241s sys 0m0.056s- The API server is sometimes lagging.- We have noticed intermittent issues with the Pod Autoscaling (HorizontalPodAutoscaler).- The API server logs are full with errors regarding `v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io` E0409 16:41:03.286962 1 available_controller.go:316] v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io failed with: Operation cannot be fulfilled on apiservices.apiregistration.k8s.io "v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io": the object has been modified; please apply your changes to the latest version and try again... E0409 16:40:53.273051 1 available_controller.go:316] v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io failed with: Get https://1.2.3.4:443: net/http: request canceled (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)... E0409 16:41:08.257156 1 available_controller.go:316] v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io failed with: Operation cannot be fulfilled on apiservices.apiregistration.k8s.io "v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io": StorageError: invalid object, Code: 4, Key: /kubernetes.io/apiservices/v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io, ResourceVersion: 0, AdditionalErrorMsg: Precondition failed: UID in precondition: ec197e11-db84-11e9-a44e-0050569a2c35, UID in object meta... E0409 16:52:03.561076 1 watch.go:233] unable to encode watch object: write tcp4 1.2.3.4:443-> 5.6.7.8:39396: write: broken pipe (&streaming.encoder{writer:(*metrics.fancyResponseWriterDelegator)(0xc4e7ca8230), encoder:(*versioning.codec)(0xc456b59710), buf:(*bytes.Buffer)(0xc4a2fb40e0)})... E0409 16:41:02.808545 1 controller.go:111] loading OpenAPI spec for "v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io" failed with: failed to retrieve openAPI spec, http error: ResponseCode: 503, Body: service unavailable... E0409 15:51:56.784911 1 controller.go:111] loading OpenAPI spec for "v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io" failed with: failed to retrieve openAPI spec, http error: ResponseCode: 503, Body: Error: 'dial tcp 2.90.2.226:443: i/o timeout'... E0409 16:39:40.358447 1 controller.go:111] loading OpenAPI spec for "v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io" failed with: failed to retrieve openAPI spec, http error: ResponseCode: 503, Body: request timed out, Header: map[]
resolution: **Work around**- Please perform a restart of the OCP control plane components "api" and "controllers" to work around this issue: # /usr/local/bin/master-restart controllers controllers # /usr/local/bin/master-restart api api
root_cause: - The `v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io` API is provided by the `metrics-server` component in the `openshift-metrics-server` namespace.- This components provides an aggregated API service. This means that every request sent to the OpenShift / Kubernetes API also goes through said aggregated API services. If this fails or misbehaves, it can affect the API discovery, rendering the overall API unstable.

title: How to control client access for glusterfs volumes?
issue: How to deny access for a specific client to a gluster volume?
How to set default access restrictions on dynamic provisioned gluster volumes in OCS?
resolution: * Allow access for a specific client on gluster volume. ~~~ # gluster volume set auth.reject 192.168.1.1 ~~~ *This will deny 192.168.1.1 for access to the gluster volume.* * Add a volumeoption to the storageclass for setting default access restrictions to the volumes created. * Take a backup of existing storageclass ~~~ # oc get sc glusterfs-storage-o yaml > glusterfs-storage.yaml ~~~ * Edit the yaml file to add the volumeoption. ~~~ # cat glusterfs-storage.yaml allowVolumeExpansion: true apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1 kind: StorageClass metadata: creationTimestamp: 2020-02-18T16:32:36Z name: gluster-heketi resourceVersion: "307433817" selfLink: /apis/storage.k8s.io/v1/storageclasses/gluster-heketi uid: 459e650b-526c-11ea-99cb-00505693c563 parameters: gidMax: "59999" gidMin: "50000" resturl: http://heketi-storage.glusterfs.svc:8080 restuser: admin secretName: heketi-secret secretNamespace: default volumenameprefix: paas-01-build volumeoptions: auth.allow "10.155.2.*" volumetype: replicate:3 provisioner: kubernetes.io/glusterfs reclaimPolicy: Retain volumeBindingMode: Immediate ~~~ * Delete the existing storageclass. At this point heketi would not be able to provision new volumes. ~~~ # oc delete sc glusterfs-storage ~~~ * Create a storagclass using the glusterfs-storage.yaml ~~~ # oc create-f glusterfs-storage.yaml ~~~

title: Openshift cluster using libreswan for ipsec communication randomly stops working?
issue: - Openshift is using libreswan opportunistic VPN for nodes communication. Sometime it fails to communicate and just restarting it fix the issue for sometime.
root_cause: - There are some (as of yet unknown) scenario's where pluto receives a kernel ACQUIRE for which it already detects it has a valid STATE object. Thus, it interprets these as a "duplicate acquire" and no action is taken. However, the state found does not belong to a valid IPsec SA, and so the tunnel is down and cannot be started because it is deemed up based on the "duplicate" check.- When this happens, packets are dropped for a lack of IPsec SA- or leaked in the clear, depending on whether this was a "private" or "private-or-clear" group state.- This is known issue to Red Hat Engineering team and reported via [Bugzilla 1822580](https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1822580) for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7 and [Bugzilla 1734058](https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1734058)

title: oc patch command does not create a image registry route or a image registry pod is not present in the openshift-image-registry project
issue: - oc patch command does not create a image registry route or a image registry pod is not present in the openshift-image-registry project ~~~ # oc patch configs.imageregistry.operator.openshift.io/cluster--patch '{"spec":{"defaultRoute":true}}'--type=merge # oc get route-n openshift-image-registry No resources found. OR # oc get pods-n openshift-image-registry No image registry pod is found / or missing ~~~
resolution: - Please confirm the status of the image registry is with the below steps: ~~~ # oc get co | grep image-registry AME VERSION AVAILABLE PROGRESSING DEGRADED SINCE image-registry 4.2.21 False True False 9s # oc get co image-registry-o yaml.. conditions:- lastTransitionTime: "2020-03-25T07:39:54Z" message: All registry resources are removed reason: Removed status: "False" ~~~- Check the variable managementState in the config cluster and change it to 'Managed' from 'Removed' ~~~ # oc get config # oc get config cluster-o yaml # oc edit config cluster Replace the value of the variable- managementState: <> from: managementState: Removed to: managementState: Managed ~~~
root_cause: - The image registry resources are in removed state.

title: Red Hat OpenShift 4 operator installation with manual approval fails with "404: Page Not Found"
issue: 404 error on operator install with link "one requires approval"
Installation of operatorhub operator with **manual approval*
in OpenShift 4.3 fails with "404: Page Not Found"
resolution: - The issue has been fixed in [4.3.5](https://errata.devel.redhat.com/advisory/51772) **Workaround** As a workaround to install the operator requiring manual approval you can perform the following steps:- Login to the OpenShift console with a user having cluster-admin permissions.- Navigate in the main menu to "installed operators".- Make sure you selected the proper namespace (for cluster wide operators, select the "openshift-operators" namespace).- Click on the item with a "Status" of "UpgradePending".- Click on the "Install Plan" (lower right corner of the screen) instead of "one requires approval".- Click on "Preview Install Plan".- Review all resources that will be created.- Once you are OK with the installation, click on "Approve".- Installation should now take place and operator should be available. Note: Red Hat recommends that you test workarounds in non-productive environment first.
root_cause: This behavior seems to be a Bug that is tracked in Red Hat Bugzilla. The issue is currently under investigation.

title: Where master and worker VMs boot from in OpenShift Container Platform 4.2 on Red Hat OpenStack Platform
issue: How to configure the boot location for master (controlPlane) and worker (compute) VM.
resolution: - If you set both of the following parameters for compute or controlPlane in install-config.yaml file, then OpenShift Container Platform creates a cinder volume from the RHCOS image, and boots the VM from this volume (boot from volume).- platform.openstack.rootVolume.size- platform.openstack.rootVolume.type- if you do not set both parameters for compute or controlPlane, then OpenShift Container Platform boots the VM with ephemeral disk (boot from image).- if you set only one of the parameters for compute or controlPlane, then you get a validation error.

title: Should we take vm snapshots for the purpose of taking backups of the nodes in Openshift  4.x

title: Failed to extend thin docker--vg-docker--pool
issue: - Getting `Failed to extend thin docker--vg-docker--pool` messages- After some time the LVM thin volume used by Docker becomes full.- How can it be cleaned up?
resolution: This `Failed to extend thin docker--vg-docker--pool` message doesn't mean the volume is full. LVM thin pool is configured to extend at 60% usage by default, so the usage is 60% at the time of this message started to appear. See [How to extend docker-pool](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/2107641) for the LVM thin pool details. You can get current usage by `docker info` command: ~~~ # docker info ~~~ OpenShift performs garbage collection of containers and container images no longer needed. Note that the container image garbage collection threshold is 90% by default, so it will be performed after this message started to appear at 60% usage. See [How to set garbage collection in OpenShift to clean up images and containers on a node](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/2045633) for garbage collection configuration. To sum up:- You'll see this `Failed to extend thin docker--vg-docker--pool` messages at 60% usage- Image garbage collection kicks in at 90% usage and reclaim spaces, so normally it won't get disk full- When the disk got full, OpenShift node service marked the node as NodeNotReady, Pods evicted and rescheduled to other nodes To cleanup unused images manually, or to confirm how much spaces reclaimed by image garbage collection, you can use the following command. Please make sure to get `docker info` output before and after the command, compare them to see how much space is reclaimed. If you still don't have enough spaces, it means either the configured disk is too small, too many pods scheduled, there're applications with large sized images or consuming a lot of disks inside container. ~~~ # docker info # docker images-q-f dangling=true | xargs--no-run-if-empty docker rmi # docker info ~~~

title: Why does Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 3.11 node logs error "systemd Failed to set up mount unit: Invalid argument"  frequently?
issue: - In Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 3.11 node, the following line is seen logged frequently. ~~~ systemd Failed to set up mount unit: Invalid argument ~~~- It's frequency is so high that the `/var/log` filesystem fills up. ~~~ $ egrep-v "systemd: Failed to set up mount unit: Invalid argument" var/log/messages | wc-l 105460 ~~~- Installed version of `systemd` is as follows. ~~~ $ grep systemd installed-rpms oci-systemd-hook-0.2.0-1.git05e6923.el7_6.x86_64 systemd-219-67.el7_7.2.x86_64 systemd-libs-219-67.el7_7.2.x86_64 systemd-sysv-219-67.el7_7.2.x86_64 ~~~
resolution: - The `systemd` fails to identify the `mount` arguments as valid ones because of the lengthy names, causing this issue.- The limit is of `255 bytes`. Any `mount` names longer than that would be considered invalid and thus leading to this error message.- In Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform, `systemd` read the `mount` information from `/proc/self/mounts` and converts the same using `systemd-escape` utility.- To quickly fix this issue, identify the mounts which have longer names and try reducing the projects' names/applications' names to lesser characters.
root_cause: - Longer project names/application names can easily cause having longer names to the `/proc/self/mounts` mount argument causing this issue.- The limit for the `systemd` argument is 255 bytes in total.- To increase the limit to higher value, a bug has been filed with [Red Hat Systemd Engineering](https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1779813 "Bug 1779813- Increase UNIT_NAME_MAX in unit-name.h ") which is yet to get fixed due to the collateral impacts and regressions.

title: How to check the Health Index of an image in Red Hat Container Catalog
issue: - Each image is ranked with a Health Index based in part on the age and impact of unapplied security errata across all components of a container. Refer to [this page](https://access.redhat.com/articles/2803031) for more information- It would be useful to have an API endpoint to check this Health Index
resolution: There's a public facing API which can provide such information:- To get all the information for an image (ie `redhat-openjdk-18/openjdk18-openshift`): ~~~ $ curl-s-H 'Accept: application/json' 'https://rhcc-api.redhat.com/rest/v1/repository/registry.access.redhat.com/redhat-openjdk-18%252Fopenjdk18-openshift/images' ~~~ In the response there will be an `images` array which will have all the images with their tags history and their health index (named `freshness_grade`). By iterating over this array one will be able to get the latest grade for each image.- To check just one tag (ie `redhat-openjdk-18/openjdk18-openshift:1.3-7`): ~~~ $ curl-s 'https://rhcc-api.redhat.com/rest/v1/repository/registry.access.redhat.com/redhat-openjdk-18%252Fopenjdk18-openshift/images/1.3-7' ~~~ Again, in the response there will be everything related with that tag, including the `freshness_grade` history. Again, using the time references one will be able to find the last grade applied to the image.-

title: Unable to run collectstatic with django deployment
issue: - Django python pod unable to run collect static in python module.- While redeploying django application to collect django static files following warning occurs ~~~ Collecting Django static files... WARNING: could not run 'manage.py collectstatic'. To debug, run: $ python./manage.py collectstatic--noinput Ignore this warning if you're not serving static files with Django. ~~~- With django 2.0, and 2.1 everything works fine.- But with django 2.2 collect static is failing every time.- Django example project ~~~ https://github.com/sclorg/django-ex/ ~~~- manage.py is available at: ~~~ https://github.com/sclorg/django-ex/blob/master/manage.py ~~~
resolution: The blog [Migrating Django Application](https://www.openshift.com/blog/migrating-django-applications-openshift-3) contains in general the explanation of why this is happening, and the directions needed to make collectstatic be called again. The blog contains the directions to fix it, but we can make it more concise. Take the `.s2i` directory from this repository and place it in the app codebase. ~~~ (https://github.com/openshift-evangelists/action-hooks) ~~~ Update the `.s2i/environment` file to define `DISABLE_COLLECTSTATIC=1` as per the blog. Update the `.s2i/action-hooks/build` file to call `collectstatic` as per the blog. ~~~ python /opt/app-root/src/manage.py collectstatic-- noinput ~~~ Doing these steps should result in `collectstatic` being called during the build process. **Disclaimer**: Links contained herein to external website(s) are provided for convenience only. title: How does CPU Requests and CPU Limits correspond to Linux platform specific parameters?
issue: - In the context of the OpenShift Container Platform, how does `CPU Requests` and `CPU Limits` correspond to Linux platform specific parameters: `cpu.cfs_quota`, `cpu.cfs_period_us` and `cpu.shares`?- How does one set `cpu.cfs_quota`, `cpu.cfs_period_us` and` cpu.shares`, in the context of the OpenShift Container Platform?
resolution: This document assumes that the reader is familiar with the [CPU accounting controller](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/cgroup-v1/cpuacct.txt) and the underlying [CFS scheduler](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/scheduler/sched-design-CFS.html), in particular, [CFS Bandwidth Control](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/scheduler/sched-bwc.txt). In the context of OpenShift, CPU is measured in units called *millicores*. #####CPU Requests:- Each container in a pod can specify the amount of CPU it requests on a node. The scheduler uses CPU requests to find a node with an appropriate fit for a container- The CPU request represents a baseline amount of CPU that your container may consume, but if there is no contention for CPU, it can use all available CPU on the node. If there is CPU contention on the node, CPU requests provide a relative weight across all containers on the system for how much CPU time the container may use In the case of the Linux kernel, containers that specify CPU limits, will be enforced by the CFS quota mechanism. This is enabled by default. #####CPU Limits:- Each container in a pod can specify the amount of CPU it is limited to use on a node. CPU limits control the maximum amount of CPU that your container may use independent of contention on the node. If a container attempts to exceed the specified limit, the system will throttle the container. This allows the container to have a consistent level of service independent of the number of pods scheduled to the node. If CPU Requests value is not specified and CPU Limits value is non-zero then the CPU Limits value is used to compute the cpu shares value- an excerpt of `generateLinuxContainerConfig()` is illustrated below:- File: [release-4.2/vendor/k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container_linux.go](https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/release-4.2/vendor/k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container_linux.go) ~~~ func (m *kubeGenericRuntimeManager) generateLinuxContainerConfig(container *v1.Container, pod *v1.Pod, uid *int64, username string) *runtimeapi.LinuxContainerConfig {lc:= &runtimeapi.LinuxContainerConfig{Resources: &runtimeapi.LinuxContainerResources{}, SecurityContext: m.determineEffectiveSecurityContext(pod, container, uid, username),} var cpuShares int64 cpuRequest:= container.Resources.Requests.Cpu() cpuLimit:= container.Resources.Limits.Cpu() memoryLimit:= container.Resources.Limits.Memory().Value() oomScoreAdj:= int64(qos.GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust(pod, container, int64(m.machineInfo.MemoryCapacity))) if cpuRequest.IsZero() &&!cpuLimit.IsZero() {cpuShares = milliCPUToShares(cpuLimit.MilliValue())} else {cpuShares = milliCPUToShares(cpuRequest.MilliValue())} ~~~ See `milliCPUToShares()`. If a CPU Request value is specified, the cpu shares value is computed as follows: ~~~ shares = (CPU Requests * 1024) / 1000 ~~~ Also, if the specified CPU Requests value is 0 then cpu shares value is set to the minimum value, which is 2; and if the computed cpu shares value is less than the minimum then the cpu shares value is set to 2. #####CFS period: Specifies a period of time in microseconds, for how regularly a cgroup's access to CPU resources should be reallocated. In the context of Kubernetes, the CFS period is [hard-coded to 100000](https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/release-4.2/vendor/k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/cm/helpers_linux.go) (which is equivalent to 100ms), since the Kubernetes-specific feature namely `CPUCFSQuotaPeriod` is *disabled* by default (see [release-4.2/vendor/k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/features/kube_features.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/features/kube_features.go)). #####CFS quota: Specifies the total amount of time, in microseconds, for which all tasks in a cgroup can run during one period. See `milliCPUToQuota()`. The CFS quota is computed using the CPU Limits and the derived (see above) CFS period value: ~~~ quota = (CPU Limits * 100000) / 1000 ~~~ If the computed quota is less than the minimum, which is 1000, then the quota value is set to 1000. ~~~ if m.cpuCFSQuota {cpuPeriod:= int64(quotaPeriod) if utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(kubefeatures.CPUCFSQuotaPeriod) {cpuPeriod = int64(m.cpuCFSQuotaPeriod.Duration / time.Microsecond)} cpuQuota:= milliCPUToQuota(cpuLimit.MilliValue(), cpuPeriod) lc.Resources.CpuQuota = cpuQuota lc.Resources.CpuPeriod = cpuPeriod} ~~~ The in-memory data structure (shown below) is populated accordingly. ~~~ type LinuxContainerResources struct {CpuPeriod int64 CpuQuota int64 CpuShares int64 MemoryLimitInBytes int64 OomScoreAdj int64 CpusetCpus string CpusetMems string...} ~~~ For example, with CPU Limits and CPU Requests set to 3500 and 5700, respectively, a container would be permitted to fully utilise 3.5 CPUs. The conversion to platform-specific, Linux, values is illustrated below: ~~~ cpu.cfs_period_us 100000 cpu.cfs_quota_us 350000 (3500 * 100000) / 1000 cpu.shares 5836 (5700 * 1024) / 1000 ~~~ Now, the CPU Requests directly corresponds to `cpu.shares`. The *shares* value specifies a relative share of CPU time available to all tasks in container (or cgroup); the amount of CPU time (or bandwidth) that is available to a container, may vary depending on the number of containers that exist on the node. Also note that shares of CPU time are distributed per CPU cores on a multi-core system. In other words, if a container is limited to less than 100% of a CPU, on a multi-core system, it may use 100% of each individual CPU core.

title: OpenShift 4.x installation never completes, bootstrap logs with: etcd-client.crt: no such file or directory
issue: - Installation never completes
resolution: - Every time this issue has been reported it was overcome by a new run of the installation- Root cause is currently under investigation
