title: In Red Hat Fuse 7, what are the differences among Fuse on Karaf, Fuse on EAP, and Fuse on Springboot?
issue: In Red Hat Fuse 7, what are the differences among Fuse on Karaf, Fuse on EAP, and Fuse on Springboot? How do we choose among the three options?
resolution: The core technology among the three choices is Apache Camel; since Camel is very versatile framework, it has been ported to containers (Karaf, Springboot, EAP). Camel will also be the integration framework for Quarkus and Camel-K (Serverless on Openshift). 1. Fuse on Karaf- Red Hat acquired Fusesource in 2016, and back then Camel on Karaf was the only supported platform. If you have old code that needs to be ported from 6.x to 7.x, this would be the most straight forward port. If you start from scratch, Karaf may not be the choice as it deals with OSGi and bundles which may to be difficult if you are not familiar with them. 2. Fuse on EAP- As Fusesource continued to merge with JBoss, we found many customers are on EAP platform, and they also want to use Camel for integration. Back in Camel on Karaf, the developers have to create the components (endpoints like jms connections, etc) and injected their bundles (jars) into Karaf. However, EAP has most of this endpoints created through JCA connectors for DB and JMS, and developers just need to configure them (like datasource and mdb) and just use annotation to inject these resources. Many of the components will need to be rewritten to fit the JEE style. Hence, there is an option of Fuse on EAP installer, and it is make Camel runs and fits better within EAP. So, if you use EAP/JEE and want to integrate within EAP, Fuse on EAP is the choice. 3. Fuse on Springboot- As Springboot was getting more popular, we have customers requests for Camel to run on Springboot. Springboot uses declarative way (application.properties and *-starter) to create a containerless uber jar; Camel evolves accordingly as it ported most of its components to have spring boot starters. In short, either EAP or springboot would be what most developers choose if they don't have legacy baggage.-- Moving forward: As Red Hat is preparing for supporting the trend of Microservices, containers, serverless; Red Hat expects Quarkus will gain more popularity. Springboot is pretty heavy weight; besides, if you want to adopt microservices, you will need all the spring-cloud management (hystrix, all the netflix components no one supports and develop now etc) to really run microservices. Based on my observation, the current (early 2020), application containers deployed in Openshift are most likely be monolithic spring-boot and not fully microservices. It is a progress. Red Hat took a different approach: we choose Container, Kubernetes, Openshift as the fundamental platform, and use many knative components (Istio, Promentheus, Grafana, Config Map / Secrets, Ingress / Routes) to fill-in the gaps of Spring Cloud. The choice of Openshift and Knative is simple, and it is to support Polygot (beyond just java. Spring cloud is java centric, and afaik it can't move beyond Spring). The choice of Quarkus is pretty obvious as well, a much more lightweight framework and make it easy for Java developers to adopt and port to containers.

title: Why does the `oracle` resource fails to start with error - status: SP2-0640: Not connected ?
issue: - The `oracle` resource fails to start with error: ~~~ oracle(oracledb)[17177]: ERROR: oracle prd can not be mounted (status: SP2-0640: Not connected) ~~~- The `oracle` resource can be started when `unmanaged` and monitored, but it refuses to start from the cluster when `managed`.
resolution: - Validate that the password for `monuser` is valid and has not expired.- Confirm if cluster is able to perform `connect / as sysdba` over the database.
root_cause: - The issue is in `sqlnet.ora` file which has been modified and added one parameter `SQLNET.AUTHENTICATION_SERVICES = (NONE)`. This parameter disables the OS login to the database and login to database requires username and password. ~~~ SQLNET.ALLOWED_LOGON_VERSION_CLIENT = 8 SQLNET.ALLOWED_LOGON_VERSION_SERVER = 8 ~~~

title: Zync creates multiple conflicting routes when APICAST_PATH_ROUTING=true and "deployment_option":"hosted"
resolution: When `APICAST_PATH_ROUTING` is set to true, `APIcast` should have the parameter `"deployment_option"` set to `"self_managed"`. This prevents `Zync` from creating the routes automatically when a `Service` is created or updated. From the Service's Integration Settings page, select the option `APIcast self-managed`. Integration Settings on **3scale 2.6** are accessible through the Admin Portal at: `https://${ADMIN_PORTAL_URL}/apiconfig/services/${SERVICE_ID}/integration > edit integration settings` the same settings on **3scale 2.7** can be found here: `https://${ADMIN_PORTAL_URL}/apiconfig/services/${SERVICE_ID}/settings` Note that the Public Base URLs for the services will be cleared when the deployment option is set to self-managed: * If this is a new 3scale deployment and you are creating new services, populate the Public Base URLs for staging and production. * If you already had the services from the previous 3scale version then you can retrieve the Public Base URL ahead of time with the workaround described in this issue [THREESCALE-4861](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/THREESCALE-4861?focusedCommentId=14025402&page=com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.issuetabpanels%3Acomment-tabpanel#comment-14025402). Then you'll need to create the route pointing to apicast-staging|production from OpenShift.
root_cause: This behavior is expected if the parameter `"deployment_option"` is set to `"hosted"`, as it instructs Zync to create the routes automatically. When `APICAST_PATH_ROUTING=true` and the Public Base URLs are set to be identical across different Services, the routes created by `Zync` will conflict.

title: How to upgrade service catalog and brokers post installation?
issue: - The service catalog didn't upgrade at the time of the cluster upgrade.- The service catalog was disabled at the time of cluster upgrade. ~~~ [OSEv3:vars] openshift_enable_service_catalog=false template_service_broker_install=false ansible_service_broker_install=false ansible_service_broker_remove=true template_service_broker_remove=true openshift_service_catalog_remove=true ~~~
resolution: - The following variable needs to be added to the inventory with the correct image tag to upgrade the service catalog and brokers. ~~~ openshift_service_catalog_image_version="v3.11.200" ~~~- The current version can be identified with the `oc version` command that needs to be used for the upgrade. ~~~ # oc version oc v3.11.200 kubernetes v1.11.0+d4cacc0 features: Basic-Auth GSSAPI Kerberos SPNEGO Server https://cluster.example.com:443 openshift v3.11.200 kubernetes v1.11.0+d4cacc0 ~~~- The following playbook needs to be run with the inventory containing the service catalog image version variable. ~~~ /usr/share/ansible/openshift-ansible/playbooks/openshift-service-catalog/config.yml ~~~- All the `serviceinstance` and `servicebindings` will persist and won't be removed.
root_cause: - The service catalog and brokers were disabled at the time of the cluster upgrade.

title: Add a new Gluster node in a cluster running on Independent mode. What needs to be done on Gluster side and on OpenShift side
issue: Need to add a new Gluster node in a cluster running with Independent mode on OpenShift Container Storage version 3.11
resolution: - Follow the Appendix 2 of the Deployment guide on the new node, this procedure will install the daemons, configure the firewall and enable the services. [Install a New Node- Independent Mode](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_container_storage/3.11/html/deployment_guide/cns_deploy_optional#chap-Documentation-Container_Ready_Storage_independent)- Add the new node on the cluster using Heketi, so you will need to access Heketi. ~~~ # oc project # oc rsh ~~~ Add a new node to the cluster by using Heketi CLI. Following shows an example of how to add new node in zone 1 to `597fceb5d6c876b899e48f599b988f54 ` cluster using the CLI: ~~~ $ heketi-cli node add--zone=1--cluster=597fceb5d6c876b899e48f599b988f54--management-host-name=node4.example.com--storage-host-name=192.168.10.104 ~~~ Just run this command, which is the last part of the procedure on the documentation: [Adding a new Node](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_container_storage/3.11/html/operations_guide/chap-documentation-red_hat_gluster_storage_container_native_with_openshift_platform-managing_clusters#sect_Adding_New_Nodes) To find the cluster ID you can use the command: ~~~ $ heketi-cli cluster list ~~~- Adding a new device to the new node. After add the new node you need to add a device for this new node: [Adding a new Device](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_container_storage/3.11/html/operations_guide/chap-documentation-red_hat_gluster_storage_container_native_with_openshift_platform-managing_clusters#sect_Adding_New_Devices)

title: Why Red Hat changed the default port 8443 to 443 in updating OpenShift 3.X to OpenShift 4.X
issue: y Red Hat changed the default port 8443 to 443 in updating OpenShift 3.X to OpenShift 4.X. Customer know how to switch the port but what to know why is the change
resolution: "For use by the OpenShift Container Platform web console, shared with the API server." In 3.11 we access console using openshift_master_cluster_public_hostname which is nothing but hostname "https://openshift.example.com:8443" which resolves to lb and this points to master api server on port 8443. While in Openshift 4 master api server are not publicly accessible and we access console only using console route on port 443 using console route and doesnt require port to be mentioned in the url. In openshift 4: apiserver port mapping is like below: https Service 443 TCP Pod 8443 Similarly for console: https Service 443 TCP Pod 8443

title: Tasks assigned to group are not available in RHPAM when using RHSSO
issue: - We have RH PAM 7.6 integrated with RH-SSO running on openshift. RH-SSO is connected to Ping. Users are able to login and view tasks assigned to them. i.e Reserved tasks. But tasks assigned to group they belong to are not returned in the API as well as the Task inbox. i.e Ready tasks that are assigned to my group are not available. PAM with no SSO integration on my local machine returns group tasks successfully.
resolution: As I told you before and as we could see in the remote session, you have to create the groups in the "Configure-> Roles" on RHSSO. Then you have to go to the "Manage-> Groups", select the group, edit, go to the "Role Mappings" and assign the created role. In this way, that group will appear in the RHPAM. For instance, following you can see a better example: 1. Group "APP-IT-FSA-UI-DEV" is defined in your RHSSO. 2. User "y6580" belongs to the group "APP-IT-FSA-UI-DEV" that you can see in the RHSSO "Users-> y6580-> Groups". 3. You have to add manually "APP-IT-FSA-UI-DEV" as a role in the RHSSO "Configure-> Roles". 4. Go to "Manage-> Groups" and "Edit" the group "APP-IT-FSA-UI-DEV". Go to "Role Mappings" and assign the role "APP-IT-FSA-UI-DEV" created in (3). When you finish and go to the RHPAM, you will see the "APP-IT-FSA-UI-DEV" group created in the settings and assigned to the user "y6580". After that you can configure your process and set the "group" to the user task. After following the above steps in your environment, everything worked as expected.---------------------- I've been discussing about the groups/roles mapping in RHSSO and as we could see in this case, groups created in RHSSO are not mapped anywhere in RHPAM. The reason is there's no significant difference between roles and groups in RHPAM besides the fact that roles are reserved for some specific privileges. In EAP also groups/roles are configured in same way, that is if its not a role, it is considered a group. The reserved roles in RHPAM are the "admin", "analyst", "developer", "manager", "process-admin", "user", and "rest-all" for Business Central and the "kie-server" for Process Server [1]. So if you create those roles in the "[RHSSO] Configure-> Roles", they will appear as roles in RHPAM while if you create different roles, as for instance "APP-IT-FSA-UI-DEV", they will appear as groups in RHPAM. Now the question is how those "roles" can be automatically created when the external user database and RHSSO are synchronized. As I suppose that you configured your RHSSO federating your existing external user database [2], so the idea is to map the groups from your external user database into roles in RHSSO. In that way, you would skip the extra manually step that we discussed before. Then, what is the meaning of Groups in RHSSO if they are not used? The RHSSO is a separate project and groups in RHSSO are for a different use case, so the confusion lies in how business central treats groups vs roles. Groups/Roles are very well separated in RHSSO but its not the case in EAP/RHPAM. We are looking into possibility of using RHSSO groups in RHPAM in a future although it is not still in the roadmap. [1] https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_process_automation_manager/7.6/html/integrating_red_hat_process_automation_manager_with_red_hat_single_sign-on/roles-users-con [2] https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_single_sign-on/7.3/html/server_administration_guide/user-storage-federation

title: Inconisistent versioning standards for containers on Red Hat  Customer Portal
issue: When looking to pull down Redhat's node.js 8 container, I noticed inconsistencies in the versioning for node.js and the way it is being referenced now vs. the way it was referenced for previous versions. I would like to see consistent version standards (preferably the rhscl/mysql method which includes node.js' version # in the container version # as similar to mysql). I've also noticed inconsistent naming conventions (or highly confusing naming conventions) regarding JWS 3.0 vs. 3.1 where jws 3.0 is on 1.3-## and jws 3.1 is on 1.1-##. This makes it difficult to automate without a clear, precise standard that doesn't change. Mysql's approach seems to be superior as it includes the mysql version followed by the container version, which makes the most sense from an administrative and transparency standpoint.
resolution: Hello, Here is a snippet from the mail Marek Goldmann sent regarding this issue: "Our images do follow middleware naming and versioning convention which we established long time ago. This won't change. You can find more details about it here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1oFv6Vo38bgmH1oyt5YKloUF5i3LzkO4jFD8i9uzBajk/edit#heading=h.b3lmslvipus7 This scheme is consistent and easy to understand once you get why we choose it. Unfortunately, I just realized that this is something that is missing in the doc. I'll try to shortly name these reasons here. First of all, on the OpenShift platform we have to work with two (and in fact three, but about it later), conflicting versions. Let's focus on EAP 7.0 image here, as an example. OpenShift version (currently 3.6) Product version (7.0) So, now we have two options- we can use OCP or product versions for our versioning scheme. If we choose OCP- we need to rebuild every image to release on new version of OCP which is not a great deal. If we base on the product version- we have no option to include changes that would be required to support running this particular product on new OCP version. Let me introduce other, most important from the OCP POV, part of the image: integration scripts. A product image consist from: OS and required libraries Product Integration/support scripts that actually make it possible to run this particular product in the OpenShift environment. After debating what to do with the versioning we decided to use version on the integration scripts as the image version and this is what you see as the version. This gives us ability to support particular product on selected OpenShift platform at the same time not being blocked by any incompatible changes that may be introduced by the OpenShift team or simply by changing the way how the integration works. I can give you one example: we introduced clustering protocol called DNS_PING which was used in the early images, we found out that this was unreliable at that point, so we changed completely how images find each other in OpenShift and we moved to OPENSHIFT_PING, a different protocol. Exactly zero changes were made to the main product (no product update) and OpenShift version stayed the same. We just changed a major part of the image in a breaking way. We must have an option to do it and we had- our, middleware naming scheme. Now, back to mentioned MySQL versioning. https://access.redhat.com/containers/?tab=tags#/registry.access.redhat.com/rhscl/mysql-57-rhel7 Tag of the container (after ":") is in following format: VERSION:RELEASE. In your example, MySQL container image tag is: 5.7-3.16. The "5.7" is the product version, in this case. Everything else is a release number. "3" is main release number, "16" is number or rebuilds for this image. There are additional tags attached: "5.7" and "latest". With this approach it is impossible to introduce breaking changes and to have a meaningful "floating" tag pointing to it. If we use "5.7" it would mean that we could have added a breaking change to the image and it would be fetched by customers. Of course, MySQL is different from EAP and that's the whole point. You cannot expect it to follow the same versioning scheme because it simply doesn't work. EAP integration is much more depending on the actual OpenShift capabilities than any of the RHSCL container images. The same thing applies to any middleware products, in fact."- Fatima Hello, The team has discussed and presented the following theory: "Our images do follow middleware naming and versioning convention which we established long time ago. This won't change. It is very important to use product codes, for example: Red Hat JBoss Enterprise Application Platform(Official name), JBoss EAP(approved abbr), eap(product code). For our versioning scheme we use two types of tags: Floating — where the tag can point to different images in a time (for example when we update an image and assign the “latest” tag to it). At a given point in time- a floating tag can be applied to a single image. When a new image will be tagged with this tag- old image will lose it. Static — where the tag cannot be assigned to other image. This tag includes also release number. A release number is just an incremented number of the build. It is increased by 1 after every rebuild of the image. A container image name consists of a name and a tag: NAME:TAG. Let’s consider the jboss-eap-6/eap64-openshift image. This is the EAP 6.4 image intended to use in OpenShift environment. The same image can have applied following tags: jboss-eap-6/eap64-openshift:1.4-1- this is a static tag (note the release number after the dash) jboss-eap-6/eap64-openshift:1.4- this is a floating tag pointing to latest image in the 1.4 version jboss-eap-6/eap64-openshift:latest- this is floating tag pointing to latest image When we build above image it gets following tags: 1.4-1, 1.4 and latest. If we rebuild that image, new image gets following tags: 1.4-2, 1.4 and latest. This means that floating tags 1.4 and latest have been moved to the new image and the 1.4-1 image lost them. Below you can find naming and versioning rules for OpenShift images. S ${VENDOR}-${PRODUCT}-${MAJOR}[-${RELEASE_MODIFIER}]/${PRODUCT}${MAJOR}${MINOR}[-${SUBPRODUCT}]-openshift:${STREAM_MAJOR}-${STREAM_MINOR}-${RELEASE} F: ${VENDOR}-${PRODUCT}-${MAJOR}[-${RELEASE_MODIFIER}]/${PRODUCT}${MAJOR}${MINOR}[-${SUBPRODUCT}]-openshift:${STREAM_MAJOR}-${STREAM_MINOR} F: ${VENDOR}-${PRODUCT}-${MAJOR}[-${RELEASE_MODIFIER}]/${PRODUCT}${MAJOR}${MINOR}[-${SUBPRODUCT}]-openshift:latest where, S- static tag F- floating tag VENDOR is a string identifying the BU (or similar) responsible for the product. For CE images in almost all cases it is jboss, but sometimes redhat- it depends on the product name. PRODUCT The product this is part of. For JBoss products e.g. eap. PRODUCTGEN The major relevant generation of the product that is relevant for user experience in the context of the images if needed- e.g. 6 for EAP 6.4. PRODUCTCODE Same as PRODUCT earlier, but with a version suffix. In most cases we suffix the major and minor version of the product, e.g. eap64 for EAP 6.4. Can have a modifier if it’s a variant or the combination is very important: e.g. webserver30-tomcat8 for a JWS image with Tomcat 8. SUBPRODUCT (optional) Some products (for example JWS) have subproducts: Tomcat 7 or Tomcat 8. For JWS the subproduct should be tomcat7 or tomcat8. If there is no subproduct- that part is omitted. RELEASE_MODIFIER (optional)- this can have one of the values: alpha, beta or tech-preview. Used to differentiate between stable and pre-releases. MAJOR and MINOR are the two most significant values from the image release version triplet, which is of the form major.minor.micro following semantic versioning. STREAM_MAJOR and STREAM_MINOR are independent versions that are tied to the image. With OpenShift images we cannot stick to the OpenShift versions (different lifecycle compared to the OpenShift releases) nor we cannot stick with the product versions (we can release image with a breaking change that uses the same version of the product). Instead we introduce new version in which we version the integration scripts and thus the image itself, not the product, not the OpenShift version Examples jboss-eap-6/eap64-openshift:1.4-1 jboss-eap-6/eap64-openshift:1.4 jboss-eap-6/eap64-openshift:latest jboss-webserver-3/webserver30-tomcat7-openshift:1.3 jboss-decisionserver-6/decisionserver63-openshift:1.4 jboss-eap-7-tech-preview/eap71-openshift:1.0 (tech preview OCP image for EAP 7.1) redhat-sso-7/sso70-openshift:1.4 redhat-openjdk-18/openjdk18-openshift:1.1 This scheme is consistent and easy to understand once you get why we choose it. Unfortunately this is something that is missing in the documentation. We'll try to shortly name these reasons here. First of all, on the OpenShift platform we have to work with two (and in fact three, but about it later), conflicting versions. Let's focus on EAP 7.0 image here, as an example. 1. OpenShift version (currently 3.7) 2. Product version (7.0) So, now we have two options- we can use OCP or product versions for our versioning scheme. If we choose OCP- we need to rebuild every image to release on new version of OCP which is not a great deal. If we base on the product version- we have no option to include changes that would be required to support running this particular product on new OCP version. Let me introduce other, most important from the OCP POV, part of the image: integration scripts. A product image consist from: 1. OS and required libraries 2. Product 3. Integration/support scripts that actually make it possible to run this particular product in the OpenShift environment. After debating what to do with the versioning we decided to use version on the integration scripts as the image version and this is what you see as the version. This gives us ability to support particular product on selected OpenShift platform at the same time not being blocked by any incompatible changes that may be introduced by the OpenShift team or simply by changing the way how the integration works. Now, back to mentioned MySQL versioning. https://access.redhat.com/containers/?tab=tags#/registry.access.redhat.com/rhscl/mysql-57-rhel7 Tag of the container (after ":") is in following format: VERSION:RELEASE. In your example, MySQL container image tag is: 5.7-3.16. The "5.7" is the product version, in this case. Everything else is a release number. "3" is main release number, "16" is number or rebuilds for this image. There are additional tags attached: "5.7" and "latest". With this approach it is impossible to introduce breaking changes and to have a meaningful "floating" tag pointing to it. If we use "5.7" it would mean that we could have added a breaking change to the image and it would be fetched by customers. Of course, MySQL is different from EAP and that's the whole point. You cannot expect it to follow the same versioning scheme because it simply doesn't work. EAP integration is much more depending on the actual OpenShift capabilities than any of the RHSCL container images. The same thing applies to any middleware products, in fact." If you have any more questions feel free to ask. Have a nice day. Thanks, Fatima Shaikh, RHCE. Associate Technical Support Engineer. Pune, Red Hat INC.

title: Getting i/o timeout erros while pulling or pushing an image
issue: - Node is not able to pull any images from the registry.- In /var/log/messages, node service logs. ~~~ Apr 15 09:27:56 node.example.com atomic-openshift-node: E0415 10:27:56.703803 16224 remote_runtime.go:92] RunPodSandbox from runtime service failed: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = Get https://registry.redhat.io/v1/_ping: dial tcp 10.0.5.5:443: i/o timeout Apr 15 09:27:56 node.example.com atomic-openshift-node: E0415 10:27:56.703886 16224 kuberuntime_sandbox.go:56] CreatePodSandbox for pod "master-api-node.example.com_kube-system(6992a0c85b90dd221832cedfe13eabb4)" failed: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = Get https://registry.redhat.io/v1/_ping: dial tcp 10.0.5.5:443: i/o timeout ~~~- Docker service logs. ~~~ Apr 15 10:27:37 node.example.com dockerd-current[1645]: time="2020-04-15T09:27:37.673505294+01:00" level=error msg="Attempting next endpoint for pull after error: Get https://registry.redhat.io/v2/: net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)" Apr 15 10:28:07 node.example.com dockerd-current[1645]: time="2020-04-15T09:28:07.687521261+01:00" level=error msg="Attempting next endpoint for pull after error: Get https://registry.redhat.io/v1/_ping: dial tcp 10.0.5.5:443: i/o timeout" Apr 15 10:28:10 node.example.com dockerd-current[1645]: time="2020-04-15T09:28:10.661157241+01:00" level=error msg="Handler for GET /v1.26/images/registry.redhat.io/openshift3/ose-pod:v3.11.200/json returned error: No such image: registry.redhat.io/openshift3/ose-pod:v3.11.200" ~~~
resolution: - While using proxy variables, ensure that registry.redhat.io and sso.redhat.com are whitelisted by the proxy and/or network firewall. Refer this: [Troubleshooting Authentication Issues with registry.redhat.io](https://access.redhat.com/articles/3560571)- Ensure the proxy settings applied in `/etc/origin/master/master.env`, `/etc/sysconfig/docker`, `/etc/sysconfig/atomic-openshift-node` are identical and correctly configured.- An inconvenience with the configuration of the firewall can be a possible reason, check for the active firewall rules, if it is blocking any traffic.
root_cause: Proxy setting was mismatched between `/etc/sysconfig/docker` and the `/etc/origin/master/master.env`

title: crio service fails to start with overlay2 storage driver
issue: - We cannot get crio service to start with overlay2 storage driver.- We are seeing these errors in `/var/log/messages`: ~~~ systemd[1]: Starting Open Container Initiative Daemon... level=fatal msg="kernel does not support overlay fs: overlay: the backing xfs filesystem is formatted without d_type support, which leads to incorrect behavior. Reformat the filesystem with ftype=1 to enable d_type support. Running without d_type is not supported.: driver not supported" systemd[1]: crio.service: main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE systemd[1]: Failed to start Open Container Initiative Daemon. systemd[1]: Unit crio.service entered failed state. systemd[1]: crio.service failed. ~~~
resolution: This can be prevented by creating another xfs filesystem for `/var` where you can use `d_type` without an invasive reformat of the root filesystem. This would then need to be mounted on `/var/lib/containers/storage`
root_cause: - The root filesystem, where `/var/lib/containers/storage` is mounted is `ftype=0`, so `d_type` is not enabled. The overlay2 storage driver checks for the compatibility of the underlying xfs filesystem and is dependant on a directory entry type, referred to here as `d_type`. This is a data field within the data structure that is used to point to the type of file the directory entry is representing, i.e. a directory, file, pipe, char device, a socket file, etc.

title: Outbound network traffic slow because DNS lookup is slow to respond or timeout
issue: Running a curl, wget or some similar network function can cause delays for multiples of 5 seconds while looking up domain name resolution. Not all commands are affected, for example dig and nslookup are immune even though they are DNS lookup commands.
resolution: This occurs because of a race condition while doing DNS lookups. There is no fix for this as of now but the issue can be mitigated by ensuring only one DNS request is is called at a time. This can be achieved by setting `single-request-reopen` in the resolv.conf file. There are 2 methods of doing this:- configuration at the pod level;- configuration at the node level. Only the first solution is suitable for OSD. ### POD Level changes Suitable for OSD and OCP. The goal is to add the DNS option to the pods specification, similar to the following example: ~~~ apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: labels: run: testing name: testing spec: containers:- args:- /bin/bash--c- "sleep 600" image: registry.redhat.io/rhel7/rhel-tools imagePullPolicy: Always name: testing resources: {} securityContext: runAsUser: 1002870000 stdin: true stdinOnce: true terminationMessagePath: /dev/termination-log terminationMessagePolicy: File tty: true dnsConfig: < <---- Add DNS Options options: < <---- Add DNS Options- name: single-request-reopen < <---- Add DNS Options dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst enableServiceLinks: true imagePullSecrets:- name: default-dockercfg-svbkq priority: 0 restartPolicy: Never ~~~ This is best done in the deployment config so that it is available to all pods that are created. Either by adding the DNS options to a new yaml definition or editing an existing with deployment config. For example: ~~~ $ oc edit dc ${dcToedit} ## Add the aditional lines ## save; and exit. OR $ oc patch dc ${dcToedit}--patch='{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"dnsConfig":{"options":[{"name":"single-request-reopen"}]}}}}}' ~~~ ## Node Level changes Depending on the DNS policy used for pods, the DNS option can be added to the /etc/resolv.conf. By adding the following line. ~~~ options single-request-reopen ~~~ This file is maintained by OpenShift and can be modified using the the following Red Hat solution [Update nameservers used by OCP 4](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/4518671 "Red Hat Solution")
root_cause: A problem occurs when two UDP packets are sent via the same socket at the same time from different threads. UDP is a connection-less protocol, so no packet is sent as a result of the connect(2) syscall (opposite to TCP) and thus, no conntrack entry has been created after the call. The entry is created only when a packet is sent. This leads to the following possible races:- Neither of the packets finds a confirmed conntrack in the 1. nf_conntrack_in step. For both packets two conntrack entries with the same tuples are created.- Same as in the above case, but a conntrack entry of one of the packets is confirmed before the other has called 3. get_unique_tuple. The other packet gets a different reply tuple usually with the source port changed.- Same as in the 1st case, but two different rules with different endpoints are selected in the step 2. ipt_do_table. The GNU C Library and musl libc both perform A and AAAA DNS lookups in parallel. One of the UDP packets might get dropped by the kernel due to the races, so the client will try to re-send it after a timeout which is usually 5 seconds. It is worth mentioning that the problem is not only specific for Kubernetes- any Linux multi-threaded process sending UDP packets in parallel is prone to this race condition. [Explanation provided by MARTYNAS PUMPUTIS](https://www.weave.works/blog/racy-conntrack-and-dns-lookup-timeouts "Racy conntrack and DNS lookup timeouts")

title: TLS errors after Certificates are redeployed
issue: After redeploying certificates using "/usr/share/ansible/openshift-ansible/playbooks/openshift-master/redeploy-certificates.yml". Getting the following errors:- TLS certificate error "error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)"- Project and pods stuck in terminating state.
resolution: After running the playbook, we must regenerate any service signing certificate or key pairs by deleting existing secrets that contain service serving certificates or removing and re-adding annotations to appropriate services. For more details refer to the doc [https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/3.11/install_config/redeploying_certificates.html](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/3.11/install_config/redeploying_certificates.html) It is possible that the pods are using an old certificate, so we need to update the secrets.We can also delete the secrets and wait to be re-generated, and recreate the pods in order to use new secrets. However the option of recreating pods must be under the users discretion in production environment.

title: OCS 3.11 - How to lock a BHV to prevent new gluster block volumes allocation on it
issue: In cases that for some reasons space is getting full on a Block Hosting Volume (BHV) it may be required to lock it, so the BHV won't be eligible to allocate new gluster block volumes. **NOTE*

This document should be published as internal, this option should be used only when indicated by Redhat Support. There should be no need to block a BHV as it should never become full, but it has been found situations when the BHV gets full (ie when customers have expanded the BHV)
resolution: Lock a Block Hosting Volume (BHV) with this command: ~~~ # heketi-cli volume set-block-hosting-restriction locked ~~~ That way that BHV won't be used to allocate new block volumes. You can unlock that restriction with this other command: ~~~ # heketi-cli volume set-block-hosting-restriction unlocked ~~~ **Note** You can find the ID of your BHV with command `heketi-cli volume list` See also document: [How To Identify Block Volumes and Block Hosting Volumes in Openshift Container Storage?](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/3897581)

title: What is the use of "HostPrefix" when using third party CNI(Calico)?
issue: - `Calico` is used for IP management across the cluster then what is the role of `HostPrefix`?- Why `HostPrefix` is a mandatory field in the `install-config.yaml` file?
resolution: - The `cidr` field denotes the complete network of the cluster and IPs of the pods will be of the same range. For example: ~~~ networking: clusterNetwork:- cidr: 10.128.0.0/14 hostPrefix: 23 ~~~- The `cidr` value "10.128.0.0/14" is the cluster network and all the pods will fall under this CIDR range within the cluster.- And using a default value for HostPrefix that is given in the [document](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.4/installing/installing_bare_metal/installing-bare-metal-network-customizations.html#installation-bare-metal-config-yaml_installing-bare-metal-network-customizations) which is "/23".- To further divide the `cidr` big subnet into small subnets, the subnet prefix is needed.- In OCP v3.x, the subnet prefix can be calculated by using the `HostSubnetLength` parameter.- For example, here the `cidr` has `/14` and to break it into the small subnet that is `/23` then the `HostSubnetLength` would be `9`.- But in OpenShift version v4.x, the `HostPrefix` is used at the place of `HostSubnetLength`, where we can directly specify the prefix for the small subnets i.e `23` by default.- These subnets will be assigned to each of the nodes within the cluster.- Thus, the pods on the nodes will have the IP of that "/23" subnet only. See the snippet below: ~~~ # oc get network.config cluster-o yaml apiVersion: config.openshift.io/v1 kind: Network metadata:... name: cluster... spec: clusterNetwork:- cidr: 10.128.0.0/14 hostPrefix: 23 # oc get hostsubnet NAME HOST HOST IP SUBNET master-0.openshift.example.com master-0.openshift.example.com 10.0.x.x 10.130.x.x/23 master-1.openshift.exampe.com master-1.openshift.example.com 10.0.x.x 10.129.x.x/23 master-2.openshift.example.com master-2.openshift.example.com 10.0.x.x 10.128.x.x/23 worker-0.openshift.example.com worker-0.openshift.example.com 10.0.x.x 10.128.x.x/23 worker-1.openshift.example.com worker-1.openshift.example.com 10.0.x.x 10.131.x.x/23 ~~~- According to the `HostPrefix` value "23", all the nodes have the subnet `/23`.- Whereas the `Calico` manages the IP allocation of the pods with the help IP pools. See the [document](https://www.tigera.io/blog/calico-ipam-explained-and-enhanced/) of Calico.- IP pools are configured with a particular range of IPs that can be assigned to pods. IP pools are configured by cluster administrators and can be used by the `calicoctl` utilities.- And the IP pool is dependent on `BlockSize`- BlockSize is nothing but blocks of IPs created according to the CIDR.- The default value for BlockSize is "26" which means only 62 IPs are available for the allocation.

title: Mapping single route to multiple services
issue: - Requirement if to map the “same” single route – myappln.mydomain.com/ to map to service-1, servive-2, service-3 etc. based on the filtering done on the /- Is there any other Redhat approved/supported stack to replace the default HAProxy, such as Nginx where we have much advanced routing possibilities?- Will the mentioned github [link](URL "https://github.com/elyscape/origin-router-regexp") be supported by Redhat
resolution: - A route is usually associated with one service through the to: token with kind: Service, It is possible to have as many as four services supporting the route. The portion of requests that are handled by each service is governed by the service weight.- Path based routes specify a path component that can be compared against a URL (which requires that the traffic for the route be HTTP based) such that multiple routes can be served using the same host name, each with a different path. Routers should match routes based on the most specific path to the least; however, this depends on the router implementation. The host name and path are passed through to the backend server so it should be able to successfully answer requests for them. For example: a request to http://example.com/foo/ that goes to the router will result in a pod seeing a request to http://example.com/foo/. **Workaround 1**: Setting route with a path ~~~ apiVersion: v1 kind: Route metadata: name: route-unsecured spec: host: www.example.com path: "/test" to: kind: Service name: service-name ~~~- There is no approved/supported stack to replace the default HaProxy which RedHat provides.- The methodology mentioned in the Github [Link](URL "https://github.com/elyscape/origin-router-regexp") is not supported as it is an Upstream product.

title: CLI commands in ose-cli are slow to complete
issue: - CLI commands like `$ oc get pods` are slow to complete when ran within an ose-cli container compared to when they are run from a client machine.
resolution: - The HOME environment variable can be set when the container is started directly: ~~~ $ oc run-it--image=registry.redhat.io/openshift4/ose-cli:latest bash--as=user--env=HOME=/tmp ~~~- When using a deployment, deployment configuration or job it can be added to the resource definition. This would for instance add it to a deployment configuration named dc-name: ~~~ $ oc set env dc/dc-name HOME=/tmp ~~~
root_cause: - The oc client tries to cache date in a.kube directory located in the HOME directory of the user.- When the user id is from a high range (per default with restricted scc) there is no matching user defined in the image and HOME is populated with the root directory /.- The user inside the image is however missing the permissions to write to the root directory

title: Elasticsearch is in Red state.
issue: - Some of the index created for the projects are in the Unassigned state, with the reason "UNASSIGNED ALLOCATION_FAILED".
resolution: - Redeploy logging with a new with an alternate storage backend like Gluster block storage.
root_cause: - Gluster FS is unsupported and likely the [reason] (https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/3.11/install_config/aggregate_logging.html#aggregated-logging-persistent-storage:) many issues are faced due to it.- Using NFS storage as a volume or a persistent volume, or using NAS such as Gluster, is not supported for Elasticsearch storage, as Lucene relies on file system behavior that NFS does not supply. Data corruption and other problems can occur.

title: Upgrading the OpenShift Container Platform Aggregating Container Logging stack fails
issue: - The Playbook used for upgrading the OpenShift Container Platform Aggregating Container Logging stack fails with the following error message: Initialization: Complete (0:01:00) Logging Install: In Progress (1:16:23) This phase can be restarted by running: playbooks/openshift-logging/config.yml Cluster logging-es was unable to recover to a green state. Please see documentation regarding recovering during a rolling cluster restart.
resolution: - Please upgrade to Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform [3.11.232](https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHBA-2020:2477) to mitigate this issue. **Workaround**- Make sure that the Elasticsearch cluster is in a healthy state. $ oc exec-c elasticsearch-- \ curl-s \--key /etc/elasticsearch/secret/admin-key \--cert /etc/elasticsearch/secret/admin-cert \--cacert /etc/elasticsearch/secret/admin-ca https://localhost:9200/_cat/health?v- Setup `cluster.routing.allocation.enable` to `primaries` when purposely bringing down nodes: $ oc exec-c elasticsearch-- \ curl-s \--cacert /etc/elasticsearch/secret/admin-ca \--cert /etc/elasticsearch/secret/admin-cert \--key /etc/elasticsearch/secret/admin-key \-XPUT 'https://localhost:9200/_cluster/settings' \-d '{"transient": {"cluster.routing.allocation.enable": "primaries"}}' **NOTE:** we set `cluster.routing.allocation.enable` to `primaries` (instead of `none`) to enable allocation of the new indices that are created during the upgrade.- Once complete, for each dc you have for an Elasticsearch cluster, run oc rollout latest to deploy the latest version of the dc object: $ oc scale dc--replicas=0- Once scale down is complete, for each dc you have for an Elasticsearch cluster, run oc rollout latest to deploy the latest version of the dc object: $ oc rollout latest- Perform the elasticsearch upgrade with the Playbook as described in the [official documentation](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/openshift_container_platform/3.11/html-single/upgrading_clusters/index#upgrading-efk-logging-stack)- Once deployment is complete, for each dc you have for an Elasticsearch cluster, scale up the nodes $ oc scale dc--replicas=1
root_cause: - When shard balancing is enabled, `elasticsearch` will try to migrate shards from an already upgraded node (e. g. version 5.6.16) to an older node (e. g. version 5.613), which is not possible. Therefore the Playbook will timeout eventually.

title: Why is Heketi Failing to Delete a Gluster Block Volume in OCS 3.11?
issue: In the output of the command `heketi-cli server operations info`, there's a stale entry, corresponding to the deletion of a Gluster block volume: sh-4.2# heketi-cli server operations info Operation Counts: Total: 1 In-Flight: 0 New: 0 Failed: 0 Stale: 1 sh-4.2# heketi-cli server operations list Id:3fb2f475440be3e37753433f3e69a317 Type:delete-block-volume Status:stale sh-4.2# heketi-cli server operations info 3fb2f475440be3e37753433f3e69a317 Id: 3fb2f475440be3e37753433f3e69a317 Type: delete-block-volume Status: stale Changes: Delete block volume: 74fc56f92b30daa37fd1d4ce73360e6e
After running the commands `heketi-cli server operations info && sleep 30 && heketi-cli server operations list`, still the same stale entry is listed.
How to remove then this operation?
resolution: 1. Identify first the block-hosting volume associated to the block volume that cannot be removed. Following the example in the previous section, the output of `heketi-cli server operations info < operation-id > `provides this information: [...] Delete block volume: 74fc56f92b30daa37fd1d4ce73360e6e 2. Using the block volume id, rsh to the Heketi pod and find the corresponding block-hosting volume: heketi-cli--user admin--secret $HEKETI_ADMIN_KEY blockvolume info 74fc56f92b30daa37fd1d4ce73360e6e The output will be similar to: Name: blk_glusterfs_bk1_52cf3138-affe-11e8-9d08-0a580a830004 Size: 5 Volume Id: 74fc56f92b30daa37fd1d4ce73360e6e... Block Hosting Volume: 4c9d42b87e78151f5344676f1b318f65 3. Lock / restrict access to this block-hosting volume in Heketi. From the Heketi pod: heketi-cli volume set-block-hosting-restriction locked 4c9d42b87e78151f5344676f1b318f65 4. Remove the storage space reserved by the Posix translator in the Gluster side. From any gluster pod: gluster v set vol_4c9d42b87e78151f5344676f1b318f65 storage.reserve 0 5. Manually delete the block-volume in the Gluster side. From any gluster pod: gluster-block delete vol_4c9d42b87e78151f5344676f1b318f65/blockvol_74fc56f92b30daa37fd1d4ce73360e6e force 6. Once the block volume is removed, set back the reserved space to 1%, as it's the default, and unlock the access to the block-hosting volume: gluster v set vol_4c9d42b87e78151f5344676f1b318f65 storage.reserve 1 heketi-cli volume set-block-hosting-restriction unlocked 4c9d42b87e78151f5344676f1b318f65
root_cause: * Gluster block uses the shard translator to accommodate large PV requests. Then, a single block-volume is split in many shard 'chunks' inside the block-hosting volume. * This translator sets file deletion to the background by creating a 0-byte marker file under the directory.shard/remove_me inside the brick folder. This is to avoid deleting large number of shards synchronously which can be a slow operation, and might lead to applications timing out. It's also needed to guarantee the atomicity of the operation. This 0-byte file is later picked up by a background task to finish up the deletion. * If the creation of these 'remove_me' files fail for any reason, the deletion of the block volume will fail. * This problem is commonly observed for block-volumes contained in block-hosting volumes that have been expanded. If the distribute count of the block-hosting volume is higher than one, then this is the case. As a general advice, please **avoid expanding block-hosting volumes**. If a block-hosting volume is getting out of space, Heketi will, by default, create a new one automatically.

title: Additional PVCs required in openshift-monitoring namespace after upgrading from 4.3 to 4.4.4
issue: - Additional PVCs required in openshift-monitoring namespace after upgrading from 4.3 to 4.4.4 even when the old PVCs are in place.
resolution: - This issue can become a blockage in upgrade action of OCP cluster from 4.3 to 4.4 if dynamic provisioning is not used.- If dynamic provisioning is used then there will be additional PVCs getting created even if the old PVCs are in place.- This issue was tracked using the Bugzilla [Bug 1833427](https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1833427) and has also got fixed with the Red Hat Openshift 4.4.9- It is advised to update the cluster to either the fixed or higher version of Red Hat Openshift Cluster.
root_cause: - Before upgrade: ~~~ # oc get pvc NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY ACCESS MODES STORAGECLASS AGE prom-prometheus-k8s-0 Bound pvc-af243bba-8281-4617-965b-a9cf43adcf41 1Gi RWO gp2 4h59m prom-prometheus-k8s-1 Bound pvc-679cf5a9-83d7-4927-b15f-fbfecf824720 1Gi RWO gp2 4h59m # oc get cm cluster-monitoring-config-o yaml apiVersion: v1 data: config.yaml: | prometheusK8s: volumeClaimTemplate: metadata: name: prom <==== PVC-prefix-name spec: storageClassName: gp2 resources: requests: storage: 1Gi kind: ConfigMap ~~~- Here, it was already PVCs were present with PVC-prefix-name: "prom"- But after upgrade to 4.4.4, it is observed that additional PVC with default PVC-prefix-name got created and new PVCs are getting used by the respective pods.- After upgrade ~~~ # oc get pvc NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY ACCESS MODES STORAGECLASS AGE prom-prometheus-k8s-0 Bound pvc-af243bba-8281-4617-965b-a9cf43adcf41 1Gi RWO gp2 4h59m prom-prometheus-k8s-1 Bound pvc-679cf5a9-83d7-4927-b15f-fbfecf824720 1Gi RWO gp2 4h59m prometheus-k8s-db-prometheus-k8s-0 Bound pvc-ef25921b-1a59-4145-ad9f-14904f0feb97 1Gi RWO gp2 109m prometheus-k8s-db-prometheus-k8s-1 Bound pvc-6e8ea9fd-eb97-4a3a-a1ef-32319b615fa1 1Gi RWO gp2 109m # oc describe pod prometheus-k8s-0 Volumes: prometheus-k8s-db: Type: PersistentVolumeClaim (a reference to a PersistentVolumeClaim in the same namespace) ClaimName: prometheus-k8s-db-prometheus-k8s-0 ReadOnly: false ~~~- Version-Release number of selected component (if applicable): ~~~ # oc get clusterversion NAME VERSION AVAILABLE PROGRESSING SINCE STATUS version 4.4.4 True False 69m Cluster version is 4.4.4 ~~~

title: The resource limits in Pods sometimes are greater than the limits configured in DeploymentConfig
issue: The pods are not respecting the limits and resource mentioned in DC. The actual value of resource taken by pod is not what specified in DC. The value is highly randomized and the issue is occuring in projects both with or wihout resource quota and limits.
resolution: - Check if the admission controller is configured or not. This can be checked in master-config file[/etc/origin/master/master-config.yaml]. Check if **"ClusterResourceOverride"** in master-config.yaml under "admissionConfig.pluginConfig" is configured properly.- Also check if there is any discrepancy in master-config.yaml across all the master in the cluster.
root_cause: The cause seems do be due to fault of admission controller. The admission controller intercepts the call made to api-server. The admission controllers can be both validating and mutating. The call the api servers is intercepted and mutated wrongly. This could be due to the wrong configuration of admission controller or due to some discrepancy among master-config.yaml file across the masters.

title: Cluster Monitoring Operator - Prometheus port 9090 not exposed
issue: - The cluster monitoring operator creates a service "prometheus-operated" pointing to port 9090 of Prometheus that is supposed to allow other pods on the cluster to access the Prometheus pod without going through the oauth-proxy- Unfortunately, the StatefulSet of Prometheus only exposes the container port 9091 of the oauth-proxy but not the port 9090 of Prometheus. Because of that, trying to access the "prometheus-operated" service results in a connection refused error
resolution: - There is a way to use the Bearer Token, more precisely via Roundtripper[0]. Unfortunately there is no way to use without proxy-oauth- Please set the RoundTripper in the config when you instantiate the client, the round tripper is intended to be used to inject the token into the request- There are two options two fix this- Either: The cluster-monitoring-operator should not create the service "prometheus-operated" if port 9090 is not exposed in the StatefulSet- Or: The StatefulSet should expose port 9090 if the service "prometheus-operated" stays
root_cause: I explicitly need to access the Prometheus WITHOUT authentication as I'm querying it from a piece of Go code that runs in the same namespace as the Prometheus ("openshift-monitoring") and to my knowledge the Go Prometheus client (https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang) has no possibility to set the Bearer token for queries, otherwise I would've done it. That's why I tried to access it from the same namespace via the "prometheus-operated" service that is setup by the operator and looks like it is designed for exactly this purposes of accessing the Prometheus without authentication from within the cluster. As this service is giving me "connection refused", I'm asking you to please check if there's a bug in the StatefulSet of Prometheus as I can see no exposure of port 9090 there even thought there is a service pointing to it.

title: Autoscalling does not scale, errors out with NotTriggerScaleUp' pod didn't trigger scale-up (it wouldn't fit if a new node is added)
issue: Autoscalling does not scale, errors out with NotTriggerScaleUp' pod didn't trigger scale-up (it wouldn't fit if a new node is added)
resolution: From the shared details the volume(pvc) is created in "us-gov-west-1c" zone ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Source: Type: AWSElasticBlockStore (a Persistent Disk resource in AWS) VolumeID: aws://us-gov-west-1c/vol-053ff64c844363dd4 FSType: ext4 Partition: 0 ReadOnly: false ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ However if you can see the pod is in "us-gov-west-1a" zone ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ W0627 21:06:40.294967 1 aws_manager.go:561] Found multiple availability zones for ASG "PROD-OCP-App-Group", using us-gov-west-1a I0627 21:06:40.419679 1 scale_up.go:92] Upcoming 0 nodes ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ The cause for this issue is limitation of aws-ebs volumes unlike aws-EFS storage. [An EBS volume and the instance to which it attaches must be in the same Availability Zone.] Quick fix would be either creating volumes in us-gov-west-1a zone or creating application in us-gov-west-1c zone, To match the AZ. I would recommend for OpenShift is to control where your volumes are created and where your pods are scheduled: 1. To create volumes in pre-determined zones, you can create custom StorageClass objects for each zone you want to use. For more information on storageclass for aws-ebs please follow doc[1] 2.To specify the zones where your pods with PVs are scheduled, you can use affinity or nodeSelector. For more information on node selector please follow doc[2] [1] https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/3.11/install_config/persistent_storage/dynamically_provisioning_pvs.html#aws-elasticblockstore-ebs [2] https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/3.11/admin_guide/scheduling/node_selector.html#admin-guide-sched-selector-config Hope the shared information helps you, In case of queries please dont hesitate to ask.

title: OpenShift pods are failing to be provisioned with insufficient cpu/memory even though the nodes' usage are pretty low
issue: From the pod's events ~~~ 0/X nodes are available: X node (s) didn't match node selector, X Insufficient cpu, X Insufficient memory. ~~~

Output of `oc adm top node` show low usage of resources ~~~ CPU consumption of nodes: NAME CPU(cores) CPU% MEMORY(bytes) MEMORY% node1.example 731m 18% 36485Mi 56% node2.example 593m 14% 30198Mi 47% node3.example 529m 13% 28414Mi 44% ~~~
resolution: You can use one the following resolutions that suites the best for the workload. 1. Increase the amount of physical resources for the node: * Increase the memory * Increase the CPU 2. Tune the resources/limits for each Deployment until the exhausted resource is lowered: ~~~ oc set resources dc--limits=memory=,cpu=--requests=memory=,cpu= ~~~ 3. Add more compute resource to the cluster.
root_cause: Since it is not possible to allocate more than 100% of resource requests, in this case the `Deployments` have allocated 99% of Memory/CPU requests and/or limits. Another point to consider is that If the environment is not configured with overcommit the limits cannot be higher than 100%. The output of `oc adm top node` might show's that the node has resources available at the moment, that is a true statement, but the request for applications cannot go beyond 99%. That is why we can have the node showing low memory usage and not being able to create new Pod's.

title: How to clean-up completed pods in Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform
issue: We use Spring Cloud Data Flow to manage Batch and Stream use cases on OpenShift. If you launch a Spring Tasks, a new Pod is created which runs to completion. After completion the pod is in status Completed. My understanding of garbage collection is, that OpenShift would remove such pods regularly, especially if there is no other reference to the pod. But such pods are not removed and has to be deleted manually.
resolution: In Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 3.x, there does not appear to be a solution available as `jobs` are intended to be clean-up by the operator to make sure successful and failed jobs can be reviewed after completion. In Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 4.x, [TTL Controller](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/#clean-up-finished-jobs-automatically) has reached `alpha` state which does allow a TTL (Time To Live) being set to have `jobs` automatically cleaned-up. Not yet production ready as it's `alpha` state but probable the most suitable `kubernetes` option available.

title: Worker machines stuck in provisioned state in OpenShift 4 on RHV
issue: - While performing an IPI installation for RHOCP on RHV cloud provider, the worker machines remain in a provisioned state ~~~ [root@bastion ~]# oc-n openshift-machine-api get machine NAME PHASE TYPE REGION ZONE AGE openshift-stage-wz4zh-master-0 Running 22h openshift-stage-wz4zh-master-1 Running 22h openshift-stage-wz4zh-master-2 Running 22h openshift-stage-wz4zh-worker-0-8w2xb Provisioned 17h openshift-stage-wz4zh-worker-0-ckzxm Provisioned 21h openshift-stage-wz4zh-worker-0-n8qtb Provisioned 21h ~~~- On checking the output of the node, the worker nodes look good and workloads are scheduled on them but as shown above the status should change to `Running`. ~~~ [root@bastion ~]# oc get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION openshift-stage-wz4zh-master-0 Ready master 22h v1.17.1+912792b openshift-stage-wz4zh-master-1 Ready master 22h v1.17.1+912792b openshift-stage-wz4zh-master-2 Ready master 22h v1.17.1+912792b openshift-stage-wz4zh-worker-0-8w2xb Ready worker 18h v1.17.1+912792b openshift-stage-wz4zh-worker-0-ckzxm Ready worker 21h v1.17.1+912792b openshift-stage-wz4zh-worker-0-n8qtb Ready worker 21h v1.17.1+912792b ~~~
resolution: - Above mentioned issue has been reported to the engineering team in the following bugzilla [BZ-1854787](https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1854787)- The reported issue is been actively worked on by the engineering team and the fix should be available in the future releases. **Workaround**- Collect the VM ID from RHV UI: (**Compute-> Virtual Machines-> click VM in question-> on the right see: VM ID:**)- Once the VM-ID is available for the machine, substitue the values and the node name first and then the machine name in the following commands, ~~~ # oc patch node openshift-stage-wz4zh-worker-0-8w2xb--type merge--patch '{"spec":{"providerID":"**VM ID value here**"}}' # oc-n openshift-machine-api patch machine openshift-stage-wz4zh-worker-0-8w2xb--type merge--patch '{"spec":{"providerSpec":{"value":{"id":"**VM ID value here**"}}}}' ~~~- This will get fresh CSR for the nodes which could be listed with the following command, waiting for another 5 minutes will auto approve the `CSR` ~~~ # oc get csr # oc adm certificate approve ~~~- Once the csr is approved, the machines would be in Running state and could be check with the following command. ~~~ # oc get machines-n openshift-machine-api ~~~

title: Basic Information to Collect to Troubleshoot OpenShift Container Storage 3.x Cases
issue: Which information should be provided to Red Hat Support Services when opening a case regarding Openshift Container Storage 3.x?
resolution: #### OCS version This is the information required to figure out which OCP / OCS versions are running:- Openshift version running: `oc version` from the master node.- Heketi version running: `rpm-qa | grep heketi`from the Heketi pod.- Gluster version running: `rpm-qa | grep gluster`from the Gluster pods. #### Heketi troubleshooting- Collect the logs of the Heketi pod. From the master node run `oc logs `- Gather a clean Heketi DB dump. 1. For OCS versions < 3.11.x, please follow the steps in document [How to export and import Heketi database in Openshift Container Storage-3.9 or newer version?](https://access.redhat.com/articles/3687641) to get a clean copy of the DB. 2. For OCS version 3.11.x, please follow the steps below:- Set the Heketi mode to `local-client`to prevent further volume operations reaching the database while the DB dump is being taken. This will briefly stop volume provisioning, but it's required to get a consistent view of the database. heketi-cli server mode set local-client- Check that the number of operations is zero: `heketi-cli server operations info`- Collect a DB dump, the output of `gluster volume info`and the current PVs created in Openshift, to have a full picture of the volume configuration: heketi-cli db dump > heketi-$(date-I).json (from the Heketi pod) gluster volume info > gluster-info-$(date-I).txt (from any Gluster pod) oc get pv--all-namespaces-o yaml > pvs-$(date-I).yaml (from the master node)- Once this information is collected, resume the normal Heketi operation mode: `heketi-cli server mode set normal` #### Gluster pods troubleshooting- Collect the output of the following script and upload the file `/tmp/gluster-logs-$(date +%m.%d.%Y).out`available in the master node (please note that the script assumes that the Gluster pods are running in the `glusterfs`namespace. If this is not the case, adjust the script as required): for pod in $(oc get pods--all-namespaces-o wide | grep glusterfs| awk '{print $2}'); do echo "*** start: $pod ***";oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod ps ax;oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod gluster volume info;oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod gluster volume status;oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod tail-n100 /var/log/glusterfs/glusterd.log;oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod gluster pool list;oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod gluster peer status;oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod df;oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod systemctl status glusterd.service;oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod systemctl status gluster-blockd.service;oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod systemctl status gluster-block-target.service;oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod systemctl status tcmu-runner.service;oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod journalctl-xe--no-pager;oc rsh-n glusterfs $pod ls-l /;echo "*** end: $pod ***"; echo; echo; echo; done > /tmp/gluster-logs-$(date +%m.%d.%Y).out 2> &1- Additionally, upload a tarball of the directory `/var/log/glusterfs`from the nodes hosting the Gluster pods.- For LVM configuration / space mismatch issues between Heketi and the Gluster pods, collect the following outputs *from each gluster pod* lvs--all--units k--reportformat=json > lvs-NODENAME-$(date-I).js vgs--all--units k--reportformat=json > vgs-NODENAME-$(date-I).json #### Gluster block * Sosreports of the Openshift nodes running the Gluster pods. If this is not possible, at least a tarball of the directory `/var/log/glusterfs/gluster-block` from each node. * The output of `targetcli ls`from the three Gluster pods. * A tarball of the directory `/etc/target` from the three Gluster pods. #### Installation / upgrades * The inventory file being used. * If any particular playbook execution is failing, the output of: ansible-playbook-i-vvv

resolution: So here is the summary:--- KVM host has NUMA configuration enabled-- VMs (Openshift worker nodes) doesn't have NUMA configuration enabled-- Openshift starts "topologymanager" with "single-numa-node policy"-- After disabling "single-numa-node policy" from kubeletconfig, node going into hung status with "BUG: soft lockup" error resolved.-- To disable "topologymanager" from using "single-numa-node policy" you altered line highlighted here [1]. [1] ~~~ cat < < EOF > cpumanager-kubeletconfig.yaml apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1 kind: KubeletConfig metadata: name: cpumanager-enabled spec: machineConfigPoolSelector: matchLabels: custom-kubelet: cpumanager-enabled kubeletConfig: cpuManagerPolicy: static cpuManagerReconcilePeriod: 5s topologyManagerPolicy: single-numa-node < < < numa configuration for topologyManagerPolicy EOF ~~~
root_cause: I see that NUMA is enabled on the KVM Host but I couldn't see that on worker node VM vm-router-0 [y] answer: I didn't manually enable numa on kvm host, if it is enabled, it is enabled by os install program. If it is not enabled on vm-router-0, that means numa machine config is not applied to vm-router-0.-- However we see below message "container_manager_linux.go:300] [topologymanager] Initilizing Topology Manager with single-numa-node policy", which suggest that Topology Manager started with "single-numa-node policy". answer: single-numa-node policy is applied by machine configuration.-- Having said that this is also to be noted that Topology Manager feature is alpha feature in Openshift and wouldn't be supported.[1] answer: yes, if numa causes the issue, it is un-supported. Thank you very much.

title: After replacing CA cert in OCP, SSO disappears from the console
issue: After following the steps from [https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.5/security/certificates/replacing-default-ingress-certificate.html](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.5/security/certificates/replacing-default-ingress-certificate.html "https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.5/security/certificates/replacing-default-ingress-certificate.html") to replace Ingress certificate with Let's Encrypt Certificates, you are seeing that the certificates are still not trusted and SSO login from the OpenShift console disappears.
resolution: Mistake 1: Occurred the Step 1 of the documentation where we create a `ca-letsencrypt` `configMap` we have incorrectly used **ISGR Root X1** certificate instead of **Let's Encrypt Authority X3** certificate. Mistake 2: Occurred in Step 3 of the documentation where we forgot to provide **Full Chain** (server + Let's Encrypt Authority X3 + ISGR Root X1) see middle line in Fig. 1 to the `--cert` parameter.
root_cause: ![https://letsencrypt.org/certs/isrg-keys.png](https://letsencrypt.org/certs/isrg-keys.png "Lets Encrypt") Fig. 1 Step 1: Create a ConfigMap that includes only the root CA certificate used to sign the wildcard certificate: ~~~ oc create configmap ca-letsencrypt--from-file=ca-bundle.crt=lets-encrypt-x3.crt-n openshift-config ~~~ Step 2: Update the cluster-wide proxy configuration with the newly created ConfigMap: ~~~ oc patch proxy/cluster--type=merge--patch='{"spec":{"trustedCA":{"name":"ca-letsencrypt"}}}' ~~~ Step 3: Create a secret that contains the wildcard certificate chain and key: ~~~ oc create secret tls apps-wildcard--cert=fullchain.pem--key=key.pem-n openshift-ingress ~~~ Step 4: Update the Ingress Controller configuration with the newly created secret: ~~~ oc patch ingresscontroller.operator default--type=merge-p '{"spec":{"defaultCertificate": {"name": "apps-wildcard"}}}'-n openshift-ingress-operator ~~~ Make sure that the **Let's Encrypt Authority X3 certificate (intermediate)** is trusted in `openshift-authentication` project in `v4-0-config-user-idp-0-ca` `configMap` Without this change, OCP doesn't trust the certificate and SSO login option from the cluster console disappears.

title: Missing /etc/mtab symlink in CRI-O containers
resolution: Possible workarounds:- Change the target to `/proc/mounts` in your scripts.- Create new `Dockerfile` which will contain the symlink to `/proc/mounts`. ~~~ RUN ln-sv../proc/self/mounts /etc/mtab ~~~
root_cause: In OpenShift Container Platform 3.11 we are using Docker container technology. And Docker adds this symbolic link for `/etc/mtab` to all containers everytime if the Dockerfile doesn't contain the entry for symlink. [https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/b3e9f7b13b0f0c414fa6253e1f17a86b2cff68b5/daemon/initlayer/setup_unix.go#L20](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/b3e9f7b13b0f0c414fa6253e1f17a86b2cff68b5/daemon/initlayer/setup_unix.go#L20) ~~~ // Setup populates a directory with mountpoints suitable // for bind-mounting things into the container. // // This extra layer is used by all containers as the top-most ro layer. It protects // the container from unwanted side-effects on the rw layer. func Setup(initLayerFs containerfs.ContainerFS, rootIdentity idtools.Identity) error {// Since all paths are local to the container, we can just extract initLayerFs.Path() initLayer:= initLayerFs.Path() for pth, typ:= range map[string]string{"/dev/pts": "dir", "/dev/shm": "dir", "/proc": "dir", "/sys": "dir", "/.dockerenv": "file", "/etc/resolv.conf": "file", "/etc/hosts": "file", "/etc/hostname": "file", "/dev/console": "file", "/etc/mtab": "/proc/mounts",} ~~~ The CRI-O doesn't seems to do it. title: How to make a custom CA bundle for CodeReady Workspaces 2.x
issue: Users will sometimes use an institutional Certificate Authority to sign certificates. In this case, special steps must be taken to tell CodeReady Workspaces about the CAs.
resolution: A custom group of certificates can be used with CRW 2.2. Examples of certificates that might be needed:- An OpenShift CA certificate- An institutional Root CA certificate- An institutional Intermediate CA certificate To group these CAs together and make them usable in CRW 2.2: oc-n openshift-ingress get secret custom-ca-ojson | jq-r '.data."tls.crt"' | base64-d > ca.crt cat intermediary.pem > > ca.crt cat rootcert.pem > > ca.crt oc-n codeready-operator delete secret self-signed-certificate oc-n codeready-operator create secret generic self-signed-certificate--from-file=ca.crt The above steps will make a secret, 'self-signed-certificate' which has a data component called 'ca.crt'. Per the CRW documentation, a secret of this type will be used to place the CAs where CRW can use them. The CA bundle can be validated: // Use your real domain name echo | openssl s_client-servername devfile-registry-codeready-operator.apps.my.domain-connect devfile-registry-codeready-operator.apps.my.domain:443-CAfile /path/to/my/cabundle/ca.crt // Alternative export WORKSPACE_POD=`oc-n crw get pods | grep workspace | awk '{print $1}'` export THEIA_CONTAINER=`oc-n crw get pod workspacepodname-ojson | jq-r '.spec.containers[-1].name'` oc-n crw exec-ti $WORKSPACE_POD-c $THEIA_CONTAINER-- bash curl--cacert /path/to/mybundle/ca.crt https://devfile-registry-codeready-operator.apps.mydomain/resources/ (this assumes you have: oc-n codeready-operator get checluster codeready-workspaces-ojson | jq-r '.spec.server.selfSignedCert' == true)
