title: How to Check Azure Red Hat OpenShift (ARO)  Load Balancer Health Probe Status and Filter by Specific Port
issue: - My ARO load-balancer seems not reachable, how can I check if the load-balancer port is healthy?
resolution: ### Introduction Azure Load Balancer utilizes health probes to monitor the status of your instances. If an instance fails to respond to a health probe, the Load Balancer ceases to direct new connections to that instance. This article provides instructions on how to check the status of health probes through the Azure portal and how to filter the metrics for a specific load balancer port's health probe status. ### Checking Health Probe Status Follow these steps to access the status of health probes: 1. Sign in to your account on the Azure portal. 2. From the left-hand menu, select "All resources". 3. Click on the Load Balancer resource for which you want to check the health probe status. 4. In the Load Balancer resource's left-hand menu, under "Settings", click on "Health probes". You will now see a list of all health probes configured for your Load Balancer, along with their configurations. Please note that the Azure portal does not directly provide the status of these health probes. ### Monitoring Health Probe Status with Azure Monitor To monitor the health of your Load Balancer, follow these steps: 1. In the Load Balancer resource's left-hand menu, under "Monitoring", click on "Metrics". 2. On the chart, select the "Health Probe Status" metric. 3. Specify the time range and the aggregation (Average, Minimum, Maximum, or Total). ### Filtering Health Probe Status by Specific Port When viewing the "Health Probe Status" metric, you can filter the results by specific ports as follows: 1. Under the "Metrics" section, find and click on the "Add filter" button. 2. A drop-down menu will appear. Select "Frontend Port" from the options. 3. Select the specific port number you wish to filter, e.g. 6379 for Redis service. The metrics chart will now reflect the health probe status for the specified port only. ### Conclusion Monitoring the health probe status is essential to ensure the efficient operation of your Azure Load Balancer. Always refer to the official Azure documentation or use Azure CLI help commands for the most accurate and up-to-date information. Remember, Azure CLI (the `az` command) does not have a built-in command to check the health probe status directly. The methods outlined in this KCS are the recommended ways to view and filter health probe statuses.![1](https://access.redhat.com/sites/default/files/images/azure-lb-healthy-probe.png)![2](https://access.redhat.com/sites/default/files/images/azure-lb-healthy-probe-port-filter.png)![3](https://access.redhat.com/sites/default/files/images/azure-lb-healthy-probe-status.png)

title: Cluster installation failed with error code OCM3034: VcpuLimitExceeded
product: Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS
issue: **Disclaimer:*

*Links contained herein to external website(s) are provided for convenience only. Red Hat has not reviewed the links and is not responsible for the content or its availability. The inclusion of any link to an external website does not imply endorsement by Red Hat of the website or their entities, products or services. You agree that Red Hat is not responsible or liable for any loss or expenses that may result due to your use of (or reliance on) the external site or content.*- Cluster installation failed with error code **OCM3034: VcpuLimitExceeded**.- Following error message was observed in **install logs**: ~~~ error:: reconciler failed to Create machine: failed to launch instance: error launching instance: You have requested more vCPU capacity than your current vCPU limit of 32 allows for the instance bucket that the specified instance type belongs to. Please visit http://aws.amazon.com/contact-us/ec2-request to request an adjustment to this limit. ~~~
resolution: To resolve this, **free up capacity** or **increase quota** and **try again**. EC2 vCPU limit increases are submitted as a vCPU value. To request an increase, first determine how many vCPUs that your On-Demand Instances are using. You can use the [vCPU limits calculator](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-on-demand-instances.html#vcpu-limits-calculator) to measure the number of vCPUs that you are currently using against vCPU-based limits to determine the appropriate service limit increase to request. You can create a service limit request directly from the vCPU limits calculator. ###Solution: ####Request an On-Demand Instance limit increase 1. Sign in to the [Amazon EC2 console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/ec2/). 2. In the Region selector, choose the AWS Region where you want to request a vCPU increase. 3. (Optional) To view the instances that are already running, from the **EC2 Dashboard**, under **Resources**, choose **Instances (running)**. 4. In the navigation pane, Choose **Limits**. 5. Choose **Calculate vCPU limit** to access the vCPU limits calculator. 6. In the **Limits calculator** page, choose **Add instance type**. 7. For **Instance type**, select an available instance type from the dropdown list. 8. For **Instance count**, enter the number of new instances (of the type that you chose in step 6) that you want. 9. Continue adding instance types as needed. 10. Review the Limits calculation section, choose **Request on-demand limit increase** to submit a service limit increase request. The value in the **New limit** field is the number of vCPUs that you must request.
root_cause: The install requires more vCPU capacity than the current vCPU limit. Customers are limited to running one or more On-Demand Instances in an AWS account, and Amazon EC2 measures usage towards each limit based on the total number of vCPUs (virtual central processing unit) that are assigned to the running On-Demand instances in your AWS account.

title: How to create an Automation Hub instance on Azure Red Hat OpenShift (ARO)?
issue: - How to create an Automation Hub instance on Azure Red Hat OpenShift (ARO)?
resolution: ### 1. Prepare ARO instance and install the AAP Operator- Confirm to login to the cluster with `oc` command. ~~~ $ oc login--username kubeadmin https://api.XXXXXXXX.japaneast.aroapp.io:6443/ Authentication required for https://api.XXXXXXXX.japaneast.aroapp.io:6443 (openshift) Username: kubeadmin Password: Login successful. it give access to 69 projects, the list has been suppressed. it can list all projects with 'oc projects' Using project "default". ~~~ ### 2. prepare a cluster role and its binding- Create the following files to define the role. #### clusterrole.yml ~~~--- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: ClusterRole metadata: name: system:azure-cloud-provider rules:- apiGroups: [''] resources: ['secrets'] verbs: ['get','create'] ~~~ #### clusterrolebinding.yml ~~~--- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: ClusterRoleBinding metadata: name: system:azure-cloud-provider roleRef: kind: ClusterRole apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io name: system:azure-cloud-provider subjects:- kind: ServiceAccount name: persistent-volume-binder namespace: kube-system ~~~- Apply them. ~~~ $ oc apply-f clusterrole.yml clusterrole.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/system:azure-cloud-provider created $ oc apply-f clusterrolebinding.yml clusterrolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/system:azure-cloud-provider created ~~~ ### 3. create a storage class- On the Azure console at `Home` > `Storage accounts`, you can find the information about the storage account associated with the ARO cluster.- Storage account: clusterXXXXX- Resource group: aro-XXXXXXXX #### storageclass.yml ~~~ kind: StorageClass apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1 metadata: name: azure-files provisioner: kubernetes.io/azure-file parameters: location: skuName: Standard_LRS storageAccount: clusterXXXXX resourceGroup: aro-XXXXXXXX mountOptions:- dir_mode=0777- file_mode=0777- noperm reclaimPolicy: Delete volumeBindingMode: Immediate ~~~- Apply and confirm it. ~~~ $ oc apply-f storageclass.yml storageclass.storage.k8s.io/azure-files created $ oc describe sc/azure-files... ~~~ ### 4. install an Automation Hub instance- Go to Installed Operators > Ansible Automation Platform > `Automation Hub` tab > press the `Create AutomationHub` button > fill in these forms. ~~~- Name: (your instance name for AH)- Storage type: select `File`- File storage access mode: ReadWriteMany (by default)- File storage size: 100Gi (by default)- File storage class: azure-files (created by the step [3]) ~~~- Next press the `Create` button to proceed.- When the deployment is successful, login to the Web UI for the Automation Hub instance.- URL: Networking > Routes > (AH instance) > Location- Password for admin user: Workloads > Secrets > (AH instance)-admin-password > Data

title: About changing the pids_limit in OSD or ROSA
product: Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS
issue: - How to change the value of `pids_limit`/`pidsLimit` in OSD or ROSA.- Is it possible to customize `crio.conf` in OSD or ROSA?
resolution: The specific `pidsLimit` is not user configurable on any OSD or ROSA cluster before 4.11. > **Note:** For OSD/ROSA 4.11 or newer, please refer to [Change pids_limit in OSD/ROSA 4.11 and newer](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/6986931). As of the following versions, the default per-pod `pidsLimit` is `4096`: * 4.8.35 * 4.9.26 * 4.10.6 To enable this new default value, please upgrade the OSD/ROSA cluster to any of these or newer versions. > **Note:** In previous OSD/ROSA versions, the default per-pod `pidsLimit` was the OpenShift default of `1024`.
root_cause: It's not possible to customize CRI-O configurations in OSD or ROSA before 4.11. While it's not possible to configure the `pidsLimit` or other CRI-O configurations in OSD or ROSA, the fleet wide default `pidsLimit` was changed per the above resolution. Refer to the documentation for additional information: [Compute nodes in OSD](https://docs.openshift.com/dedicated/osd_architecture/osd_policy/osd-service-definition.html#compute_osd-service-definition), [Compute nodes in ROSA](https://docs.openshift.com/rosa/rosa_architecture/rosa_policy_service_definition/rosa-service-definition.html#rosa-sdpolicy-compute_rosa-service-definition).

title: Shards will be not be allocated on this node. reason: Disk Watermark Low
issue: - Elasticsearch jobs are not running properly and its health status is yellow and the logs contain below warning ~~~ $ oc exec-n openshift-logging $ES-c elasticsearch-- es_util--query=_cluster/allocation/explain disk_threshold","decision":"NO","explanation":"the node is above the low watermark cluster setting [cluster.routing.allocation.disk.watermark.low=85%], using more disk space than the maximum allowed [85.0%] ~~~
resolution: - Increase the Elasticsearch storage- Add a new data node to the cluster- Reduce the [log retention](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.11/logging/config/cluster-logging-log-store.html#cluster-logging-elasticsearch-retention_cluster-logging-store)- If none of the above options are applicable then [delete the old indices](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.11/logging/troubleshooting/cluster-logging-troubleshooting-for-critical-alerts.html#elasticsearch-node-disk-flood-watermark-reached)
root_cause: - Elasticsearch does not allocate shards to nodes that reach the low watermark. The default value is 85%, meaning that Elasticsearch will not allocate shards to nodes that have more than 85% disk used- Elasticsearch considers the available disk space on a node before deciding whether to allocate new shards to that node or to actively relocate shards away from that node.

title: Add DockerHub pull secret globally to OpenShift 4.X
issue: - Globally define DockerHub pull secret in OpenShift instead of defining it in individual projects.- Unable to pull images from DockerHub due to pull rate limit.
resolution: - Requirement- [Free Docker or Docker Pro or Docker Team Account](https://hub.docker.com/) {EXTERNAL}- Docker Client- You should have access to the OpenShift cluster as a user with the cluster-admin role. **1.** Login to your Docker account using Docker client. ~~~ $ docker login Username: xxxxxxx Password: Login Succeeded ~~~ **2.** Review the config.json in ~/.docker ~~~ $ cat ~/.docker/config.json {"auths": {"https://index.docker.io/v1/": {"auth": "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"}}}....REDACTED.... ~~~ **NOTE** For v4.9 and above, the usage of https can block the retrieval of OCI images from the docker.io registry. See [article](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/6725261) for more details. **3.** Create empty directory `pull-secret`. ~~~ $ mkdir pull-secret ~~~ **4.** Extract global `pull-secret` from OpenShift. ~~~ $ oc extract secret/pull-secret-n openshift-config--to=pull-secret pull-secret/.dockerconfigjson ~~~ **5.** Convert `pull-secret` in a pretty readable format. ~~~ $ cat pull-secret/.dockerconfigjson | python-m json.tool > pull-secret/dockerconfigjson ~~~ **6.** Carefully edit OpenShift global `pull-secret` and append Docker `pull-secret`. ~~~ $ vim pull-secret/dockerconfigjson {"auths": {"cloud.openshift.com": {"auth": "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx....REDACTED....xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", "email": "xxxxxxxxx@xxxxx.xxxx"}, "quay.io": {"auth": "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx....REDACTED....xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", "email": "xxxxxxxxx@xxxxx.xxxx"}, "registry.connect.redhat.com": {"auth": "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx....REDACTED....xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", "email": "xxxxxxxxx@xxxxx.xxxx"}, "registry.redhat.io": {"auth": "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx....REDACTED....xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", "email": "xxxxxxxxx@xxxxx.xxxx"}, "https://index.docker.io/v1/": {"auth": "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"}} ~~~ **7.** Test the `pull-secret` before applying it to OpenShift. ~~~ $ podman pull docker.io/library/httpd:latest--authfile=pull-secret/dockerconfigjson ~~~ Proceed only if the image pull is successful **8.** Update the global `pull-secret` in OpenShift. ~~~ $ oc set data secret/pull-secret-n openshift-config--from-file=.dockerconfigjson=pull-secret/dockerconfigjson ~~~ **9.** This update is rolled out to all nodes, which can take some time depending on the size of your cluster. During this time, nodes are drained and pods are rescheduled on the remaining nodes. The above point 9 is NOT valid for OCP 4.7.4 and above, as changes to the global pull secret no longer trigger a node drain or reboot. See [documentation](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.10/openshift_images/managing_images/using-image-pull-secrets.html#images-update-global-pull-secret_using-image-pull-secrets).
root_cause: - The rate limits of 100 container image requests per six hours for anonymous usage, and 200 container image requests per six hours for free Docker accounts are in effect since November 20, 2020. Image requests exceeding these limits will be denied until the six hour window elapses.

Error: self-signed certificate in certificate chain $onExtensionRuntimeError @ workbench.web.main.js:2042 S @ workbench.web.main.js:1584 (...) workbench.web.main.js:2042 Error: Cannot get workspace pod. title: How to increase Backingstore size in ODF
issue: Backingstore is full. How to expand it
resolution: oc edit backingstore ~~~ spec: pvPool: numVolumes: 1 <---- Edit it to 2 resources: requests: storage: 50Gi secret: {} storageClass: ocs-storagecluster-cephfs type: pv-pool ~~~ A new pvc will be created: oc get pv|grep cephfs ~~~ pvc-86c619f7-5cd3-46ed-b4d1-3fbccab0e40f 40Gi RWO Delete Bound openshift-storage/test-2-noobaa-pvc-ff1e906e ocs-storagecluster-cephfs 3s <--- pvc-90405135-aee3-4cbb-83a2-751ec59d2f25 40Gi RWO Delete Bound openshift-storage/test-2-noobaa-pvc-3e7177a5 ocs-storagecluster-cephfs 5d3h ~~~ Backingstore will be in Creating state for a few minutes during scaling. Once expanded, it comes to Ready state: ~~~ oc get backingstore NAME TYPE PHASE AGE noobaa-default-backing-store s3-compatible Ready 6d2h test-2 pv-pool Ready 12d <-- ~~~
root_cause: - Size of backingstore is not suitable for high workloads

title: The machine has been without a Running or Deleting phase for more than 60 minutes in RHOCP 4
issue: - Receiving below alert after a fresh installation of the RHOCP cluster: ~~~ Warning The machine has been without a Running or Deleting phase for more than 60 minutes ~~~
resolution: > **IMPORTANT NOTE:** For the control plane nodes, refer to the documentation for [Replacing an unhealthy etcd member](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.14/backup_and_restore/control_plane_backup_and_restore/replacing-unhealthy-etcd-member.html).- Delete the compute `machine` object and `machineset` manually in `openshift-machine-api` namespace. ~~~ $ oc get machine-n openshift-machine-api $ oc delete machine-n openshift-machine-api $ oc get machineset-n openshift-machine-api $ oc delete machineset-n openshift-machine-api ~~~ > **Note:** The name of the `machine` object and `machineset` which are in the `Provisioning` state should not match with the running `Nodes`in the cluster.- After the above step, If the `machines` stuck in deleting state, check the `machine-api-operator` pod logs: ~~~ $ oc get pods-n openshift-machine-api [...] $ oc logs-n openshift-machine-api-c machine-api-operator [machine-api-operator-pod_name] ~~~
root_cause: Kubernetes `manifest` files that define the `control plane` `machines` and `compute` `machine-sets` were not removed before installing the cluster- See: [Creating the Kubernetes manifest and Ignition config files](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.10/installing/installing_vsphere/installing-restricted-networks-vsphere.html#installation-user-infra-generate-k8s-manifest-ignition_installing-restricted-networks-vsphere) point 2, for more details.

title: SRV lookup is failing after OpenShift Container Platform 4.13 update
issue: Since the update of the cluster from 4.12 to 4.13, there is at least one application that is having issues resolving dns. Logs from the `dns-default` pod are showing below error. [INFO] 10.94.51.166:37161- 6766 "SRV IN_example._tcp.foo-bar-abc-123-xyz-456-foo-000.abcde.example.net. udp 76 false 512"-- 0 5.001094875s [ERROR] plugin/errors: 2_example._tcp.foo-bar-abc-123-xyz-456-foo-000.abcde.example.net. SRV: dns: overflowing header size
resolution: Red Hat is aware about this issue and investigating it in OCPBUGS-27397 which is private. To raise questions or obtain more information, contact [Red Hat Technical Support](https://access.redhat.com/support/contact/technicalSupport). ### Workaround 1 * Set the `DNS` Cluster Operator in Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 4 to `unmanaged` state, following [How to set CoreDNS Operator into unmanaged state](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/6243031). * Replace the `image` in the `dns-default` `DaemonSet` found in the `namespace` called `openshift-dns` with a `coredns` `image` from Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 4.12. * The respective Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 4.12 `image` can be found in [release.txt](https://mirror.openshift.com/pub/openshift-v4/x86_64/clients/ocp/4.12.45/release.txt) for the respective version. The example here (`image` would be `quay.io/openshift-release-dev/ocp-v4.0-art-dev@sha256:9b39ea51a646fa4796803e654e78466dd73dfdca75de8f6057a7abd0caf0cc5d`) points to Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 4.12.45 but can be exchanged with any version available from Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 4.12. * Once the change in the `DaemonSet` is applied, wait for the `pods` to be rolled out and then verify that lookup of the problematic DNS query is working again. ### Workaround 2 * Configure `forwardPlugin` as per [Using DNS forwarding](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.14/networking/dns-operator.html#nw-dns-forward_dns-operator) for the affected domain and enforce DNS over TCP by setting `protocolStrategy` to `TCP`. An example of such a configuration can be found below. $ oc get dns.operator default-o yaml apiVersion: operator.openshift.io/v1 kind: DNS metadata: creationTimestamp: "2024-01-11T09:14:03Z" finalizers:- dns.operator.openshift.io/dns-controller generation: 8 name: default resourceVersion: "4232322" uid: c8f5c627-2010-4c4a-a5fe-ed87f320e427 spec: logLevel: Normal nodePlacement: {} operatorLogLevel: Normal servers:- forwardPlugin: policy: Random protocolStrategy: TCP upstreams:- 1.1.1.1 name: example zones:- example.net upstreamResolvers: policy: Sequential transportConfig: {} upstreams:- port: 53 type: SystemResolvConf
root_cause: While Microsoft Azure DNS is mentioned here, it's important to understand that other 3rd party DNS server may behave the same way and therefore trigger the same affected as documented below. Microsoft Azure DNS though is used in this example to explain the behavior and because it can be quickly reproduced there. * When Extended DNS (EDNS) is used and a record is larger than `bufsize`, Microsoft Azure DNS for example sets the `TC` bit (which is expected). * When EDNS is_NOT_ used and a record is larger than 512 (the max without EDNS byte size), Microsoft Azure DNS does_NOT_ set the `TC` bit and returns more than 512 (which is rather unexpected when considering [RFC 1035](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1035#section-4.2.1)). * `CoreDNS` 1.10.0 (Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 4.12 and before) always added EDNS, avoiding this unexpected situation in Microsoft Azure DNS. * `CoreDNS` 1.10.1 (Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 4.13 and later) only uses EDNS if the source query has it, which exposes this unexpected situation as a non-EDNS request now can make it to the configured upstream DNS server (whereas previously, all request were EDNS). * `CoreDNS` panics if the response is larger than expected and will fail to provide an answer to the query.

title: Large number of restarts for ovnkube-master pods on OCP4
issue: - All newly created pods are pending with `ContainerCreating` status.- One or more of the `ovnkube-master` pods have an high number of restarts.- All the pods in `ContainerCreating` status have the same warning `FailedCreatePodSandBox` and message similar to the following: ~~~ Failed to create pod sandbox: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to create pod network sandbox: error adding pod to CNI network "multus-cni-network": [container_name]: error adding container to network "ovn-kubernetes": CNI request failed with status 400: '[container_name] [pod_name] failed to get pod annotation: timed out waiting for annotations: context deadline exceeded ~~~
resolution: 1. Restart all the `ovnkube-master` pods in the `openshift-ovn-kubernetes` project: ~~~ $ oc delete pod ovnkube-master-xxx-n openshift-ovn-kubernetes ~~~ 2. The pods are part of a *daemonset* and will be recreated by the `network` clusteroperator. ~~~ $ oc get daemonset-n openshift-ovn-kubernetes ~~~ > **Note:** Since no changes in the ovn-kubernetes database were done, this should be a safe operation that doesn't cause interruption of service. > **Note:** Please continue monitoring all the `ovnkube-master` pods for any abnormal number of restarts, and if these are present please contact Red Hat Support providing a `must-gather` of the cluster.
root_cause: Usually the root cause of the restarts can be found in the "previous" logs for the `ovnkube-master` pods. You should review the logs of the `ovnkube-master` pods as explained in the diagnostic steps to find the exact root cause of the restarts.

title: How to downgrade broker version after an operator upgrade
issue: Is it possible to downgrade broker version after an operator upgrade?
resolution: Normally when an operator get upgraded it upgrades the version of the broker as well. In case there is a need to downgrade the broker version it is possible to add a version property to the broker CR file and then execute command: ~~~ oc apply-f ~~~ For example if after upgrading the operator to version 7.11.5, which results in broker upgrade to the same version, there is a need to downgrade to version 7.10.2 of the broker all that needs to be done is to add this to CR file: ~~~ spec: version: 7.10.2 deploymentPlan: size: 2 image: placeholder requireLogin: false ~~~ After applying the file the pods will be restarted with a version 7.10.2 of the broker. There are some caveats though:- the broker version must be within the operator`s supported broker versions- the applied CR file must be compatible with the version of the broker that we are trying to downgrade to.

title: ArgoCD RBAC does not work properly with App of Apps
issue: - User with no permission to access a project can deploy an application on a new project that deploys another application in the first project.
resolution: - If you have the Red Hat GitOps Operator installed in a Namespace that is also listed under the destination list for ArgoCD, then this is expected behavior from the operator.
root_cause: - As stated in ArgoCD upstream [documentation](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/declarative-setup/#projects): ~~~ If a Project's destinations configuration allows deploying to the namespace in which Argo CD is installed, then Applications under that project have admin-level access. RBAC access to admin-level Projects should be carefully restricted, and push access to allowed sourceRepos should be limited to only admins. ~~~

title: GitOps is failing due to "Resource not found in cluster: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1/Kustomization:undefined"
issue: - Kustomized manifests are failing to deploy- The manifests contain characters like `~` or `/`
resolution: In the values of the affected Kustomize manifest, change any `~` and `/` characters to `~0` and `~1`, respectively. For example, the following script attempts modify a resource and add the label `app.kubernetes.io/component: frontend`: ~~~yaml- op: add path: "/metadata/labels/app.kubernetes.io/component" value: "frontend" ~~~ However, this will fail; the final `/` is taken as part of the API, which will trigger a failure. This will need to be formatted like so: ~~~yaml- op: add path: "/metadata/labels/app.kubernetes.io~1component" value: "frontend" ~~~
root_cause: JSON (and by extension, Kustomize) uses the characters `~` and `/` to have special meanings, according to the [JSON Pointer RFC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6901/#section-3 "") ^[^1]. To escape these characters, the user must use `~0` for `~`, and `~1` for `/`. [^1] https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6901/#section-3

title: How to create a bindDN account in Red Hat Identity Management (IDM) for identity provider LDAP authentication?
issue: Account needed to query Red Hat Identity Management (IdM) for account for authentication to OpenShift.
A bindDN account in Red Hat Identity Management (IdM) needed for LDAP authentication for Red Hat Build of Keycloak/Red Hat Single Sign-on?
A bindDN account needed in Red Hat Identity Management (IdM) for LDAP authentication and LDAP searches?
resolution: - Create BindDN for accessing directory: ~~~ cat < < EOF > create-SVC-OCP-BINDDN.ldif dn: uid=svc-ocp-test,cn=sysaccounts,cn=etc,dc=ipa,dc=internal,dc=tkagn,dc=io changetype: add objectclass: account objectclass: simplesecurityobject uid: svc-ocp-binddn userPassword: temppassword passwordExpirationTime: 20380119031407Z nsIdleTimeout: 0 EOF ldapmodify-x-D "cn=Directory Manager"-W-H ldap://-ZZ-f./create-SVC-OCP-BINDDN.ldif ~~~- Verify service account exists: ~~~ ldapsearch-D "cn=Directory Manager"-x uid=svc-ocp-binddn-W ~~~- Change password of service account ~~~ ldappasswd-x-D "cn=Directory Manager"-W-S "uid=svc-ocp-binddn,cn=sysaccounts,cn=etc,dc=ipa,dc=internal,dc=tkagn,dc=io" ~~~
root_cause: A system account should be used rather than creating a normal user account in directory. A system account is not a real POSIX user, can't log into any systems, and doesn't own any files. The system account also has no special rights and is unable to write any data in the directory, only read. *Note: Do not use the Directory Manager account to authenticate remote services to the LDAP server*

title: How to migrate from a separately installed CodeFlare Operator in your data science cluster
issue: - Cannot use a separately installed instance of the CodeFlare Operator in Red Hat OpenShift Data Science 2.4 or later In Red Hat OpenShift Data Science 2.4 or later, the CodeFlare Operator is included in the base product and not in a separate Operator. Separately installed instances of the CodeFlare Operator from Red Hat or the community are not supported.
resolution: ### Summary This workaround involves the following steps: 1. Uninstall any installed CodeFlare Operators. 2. Remove unnecessary resources. 3. Install Red Hat OpenShift Data Science 2.4 or later. 4. Enable the Data Science Cluster. ### Procedure 1. Uninstall any installed CodeFlare Operators, as follows: (a) Log in to the OpenShift Container Platform cluster web console as a cluster administrator. (b) Click **Operators > Installed Operators**. (c) Search for **CodeFlare Operator**. (d) If any CodeFlare Operator is installed, either the Community CodeFlare Operator or the Red Hat CodeFlare Operator, uninstall it: select the Operator, and from the actions menu, click **Uninstall Operator**. 2. In a terminal window, remove any resources from the previous installation that are no longer needed, as follows: ``` oc delete crd instascales.codeflare.codeflare.dev mcads.codeflare.codeflare.dev quotasubtrees.ibm.com appwrappers.mcad.ibm.com schedulingspecs.mcad.ibm.com ``` 3. Install Red Hat OpenShift Data Science 2.4 or later, as described in the relevant installation guide. 4. Enable the Data Science Cluster, as follows: (a) In the OpenShift Container Platform cluster web console, click **Home > Search**. (b) From the **Resources** list, select the **DataScienceCluster** Custom Resource Definition (CRD). (c) Click the default instance name to open the instance details page. Starting from Red Hat OpenShift Data Science 2.4, the default instance name for new installations is **default-dsc**. The default instance name for earlier installations, **rhods**, is preserved during upgrade. (d) Click the **YAML** tab to show the instance specifications. (e) Enable the `codeflare` component by setting the `managementState` field to `Managed`. (f) Click **Save**. For more information about Red Hat OpenShift AI, see the [product documentation](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_ai_self-managed/2-latest). For more information about Red Hat OpenShift Data Science 2.4, see the [2.4 product documentation](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_data_science_self-managed/2.4).

title: Unable to clone PVC when the resource size is in bytes
issue: - When a PVC is created with a size in bytes, and then there is an attempt to clone the PVC in the OpenShift Console, the size of the clone PVC will be incredibly large- A PVC with a resource size that has no size qualifier (e.g. Mi, Gi, Ti) will be interpreted by the UI cloning process as Ti, which will result in a PVC that is far too large
resolution: - Convert the size of the PVC from bytes to another size, such as Gi- For example, a 10Gi PVC expressed in bytes would be `10737418240`, so convert from bytes to Gi, divide by 1024 three times: `10737418240 / 1024 / 1024 / 1024 = 10Gi`- Update the resource request from the size in bytes: ~~~ resources: requests: storage: 10737418240 ~~~ to the corresponding size in Gi: ~~~ resources: requests: storage: 10Gi ~~~
root_cause: - Some PVC created via YAML files or other applications, such as OpenShift Virtualization, can be created in bytes.- The OpenShift Console only understands resource sizes in Mi, Gi, Ti, or Pi.- If a PVC is expressed in bytes, the OpenShift Console may incorrectly assume the size is in Ti, resulting in cloned volumes that are much too large.

title: [RHOCP] Warning: unknown field "spec.controlPlaneHardwareSpeed" etcd.operator.openshift.io/cluster patched (no change)
issue: - I want to enable the `etcd` "Slow profile" in an RHOCP 4.14 cluster. However, the field is reported as unknown: ~~~ $ oc patch etcd/cluster--type=merge-p '{"spec": {"controlPlaneHardwareSpeed": "Slower"}}' Warning: unknown field "spec.controlPlaneHardwareSpeed" etcd.operator.openshift.io/cluster patched (no change) ~~~- I need clarification on how to enable `etcd` "Slower" profile in RHOCP.
resolution: As of 01/02/24, please note that this feature is Technical Preview (TP) on RHOCP 4.14 as per [the docs](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.14/scalability_and_performance/recommended-performance-scale-practices/recommended-etcd-practices.html#etcd-changing-hardware-speed-tolerance_recommended-etcd-practices:~:text=Tuning%20etcd%20latency,the%20development%20process.) and are_not_ recommended to be used in production clusters: ~~~ Tuning etcd latency tolerances is a Technology Preview feature only. Technology Preview features are not supported with Red Hat production service level agreements (SLAs) and might not be functionally complete. Red Hat does not recommend using them in production. These features provide early access to upcoming product features, enabling customers to test functionality and provide feedback during the development process. ~~~ Therefore, the solution below applies **ONLY** to non-production **TEST** clusters, until the feature is officially supported. 1. Enable the techpreview as per [Enabling features using feature gates](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.14/nodes/clusters/nodes-cluster-enabling-features.html) ~~~ $ oc edit featuregate cluster ~~~ and add `.spec.featureSet` as below: ~~~ spec: featureSet: TechPreviewNoUpgrade ~~~ 2. Wait ~20-30min as the new `MachineConfigs` are created, `MachineConfigPools` are updated, and scheduling on each `Node` is disabled while the change is being applied. ~~~ $ watch oc get node,mcp,clusterversion ~~~ 3. Patch `etcd/cluster`: ~~~ $ oc describe etcd/cluster | grep-i "Control Plane Hardware Speed" $ oc patch etcd/cluster--type=merge-p '{"spec": {"controlPlaneHardwareSpeed": "Slower"}}' etcd.operator.openshift.io/cluster patched $ oc describe etcd/cluster | grep-i "Control Plane Hardware Speed" Control Plane Hardware Speed: Slower $ ~~~ **IMPORTANT:** Enabling the TechPreviewNoUpgrade feature set on your cluster **cannot be undone and prevents minor version updates**. You should **not enable this feature set on production clusters**- as per [the docs](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.14/nodes/clusters/nodes-cluster-enabling-features.html#:~:text=specific%20feature%20sets%3A-,Enabling%20the%20TechPreviewNoUpgrade%20feature%20set%20on%20your%20cluster%20cannot%20be%20undone%20and%20prevents%20minor%20version%20updates.%20You%20should%20not%20enable%20this%20feature%20set%20on%20production%20clusters.,-Sample%20Feature%20Gate) See also:- [Introducing Selectable Profiles for etcd](https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/introducing-selectable-profiles-for-etcd)- [Setting tuning parameters for etcd](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.14/scalability_and_performance/recommended-performance-scale-practices/recommended-etcd-practices.html#etcd-tuning-parameters_recommended-etcd-practices)
root_cause: - It is required to enable techpreview features using feature gates, which is done by editing `featuregate/cluster`

title: Adding Local users to Quay
issue: - If Red Hat quay is configured to use external authentication (say LDAP), can users be created from quay dashboard? I mean, can we have both AD authentication plus local users at the same time?
resolution: No. One cannot do that. In an LDAP-based authentication system, user information is stored centrally in an LDAP directory server. Local user information is stored locally in the database. This is often referred to as basic user authentication. When LDAP is used for authentication, the concept of local users is often bypassed. All user authentication and authorization are handled through the LDAP directory. Both auth types are mutually exclusive

title: How to delete exited containers and dangling images in RHOCP4 ?
issue: - How to delete containers with an `exited` state using `crictl`?- How to remove `dangling/unused` images using `crictl`?
resolution: - Check the list of the containers in `Exited` state by running: ~~~ $ sudo crictl ps--state Exited ~~~- To delete the exited containers, run the below command: ~~~ $ crictl ps--state Exited | grep-v CONTAINER | awk '{print $1}' | xargs crictl rm ~~~- To remove unused images, run the below command: ~~~ $ sudo crictl rmi--prune ~~~ **NOTE**: Above command will remove all the unused images from the host, it will not **prompt for confirmation**.- To check if any dangling images present on the node: ~~~ $ podman images--filter "dangling=true"-q--no-trunc ~~~- To delete dangling images from the node: ~~~ $ sudo podman rmi $(podman images--filter "dangling=true"-q--no-trunc) ~~~
root_cause: - At the time of writing this article, there is no direct command to delete exited containers or `crictl system prune` command with `crictl` binary.

title: What is the expected impact of the Docker build strategy imageOptimiszationPolicy "SkipLayers" on the resulting image layers?
issue: When building a custom image using the Docker build strategy with "imageOptimizationPolicy" set to "SkipLayers", the resulting image still contains multiple layers
root_cause: Docker builds normally create a layer representing each instruction in a Dockerfile. Setting the `imageOptimizationPolicy` to `SkipLayers` merges all the Docker build instructions into a single layer which is applied on top of the base image. The `SkipLayers` policy *ONLY* applies to the layers that would be normally generated by the Docker build. It does not squash the layers of the base image being used. If the base image being used contains `N` layers, then the new image will contain `N+1` layers when built with the `SkipLayers` policy enabled. For example, if the base image contains 4 layers, and the Docker build contains 3 instructions to apply when building the image, the final built image would normally contain 7 layers: 4 from the base image, and 3 for the Docker build instructions. Using the `SkipLayers` policy with the same Docker build, the final built image would contain 5 layers: 4 from the base image, and 1 merged layer from all the Docker build instructions.

title: How to install the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift in a disconnected environment in OpenShift 4.x?
issue: - How to install the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift in a disconnected environment?- The installation stuck when trying to install the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift in a disconnected environment.
resolution: Check the unit file of the quay-postgres service to find the image it uses in the podman run command to create the quay-postgres container. ~~~ ExecStart=/usr/bin/podman run \--name quay-postgres \-v /home/mirror-registry/quay-install/pg-data:/var/lib/pgsql/data:Z \-e POSTGRESQL_USER=user \-e POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD=password \-e POSTGRESQL_DATABASE=quay \--pod=quay-pod \--conmon-pidfile %t/%n-pid \--cidfile %t/%n-cid \--cgroups=no-conmon \--replace \ registry.redhat.io/rhel8/postgresql-10:1-203.1669834630 ~~~ Run the podman images command to find if this image exists in the server. ~~~ # podman images ~~~ If the image doesn't exist in the server, pull it from a place that has access to the internet ~~~ # podman pull registry.redhat.io # podman pull registry.redhat.io/rhel8/postgresql-10:1-203.1669834630 # podman images postgresql-10-q # podman save 83df85f47fde-o /tmp/postgresql-10.tar ~~~ Then copy the postgresql-10.tar file to the disconnected environment and load the image into the server ~~~ # podman load < postgresql-10.tar # podman images postgresql-10 ~~~ **NOTE**: Please run the `./mirror-registry uninstall-v` command first before rerunning the `./mirror-registry install-v` command to clean the old data/file/container to prevent the server from being overwhelmed by the old data.
root_cause: The quay-postgres service cannot pull the necessary image from the internet to start the quay-postgres container.

title: Compliance Operator is unable to mount persistent volume for result server pod
issue: Compliance Operator `resultServer` pods are unable to start, with the following error observed in the pod logs: ~~~ MountVolume.MountDevice failed for volume "pvc-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx": kubernetes.io/csi: attacher.MountDevice failed to create newCsiDriverClient: driver name pxd.portworx.com not found in the list of registered CSI drivers ~~~
resolution: Make sure the `nodeSelector` and `tolerations` attributes of the `ScanSetting` custom resource are set to target the deployment to nodes that are permitted to mount persistent volumes using the Portworx CSI driver. For example, this may require specifying the `worker` role as the target in the `nodeSelector`: ``` apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1 kind: ScanSetting metadata: name: rs-on-workers namespace: openshift-compliance rawResultStorage: nodeSelector: node-role.kubernetes.io/worker: "" pvAccessModes:- ReadWriteOnce rotation: 3 size: 1Gi tolerations:- operator: Exists roles:- worker- master scanTolerations:- operator: Exists schedule: 0 1 * * * ```
root_cause: The Compliance Operator result server pod mounts a persistent volume (PV) that stores the raw Asset Reporting Format (ARF) scan results. The `nodeSelector` and `tolerations` attributes of the `ScanSetting` custom resource enable you to configure the location of the result server pod. Many examples of `ScanSetting` definitions specify the `master` node role in the `nodeSelector`. In environments where control plane nodes are not permitted to mount persistent volumes, you must use the `worker` role instead.

title: After scaling up a machineset or recreating a master node, the node never finishes the boot process..
issue: - After executing the replacement of an unhealthy etcd member whose machine is not healthy or scaling up a machine set, the new node gets stuck in the boot process. The node is able to fetch its ignition config from the cluster but after the node's nic is up, the process gets stuck and never moves forward.- Restarting the node doesn't fix the issue.- Removing the machine object and adding it again doesn't solve the issue.
resolution:
The workaround for this issue requires to upload a most recent image template to the cluster, depending on the platform, the instructions are provided in the official documentation: [Openstack Platform](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.12/installing/installing_openstack/installing-openstack-user.html#installation-osp-creating-image_installing-openstack-user) [Vmware vSphere](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.12/installing/installing_vsphere/installing-vsphere-network-customizations.html#installation-vsphere-machines_installing-vsphere-network-customizations) [RHV](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.12/installing/installing_rhv/installing-rhv-user-infra.html#installation-rhv-specifying-rhcos-image-settings_installing-rhv-user-infra) As the cluster was first installed in Openshift 4.6 or older, ignition data is probably not valid for a newer template image. So a new secret must be created for master and worker nodes. The following steps outline the full workaround process: 1. Check if ignition data from machine-api secrets is version 2.x (it might be necessary to install the jq package to execute the command in the bastion where oc commands will be executed): ~~~ $ oc get secret worker-user-data-n openshift-machine-api-o jsonpath='{.data.userData}' | base64-d |jq.ignition.version "2.2.0" $ oc get secret master-user-data-n openshift-machine-api-o jsonpath='{.data.userData}' | base64-d |jq.ignition.version "2.2.0" ~~~ 2. Backup the original secrets: ~~~ $ oc get secret worker-user-data-n openshift-machine-api-o yaml > worker-user-data-new.yaml $ oc get secret master-user-data-n openshift-machine-api-o yaml > master-user-data-new.yaml ~~~ 3. Decode the ignition data from base64 and save it to a file: ~~~ $ oc get secret worker-user-data-n openshift-machine-api-o jsonpath='{.data.userData}' | base64-d | jq. > worker.ign $ oc get secret master-user-data-n openshift-machine-api-o jsonpath='{.data.userData}' | base64-d | jq. > master.ign ~~~ 4. Transform the ignition content from version 2.x to 3.1.0. For this, replace the word `append` with `merge` and change the ignition version to `3.1.0`. As an example: Original ignition data 2.2.0: ~~~ {"ignition": {"config": {"append": [{"source": "https://192.168.1.210:22623/config/worker", "verification": {}}]}, "security": {"tls": {"certificateAuthorities": [{"source": "data:text/plain;charset=utf-8;base64,", "verification": {}}]}}, "timeouts": {}, "version": "2.2.0"}, "networkd": {}, "passwd": {}, "storage": {}, "systemd": {}} ~~~ Converted to 3.1.0 ignition data: ~~~ {"ignition": {"config": {"merge": [{"source": "https://192.168.1.210:22623/config/worker", "verification": {}}]}, "security": {"tls": {"certificateAuthorities": [{"source": "data:text/plain;charset=utf-8;base64,", "verification": {}}]}}, "timeouts": {}, "version": "3.1.0"}, "networkd": {}, "passwd": {}, "storage": {}, "systemd": {}} ~~~ This step needs to be executed for both worker.ign and master.ign. In this example, the fixed versions were saved as master.ign.3 and worker.ign.3. 5. Encode the new worker.ign.3 and master.ign.3 to base64: ~~~ $ cat worker.ign.3 | tr-d '[:space:]' |base64-w0 > worker.ign.base64 $ cat master.ign.3 | tr-d '[:space:]' |base64-w0 > master.ign.base64 ~~~ 6. Replace the base64 encoded from the correspondent output file from the previous step in worker-user-data-new.yaml and master-user-data-new.yaml. Change the name of the secret in `.metadata.name` field and remove `.metadata.uid`, `.metadata.creationTimestamp` and `.metadata.resourceVersion` like the following example: master-user-data-new.yaml ~~~ apiVersion: v1 data: disableTemplating: dHJ1ZQo= userData:  kind: Secret metadata: name: master-user-data-new namespace: openshift-machine-api type: Opaque ~~~ worker-user-data-new.yaml ~~~ apiVersion: v1 data: disableTemplating: dHJ1ZQo= userData:  kind: Secret metadata: name: worker-user-data-new namespace: openshift-machine-api type: Opaque ~~~ 7. Once the secret data contains the fixed ignition 3.1.0 encoded data, create the secrets from the files: ~~~ $ oc create-f master-user-data-new.yaml-n openshift-machine-api secret/master-user-data-new created $ oc create-f worker-user-data-new.yaml-n openshift-machine-api secret/worker-user-data-new created $ oc get secrets-n openshift-machine-api | grep new master-user-data-new Opaque 2 113s worker-user-data-new Opaque 2 40s ~~~ 8. Obtain machine object names for master nodes: ~~~ $ oc get machine-l machine.openshift.io/cluster-api-machine-role=master-n openshift-machine-api NAME PHASE TYPE REGION ZONE AGE ocp4-sqqgc-master-0 Running 28d ocp4-sqqgc-master-1 Running 28d ocp4-sqqgc-master-2 Running 28d ~~~ 9. Obtain the machineset name that needs to be fixed: ~~~ $ oc get machineset-n openshift-machine-api NAME DESIRED CURRENT READY AVAILABLE AGE ocp4-sqqgc-worker 3 3 2 2 28d ~~~ 10. Backup every object before changing them and keep them for further reference in case you need to rollback: ~~~ $ oc get machine ocp4-sqqgc-master-0-n openshift-machine-api-o yaml > ocp4-sqqgc-master-0_machine.yaml $ oc get machine ocp4-sqqgc-master-1-n openshift-machine-api-o yaml > ocp4-sqqgc-master-1_machine.yaml $ oc get machine ocp4-sqqgc-master-2-n openshift-machine-api-o yaml > ocp4-sqqgc-master-2_machine.yaml $ oc get machineset ocp4-sqqgc-worker-n openshift-machine-api-o yaml > ocp4-sqqgc-worker_machineset.yaml ~~~ 11. Patch the machine objects and machineset object using the new template name and the new secret name: ~~~ $ export WORKER_SECRET=worker-user-data-new $ export MASTER_SECRET=master-user-data-new $ export TEMPLATE_NAME=rhcos-4.12.30 $ oc patch machine ocp4-sqqgc-master-0--type merge--patch "{"spec":{"providerSpec":{"value":{"template":"${TEMPLATE_NAME}","userDataSecret":{"name":"${MASTER_SECRET}"}}}}}" $ oc patch machine ocp4-sqqgc-master-1--type merge--patch "{"spec":{"providerSpec":{"value":{"template":"${TEMPLATE_NAME}","userDataSecret":{"name":"${MASTER_SECRET}"}}}}}" $ oc patch machine ocp4-sqqgc-master-2--type merge--patch "{"spec":{"providerSpec":{"value":{"template":"${TEMPLATE_NAME}","userDataSecret":{"name":"${MASTER_SECRET}"}}}}}" $ oc patch machineset ocp4-sqqgc-worker--type merge--patch "{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"providerSpec":{"value":{"template":"${TEMPLATE_NAME}","userDataSecret":{"name":"${WORKER_SECRET}"}}}}}}}" ~~~ 12. Check that the changes were applied. In this example we expect the template is rhcos-4.12.30 and secrets are master-user-data-new for masters machine object and worker-user-data-new for machineset: ~~~ $ for i in $(oc get machine-o name-l machine.openshift.io/cluster-api-machine-role=master); do oc get $i-o jsonpath='{.spec.providerSpec.value.template}{"
"}{.spec.providerSpec.value.userDataSecret.name}{"
"}';done rhcos-4.12.30 master-user-data-new rhcos-4.12.30 master-user-data-new rhcos-4.12.30 master-user-data-new $ for i in $(oc get machineset-o name); do oc get $i-o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.providerSpec.value.template}{"
"}{.spec.template.spec.providerSpec.value.userDataSecret.name}{"
"}';done rhcos-4.12.30 worker-user-data-new ~~~ 13. Now that all the changes are in place, delete the machine object that is stuck in the `Provisioning` state, this should trigger a new node creation using the new template and the new secret: ~~~ $ oc get machine |grep-i Provisioned ocp4-sqqgc-worker-ckvpt Provisioned 10d $ oc delete machine ocp4-sqqgc-worker-ckvpt ~~~ After some time, the deployment should work correctly and the machine should transition to `Provisioned` state and then to the `Running` state: ~~~ $ oc get machine NAME PHASE TYPE REGION ZONE AGE ocp4-sqqgc-master-0 Running 31d ocp4-sqqgc-master-1 Running 31d ocp4-sqqgc-master-2 Running 31d ocp4-sqqgc-worker-sb2ms Running 31d ocp4-sqqgc-worker-vjdvg Running 29d ocp4-sqqgc-worker-xbq67 Provisioned 7m15s $ oc get machine NAME PHASE TYPE REGION ZONE AGE ocp4-sqqgc-master-0 Running 31d ocp4-sqqgc-master-1 Running 31d ocp4--sqqgc-master-2 Running 31d ocp4-sqqgc-worker-sb2ms Running 31d ocp4-sqqgc-worker-vjdvg Running 29d ocp4-sqqgc-worker-xbq67 Running 7m59s $ oc get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION ocp4-sqqgc-master-0 Ready master 31d v1.25.16+5c97f5b ocp4-sqqgc-master-1 Ready master 31d v1.25.16+5c97f5b ocp4-sqqgc-master-2 Ready master 31d v1.25.16+5c97f5b ocp4-sqqgc-worker-sb2ms Ready worker 31d v1.25.16+5c97f5b ocp4-sqqgc-worker-vjdvg Ready worker 28d v1.25.16+5c97f5b ocp4-sqqgc-worker-xbq67 Ready worker 67s v1.25.16+5c97f5b ~~~
root_cause: The issue is explained in detail in the following [Red Hat solution](https://access.redhat.com/articles/7053165) including the background and why it affects Openshift. It is also being tracked in the following [bug](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPBUGS-15087).

title: How to configure user-workload to scrape the federation endpoint of ServiceMesh Prometheus instance in OpenShift 4
issue: - How to scrape the federation endpoint of the ServiceMesh Prometheus instance from the user workload instance
resolution: Its possible to configure the User workload Prometheus instance to scrape the federation endpoint of the mesh owned prometheus instance. This can be achived using a `serviceMonitor` object. ~~~ apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1 kind: ServiceMonitor metadata: name: istio-federation namespace: istio-system spec: endpoints:- honorLabels: true honorTimestamps: true interval: 30s params: 'match[]':- '{job="kubernetes-pods"}'- '{job="kubernetes-services"}' path: /federate scrapeTimeout: 30s targetPort: 9090 selector: matchLabels: app: prometheus ~~~ Using the above configuration, all of the metrics scraped from any namespaces that are a member of the mesh will be ingested with the labels ~~~ kubernetes_namespace = $ORIGIN_PROJECT_NAME namespace = istio-system ~~~ Meaning that the ingested metrics will only be visable to cluster administrators or user with access to the istio-system namespace. title: After adding MicroShift cluster to Red Hat ACM the access to application breaks

resolution: Currently this issue is reported in the Jira Link- [\[ACM-8347\] Importing microshift cluster breaks routes in microshift](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/ACM-8347). Engineering is working on the mitigation of the issue.
root_cause: When the cluster is imported to the RHACM, the iptables are updated with the rule to route the traffic to the Service. title: free command shows Java process size much smaller than the initial heap size
issue: Tomcat is starting with the initial and max heap set to 6144m; however, `free` output shows memory usage far below the initial heap size: ~~~ $ ps-ef | grep-i java tomcat85 7 1 73 17:52 pts/0 00:00:51 /etc/alternatives/jre/bin/java-Xms6144m-Xmx6144m org.apache.catalina.startup.Bootstrap start # free-m total used free shared buff/cache available Mem: 15866 775 13180 11 1910 14757 Swap: 4515 0 4515 ~~~
resolution: By default, the initial Java heap (e.g. `-Xms`) is reserved as virtual memory. Linux does not back the pages with actual physical memory until the pages are used. `-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch` can be used to force Linux to back the initial Java heap pages with physical memory on JVM startup. The trade offs are startup time, application speed, and JVM process size. The application will run faster with pretouching, but at the cost of a longer startup time and increased process size.

title: Obtaining an OpenShift token using AzureAD authentication via OAuth endpoint
issue: - How to get Red Hat OpenShift token?- How to know which endpoint the Oauth access token should be presented to, to get an OpenShift token in return?
resolution: The following steps can be implemented to access the Oauth endpoint to get an OpenShift token by providing an AzureAD bearer token: 1. Store the azure token in the AZURE_TOKEN variable: $ AZURE_TOKEN=$(az account get-access-token--resource https://--output tsv-- query accessToken) 2. Store the endpoint in the OAUTH_ENDPOINT variable: $ OAUTH_ENDPOINT="https:// /oauth/token/request" 3. Make a curl request to get the openshift token and store in the OPENSHIFT_TOKEN variable $ OPENSHIFT_TOKEN=$(curl-s-k-X POST \-H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \-d "client_id=openshift-challenging-client" \-d "grant_type=token" \-d "provider_id=azure" \-d "api_url=https:// " \-d "access_token=${AZURE_TOKEN}" \ $OAUTH_ENDPOINT | jq-r.access_token) 4. Verify the openshift token: $ echo $OPENSHIFT_TOKEN

title: [WIP] What options do I have to run a nested container inside of an OpenShift pod?
issue: - I am attempting to run a container tool like `podman`, `buildah`, or `skopeo` inside of an OpenShift pod.- This may be a part of a CI/CD pipeline, such as Jenkins, and jobs must run a container within an OpenShift pod.- Users in a pod may need access to either `podman build` or `podman run` commands within the pod to- How do I run a nested container inside of an OpenShift pod?
resolution: - Based on your current version of OpenShift and current features in development, `podman` inside of a pod may behave differently than it would directly on a Red Hat Enterprise Linux host.- It is expected that `podman build` and `buildah build`/`buildah bud` operations inside of a pod should work.- As of the current writing of this article, there is no direct support for performing a `podman run` inside of a pod, or full nesting of a running container inside of a pod.- This can still be accomplished but requires high levels of privilege escalation which is very insecure.- A solution to this is actively in development and is reliant on two upstream Kubernetes features:- `ProcMounts`- `UserNamespacesSupport`- Please refer to the following sections in this document on how best to accomplish running nested containers based on your needs. ### Building container images inside of an OpenShift Pod- If you only need to *build* container images inside of an OpenShift pod, this can be accomplished in a number of ways.- Building container images inside of OpenShift pods should work natively as a rootless user provided the container utility (`podman`, `buildah`, etc) is configured correctly in the container image being used in the pod.- Red Hat provides base images of `podman` and `buildah` which can be used to run rootless container image builds inside of an OpenShift pod:- [Red Hat Universal Base Image 8- podman Image](https://catalog.redhat.com/software/containers/ubi8/podman/6113ec146e1e42ca4d6decca?architecture=amd64&image=65cba2bfa05d0c424860a686&container-tabs=overview)- [Red Hat Universal Base Image 9- podman Image](https://catalog.redhat.com/software/containers/ubi9/podman/618aa2ad4ae373968756826c?architecture=amd64&image=65a8faa3d59cca758b7d41c3&container-tabs=dockerfile)- [Red Hat Universal Base Image 8- buildah Image](https://catalog.redhat.com/software/containers/ubi8/buildah/602686f7b16b1eb2e30807ee?architecture=amd64&image=65cba3380378193680dd33f9&container-tabs=dockerfile)- [Red Hat Universal Base Image 9- buildah Image](https://catalog.redhat.com/software/containers/ubi9/buildah/61959488b0df17a5d66395f6?architecture=amd64&image=65a8f9eb7e70d3e4e689f960&container-tabs=dockerfile)- If you wish to add `podman` or `buildah` to your existing container image, such as within a CI/CD pipeline, you can insert the following into your `Containerfile` or `Dockerfile` to configure a rootless environment for container image builds, customizing as required for your environment: ~~~ # Install required packages for podman-in-a-pod RUN rpm--restore--quiet shadow-utils && \ dnf-y install crun podman netavark fuse-overlayfs && \ rm-rf /var/cache/* /var/log/dnf* /var/log/yum.* # Configure the podman user and configuration files RUN useradd podman-u 1000 && \ echo podman:10000:5000 > /etc/subuid && \ echo podman:10000:5000 > /etc/subgid && \ mkdir-p /home/podman/.local/share/containers && \ mkdir-p /home/podman/.config/containers && \ curl-L https://raw.githubusercontent.com/containers/libpod/master/contrib/podmanimage/stable/containers.conf-o /etc/containers/containers.conf && \ curl-L https://raw.githubusercontent.com/containers/libpod/master/contrib/podmanimage/stable/podman-containers.conf-o /home/podman/.config/containers/containers.conf && \ chown podman:podman-R /home/podman # chmod containers.conf and adjust storage.conf to enable Fuse storage. RUN chmod 644 /etc/containers/containers.conf; sed-i-e 's|^#mount_program|mount_program|g'-e '/additionalimage.*/a "/var/lib/shared",'-e 's|^mountopt[[:space:]]*=.*$|mountopt = "nodev,fsync=0"|g' /etc/containers/storage.conf RUN mkdir-p /var/lib/shared/overlay-images /var/lib/shared/overlay-layers /var/lib/shared/vfs-images /var/lib/shared/vfs-layers; touch /var/lib/shared/overlay-images/images.lock; touch /var/lib/shared/overlay-layers/layers.lock; touch /var/lib/shared/vfs-images/images.lock; touch /var/lib/shared/vfs-layers/layers.lock # Ensure this is configured to allow for proper user namespace behavior ENV_CONTAINERS_USERNS_CONFIGURED="" ~~~

title: How to change cipher suite?
issue: - The defaults TLS protocol and cipher suites in the registry are defined in code [here](https://github.com/quay/quay/blob/2a4ac0930608f6d64bbf55b595736da2518a4bea/conf/init/nginx_conf_create.py#L12C1-L55 "here"). How to use different cipher suite such that its accepted by Quay?
resolution: Ensure Quay is offline when makin \ changes for the ciphers to take effect. 1. Locate Quay's Config.yaml File: The location of Quay's config.yaml file on OMR depends on the installation directory. To find the install directory, use either of the following methods:- Execute podman inspect quay-app and retrieve the information from the container description.- Check the systemd unit file with the following command (for root installations): ``` $ cat /etc/systemd/system/quay-app.service ``` 2. Identify the relevant directory for Quay's configuration is the one that mount-binds to /conf/stack within the container. 3. Edit and add SSL directives: Open the Quay config.yaml file located in the identified directory and edit it to add SSL_CIPHERS Directive. Specify the desired list of ciphers within square brackets: yaml ``` SSL_CIPHERS: [cipher1, cipher2,...] ```

title: Adopt a Previously Deployed ZTP Cluster into ACM
product: Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management for Kubernetes
issue: An OpenShift cluster previously deployed via ZTP needs to be re-added to an ACM hub cluster or migrated to another ACM hub cluster.
resolution: This is based on https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7006147, but instead opts for Hive Adoption instead of ACM Import. Both methods are valid, but Hive adoption will result in proper status of the resources re-created by GitOps. N.B. this process will not work without a valid system:admin kubeconfig or, if the kubeconfig is not available, SSH access to the target cluster. **Retrieve the clusterID and infrastructureID from the target** 1. Authenticate to the cluster to be adopted. If you do not have a copy of the kubeconfig for the system:admin user, proceed to step 2. Otherwise skip to step 3. ~~~ export CLUSTERNAME= export KUBECONFIG=/path/to/kubeconfig ~~~ 2. Retrieve the system:admin kubeconfig from the target cluster ~~~ export NODE=$(oc get nodes-ocustom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name--no-headers | head-n1) ssh core@$NODE "sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/static-pod-resources/kube-apiserver-certs/secrets/node-kubeconfigs/lb-ext.kubeconfig /home/core/kubeconfig && sudo chown core:core /home/core/kubeconfig" scp core@$NODE:kubeconfig. ~~~ 3. Retrieve the cluster ID and infrastructure ID from the target cluster ~~~ export CLUSTER_ID=$(oc get clusterversion/version-ojson | jq-r '.spec.clusterID') export INFRA_ID=$(oc get infrastructure cluster-ojson | jq-r '.status.infrastructureName')) ~~~ **Authenticate to the hub cluster that will adopt the target cluster** ~~~ export KUBECONFIG=/path/to/hub-kubeconfig ~~~ **Authenticate to the ArgoCD Application** ~~~ argoPass=$(oc get secret/openshift-gitops-cluster-n openshift-gitops-o jsonpath='{.data.admin\.password}' | base64-d) argoURL=$(oc get route openshift-gitops-server-n openshift-gitops-o jsonpath='{.spec.host}{"\n"}') argocd login--insecure--grpc-web $argoURL--username admin--password $argoPass ~~~ **Disable Auto-Sync** ~~~ argocd app set clusters--sync-policy none oc get applications-n openshift-gitops clusters-ojson | jq.spec {"destination": {"namespace": "clusters-sub", "server": "https://kubernetes.default.svc"}, "project": "ztp-app-project", "source": {"path": "clusters", "repoURL": "ssh://git@ /path/to/site-configs-repo.git", "targetRevision": "main"}, "syncPolicy": {"syncOptions": ["CreateNamespace=true"]}} ~~~ **Prepare the SNO for Adoption into Git** 1. Clone the clusters repository locally ~~~ git clone gitlab.com/path/to/site-configs-repo.git... remote: Enumerating objects: 520, done. remote: Counting objects: 100% (170/170), done. remote: Compressing objects: 100% (68/68), done. remote: Total 520 (delta 85), reused 146 (delta 67), pack-reused 350 Receiving objects: 100% (520/520), 54.33 KiB | 13.58 MiB/s, done. Resolving deltas: 100% (267/267), done. ~~~ 2. In the clusters repository, create the BareMetalHostOverride.yaml file if it doesn't already exist. ~~~ cd site-configs-repo/clusters/site-configs/ vim BareMetalHostOverride.yaml cat BareMetalHostOverride.yaml--- apiVersion: metal3.io/v1alpha1 kind: BareMetalHost metadata: name: "{{.Node.HostName}}" namespace: "{{.Cluster.ClusterName}}" annotations: argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "1" inspect.metal3.io: "{{.Node.IronicInspect}}" bmac.agent-install.openshift.io/hostname: "{{.Node.HostName}}" bmac.agent-install.openshift.io/installer-args: "{{.Node.InstallerArgs}}" bmac.agent-install.openshift.io/ignition-config-overrides: "{{.Node.IgnitionConfigOverride}}" bmac.agent-install.openshift.io/role: "{{.Node.Role}}" baremetalhost.metal3.io/detached: "assisted-service-controller" labels: infraenvs.agent-install.openshift.io: "{{.Cluster.ClusterName}}" spec: bootMode: "{{.Node.BootMode}}" externallyProvisioned: true bmc: address: "{{.Node.BmcAddress}}" disableCertificateVerification: true credentialsName: "{{.Node.BmcCredentialsName.Name}}" bootMACAddress: "{{.Node.BootMACAddress}}" automatedCleaningMode: disabled online: true rootDeviceHints: "{{.Node.RootDeviceHints}}" userData: "{{.Node.UserData}}" ~~~ 3. Update the SiteConfig for the spoke to reference the override ~~~ git diff diff--git a/clusters/site-configs/.yaml b/clusters/site-configs/.yaml index 17caf00..b6a30b8 100644--- a/clusters/site-configs/.yaml +++ b/clusters/site-configs/.yaml @@-43,8 +43,8 @@ spec: exclude:- 03-sctp-machine-config-worker.yaml- 03-sctp-machine-config-master.yaml + crTemplates: + BareMetalHost: "BareMetalHostOverride.yaml" clusterNetwork:- cidr: "fd01::/48" hostPrefix: 64 ~~~ 4. Ensure the SNO exists in the kustomization.yaml file ~~~ cat kustomization.yaml apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: Kustomization generators:-.yaml ~~~ 5. Your directory tree should look similar to the following ~~~ tree-L 1. ├── BareMetalHostOverride.yaml ├── kustomization.yaml ├── extra-manifest-dir ├──.yaml 1 directory, 3 files ~~~ **Sync the policies and clusters** ~~~ argocd app sync policies [output truncated] argocd app sync clusters [output truncated] ~~~ **Verify if there are differences between manifests in git and present on the cluster. If there are, fix on the cluster and verify all is healthy (no diff in our case)** ~~~ argocd app diff clusters oc get apps-A NAMESPACE NAME SYNC STATUS HEALTH STATUS openshift-gitops clusters Synced Healthy openshift-gitops policies Synced Healthy ~~~ **Restore the sync policy (your original sync policy may be different)** ~~~ argocd app set clusters--sync-policy auto--allow-empty--self-heal--auto-prune oc get applications-n openshift-gitops clusters-ojson | jq.spec {"destination": {"namespace": "clusters-sub", "server": "https://kubernetes.default.svc"}, title: Application is receiving traffic without sidecar injected

resolution: It is a known issue reported at [OCPBUGS-30256](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPBUGS-30256)- If this issue is being faced on your node, raise a Red Hat Support case immediately.
root_cause: The `nmstatectl persist-nic-names` is a functionality that creates `.link` files under `/etc/systemd/network/` that save NIC name based on its MAC address. title: Broker is trying to reconnect after scale down
issue: After a scale down we can see that the remaining broker is trying to reconnect to the missing cluster memeber
resolution: This is expected behaviour. After the scale down the operator launches the drainer process to drain any remaining messages. This will be detected by the remaining brokers which will try to reconnect to it. By default in OpenShift environment this will take 10 attempts and may take over 10 minutes to completes.

title: Configure multiple static IP in RHCOS during OCP installation using UPI in vSphere
issue: - How to configure multiple static IPs on a node during deployment of OCP 4. x UPI on vSphere.- When configuring two network interfaces on a node either using Kernel Args or Machine config file during your manifest/install stage [Official Document](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.14/installing/installing_vsphere/installing-vsphere-installer-provisioned-network-customizations.html), below possible issues are faced 1. resolution: We can configure multiple network interfaces through kernel arguments for cluster nodes during the deployment of OpenShift Container Platform 4. x with the User Provisioned Infrastructure installer passing multiple "IP" parameters into the guestinfo.afterburn.initrd.network-kargs. ~~~ ip=10.x.x.x::10.y.y.y:255.255.255.0:[Hostname]:ens192 [...] export IPCFG="ip=::::::none nameserver=srv1 ip=::::::none nameserver=srv1" ~~~

title: ImageStreams are pulling images from private registry without authentication
issue: + We have discovered that there are many anonymous pulls of images from our private image registry. + We have identified that these pulls are initiated by ImageStreams from the default `openshift` namespace. + Our security policy allows only authenticated pulls, but the registry does not reject unauthenticated ones.
resolution: To force the ImageStream authentication we can: + Create an `on-prem` pull-secret in namespace `openshift`. + Link the `on-prem` pull-secret to the `default` Service Account.
root_cause: + By default ImageStreams do not reference any authentication. + By default OpenShift internal ImageStreams use the Service Account (SA) called `default`. + If we see anonymous pull requests, pull-secret does not have the on-prem/mirror registry configured.

title: "PrometheusOperatorRejectedResources" alert firing continuously in a Red Hat OpenShift Service  in RHOCP 4
product: Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS
issue: - Continuous **"PrometheusOperatorRejectedResources"*

warning from the AlertManager.- Prometheus operator shows the following warning log repeatedly: ~~~ level=warn ts=2022-07-29T16:17:27.361540578Z caller=operator.go:1832 component=prometheusoperator msg="skipping servicemonitor" error="it accesses file system via bearer token file which Prometheus specification prohibits" servicemonitor=openshift-logging/monitor-elasticsearch-cluster namespace=openshift-user-workload-monitoring prometheus=user-workload ~~~
resolution: As per the description of the **"Red Hat OpenShift Logging"** operator, it is a pre-requisite to enable monitoring on namespace openshift-logging. This can be resolved by setting the label **openshift.io/cluster-monitoring=true** on the **affected namespace**. ~~~ oc label namespace openshift-logging openshift.io/cluster-monitoring=true ~~~ **For Customers using ROSA** Please note that the **customers cannot directly set this label** as "openshift-logging" comes under the Red Hat managed namespaces. If the customers attempt to set any label on the managed namespaces (i.e., starting with **openshift-**), it will be **blocked** and the following error log is displayed: ~~~ Error from server (Prevented from accessing Red Hat managed namespaces. ~~~ **In order to enable the cluster monitoring by applying the above label, please open a support case with us by clicking** [here](https://access.redhat.com/support/cases/#/case/new/open-case?caseCreate=true).
root_cause: The **"PrometheusOperatorRejectedResources"** alert fires when the Prometheus operator rejects some resources in a particular namespace due to some misconfiguration in the service or UWM. Here, the "openshift-logging" namespace under user workload monitoring (UWM) is being rejected by Prometheus operator. "openshift-logging" monitoring is expected to be in UWM and thus, Red SRE is not alerted for it (it's also a warning alert). The Prometheus Operator would expect cluster monitoring to be enabled for it.

title: High memory consumption in RHOCP 4 nodes caused by duplicated IngressController haproxy processes
issue: - Why the `IngressController` `pods` are creating several `haproxy` processes and increasing the memory consumption in the OCP nodes?
resolution: There are two most affordable resolution for the issue: 1- Identify the cause of long-lived connections in application side and apply configurations to terminate them. Example: Configure session timeouts for the users 2- Configure `Ingress Sharding` for the `IngressController` according to the suggested in the [documentation](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.13/networking/ingress-sharding.html)
root_cause: The Openshift `IngressController` needs to keep its `haproxy` configuration updated considering the most updated `endpoints` from pods referenced by the `services` from the routes. In case of any pod deleting or adding events present in the configuration, the `haproxy` configuration will be renewed. In this phase, the `router pod` will create a new process and the older haproxy process will receive a `SIGUSR1` signal to finish the process but only when all established sessions are terminated. The detailed situation can increase the nodes CPU and memory consumption where the router pods are running due the quantity of duplicated haproxy processes created in the container. The situation getting worse when you have long-lived sessions established with application `routes`. In case of long-lived sessions, the sessions that are established in the `haproxy` for several hours, the older processes will be running in the container still those sessions are terminated by the clients. As higher the age that the sessions keep established in the ingresscontroller, as higher will be the quantity of running haproxy processes. The IngressController implementations with high quantity of configured routes without route sharding has more chances of creating duplicated haproxy processes due the quantity of configured pods in its haproxy configuration. Any pod deleting or creating will trigger the haproxy process reloading.

root_cause: A recent change in the Azure cloud controller manager has set a new default for virtual machines to use the Virtual Machine Scale Set (VMSS) type. This change is benign when using the cloud controller manager on Azure. When deploying to Azure Stack Hub there is an issue that arises between the virtual machine type and the load balancer type for Azure Stack Hub. Azure Stack Hub uses “basic” style load balancers instead of “standard” style, as defined by Azure. Virtual machines of the VMSS type are not allowed to be added to “basic” style load balancers. When the changes to the default virtual machine type are combined with the load balancer rules for Azure Stack Hub, this results in a scenario where new nodes are not added to the primary load balancer for the cluster.

title: Defining resourceHealthChecks  for resources with no group does not work in GitOps operator
issue: - GitOps operator does not correctly implement the reourceHealthChecks for resources with no group.
resolution: - Red Hat is aware of the issue and the bug is being tracked here at [GITOPS-3591](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/GITOPS-3591)
root_cause: When creating resourceHealthChecks for resources in default group, the operator appends an underscore(_) to the generated value, example: `resource.customizations.health._Service:` in `argocd-cm` configmap which does not work.

title: ERROR WFLYJCA0115: Module for driver [com.mysql] or one of it dependencies is missing occurs during container startup
product: Red Hat JBoss Enterprise Application Platform
issue: If the customized `standalone-openshift.xml` is brought from EAP 7.2 or earlier container to EAP 7.3 container, the following error occurs during container startup. ~~~ 02:50:56,675 ERROR [org.jboss.as.controller.management-operation] (ServerService Thread Pool-- 42) WFLYCTL0013: Operation ("add") failed- address: ([("subsystem" => "datasources"), ("jdbc-driver" => "mysql")])- failure description: "WFLYJCA0115: Module for driver [com.mysql] or one of it dependencies is missing: [com.mysql]" 02:50:56,705 ERROR [org.jboss.as.controller.management-operation] (ServerService Thread Pool-- 42) WFLYCTL0013: Operation ("add") failed- address: ([("subsystem" => "datasources"), ("jdbc-driver" => "postgresql")])- failure description: "WFLYJCA0115: Module for driver [org.postgresql] or one of it dependencies is missing: [org.postgresql]" ~~~
resolution: Remove the following ` ` settings in `standalone-openshift.xml` as below: ~~~ @@-147,12 +147,6 @@ org.h2.jdbcx.JdbcDataSource-- com.mysql.jdbc.jdbc2.optional.MysqlXADataSource--- org.postgresql.xa.PGXADataSource- ~~~ If you need a MySQL or PostgreSQL driver, you can add these using the [Deploy custom configuration files, modules, and source deployments on JBoss EAP for Openshift](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/1524553) knowledge base solution. Make sure the user used to connect to `CLI` has read permission to custom module directory.
root_cause: The JDBC driver bundled with the EAP container has been removed from the EAP 7.3 container. These drivers had already been deprecated in EAP 7.2 container.

title: new machineconfig generated without reason
issue: What are you experiencing? What are you expecting to happen? We have experienced a new MachineConfig being generated for all our MCPs, and this triggered the update of the MCPs during the day, causing issues. We do not expect to have this behavior, without any advice, or control. As a workaround, when we identified the issue, we patched all MCPs with the spec.paused=true, to avoid all our nodes to be restarted, but we cannot keep the paused=true, but, before changing back the paused=false we need no understand what happened here. Define the value or impact to you or the business This kind of behavior have a high impact in our business, because when a MCP update, it will update/restart all the related nodes. Where are you experiencing this behavior? What environment? In all our MCPs, of the SUL-PROD cluster When does this behavior occur? Frequency? Repeatedly? At certain times? It happened about a hour ago, this is the first time we saw it.
resolution: Hello, Me and Bruno were able to reproduce the issue. The conclusion is:- Just rebooting the master node were the controller pod is running doesn't trigger the mc containerruntime recreation [1]- Also Upgrades doesn't trigger the mc containerruntime recreation [2]- mc containerruntime is created if it does not exist *and* the controller pod is recycled [3] So the advice to avoid this situation is:- remove the ContainerRuntimeConfig CR- do not remove mc related to ContainerRuntimeConfig- recycle the controller pod in a controlled window change Let us know if you have any question. Best regards, Clésio Takahashi, RHCE Hybrid Cloud Infrastructure Red Hat Inc.
