title: Understanding TCP Source Port Reuse and TIME_WAIT in OpenShift Node vs. Pod Communications
issue: How does TCP source port reuse and the TIME_WAIT state differ for connections originating directly from an OpenShift node versus from a Pod? This clarification is necessary to understand the default behavior of outbound connections that undergo Network Address Port Translation (NAPT) with different Container Network Interface (CNI) plugins like OVN-Kubernetes and OpenShiftSDN.
resolution: The management of TCP sockets, `TIME_WAIT` state, and source port reuse varies significantly depending on whether the connection originates from a node or a Pod. Connections from Pods to external destinations are handled by the CNI's NAPT mechanism, which behaves differently from the node's native TCP stack. Below are three distinct patterns of behavior. For detailed commands and example outputs, refer to the "Diagnostic Steps" section. 1. **TCP Session Originating from a Node**- When a TCP session is initiated directly from a node, it is managed by the host's standard Linux TCP stack.- After the connection closes, the socket enters a `TIME_WAIT` state for approximately 60 seconds, which can be verified with the `ss` command.- During this period, any attempt to create a new connection using the exact same source port will fail with an "Address already in use" error. 2. **Pod Session with OVN-Kubernetes NAPT**- When a Pod initiates an external connection, the traffic is processed by `conntrack` (Netfilter) on the node to perform NAPT.- The `conntrack` table manages these connections, and after a session closes, the entry remains in `TIME_WAIT` for approximately 120 seconds.- If two Pods on the same node attempt to establish external connections using the same source port, the NAPT mechanism ensures that the source ports of the outbound traffic do not overlap by assigning a different, available port to the second connection. 3. **Pod Session with OpenShiftSDN NAPT**- Similar to OVN-Kubernetes, outbound connections from Pods are managed via NAPT.- While the `conntrack` output does not directly show the port translation, observing the destination port of the return traffic reveals that different ports are being used.- This behavior is definitively confirmed with a `tcpdump` packet capture, which shows that the node assigns a different source port to the second connection.
root_cause: The difference in behavior stems from the two distinct mechanisms managing the connections.- **Node-level connections** are governed directly by the Linux kernel's TCP/IP stack, where `TIME_WAIT` prevents the immediate reuse of a socket tuple and is visible with tools like `ss`.- **Pod-to-external connections** are managed by the `conntrack` system as part of the CNI's NAPT implementation. `conntrack` maintains its own connection tracking table with different timers and logic. It ensures that even if multiple Pods try to use the same source port internally, they are mapped to unique, available source ports on the node for the outbound connection, thus preventing conflicts.

title: How OpenShift Monitoring Prometheus Deletes Data Blocks Based on Retention Time
issue: How does the Prometheus instance in OpenShift Monitoring identify and delete data blocks that have exceeded the configured retention period?
resolution: The Prometheus server included with the OpenShift Monitoring stack enforces data retention by deleting entire compacted data blocks. This cleanup process runs periodically every two hours. For each data block, Prometheus inspects the `maxTime` timestamp within its corresponding `meta.json` file. If this `maxTime` is older than the configured retention period (e.g., 15 days), the entire block is removed from the persistent volume.
root_cause: This mechanism is a core design feature of the Prometheus Time Series Database (TSDB). The TSDB is architected to work with immutable, time-bounded blocks of data for performance and efficiency. Instead of deleting individual metrics, Prometheus manages data at the block level. The key metadata for each block is stored in a `meta.json` file.- Further details on this data structure are available in the [Prometheus On-Disk Layout documentation](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/storage/#on-disk-layout). The retention policy is specifically enforced by a function that compares a block's `maxTime` against the retention threshold.- This logic can be viewed directly in the `BeyondTimeRetention()` function within the [Prometheus source code on GitHub](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/tsdb/db.go).

title: Removing Orphaned Cephfs Subvolumes and Snapshots in ODF
issue: Sometimes Cephfs subvolumes and snapshots become orphaned in ODF. That is to say, Cephfs subvolumes and snapshots lose their connection to their requisite PV in Openshift. The result is that ODF ends up housing more data than it should. This data cannot be accessed by Openshift, making it essentially useless. The following document is an effort to describe how to check for and remove cephfs snapshots and subvolumes.
resolution: This solution focuses only on cleaning Orphaned Cephfs Subvolumes and Snapshots. To implement strategies to prevent the issue from happening in the first place: [CephFS VolumeSnapshot creation (and restore) takes a very long time to complete](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/6931531). **NOTE: Use this process at your own risk. Removal of cephfs subvolumes or snapshots that are not orphans can result in data loss. If at any point you are confused by this process or run into any errors you do not understand, please contact Red Hat Support.** ### Checking For and Removing Cephfs Snapshots 1. Get a list of your Cephfs snapshots and their requisite csi-volume names in Openshift, and save it to a file. ~~~ # oc get volumesnapshotcontent-o 'custom-columns=Name:.spec.volumeSnapshotRef.name,PARENT-CSI-VOL+CEPH-CSI-VOL-SUFFIX-ID:.spec.source.volumeHandle,SNAP-SUFFIX-ID:.status.snapshotHandle,SNAP-CLASS-NAME:.spec.volumeSnapshotClassName' | sed-n '1p; /cephfs/p' > /tmp/cephfs_volumesnapshots.txt ~~~ 2. Get a list of all cephfs snapshots in Ceph. First rsh into the [rook-ceph-tools pod](https://access.redhat.com/articles/4628891) and run the following command: ~~~ # for i in `ceph fs subvolume ls ocs-storagecluster-cephfilesystem csi | jq-r '.[].name'`; do echo subvolume $i:; echo-----; ceph fs subvolume snapshot ls ocs-storagecluster-cephfilesystem $i csi; echo-----; done > /tmp/snaplist.txt ~~~ 3. Exit the pod, then copy the list of snapshots from the rook-ceph-tools pod to your local /tmp directory: ~~~ # exit # oc exec-n openshift-storage $(oc get pods-l app=rook-ceph-tools--no-headers-n openshift-storage | awk '{print $1}')-- cat /tmp/snaplist.txt > /tmp/snaplist.txt ~~~ 4. Compare both files and output only the orphans and it's parent to a new file called `orphaned_snapshots.txt`: ~~~ awk 'NR> 1 {print substr($3, length($3)-35)}' /tmp/cephfs_volumesnapshots.txt | sort | grep-v-f- /tmp/snaplist.txt | grep-o 'csi-snap-[a-f0-9-]\{36\}' | awk 'NR> 1 {print substr($3, length($3)-35)}' /tmp/cephfs_volumesnapshots.txt | sort | grep-v-f- /tmp/snaplist.txt | grep-o 'csi-snap-[a-f0-9-]\{36\}' | awk ' BEGIN {while ((getline pattern < "/dev/stdin") > 0) patterns[pattern] = 1} /^subvolume/ {subvol = $0} {for (pattern in patterns) if ($0 ~ pattern) {print subvol; print $0; echo; break}} ' /tmp/snaplist.txt > /tmp/orphaned_snapshots.txt ~~~ 5. All orphaned snapshots are listed in `orphaned_snapshots.txt`, the orphaned snapshot's parent is listed directly above it (if nothing is listed in this file, you have no orphans): ~~~ subvolume csi-vol-26ff197a-25e6-4b67-bd3f-0a6fc55299fe: <-------- Parent of csi-snap-f31ccf25-5976-42c0-8b18-dc897f9be650 "name": "csi-snap-f31ccf25-5976-42c0-8b18-dc897f9be650" <-------- Orphaned Snapshot subvolume csi-vol-788285d0-a4ab-47a6-bc25-c16ae4649168: <-------- Parent of csi-snap-393e63a0-aa78-421b-a378-b34f4b22290b "name": "csi-snap-393e63a0-aa78-421b-a378-b34f4b22290b" <-------- Orphaned Snapshot ~~~ 6. To get rid of the orphaned snapshots, you need to issue the following command in the rook-ceph-tools pod for each of the listed orphans: ~~~ # ceph fs subvolume snapshot rm ocs-storagecluster-cephfilesystem ${subvolume} ${snap}--group_name csi ~~~ Replace `${subvolume}` with the parent cephfs subvolume of the orphaned snapshot, and `{snap}` with the snapshot name. For example, to remove `csi-snap-f31ccf25-5976-42c0-8b18-dc897f9be650`: ~~~ # ceph fs subvolume snapshot rm ocs-storagecluster-cephfilesystem csi-vol-26ff197a-25e6-4b67-bd3f-0a6fc55299fe csi-snap-f31ccf25-5976-42c0-8b18-dc897f9be650--group_name csi ~~~ 7. Enact Step 6 for each of the orphaned snapshots listed in `orphaned_snapshots.txt` ### Checking For and Removing Cephfs Subvolumes 1. Get a list of all cephfs PVs in Openshift and their requisite volumeHandle attributes, and save it to a file.: ~~~ # oc get pv-o 'custom-columns=NAME:.spec.claimRef.name,PVNAME:.metadata.name,STORAGECLASS:.spec.storageClassName,VOL-NAME:.spec.csi.volumeHandle' | grep cephfs > /tmp/cephfs_pvs.txt ~~~ 2. Get a list of all cephfs subvolumes in Ceph. First rsh into the [rook-ceph-tools pod](https://access.redhat.com/articles/4628891) and run the following command: ~~~ # ceph fs subvolume ls ocs-storagecluster-cephfilesystem csi | jq-r '.[].name' > /tmp/cephfs_subvolumes.txt ~~~ 3. Exit the pod, then copy the list of cephfs subvolumes from the rook-ceph-tools pod to your local /tmp directory: ~~~ # oc exec-n openshift-storage $(oc get pods-l app=rook-ceph-tools--no-headers-n openshift-storage | awk '{print $1}')-- cat /tmp/cephfs_subvolumes.txt > /tmp/cephfs_subvolumes.txt ~~~ 4. Compare both files and output only the orphaned subvolumes to a new file called `orphaned_subvolumes.txt`: ~~~ grep-v "$(awk '{print $4}' /tmp/cephfs_pvs.txt | grep-o '[0-9a-f]\{8\}-[0-9a-f]\{4\}-[0-9a-f]\{4\}-[0-9a-f]\{4\}-[0-9a-f]\{12\}')" /tmp/cephfs_subvolumes.txt > /tmp/orphaned_subvolumes.txt ~~~ 5. All orphaned cephfs subvolumes are listed in `orphaned_subvolumes.txt` (if nothing is listed in this file, you have no orphans): ~~~ # cat /tmp/orphaned_subvolumes.txt csi-vol-806f4943-cf3b-48c2-b29d-9f544e01fbaa <-------- Orphaned Cephfs Subvolume csi-vol-1489c09e-e11b-4160-9836-e6fc36e43075 <-------- Orphaned Cephfs Subvolume ~~~ 6. To get rid of the orphaned subvolumes, you need the to issue the following command in the rook-ceph-tools pod for each of the listed orphans: ~~~ # ceph fs subvolume subvolumes rm ocs-storagecluster-cephfilesystem ${subvolume}--group_name csi ~~~ Replace `${subvolume}` with a subvolume name from `orphaned_subvolumes.txt`. For example, to remove `csi-vol-806f4943-cf3b-48c2-b29d-9f544e01fbaa`: ~~~ # ceph fs subvolume rm ocs-storagecluster-cephfilesystem csi-vol-806f4943-cf3b-48c2-b29d-9f544e01fbaa--group_name csi ~~~ 7. Enact Step 6 for each of the orphaned subvolumes listed in `orphaned_subvolumes.txt`
root_cause: There are many reasons that orphaned cephfs subvolumes and cephfs snapshots can become orphaned. The most common is backup solutions (OADP, Velero, Kasten, etc.) have timeout values that are set too low. If you are encountering this issue frequently and use any of the stated backup solutions, please reference [1]. It goes over why this happens, and how to correct it. [1] https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7128329

title: ODF ocs-osd-removal-job pod failed : not found osd.X in OSDDump
issue: - Trying to redeploy a new OSD (in this example / whole document we assume osd-1 has the issue), the osd pod is in pending: ~~~ rook-ceph-osd-1-5dfc7f94dc-6bnzp 0/2 Pending 0 2m15s ~~~- There is no osd.1 present in ceph layer (`ceph osd df` and `ceph osd dump`)- osd-1 deployment exist in openshift, but there is no `rook-ceph-osd-prepare` pod created for this osd- From the bastion try to delete the osd (so after deletion rook will trigger the creation of a new osd) ~~~ # oc process-n openshift-storage ocs-osd-removal-p FORCE_OSD_REMOVAL=true-p FAILED_OSD_IDS=1 | oc create-f- ~~~ but the ocs-osd-removal-job pod fails with the error ~~~ # oc logs-n openshift-storage job ocs-osd-removal-job-xxxx [client.admin] keyring = /var/lib/rook/openshift-storage/client.admin.keyring 2024-02-27 12:56:38.658774 D | exec: Running command: ceph osd dump--connect-timeout=15--cluster=openshift-storage--conf=/var/lib/rook/openshift-storage/openshift-storage.config--name=client.admin--keyring=/var/lib/rook/openshift-storage/client.admin.keyring--format json 2024-02-27 12:56:38.965991 I | cephosd: validating status of osd.1 2024-02-27 12:56:38.966192 C | multus-validation: failed to get osd status for osd 1: not found osd.1 in OSDDump ~~~
resolution: - Scale down ocs-operator and rook-ceph-operator to have more control on the creation process ~~~ # oc scale deploy ocs-operator rook-ceph-operator--replicas=0 ~~~- Scale down the osd.1 deployment: ~~~ # oc scale deploy rook-ceph-osd-1--replicas=0 ~~~- Get the PVC name associated to osd-1: ~~~ # oc get deploy rook-ceph-osd-1-o yaml|grep "claim" ~~~- **Workaround.1**: Manually delete osd-1 deployment and delete the associated PVC ~~~ # oc delete deployment rook-ceph-osd-1 # oc delete pvc ~~~- Continue with below step [1]- **Workaround.2**: on ceph toolbox pod: `ceph osd create 1`--> that create a new dummy osd.1- Check new osd is present with `ceph osd dump`: ~~~ osd.1 down in weight 1 up_from 0 up_thru 0 down_at 0 last_clean_interval [0,0) exists,new ~~~- From bastion delete the osd.1: this process should delete the deployment of osd.1, the PVC of osd.1, the PV of osd.1 and the osd.1 in ceph config: ~~~ # oc process-n openshift-storage ocs-osd-removal-p FORCE_OSD_REMOVAL=true-p FAILED_OSD_IDS=1 | oc create-f- ~~~- Continue with below steps:- [1] When PV is based on the LSO (Local Storage Operator), If the PV of osd.1 is still present as `Released`, then manually delete that PV: after that the same PV name should appear as `Available`- Clean up any possible previous ceph label on that disk, from the OCS node where that disk is present: ~~~ # for gb in 0 1 10 100 1000; do dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/path_to_device_of_osd bs=1K count=200 oflag=direct,dsync seek=$((gb * 1024**2)); done ~~~ NOTE1. If the disk was encrypted, follow [Step 8 of 5.1. Replacing operational or failed storage devices on clusters backed by local storage devices](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_data_foundation/4.18/html/replacing_devices/openshift_data_foundation_deployed_using_local_storage_devices#replacing-operational-or-failed-storage-devices-on-clusters-backed-by-local-storage-devices_rhodf) to remove encrypted device NOTE2. Check that the disk has NO ceph label on it: ~~~ # head--bytes=60 /dev/path_to_device_of_osd ~~~- Then scale up the ocs-operator, that triggered the creation of new osd-prepare pod that created a new osd.1 with a new PVC ~~~ # oc scale deploy ocs-operator rook-ceph-operator--replicas=1 ~~~- Monitor with "oc get pod-w" the creation of a new osd.1
root_cause: - Could not be identified, during previous removal operation, there was some failure that did not completely removed the osd, but only from ceph side.

title: Upgrading OpenShift AI (RHOAI)
issue: What are the upgrade paths in Red Hat OpenShift AI?
How to upgrade to the next minor version of RHOAI?- Is there any tool/application available to assist with upgrade strategy for the Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI)?
resolution: Customers can now use the [Red Hat Openshift AI Upgrade Graph visualizer and update planner](https://access.redhat.com/labs/rhoaiupi/update_path/), to view channel graphs or plan an upgrade from one version to another. The query parameter needs to be specified based on the RHOAI cluster's channel. The allowed channels are listed in the [Red Hat OpenShift AI Self-Managed Life Cycle](https://access.redhat.com/support/policy/updates/rhoai-sm/lifecycle) official documentation. **Important** ~~~ By default, the Red Hat OpenShift AI Operator follows a sequential update process. This means that if there are several versions between the current version and the version that you intend to upgrade to, Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM) upgrades the Operator to each of the intermediate versions before it upgrades it to the final, target version. If you configure automatic upgrades, OLM automatically upgrades the Operator to the latest available version, without human intervention. If you configure manual upgrades, a cluster administrator must manually approve each sequential update between the current version and the final, target version. ~~~
root_cause: A definitive document containing the RHOAI upgrade paths does not exist.

title: Adding compute nodes to a disconnected cluster installed using Agent Based Installation in RHOCP4
issue: - How to add a new compute node to disconnected cluster after it has been installed using Agent Based Installer (ABI).
resolution: Starting with OpenShift 4.17, it is possible to [add compute nodes to on-premise clusters](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.17/html/release_notes/ocp-4-17-release-notes#ocp-4-17-adding-nodes-to-on-prem_release-notes) using the new `oc adm node-image` command. As per that document: "*This process can be used regardless of how you installed your cluster*". There is also a RFE for adding compute nodes for appliance using ABI: [enable day2 add node for appliance using agent-install](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/AGENT-838), still in progress. ### OpenShift version 4.17 and newer Currently, this procedure is only supported for some platforms: `baremetal`, `vsphere`, `none` and `external`. Refer to [adding worker nodes to an on-premise cluster](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.17/html/nodes/working-with-nodes#adding-node-iso) for additional information. ### OpenShift version 4.12 to 4.16 For the Agent-based installation method, OpenShift versions 4.12 to 4.16 does not cover day 2 procedure of adding/scaling nodes. However, there is a workaround that can be followed: 1. An `ignition` file(i.e.`worker.ign`) will be required:- To retrieve the ignition from RHOCP cluster, follow the steps mentioned in [how to retrieve Master or Worker Ignition Configuration from OpenShift Container Platform 4?](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/5504291). 2. Follow the documentation for [adding compute machines to bare metal](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.16/html/machine_management/managing-user-provisioned-infrastructure-manually#adding-bare-metal-compute-user-infra) (this method is usually followed for bare-metal UPI installed cluster).
root_cause: Starting with OpenShift 4.17, it is possible to [add compute nodes to on-premise clusters](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.17/html/release_notes/ocp-4-17-release-notes#ocp-4-17-adding-nodes-to-on-prem_release-notes).

title: Prometheus targets are down with "connection reset by peer" error in RHOCP 4
issue: - After creating servicemonitor for an application which resides in a namespace that is a `Service Mesh` member, the target reports down with error `connection reset by peer`: ~~~ Login => Administrator View => Observe => Targets => Click on the target and check the error ~~~
resolution: - Identify the application for which targets are reporting down with error `connection reset by peer`: ~~~ $ oc project $ oc get deployment // This can also be daemonset, statefulset or similar resource ~~~- Edit the resource and add below labels. Replace in the label with port on which application is generating the metrics: ~~~ $ oc edit deployment-n spec: template: metadata: annotations: traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeInboundPorts: " " < < < <==== Add this line traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeOutboundPorts: " " < < < <==== Add this line sidecar.istio.io/inject: "true" ~~~- Save the config and the target will start reporting up in a couple of minutes.- If this issue still occurs in the cluster after following above steps, [open a support case](https://access.redhat.com/support/cases/#/case/new/) in the Red Hat Customer Portal referring to this solution.
root_cause: When sidecar container is inject in the application, then it drops connections which are not from `Service Mesh`, which is why `Prometheus` user-workload is not able to successfully connect to the discovered target.

title: OSSM3: Tracing output not present, despite Telemetry object being configured.
issue: - OSSM3 mesh members do not log traces within jaeger/tempo and/or kiali.- There is no trace information printed to standard out within the otel-collector pod logs even when [debugging is configured](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/troubleshooting/).
resolution: ### OpenShift Service Mesh 3- A resolution to this problem is tracked in the following Red Hat Issue.- OSSM-9932- Metrics not showing when Telemetry object is enabled in OSSM 3- As of Tuesday, September 30, 2025, the status of this bug is UNRESOLVED.. The behavior is still currently under investigation ### Workarounds- Create a unified Telemetry object containing both `metrics` and `tracing` of the form below: ~~~--- apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1 kind: Telemetry metadata: name: otel-demo namespace: istio-system spec: metrics:- overrides:- disabled: false providers:- name: prometheus tracing:- providers:- name: otel randomSamplingPercentage: 100 ~~~- Change `name: otel` to match the name within `.spec.values.meshConfig.extensionProviders` for `opentelemetry`
root_cause: - This behavior is currently under investigation.- The exact root cause for the behavior is not known at this time.

title: Unable to reconcile LogFileMetricExporter when migrating from Logging 5 to 6 in RHOCP 4
issue: - `ClusterLogForwarder` fails to deploy due to an immutable field error in the collector `DaemonSet`.- The `cluster-logging-operator` attempts to overwrite an existing `DaemonSet` with conflicting label selectors.- Log collection and forwarding disrupted.- After upgrading from OpenShift Logging v5 to Logging v6, the cluster logging operator pod fails throwing the error: ~~~ {"_ts":"2025-10-08T09:28:07.099724411Z","_level":"0","_component":"cluster-logging-operator","_message":"Reconciler error","LogFileMetricExporter":{"name":"instance","namespace":"openshift-logging"},"_error":{"msg":"Unable to reconcile LogFileMetricExporter: DaemonSet.apps \"logfilesmetricexporter\" is invalid: spec.selector: Invalid value: v1.LabelSelector{MatchLabels:map[string]string{\"app.kubernetes.io/component\":\"logfilesmetricexporter\", \"app.kubernetes.io/instance\":\"instance\", \"app.kubernetes.io/managed-by\":\"cluster-logging-operator\", \"app.kubernetes.io/name\":\"logfilesmetricexporter\", \"app.kubernetes.io/part-of\":\"cluster-logging\"}, MatchExpressions:[]v1.LabelSelectorRequirement(nil)}: field is immutable"},"controller":"logfilemetricexporter","controllerGroup":"logging.openshift.io","controllerKind":"LogFileMetricExporter","name":"instance","namespace":"openshift-logging","reconcileID":"c6c7f0d9-f0f3-46fb-add6-f61fa98033ad"} ~~~
resolution: This issue has been reported to Red Hat engineering. It is being tracked in Bug [LOG-7821](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/LOG-7821). #### Workaround: once upgraded to Red Hat Logging v6 Delete the `logfilesmetricexporter` daemonset and the Red Hat Logging Operator will recreate with the fields required: ~~~ $ oc get daemonset logfilesmetricexporter-n openshift-logging ~~~ #### Workaround: before upgrading to Red Hat Logging v6 If this issue is known by the OpenShift admin before upgrading to Red Hat Logging v6, follow the next steps 1. Before upgrading to Red Hat Logging v6, delete the `logfilemetricexporters` Custom Resource (CR) ~~~ $ oc delete logfilemetricexporters instance-n openshift-logging ~~~ 2. Upgrade to Red Hat Logging v6 following the [Red Hat Documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_logging/6.2/pdf/upgrading_logging/Red_Hat_OpenShift_Logging-6.2-Upgrading_logging-en-US.pdf) 3. Recreate the `logfilemetricexporters` CR: ~~~ $ cat < < EOF | oc create-f- apiVersion: logging.openshift.io/v1alpha1 kind: LogFileMetricExporter metadata: name: instance namespace: openshift-logging spec: nodeSelector: {} resources: limits: cpu: 500m memory: 256Mi requests: cpu: 200m memory: 128Mi tolerations: [] EOF ~~~ For more information, please open a [new support case](https://access.redhat.com/support/cases/#/case/new/) with Red Hat Support.
root_cause: The daemonsets have immutable fields that the Red Hat Logging Operator tries to modify returning the error observed.

title: 3scale TLS Protocol Support (TLS 1.1, 1.2, 1.3)
issue: Clarification is required on which TLS protocol versions are officially supported by Red Hat 3scale API Management, specifically whether TLS 1.1 is accepted:- for outbound connections from APIcast to backends, and- for inbound connections from consumers to the 3scale API gateway.
resolution: TLS 1.1 is supported by 3scale for both directions of communication:- **Inbound connections (consumer → 3scale API):** Consumers can connect to 3scale APIcast using TLS 1.1, TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3.- **Outbound connections (3scale APIcast → backend services):** APIcast can establish secure connections using TLS 1.1, TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3. Support for **custom domains** and TLS 1.2 was introduced in protocol version 1.2, but the underlying Nginx/OpenResty configuration retains compatibility with TLS 1.1 for backward compatibility.
root_cause: In the APIcast configuration (`ssl.conf`), the following directives define the protocols used for both Lua and proxy SSL contexts: ~~~ lua_ssl_protocols TLSv1.1 TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; proxy_ssl_protocols TLSv1.1 TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; ~~~ These values are present in both staging and production configurations for versions 2.14 and 2.15, confirming TLS 1.1 compatibility at the 3scale gateway level.

title: RHOSO Volume service down with partner storage backend
product: Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift
issue: Unable to create a volume due to volume service down (partner storage backend as HPE 3par).
resolution: 1. Edit the CR `OpenStackVersion` to include the custom image from partner in the `customContainerImages` block as below example to HPE 3par and Pure storage.[doc](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openstack_services_on_openshift/18.0/html/integrating_partner_content/integrating-rhoso-storage-services_osp). ~~~ apiVersion: core.openstack.org/v1beta1 kind: OpenStackVersion metadata: name: openstack... spec:... customContainerImages: cinderVolumeImages:: registry.connect.redhat.com/purestorage/openstack-cinder-volume-pure-18-0@sha256:894b1f1a9c75326097017c9c5c633ca64012f1c5ce60e1a4a479a8e78735c461 my-custom-volume: registry.connect.redhat.com/hpe3parcinder/openstack-cinder-volume-hpe3parcinder18-0@sha256:9b50891f7c4f73f262c4b733965f24ce8fc272df79d18ebe76edf729f421f142... ~~~ **NOTE:** "backend_name" This is a label or name you assign to your custom backend inside `cinderVolumes`, not `volume_backend_name`, such as pure-iscsi or my-custom-volume. This name links the container image to a specific backend configuration in your `OpenStackControlPlane` CR. 2. Check that the pod was recreated with the new image. ~~~ oc get pod-n openstack-o=jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].image}' ~~~ 3. Test creating a volume.
root_cause: The default cinder volume image does not contains the needed drivers to communicate with partner storage backend.

title: Tracking memory usage via page_owner
issue: - Memory utilization is high, although there are no processes running on the server and ballooning is not occurring (if a hypervisor is involved).- How do you determine who is using (owns) the pages of memory?
resolution: _**Disclaimer**__Like any debugging tooling, additional overhead will be introduced in some manner. Tracking `page_owner` increases memory consumption on the system. For systems with tightly tuned memory usage considerations, please ensure to test in a lower environment if possible (such as UAT, development, testing, etc) with a similar system to determine if the target system to be debugged will not incur issues from enabling `page_owner` tracking. For RHEL7 releases prior to kernel-3.10.0-1160.31.1.el7 there is a 2.15% memory increase regardless whether `page_owner` is enabled or not For RHEL7 at kernel-3.10.0-1160.31.1.el7 or later, the memory usage increase is only evident after enabling `page_owner` tracking and is roughly 2.15% of total system memory._ 1. Check if `page_owner` is enabled already- To check if `page_owner` tracking is enabled, review the output of `dmesg` and confirm the existence of its sysfs entry: # dmesg | grep page_owner [1.149165] page_owner is disabled # ls-l /sys/kernel/debug/page_owner ls: cannot access /sys/kernel/debug/page_owner: No such file or directory.- In the above output, `page_owner` is confirmed to be disabled. 2. Enable `page_owner` functionality- The below command updates only the currently booted kernel's parameters to enable `page_owner` tracking.- This will not enable it for any other kernels or any future kernel installations. # grubby--args="page_owner=on"--update-kernel=0 3. Reboot the system- The `page_owner` functionality is enabled only via kernel parameters and thus requires a reboot to take effect # reboot 4. Monitor the system after reboot for the issue to reoccur. 5. Once the issue is reproduced, collect `page_owner` debugging data- Debugging data captured by tracking `page_owner` is made available to userspace via `/sys/kernel/debug/page_owner`- The output of that file will look something like the following: Page allocated via order 0, mask 0x2135a PFN 453164 Block 885 type 2 Flags RU L M [] alloc_pages_current+0x98/0x110 []__page_cache_alloc+0x97/0xb0 []__do_page_cache_readahead+0x11f/0x280 [] ondemand_readahead+0x134/0x260 [] page_cache_async_readahead+0x80/0xa0 [] do_generic_file_read.constprop.55+0x3c9/0x510 [] generic_file_aio_read+0x1c9/0x290 [] xfs_file_buffered_aio_read+0x95/0x150 [xfs] Page allocated via order 0, mask 0x2135a PFN 453165 Block 885 type 2 Flags RU L M [] alloc_pages_current+0x98/0x110 []__page_cache_alloc+0x97/0xb0 []__do_page_cache_readahead+0x11f/0x280 [] ondemand_readahead+0x134/0x260 [] page_cache_sync_readahead+0x60/0x80 [] do_generic_file_read.constprop.55+0xdc/0x510 [] generic_file_aio_read+0x1c9/0x290 [] xfs_file_buffered_aio_read+0x95/0x150 [xfs]- With `page_owner` tracking enabled, dump the stacks produced to a file (here the output file is named `page_owner_full.txt`) # cat /sys/kernel/debug/page_owner > page_owner_full.txt- Allow this to run for an appropriate length of time. If working with a Red Hat support associate, follow their recommendation. Otherwise, for slow and gradual growth, perform data collection for several hours or days making sure to monitor the size of the file so it does not fill the filesystem. For tracking short-lived memory bursts, capture data for several seconds or minutes. When finished, terminate (with CTRL+c, `pkill cat`, etc) 6. Upload the `page_owner_full.txt` file to the case for review. ### Optionally 7. Parse the collected data- Even on systems with smaller amounts of installed memory, the data can grow to be quite voluminous.- If the kernel-tools package of version **kernel-tools-3.10.0-1160.el7** and later is available then the below command can be used to parse the data, since the binary `page_owner_sort` is already added in **kernel-tools-3.10.0-1160.el7** and later version.- Execute page_owner_sort against the captured data. The below command writes the parsed data to a file, sorted_page_owner.txt. # page_owner_sort page_owner_full.txt sorted_page_owner.txt- If the **kernel-tools-3.10.0-1160.el7** or later is not present then, work through the **"Diagnostic Steps"** section of this article to produce the page_owner_sort script which helps in parsing the captured data in page_owner_full.txt. For this article, the script will be referred to as page_owner_sort.c for the source code, and the script itself will be called page_owner_sort. 8. Review the output file- Below is an example output from `sorted_page_owner.txt`: # less sorted_page_owner.txt 98304 times: Page allocated via order 0, mask 0x280d0 [] dma_generic_alloc_coherent+0x8f/0x140 [] x86_swiotlb_alloc_coherent+0x21/0x50 [] i40iw_allocate_dma_mem+0xa0/0x100 [i40iw] [] i40iw_puda_create_rsrc+0x8c2/0xb70 [i40iw] [] i40iw_open.part.10+0xb6d/0x18f0 [i40iw] [] i40iw_open+0x3b/0x50 [i40iw] [] i40e_client_subtask+0xbd/0x130 [i40e] [] i40e_service_task+0x2e4/0x1010 [i40e] 68942 times: Page allocated via order 0, mask 0x0 [] page_cgroup_init+0x11c/0x156 [] start_kernel+0x387/0x46c [] x86_64_start_reservations+0x24/0x26 [] x86_64_start_kernel+0x154/0x177 [] start_cpu+0x5/0x14 [] 0xffffffffffffffff 49152 times: Page allocated via order 0, mask 0x280d0 [] dma_generic_alloc_coherent+0x8f/0x140 [] x86_swiotlb_alloc_coherent+0x21/0x50 [] i40iw_allocate_dma_mem+0xa0/0x100 [i40iw] [] i40iw_puda_create_rsrc+0x8c2/0xb70 [i40iw] [] i40iw_initialize_ieq+0x86/0xc0 [i40iw] [] i40iw_open.part.10+0xb90/0x18f0 [i40iw] [] i40iw_open+0x3b/0x50 [i40iw] [] i40e_client_subtask+0xbd/0x130 [i40e] [...]- In the above example output, the majority of allocations came from the `i40iw` module strongly implying a memory leak within the module.
root_cause: ### RHEL8.3 (`kernel-4.18.0-240.el8_3` and above) The initial feature was developed in Linux v4.0 and backported to RHEL 8.3 GA. This is the RHEL8 commit that introduced the feature to track allocations of particular pages: ~~~ commit 48c96a3685795e52903e60c7ee115e5e22e7d640 Author: Joonsoo Kim Date: Fri Dec 12 16:56:01 2014-0800 mm/page_owner: keep track of page owners This is the page owner tracking code which is introduced so far ago. It is resident on Andrew's tree, though, nobody tried to upstream so it remain as is. Our company uses this feature actively to debug memory leak or to find a memory hogger so I decide to upstream this feature. This functionality help us to know who allocates the page. When allocating a page, we store some information about allocation in extra memory. Later, if we need to know status of all pages, we can get and analyze it from this stored information. In previous version of this feature, extra memory is statically defined in struct page, but, in this version, extra memory is allocated outside of struct page. It enables us to turn on/off this feature at boottime without considerable memory waste. Although we already have tracepoint for tracing page allocation/free, using it to analyze page owner is rather complex. We need to enlarge the trace buffer for preventing overlapping until userspace program launched. And, launched program continually dump out the trace buffer for later analysis and it would change system behaviour with more possibility rather than just keeping it in memory, so bad for debug. Moreover, we can use page_owner feature further for various purposes. For example, we can use it for fragmentation statistics implemented in this patch. And, I also plan to implement some CMA failure debugging feature using this interface. I'd like to give the credit for all developers contributed this feature, but, it's not easy because I don't know exact history. Sorry about that. Below is people who has "Signed-off-by" in the patches in Andrew's tree. ~~~ ### RHEL7 (`kernel-3.10.0-1160.el7` and above) Not all of the RHEL8 implementation could be backported. Therefore a portion of `page_owner` was backported to RHEL7.9 GA as part of an RFE BZ request. This included a number of Red Hat specifically developed commits: ~~~ 7817f23beb3fe88c945f256ac11d04aa04a7f54e [mm] mm/page_owner: convert page_owner_inited to static key f37df91c647e6d9a411011a8ed15d4cd4b750bf3 [mm] mm/page_owner: set correct gfp_mask on page_owner 14a4f111610cb721cceef8e0a1dffcbf3a7e558e [mm] mm/page_owner: fix possible access violation e6dc363573234c6ca3b769de1e5eebc851ae3629 [mm] mm/page_owner: use late_initcall to hook in enabling 48cba4919430f45ecae31aef0f837331f96e485f [mm] mm/page_owner: remove unnecessary stack_trace field 6a3ec607d84c8617b70919fd8d06309642eed03d [mm] mm/page_owner: correct owner information for early allocated pages e26a6d2618e71ec69833712fbae3b72f480b634a [mm] mm/page_owner: keep track of page owners 86bcf7a923df6c3bc65f0625bef06bd4a6d8988a [documentation] Documentation: add new page_owner document ~~~ ### RHEL7 (3.10.0-1160.31.1.el7 and later) **Note** The patch set in the original RHEL7.9 `kernel-3.10.0-1160.el7` implementation introduced a roughly 2.15% of system memory increase to memory usage even with `page_owner` tracking disabled. As a result of issues raised by users not wanting the `page_owner` feature, an additional patch was introduced to Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7.9.z in `kernel-3.10.0-1160.31.1.el7` to reduce this increased memory usage when page_owner is disabled to 0.64%. The 2.15% memory increase will now only be seen if `page_owner` is enabled. ~~~ commit aff80dc921ceb97ca47f5a924e34fc529b8569c1 [...] mm: reduce struct page_cgroup overhead when page_owner is not enabled Bugzilla: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1948451 Upstream status: RHEL only Tested: KT-1+ integration/regression tests and verified by the reporting customer, as documented in the BZ ticket. page_owner is a tracking tool that was requested by CEE for integration in RHEL as it provides the engineers on the field with valuable information on kernel memory usage by drivers and other subsystems, without having to provide instrumented custom kernel builds to the customers. It was brought into RHEL-7.9 via RFE Bug 1781726. Given the constraints we had (and still have) for code integration into RHEL-7, it was decided to only integrate the original implementation of the feature, which requires that the data structure that is utilized to create the map of memory sections to be statically extended. As the maps of every memory section have to get allocated regardless of page_owner being enabled or disabled (it's disabled by default) the overhead of extending struct page_cgroup is is a cost paid for both cases. The total overhead cost was fully advertised as 2.15% of total system memory. Unfortunately, we hit a corner case (Bug 1948451) with a customer setup that demands reserving over 90% of the system memory to a hugepages pool which leaves the system virtually without room for its workload after this huge reservation and the noted overhead are accounted for the runtime. In order to address the aforementioned corner-case without having to backport the extensive, invasive, and risky changes that were originally dismissed, we are settling on an RHEL7-only approach where we can shave off almost 70% of that noted overhead for the default case (page_owner OFF), and the code changes are mostly concentrated on the feature code, leaving the generic code paths untouched. IOW, there's no change for the default case (page_owner off) other than the reduced memory overhead. This patch reduces the previous overhead of 88 bytes per page frame to 16 bytes per page frame (0.4% of system's memory in the default case), which will cause struct page_cgroup size to shrink from 104 bytes to 32 bytes, giving us a 69.2% overhead reduction [1-(32/104) = 0.69231] * RHEL-7.9 stock kernel: struct page_cgroup {long unsigned int flags; /* 0 8 */ struct mem_cgroup * mem_cgroup; /* 8 8 */ struct page_ext ext; /* 16 88 */ /* size: 104, cachelines: 2, members: 3 */ /* last cacheline: 40 bytes */}; * RHEL-7.9 patched kernel: struct page_cgroup {long unsigned int flags; /* 0 8 */ struct mem_cgroup * mem_cgroup; /* 8 8 */ struct page_ext ext; /* 16 16 */ /* size: 32, cachelines: 1, members: 3 */ /* last cacheline: 32 bytes */}; The code changes for this feat are not complex, and the bulk of the changes is mostly contained to mm/page_owner.c and to include/linux/page_ext.h (data struct changes) with small sprinkles of fairy dust on mm/page_cgroup.c and related headers. There are some trade-offs to consider for the case page_owner=on, obviously, as we are now shifting the heaviest part of the overhead (rightfully) to that particular use case. Because we are utilizing dynamic allocation to provide the storage for the page_owner tracking objects, the noticeable trade-offs are: i. because there is no slab size perfectly aligned with 80 bytes, (sizeof(struct page_owner) == 80), overhead for the page_owner=on case gets increased by yet another 16 bytes / page, as the objects will now come out of the kmalloc-96 bucket; ii. because kmalloc() can return NULL, if/when that happens, we'll lose the ability to track ownership for each one of the pages to which kmalloc has returned NULL. The tracking code changes deals with the NULL pointer without complications, though. ~~~

title: How to configure user defined cert for AMQ Artemis broker installed on openshift?
issue: - How to configure user defined cert for AMQ Artemis broker installed on openshift?
resolution: - Use a customer-provided signed `.pfx` certificate for the AMQ Broker’s SSL acceptor instead of the self-signed one.- The AMQ Operator expects the broker’s SSL configuration to come from a Kubernetes Secret referenced in: sslSecret: amq-tls-secret- The secret must contain:- `broker.ks` – Keystore file (JKS or PKCS#12)- `broker.ts` – Truststore file (JKS or PKCS#12)- And optionally: `keyStorePassword` `trustStorePassword` The operator mounts these into the broker pod automatically under `/etc/amq-secret-volume`. Step-by-Step Procedure- Convert the `.pfx` to separate keystore/truststore files You have the `.pfx` (PKCS#12) file, say:`xxx-broker.pfx` Extract keystore (contains key + cert): openssl pkcs12-in xxx-broker.pfx-out broker-key.pem-nocerts-nodes openssl pkcs12-in xxx-broker.pfx-out broker-cert.pem-clcerts-nokeys You may also extract CA chain if present: openssl pkcs12-in xxx-broker.pfx-out ca-chain.pem-cacerts-nokeys Now you can either: Keep them as PEM files and repackage into a `.p12` keystore, or Directly import them into a Java Keystore (JKS). Let’s use PKCS12 format that’s simpler. ``` Create broker keystore: openssl pkcs12-export \-in broker-cert.pem \-inkey broker-key.pem \-certfile ca-chain.pem \-name "amq-broker" \-out broker.ks \-password pass:changeit ```- Create truststore (optional but recommended contains CA chain): ``` keytool-import-trustcacerts-alias xxx-ca \-file ca-chain.pem \-keystore broker.ts \-storepass changeit-noprompt ```- Create the Kubernetes Secret Now create a secret containing both keystore and truststore: ``` oc create secret generic amq-tls-secret \--from-file=broker.ks=broker.ks \--from-file=broker.ts=broker.ts \--from-literal=keyStorePassword=changeit \--from-literal=trustStorePassword=changeit ```- This secret name must match the name referenced in your YAML: sslSecret: amq-tls-secret- Verify Your Broker YAML Your existing `deployment.yaml` already points correctly: ``` acceptors:- name: acceptor protocols: amqp,core port: 61616 needClientAuth: false sslEnabled: true sslSecret: amq-tls-secret verifyHost: false expose: true ```- If you need to serve over port 443 (for example, as in the Red Hat article), just expose that port in the service, not necessarily in the acceptor config the Operator typically maps routes automatically for the `console` or `amqp` protocols.- Apply and Verify Apply your updated deployment: oc apply-f deployment.yaml Then check, `oc get pods`, `oc logs `- Test SSL From your workstation or test pod: openssl s_client-connect:443-showcerts- Check that the certificate chain includes `*.xxx.com` and is signed by the expected CA. `.pfx` = `.p12` — both are PKCS#12 format; the AMQ Operator supports this.- Make sure the file encoding is binary (not base64) when creating the secret.- If your broker needs client authentication, set: needClientAuth: true and include the client CA in your truststore.

title: Image pull fails as rejected by policy in OpenShift 4
issue: When trying to deploy a container image, the deployment fails with `ImagePullBackOff` and the following error message: ~~~ Failed to pull image "registry.example.com:5000/my-project/myimage@sha256:c7be7ee7e61afee1618c09271db59f846aa5a9e17487f909793cef5f722303c0": rpc error: code = Unknown desc = Source image rejected: Running image docker://registry.example.com:5000/my-project/myimage@sha256:c7be7ee7e61afee1618c09271db59f846aa5a9e17487f909793cef5f722303c0 is rejected by policy. ~~~

When trying to deploy a container image, the deployment fails with `ImagePullBackOff` and the following error message is observed: ~~~ Failed to pull image "example.com/my-image/my-image@sha256:xxxxxxx": rpc error: code = Unknown desc = SignatureValidationFailed: copying system image from manifest list: Source image rejected: Running image docker://example.com/my-image/my-image@sha256:xxxxxxx is rejected by policy. ~~~
resolution: Add the registry to the `allowedRegistries` in the Image Controller configuration (`image.config.openshift.io/cluster`) as described in the [image controller configuration parameters](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.18/html/images/image-configuration#images-configuration-parameters_image-configuration): ~~~ [..] spec: registrySources: allowedRegistries:- quay.io- registry.redhat.io- image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000- registry.example.com:5000 ~~~ > **Note:** when using the `allowedRegistries`, make sure to include the OpenShift default set of registry hostnames (`quay.io,registry.redhat.io,image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000`) as they are required for OpenShift.
root_cause: Image registry sources can be restricted by using either a block list or an allow list. These lists are configured in the cluster `Image` configuration CR (`image.config.openshift.io/cluster`) under `.spec.registrySources` as either `blockedRegistries` or `allowedRegistries` respectively. Note that these settings are mutually exclusive: either `blockedRegistries` or `allowedRegistries` can be set, but not both at the same time. * When using an allow list (`allowedRegistries`), all registries are blocked except for those explicitly identified in the allow list. * When using a block list (`blockedRegistries`), all registries are allowed except for those explicitly identified in the block list. > **IMPORTANT NOTE:** when access to a registry is restricted this way, it is not possible to even use mirrored images from the restricted registries using the name of the restricted registry. For preventing access to a registry allowing mirrored images, please refer to [how to block access to a registry in OpenShift and use a registry mirror instead](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7106542). The container runtime policy for pulling images is defined on the OpenShift Container Platform Worker node in the file `/etc/containers/policy.json`. This file is generated by the `machine-config` Operator and is derived from the Image Controller configuration (`image.config.openshift.io/cluster`). Any changes to the `cluster` resource require a new machine configuration to be generated and pushed out to the nodes to take effect.

title: Windows stops with with HYPERVISOR_ERROR code

title: Using API v2 to review the registry's content
issue: - Want to list the available repos from the registry's catalog- Want to list the available tags from a repo- Want to list the blobs from a digest image
resolution: Providing the curl commands to access the registry. ##### How to run the queries with the RHOCP internal registry: Example with RHOCP internal registry: ~~~ # Retrieve your Token & Registry POD TOKEN=$(oc whoami-t) Registry_POD=$(oc get pod-n openshift-image-registry | grep "^image-registry-" | awk '($3 =="Running"){print $1}' | head-1) # List all repositories: oc rsh-n openshift-image-registry ${Registry_POD} curl-k-s-H "Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}" https://image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/v2/_catalog | jq-r '.' | jq # List all tags available in a repository: repo=openshift/php oc rsh-n openshift-image-registry ${Registry_POD} curl-k-s-H "Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}" https://image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/v2/${repo}/tags/list | jq-r '.' | jq # Pulling an Image Manifest repo=openshift/nginx tag="latest" oc rsh-n openshift-image-registry ${Registry_POD} curl-k-s-H "Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}" https://image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/v2/${repo}/manifests/${tag} | jq-r '.' | jq # To get the additional information from a tag or a manifestID. As an example here based on the manifestID from the POD logs: repo=openshift/nginx sha256sum_val="aed76750ad2d10af5745286eba75b8746a33255e4913e7a166e8e2c6506ac0c5" oc rsh-n openshift-image-registry ${Registry_POD} curl-k-Ls-H "Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json"-H "Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json"-H "Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}" https://image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/v2/${repo}/manifests/sha256:${sha256sum_val} | jq-r '.' | jq ~~~ ##### How to use the queries with an external registry (nexus, docker, Artifactory,...) 1. Set your Registry URI and PORT REGISTRY_URI= REGISTRY_PORT= # If not set the commands will assume port 5000. 2. Define your authentication method Depending of the allowed method to connect to the registry, please use one of the following:- Using username & passwd: REG_USERNAME= REG_PASSWORD= AUTHENTICATION_METHOD="-u ${REG_USERNAME}:${REG_PASSWORD}"- Using a token: TOKEN= AUTHENTICATION_METHOD="-H \"Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}\"" 3. Specify an additional PATH (optional): Some registry will require an optional PATH:- **Artifactory** may required additional path such as: artifactory/api/docker/repo_name/ Set the OPTIONAL_PATH variable (including a '/' at the end), when required. OPTIONAL_PATH="artifactory/api/docker/my_repo_name/" 4. Run the desired command: ~~~ # List all repositories: curl-k-s ${AUTHENTICATION_METHOD} https://${REGISTRY_URI}:${REGISTRY_PORT:-5000}/${OPTIONAL_PATH}v2/_catalog | jq-r '.' | jq # List all tags available in a repository: repo=openshift/php curl-k-s ${AUTHENTICATION_METHOD} https://${REGISTRY_URI}:${REGISTRY_PORT:-5000}/${OPTIONAL_PATH}v2/${repo}/tags/list | jq-r '.' | jq # Pulling an Image Manifest repo=openshift/nginx tag="latest" curl-k-s ${AUTHENTICATION_METHOD} https://${REGISTRY_URI}:${REGISTRY_PORT:-5000}/${OPTIONAL_PATH}v2/${repo}/manifests/${tag} | jq-r '.' | jq # To get the additional information from a tag or a manifestID. As an example here based on the manifestID from the POD logs: repo=openshift/nginx sha256sum_val="aed76750ad2d10af5745286eba75b8746a33255e4913e7a166e8e2c6506ac0c5" curl-k-Ls-H "Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json"-H "Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json" ${AUTHENTICATION_METHOD} https://${REGISTRY_URI}:${REGISTRY_PORT:-5000}/${OPTIONAL_PATH}v2/${repo}/manifests/sha256:${sha256sum_val} | jq-r '.' | jq ~~~
root_cause: Most of the registry used for internal and external support in RHOCP use the same API structure `v2`. It's possible to query the API to retrieve some details from the registry and confirm the presence of desired repo/tags.

title: Control Plane ingress operator and konnectivity-http-proxy appears to be making remote dns calls on tcp by default, if the dataplane infra dns is not listening on tcp, the operator goes into degrade status.
issue: - Control Plane ingress operator and konnectivity-http-proxy appears to be making remote dns calls on tcp by default, if the dataplane infra dns is not listening on tcp, the operator goes into degrade status.
resolution: - Ensure dataplane coredns traffic is able to reach infra dns on port tcp and infra dns is serving traffic on tcp.- Red Hat engineering is aware of this and it is under review to check if CoreDNS can be configure (day-2 or specifically for hcp cluster) with option [prefer_udp(RFE-8277)](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/RFE-8277).- This has been also mentioned in [HCP essential requirement doc](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.18/html/hosted_control_planes/preparing-to-deploy-hosted-control-planes#requirements-for-hosted-control-planes)
root_cause: - It appears by default ingress operator + konnectivity-http-proxy on dataplane making remote dns calls on tcp by default. Red Hat engineering is aware of this behavior and currently under investigation, [bug OCPBUGS-60631](issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPBUGS-60631). For more details, please reach out to Red Hat technical support.

title: Scheduler pod crashes during numa resources operator installation with API group resource error
issue: The scheduler pod fails with the following error during installation. `Cannot create clientset for NodeTopologyResource" err="failed to get API group resources: unable to retrieve the complete list of server APIs: topology.node.k8s.io/v1alpha2: the server could not find the requested resource`
resolution: Please update the NUMAResourcesOperator custom resource to use the correct API group nodetopology.openshift.io/v1 instead of the deprecated topology.node.k8s.io/v1alpha2, in order to align with the [documentation](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.14/scalability_and_performance/cnf-numa-aware-scheduling.html#installing-the-numa-resources-operator_numa-aware).
root_cause: The API group topology.node.k8s.io/v1alpha2 could not be found. The correct API group to use is nodetopology.openshift.io/v1. However, the deprecated API topology.node.k8s.io/v1alpha2 is currently being referenced in the NUMAResourcesOperator custom resource [documentation](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.14/scalability_and_performance/cnf-numa-aware-scheduling.html#installing-the-numa-resources-operator_numa-aware).

title: Does OpenShift AI Installation need a access to ngc.download.nvidia.cn domain?
issue: - Does OpenShift AI Installation need a access to ngc.download.nvidia.cn domain?
resolution: Access to NVIDIA domains such as **developer.download.nvidia.com** or **ngc.download.nvidia.cn** is generally **not** required for standard **RHOAI** Self-Managed **installations**. This is because RHOAI utilizes **pre-built**, CUDA-based container images hosted on Red Hat's registries (_registry.redhat.io_ and_quay.io_), and the installation process **does not** directly download content from NVIDIA. However, these NVIDIA domains would be necessary if the environment specifically pulls artifacts directly from NVIDIA, for instance:- When customizing or building CUDA-based images using NVIDIA's base images.- When deploying additional software from the NVIDIA NGC catalog, such as NGC containers, CUDA toolkits, or model libraries. In summary, the domains_developer.download.nvidia.com_ and_ngc.download.nvidia.cn_ are **only** needed for direct **pulls** from **NVIDIA**.

title: Error while creating Pod with SR-IOV CNI plug-in additional network configuration.
issue: The pod is failing to come up with below error in the events. ~~~ Warning FailedCreatePodSandBox 38s (x4785 over 20h) kubelet, worker-0.ocp4.lab.com (combined from similar events): Failed create pod sandbox: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to create pod network sandbox k8s_sriov-pod-1_openshift-sriov-network-operator_150efb80-af96-4071- be12-82538c32cace_0(986fc4eed52a417525fe0796ed50d9cb91fa61f57f3257c5bf0eu8jllasd988a): Multus: [openshift-sriov-network-operator/sriov-pod-1]: error adding container to network "sriov-net": delegateAdd: error invoking DelegateAdd- "sriov": error in getting result from AddNetwork: SRIOV-CNI failed to load netconf: LoadConf(): VF pci addr is required ~~~

The webhook of `network-resources-injector` failed. ~~~ 2025-10-10T15:15:05.526138352+09:00 W0918 07:17:05.526026 17 dispatcher.go:210] Failed calling webhook, failing open network-resources-injector-config.k8s.io: failed calling webhook "network-resources-injector-config.k8s.io": failed to call webhook: Post "https://network-resources-injector-service.openshift-sriov-network-operator.svc:443/mutate?timeout=10s": EOF ~~~
resolution: ### For a multi-node environment- Make sure you enable the Network Resource Injector and admission control webhook using the below commands. ~~~ $ oc patch sriovoperatorconfig default--patch '{"spec": {"enableInjector": true}}'--type=merge $ oc patch sriovoperatorconfig default--patch '{"spec": {"enableOperatorWebhook": true}}'--type=merge ~~~- If you find both values have already been enabled but still see the errors, ***delete the Pod and the Pod should be recreated*** or ***specify the device information in the Pod definition manually***. ~~~ resources: limits: cpu: "2" hugepages-1Gi: 1Gi memory: 1Gi openshift.io/: "1" # <========= requests: cpu: "2" hugepages-1Gi: 1Gi memory: 1Gi openshift.io/: "1" # <========= ~~~- ***The*** `resourceInjectorMatchCondition` ***featureGate will resolve the issue***. It can be enabled as a featuregate on ***4.19+***. Please refer to [the documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.19/html/networking_operators/sr-iov-operator#about-network-resource-injector_configuring-sriov-operator) for more details. ### For Single Node cluster- It is recommended to ***disable Network Resource Injector and admission control webhook values*** and the user needs to ***explicitly set the device information in the Pod definition manually***.
root_cause: * The Network Resource Injector and admission control webhook was found to be disabled. According to the [documentation of SR-IOV Network Operator](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.19/html/networking_operators/sr-iov-operator#nw-sriov-configuring-operator_configuring-sriov-operator), it is recommended setting `true` for both `enableInjector` and `enableOperatorWebhook`. ~~~ # oc get sriovoperatorconfig-n openshift-sriov-network-operator-o yaml apiVersion: v1 items:- apiVersion: sriovnetwork.openshift.io/v1 kind: SriovOperatorConfig metadata: [...] spec: configDaemonNodeSelector: feature.node.kubernetes.io/network-sriov.capable: "true" enableInjector: false <---- enableOperatorWebhook: false <---- ~~~ * It could be a transient issue that the `network-resources-injector` that is responsible to populate the SRIOV resources but it didn't receive the mutating webhook request due to a temporary network issue. * For Single Node cluster, because when you reboot the node it also reboots the webhook and there is a race between when the application pod starts and the webhook starts so we can miss the mutation. So for a Single Node cluster, it's recommended for the user to add the resource in the pod definition manually.

title: How to identify the backend disk for an OSD
issue: - How to locate the physical drive of an OSD in LSO provisioned ODF cluster?
resolution: The following procedure outlines how to find the storage device associated with an OSD in an ODF 4.x cluster. 1. Fetch the PVC names for all the OSDs using below command: ~~~ $ oc get pod-n openshift-storage-o 'custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.labels.ceph-osd- id,PVCNAME:.spec.volumes[*].persistentVolumeClaim' |grep-v none NAME PVCNAME 0 map[claimName:ocs-deviceset-lso-volumeset-0-data-1g8rk8] 1 map[claimName:ocs-ocs-deviceset-lso-volumeset-0-data-0l9dgk] 2 map[claimName:ocs-deviceset-lso-volumeset-0-data-3gbxtk] ~~~ 2. Get the hostname, PVC name, symlink or path for the devices using below command: ~~~ $ oc get pv-o 'custom-columns=HOST-NAME:.metadata.labels.kubernetes\.io/hostname,PVCNAME:.spec.claimRef.name,SYMLINK:.spec.local.path,DEV-NAME:.metadata.annotations.storage\.openshift\.com/device-name' | grep-v none HOST-NAME PVCNAME SYMLINK DEV-NAME dell-per7525-05.lab.redhat.com ocs-deviceset-lso-volumeset-0-data-1g8rk8 /mnt/local-storage/lso-volumeset/nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_a-part1 nvme0n1p1 dell-per7525-04.lab.redhat.com ocs-deviceset-lso-volumeset-0-data-0l9dgk /mnt/local-storage/lso-volumeset/nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_b-part1 nvme2n1p1 dell-per7525-04.lab.redhat.com ocs-deviceset-lso-volumeset-0-data-3gbxtk /mnt/local-storage/lso-volumeset/nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_c-part1 nvme1n1p1 ~~~ OR Follow below steps one by one for each OSDs: 1. Retrieve the node name for the OSD pod: ~~~ $ oc get po-n openshift-storage-owide | grep 'osd-id' Ex: $ oc get po-n openshift-storage-owide | grep 'osd-0' rook-ceph-osd-0-6f4c56dfb9-rb4qw 2/2 Running 0 44m 10.x.x.x dell-per7525-05.lab.redhat.com ~~~ 2. Match the OSD pod to it's respective PVC: ~~~ $ oc get-n openshift-storage-o yaml deployment rook-ceph-osd-{osd-id} | grep "ceph.rook.io/pvc:" Ex: $ oc get-n openshift-storage-o yaml deployment rook-ceph-osd-0 | grep "ceph.rook.io/pvc:" ceph.rook.io/pvc: ocs-deviceset-lso-volumeset-0-data-1g8rk8 ceph.rook.io/pvc: ocs-deviceset-lso-volumeset-0-data-1g8rk8 ~~~ 3. Locate the PV corresponding to the PVC: ~~~ $ oc get-n openshift-storage pvc Ex: $ oc get-n openshift-storage pvc ocs-deviceset-mylocalvol-0-data-1wt4gx NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY ACCESS MODES STORAGECLASS VOLUMEATTRIBUTESCLASS AGE ocs-deviceset-lso-volumeset-0-data-1g8rk8 Bound local-pv-b04cd30d 2Ti RWO lso-volumeset 43m ~~~ 4. Find the device ID: ~~~ $ oc get pv-oyaml | grep path Ex: $ oc get pv local-pv-b04cd30d-oyaml | grep path path: /mnt/local-storage/lso-volumeset/nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_a-part1 ~~~ With the hostname, path or symlink in hand, debug into the node and map the device with associated OSDs as follows: 5. Go inside the OSD node and identify the disk name for the ID that we received from the previous command output. ~~~ $ oc debug node/ # chroot /host Ex: $ oc debug node/ip-10-x-x-x.sa-east-1.compute.internal Starting pod/ip-10-x-x-x-sa-east-1computeinternal-debug-49thj... To use host binaries, run `chroot /host` Pod IP: 10.x.x.x If you don't see a command prompt, try pressing enter. sh-5.1# chroot/host sh: chroot/host: No such file or directory sh-5.1# chroot /host # ls-l /mnt/local-storage/lso-volumeset/ # ls-l /dev/disk/by-id/ Ex: sh-5.1# ls-l /mnt/local-storage/lso-volumeset/ total 0 lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 68 Aug 15 10:58 nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_a-part1-> /dev/disk/by-id/nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_a-part1 lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 68 Aug 15 10:58 nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_b-part1-> /dev/disk/by-id/nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_b-part1 lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 68 Aug 15 10:58 nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_c-part1-> /dev/disk/by-id/nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_c-part1 sh-5.1# ls-l /dev/disk/by-id/ total 0 lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 13 Aug 15 11:00 nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_a-part1->../../nvme0n1p1 lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 13 Aug 15 11:00 nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_b-part1->../../nvme2n1p1 lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 13 Aug 15 10:07 nvme-Dell_Ent_NVMe_v2_AGN_RI_U.2_1.92TB_c-part1->../../nvme1n1p1 ~~~
root_cause: - For any OSD redeployment or replacement activity, it is a crucial step to know the backend disk associated with the OSDs in Red Hat Openshift Data Foundation.

title: Multiple NVIDIA H100 GPUs Fail with Driver Errors in KubeVirt VMs on Hosted Control Plane NodePools Configured with HostDevices
issue: When attempting to pass through multiple NVIDIA H100 PCIe devices to KubeVirt Virtual Machines (VMs) provisioned via NodePools in a Hosted Control Plane (HCP) cluster, the VMs encounter hardware driver errors. This issue specifically appears when more than one GPU is assigned to a VM, even though single GPU passthrough works correctly.
resolution: - The current solution involves manually configuring the CPU model for the affected VMs to host-passthrough. While direct configuration via NodePools is not yet supported, the following workarounds can be applied.- A permanent and supported solution to allow setting the CPU model directly within the NodePool specification, and/or ensuring adequate MMIO space without manual workarounds, is being tracked by Red Hat Engineering under [OCPBUGS-55974](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPBUGS-55974) Workaround: **1. Manually Edit Individual VM Configuration and edit the VM's configuration to set cpu.model to host-passthrough** ~~~ apiVersion: kubevirt.io/v1 kind: VirtualMachine metadata: name: example-vm spec: running: true template: spec: domain: cpu: model: host-passthrough ~~~ Restart VM. **2. Set Cluster Default CPU Model (Broader Impact- Use with Caution):** This approach sets host-passthrough as the default CPU model for all VMs in the cluster that do not explicitly specify a CPU model in their spec. This can have a broad impact on other VMs and potentially affect live migration capabilities. Check the current default CPU model ~~~ oc get hco-n openshift-cnv kubevirt-hyperconverged-o yaml | yq '.spec.defaultCPUModel' ~~~ Patch the HyperConverged object to set defaultCPUModel ~~~ oc patch hco-n openshift-cnv kubevirt-hyperconverged--type=merge-p '{"spec":{"defaultCPUModel":"host-passthrough"}}' ~~~ Restart VMs. Important Note: The manual editing of individual VM configurations (Workaround 1) is generally preferred as it is less disruptive than setting a cluster-wide default.
root_cause: The issue is related to the default CPU model used by VMs within Hosted Control Plane NodePools. The default CPU model may not provide sufficient PCI MMIO (Memory-Mapped I/O) space for multiple high-end GPUs like the NVIDIA H100. While the PciMmio64Mb option was previously a workaround for similar issues, it's considered obsolete in "host-passthrough" CPU mode, where qemu is expected to handle MMIO automatically. However, the VMs provisioned by NodePools do not expose a direct option to configure the CPU model, preventing the use of host-passthrough for these specific VMs by default.

title: In Openshift Virtualization the Custom RBAC Role with resourceNames field does not effectively filter the results of that list operation for VMs.
issue: - Standard RBAC is primarily designed to work at the namespace level. A rule that grants access to a resource type (like virtualmachines) will apply to all instances of that resource within the namespace. The resourceNames field, which is meant to limit access to specific resources, does not reliably filter the output of list commands.
resolution: - Based on the current OpenShift architecture, it is not possible to restrict access to a specific subset of VMs within a namespace using standard RBAC policies. If a user is granted permissions to `get` or `list` the `virtualmachines` resource type in a given namespace, they will be able to see all VMs within that namespace.- The current RBAC model is designed to be scoped at the namespace level, not the individual resource level for the `virtualmachines` resource. The `resourceNames` field, while intended for this purpose, does not function as a reliable mechanism to filter which VMs a user can see in a list.- The only way to achieve a separation of access is to place the VMs in separate namespaces. * Create a dedicated namespace for each VM or for each group of VMs that a user should have access to. * Grant the user the appropriate `view` or `edit` permissions for that specific namespace using `oc policy add-role-to-user-n `.- This approach ensures that a user's permissions are contained within a specific namespace, preventing them from accessing resources in other namespaces.
root_cause: * The issue stems from a limitation in how the OpenShift and KubeVirt RBAC model processes `list` and `get` requests for `virtualmachines`. The API server evaluates permissions at the namespace level first. If a user has `list` access to `virtualmachines` in a namespace, the `resourceNames` field in a custom role does not effectively filter the results of that `list` operation. As a result, the user receives a list of all VMs in the namespace, even if they only have permissions for a subset.

title: Bootable volume fails to import from registry when the retainRevisions parameter is set to 0.
issue: Creating a bootable volume from a registry in the OpenShift console fails when the Retain revisions value is set to 0. The importer pod continuously restarts, and the import process never completes.
resolution: 1. On OpenShift console set Retain revisions to a value of 1 or higher. This is the recommended workaround.- Navigate to Virtualization > Bootable Volumes in the OpenShift console and click Add.- Choose the with form option.- Select Registry as the source type and provide a valid container image URL (e.g., quay.io/containerdisks/centos:7-2009).- Enter 1 in the Retain revisions field.- Complete the rest of the form and click Create. 2. Create the bootable volume from the command-line interface (CLI). Using the CLI does not trigger the same race condition, as the Retain revisions value is handled correctly.
root_cause: - When a bootable volume is created from the OpenShift console with the Retain revisions field set to 0, a race condition occurs. The DataImportCron controller attempts to clean up the import's snapshot and source DataVolume immediately, as a value of 0 is interpreted as "do not retain any revisions." This cleanup process happens while the import pod is still running, causing the DataSource to become unready and the importer pod to enter a continuous restart loop.- A bug has been raised to ensure the console will not accept "0" as a valid input for Retain revisions to avoid future issues. The bug can be tracked at: [CNV-66708](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/CNV-66708)

title: Does RHOCP4.16 support forwarding cluster logs to external ElasticSearch v9 via CLF?
issue: - Does Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 4.16 support forwarding cluster logs to external `ElasticSearch v9` via `ClusterLogForwarder`?
resolution: - Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 4.x at this moment doesn't support forwarding cluster logs to external `ElasticSearch v9` at this moment.- Only supported versions are `v6`, `v7`& `v8`for which details can be found by executing the command below. ~~~ # oc explain ClusterLogForwarder.spec.outputs.elasticsearch.version ~~~- Sample output can be listed as follows for above command. ~~~ VERSION: string The Elasticsearch API version for log forwarding. Valid values are 'v6', 'v7', and 'v8'. When specifying a version, the ClusterLogForwarder attempts to optimize the log payloads for the specified Elasticsearch major version, which dictates the indexing and mapping format (e.g., using 'index' or 'data_stream' semantics). Default: 'v7' (or a version appropriate to the OpenShift Logging release being used). ~~~

title: Cluster in ArgoCD fails with "Failed to load live state" after upgrade in ACM
issue: After upgrading ACM, the following appears in the argocd-server logs and can no longer sync applications to managed clusters: ``` Failed to load target state: failed to get cluster version for cluster "https://api.example.com:6443": failed to get cluster info for "https://api.example.com:6443": error synchronizing cache state: the server has asked for the client to provide credentials error synchronizing cache state: the server has asked for the client to provide credentials ```
resolution: * Modify the `application-manager` `ClusterManagementAddon` under `spec`: ~~~ installStrategy: placements:- configs:- group: addon.open-cluster-management.io name: addon-ns-config namespace: multicluster-engine resource: addondeploymentconfigs name: global namespace: open-cluster-management-global-set rolloutStrategy: type: All type: Placements ~~~ An example of addon-ns-config referenced above can be found in the [documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_advanced_cluster_management_for_kubernetes/2.14/html-single/multicluster_engine_operator_with_red_hat_advanced_cluster_management/index#config-addons-hosted) * If you need to, you can enable `ManagedServiceAccount` in the `multiclusterengine` CR: ~~~ oc patch MultiClusterEngine--type=json-p='[{"op": "add", "path": "/spec/overrides/components/-","value":{"name":"managedserviceaccount","enabled":true}}]' ~~~ You can read more on [enabling the ManagedServiceAccount in the cluster documentation (RHACM 2.14 but other releases should have their section as well)](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_advanced_cluster_management_for_kubernetes/2.12/html-single/clusters/index#managed-serviceaccount-addon)
root_cause: * The application-manager addon is in a different namespace than the managed-service account addon for those customers that have configured ACM to import MCE clusters * `ManagedServiceAccount` needs to be enabled as well in the `multiclusterengine` CR
