title: Cluster node connectivity flapping and all node IPs have MAC "00:22:bd:f8:19:ff" on Red Hat Openshift Container Platform
issue: - System/Control Plane pods have intermittent connectivity between different nodes.- Cluster Operators are flapping from healthy to degraded from time to time and get restored by themselves without any action.- Network packet captures show all traffic to come and go to the single MAC "00:22:bd:f8:19:ff" in the same network.- All cluster nodes in their ARP table have the same MAC "00:22:bd:f8:19:ff" for all their neighboor nodes.
resolution: - The customer need to check with the Network devices Vendor regarding this behavior (This topology was seen provided by Cisco feature). This is out of Scope of Red Hat Openshift Container Platform Support if the symptoms match the ones described in the "Diagnostic Steps" and "Root Cause sections" except if its proven the oposite.
root_cause: There is a Cisco ACI L2-L3 topology that differs from the classic that is called ACI Anycast Gateway. In this Cisco feature/topology the flow in a network is not the classic one that each host has its own MAC and IP and everything talk using a Switch. In this topology there is a single device with a single MAC address "00:22:BD:F8:19:FF" for replying to all ARP requests from hosts in the network. This way all hosts have in their APR tables the same MAC mapped for all hosts in the same broadcast domain. So when they want to send a packet are using as destination this same MAC to communicate with each other. This has as a result all traffic to be arriving on this device which acts like some kind of Gateway and is responsible for routing every packet to the correct host. For unknown reasons (This is Cisco Support Scope not OCP) this can stop working correctly and packets to lose their destination, getting dropped or looping in the network until their TTL expires. Then as a concequence host to host communication start flapping causing all kinds of problems like ETCD leader changes, Cluster Operators flapping, API calls to timeout and many more tasks that depend on the hostNetwork level to fail. This is seen to at least one case to be happening sporadically. Every some hours or days and to stabilize by its own. It have been seen to last at least a couple of hours on each re-occurence on the single case this has been seen but it can vary depending the case.

title: How to customize configuration on Red Hat Developer Hub (Developer Hub) Operator in Openshift 4
issue: - How to customize kubernetes resources created by the Red Hat Developer Hub (Developer Hub) Operator?- How to customize Red Hat Developer Hub (Developer Hub)'s deployment.yaml or DB statefulset?
resolution: There are the following options for customization: Mechanism | Procedure | Recommendation------------|------------|------------ Partial overwriting | User declares on the Backstage Custom Resource the spec details via `deployment.patch` for example | More recommended (for simple overwriting) `spec.application.appConfig.configMaps` | The user creates a configmap with the spec details fully | Moderate recommendation `spec.rawRuntimeConfig` | The user creates a configmap with the full section to be used | Less recommended (more advanced settings) ### Partial overwriting That's the most recommend alterntive. Example below sets a custom label and the resources to 440 milicores for request and 3Gi for limit: ~~~ spec: application: appConfig: mountPath: /opt/app-root/src extraFiles: mountPath: /opt/app-root/src replicas: 1 route: enabled: true database: enableLocalDb: true deployment: patch: spec: template: metadata: labels: label1: value1 spec: containers:- name: backstage-backend resources: limits: cpu: '1' ephemeral-storage: 5Gi memory: 3Gi requests: cpu: 440m memory: 256Mi ~~~ ### spec.application.appConfig.configMaps RHDH provides the option `spec.application.appConfig.configMaps` provides alternative for customization, as explanation on [Using the Red Hat Developer Hub operator to run Developer Hub with your custom configuration](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_developer_hub/1.4/html/configuring/provisioning-and-using-your-custom-configuration#provisioning-your-custom-configuration). ### spec.rawRuntimeConfig That's the less recommended alternative. This is possible via the Backstage Custom Resource, which is full control via `spec.rawRuntimeConfig`. This field in the Backstage CR currently allows to fully customize some of the resources created by the operator (including the application Deployment), by providing a ConfigMap with the whole resource definition. It is for advanced or uncovered scenarios given it can detail exactly how the Kubernetes resources will be created. Currently, it allows full details and later it will allow partial patches instead not fully merging, see [Janus-idp Pull 388](https://github.com/janus-idp/operator/pull/388)). With the backstage operator, the user can specify a list of app-config ConfigMaps and Backstage/RHDH will handle merging them to create the effective app-config. There is no validation from the Operator on the file, in case of issues, if the resource cannot be applied however, the error returned will be conveyed by the operator in the Backstage CR status field. ### Examples [Backstage CR with the rawRuntimeConfig field](https://github.com/janus-idp/operator/blob/main/examples/showcase-cr.yaml#L7): ~~~ apiVersion: rhdh.redhat.com/v1alpha1 kind: Backstage metadata: name: bs-showcase spec: rawRuntimeConfig: backstageConfig: showcase-config ~~~ [Deployment example](https://github.com/janus-idp/operator/blob/main/examples/showcase-config.yaml): ~~~ apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: showcase-config data: deploy: |- apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: backstage spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: backstage # backstage- template: metadata: labels: app: backstage # backstage- spec: containers:- name: backstage image: quay.io/janus-idp/backstage-showcase imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent ports:- name: http containerPort: 7007 envFrom:- secretRef: name: postgres-secrets ~~~

title: No OperatorHub for a newly deployed ARO cluster
issue: - After deploying a new ARO cluster, when customer goes to the OperatorHub page, customer sees a blank page with just the text: ~~~ "No OperatorHub items found. Please check that the OperatorHub is running and that you have created a valid CatalogSource. For more information about OperatorHub" ~~~
resolution: This issue is generally caused if the ARO cluster's pull-secret is not setup initially during deployment of the cluster, or the cluster's pull secret has expired. 1. Download your Red Hat pull secret, by accessing this [link](https://console.redhat.com/openshift/downloads#tool-pull-secret). 2. Append the Red Hat pull-secret file to the cluster's pull-secret by following this ARO [documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/openshift/howto-add-update-pull-secret). The procedure from that doc will also show you the final output to make sure it is correct.
root_cause: This issue is generally caused if your ARO cluster's pull-secret is not setup initially during deployment of the cluster or if the Pull Secret has changed. Unfortunately Azure/Microsoft doesn't do it by default due to customer privacy reasons.

title: RHACS operator pod restarting due to OOM
product: Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security for Kubernetes
issue: RHACS operator pod is getting restarted due to OOM issue. Below are the events can be seen in `rhacs-operator namespace: ~~~ Warning ProbeError pod/rhacs-operator-controller-manager-xxxx Readiness probe error: Get "http://:8081/readyz": dial tcp:8081: connect: connection refused... ~~~ From describing the pod below error logs are seen: ~~~ message: back-off 2m40s restarting failed container=manager pod=rhacs-operator-controller-manager-xxxxxxx_openshift-rhacs-operator(zzzzzzzzzz) ~~~
resolution: The solution is to increase the memory limit value of the operator pod. There are two possible ways to do it: Method | Advantage | Disadvantage-----------|-------------|------ [Set it through the ClusterServiceVersion resource](#highlight1) | Advantage: it is possible to tune only the memory limits of the`manager` container, leaving `kube-rbac-proxy` container unchanged | Disadvantage: Setting is lost after each ACS Operator upgrade. [Set it through the Subscription resource](#highlight2) | Advantage: the memory setting is preserved through updates| Disadvantage: the change will be applied to both containers inside the `rhacs-operator` pod, although only the `manager` container needs those resources. Both are details below: ### Set it through the ClusterServiceVersion {#highlight1} 1. Get the name of `rhacs-operator` csv: ~~~ $ oc-n rhacs-operator get csv | grep rhacs rhacs-operator.v4.3.4 Advanced Cluster Security for Kubernetes 4.3.4 rhacs-operator.v4.3.3 Succeeded ~~~ 2. Take a backup of `rhacs-operator` csv: ~~~ $ oc-n rhacs-operator get csv-o yaml > rhacs-operator-csv.yaml ~~~ 2. Edit it: ~~~ $ oc-n rhacs-operator edit csv ~~~ 3. Increase the `resources.limits` value of the `manager` container: ~~~ spec: containers:- args:---health-probe-bind-address=:8081---metrics-bind-address=127.0.0.1:8080---leader-elect [...] name: manager resources: limits: cpu: 200m memory: 2Gi <-- value to increase ~~~ ### Set it through the Subscription {#highlight2} Edit the `rhacs-operator` Subscription and add this `config` block under `spec`: ~~~ $ oc-n rhacs-operator edit sub rhacs-operator spec: config: resources: limits: cpu: 500m memory: 2Gi <--- pod memory increased to 2Gi requests: cpu: 100m memory: 200Mi ~~~ Note: both `limits` and `requests` need to be defined. In order to be on the safe side, the values reported here are the higher values from both the containers.

title: What information do I need to gather for troubleshooting Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management?
product: Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management for Kubernetes
issue: What information do I need to gather information for troubleshooting Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management
How do I collect system log files, configuration details and system information from a Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management (RHACM) system to provide to Red Hat Technical Support for analysis?
What data I have to provide for initial analysis of my system?
How can I generate an ACM `must-gather`?
resolution: * Please provide the 2 following items: * What kind of OpenShift you installed on, e.g., if it's on Azure Red Hat OpenShift or if it's OpenShift on OpenStack or OpenShift on Red Hat Enterprise Virtualization, etc. * The must-gather archive specific to ACM version running.--- **Note:** *For details about ACM must-gather, refer to: [ACM 2.11 Troubleshooting Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management for Kubernetes](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_advanced_cluster_management_for_kubernetes/2.11/html-single/troubleshooting/index#running-the-must-gather-command-to-troubleshoot). The documentation is version specific; ensure to select the version you are using.*--- ### Data Collection for Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management for Kubernetes (ACM) **For ACM 2.10 and later:** **Note:** *Replace `[ACM_version]` with the cluster's ACM version, for example `2.10`.* ~~~ $ oc adm must-gather--image=registry.redhat.io/rhacm2/acm-must-gather-rhel9:v[ACM_version] |& tee must-gather-collect.log ~~~ **For ACM 2.9 and earlier:** **Note:** *Replace `[ACM_version]` with the cluster's ACM version, for example `2.9`.* ~~~ $ oc adm must-gather--image=registry.redhat.io/rhacm2/acm-must-gather-rhel8:v[ACM_version] |& tee must-gather-collect.log ~~~ ### Must-gather in a disconnected environment 1. In a disconnected environment, mirror the Red Hat operator catalog images into their mirror registry. For details, refer to [Install on disconnected networks](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_advanced_cluster_management_for_kubernetes/2.9/html-single/install#install-on-disconnected-networks) 2. Run the following command to extract logs, which reference the image from their mirror registry: **For ACM 2.10 and later:** **Note:** *Replace `[ACM_version]` with the cluster's ACM version, for example `2.10`.* ~~~ REGISTRY=registry.example.com:5000 IMAGE=$REGISTRY/rhacm2/acm-must-gather-rhel9:v[ACM_version] oc adm must-gather--image=$IMAGE--dest-dir=./data |& tee must-gather-collect.log ~~~ **For ACM 2.9 and earlier:** **Note:** *Replace `[ACM_version]` with the cluster's ACM version, for example `2.9`.* ~~~ REGISTRY=registry.example.com:5000 IMAGE=$REGISTRY/rhacm2/acm-must-gather-rhel8:v[ACM_version] oc adm must-gather--image=$IMAGE--dest-dir=./data |& tee must-gather-collect.log ~~~--- **Note:** *please also share the `must-gather-collect.log` file. This will help us troubleshoot situations where must-gather collection fails.*---

title: OpenShift Virtualization: VM Operations fail after upgrade to 4.18 from 4.17.27 or above
issue: - Management operations for pre-existing, running Virtual Machines (VMs) fail.- Actions such as live migration or a graceful VM shutdown are unresponsive.- The virt-handler logs on the worker nodes repeatedly show the error: `unable to create virt-launcher client connection: can not add ghost record when entry already exists with differing socket file location`.
resolution: This has been fixed in OpenShift Virtualization 4.18.17, which is now available in the stable channel. A workaround is to manually correct the `ghost-records` of the affected VMs. 1. Get the affected VMI UUID: ~~~ # oc get vmi rhel9-blue-crawdad-23-n test-cnv-o yaml |yq '.metadata.uid' eb0fb0aa-96d9-449d-8e24-cf94eb1ab73b ~~~ 2. Correct the ghost file from the node where the VM is running: ~~~ # sed-i 's|"socketFile":"/pods|"socketFile":"//pods|g' /var/run/kubevirt-private/ghost-records/eb0fb0aa-96d9-449d-8e24-cf94eb1ab73b ~~~ If there are multiple VMs affected, sed commands to correct the ghost record can be generated using the following command: ~~~ # oc logs | grep "can not add ghost record when entry already exists with differing socket file location" | egrep-o '[a-z0-9]{8}-[a-z0-9]{4}-[a-z0-9]{4}-[a-z0-9]{4}-[a-z0-9]{12}' | awk-F ' ' '{print "sed-i \047s|\"socketFile\":\"/pods|\"socketFile\":\"//pods|g\047 /var/run/kubevirt-private/ghost-records/"$1}' | sort | uniq ~~~ 3. Restart the virt-handler pod running on this node: ~~~ # oc delete pod-n openshift-cnv ~~~
root_cause: The issue is because of mismatch in how the virt-launcher socket file path is formatted in state files (called "ghost records") between the two specific OpenShift Virtualization versions. A patch [Kubevirt PR 15522](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/15522/commits/07795d383a0f882d6525a196c3f4bd80fcbec35e) was backported to version 4.17.27 that caused the socket path in the ghost record to be saved with a single leading slash (e.g., /pods/...). This same patch was not released in stable 4.18 release although available in 4.18.16 candidate version. The virt-handler in version 4.18.13 discovers the active socket path on the host with a double leading slash (e.g., //pods/...). After the upgrade, the new 4.18.13 virt-handler starts and reads the "ghost" records left by the old 4.17.27 virt-handler. It then compares the path from the old record (/pods/...) with the the double slash (//pods/...). Because the path strings do not match exactly, the validation check fails, and virt-handler is unable to establish a connection to manage these VMs. [Jira CNV-69894](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/CNV-69894) is tracking the release of the availability of the fix in the stable channel for 4.18. *Note:* Attempting to avoid the issue by avoid the OpenShift Virtualization operator to 4.17.27, for example staying on operator version 4.17.21 prior to the Operator 4.18 upgrade, does not work because the upgrade process requires going to 4.17.27 before it will allow upgrading to 4.18. *Note:* Care was taken to make sure these versions refer specifically to the operator, NOT the versions of the RHOCP cluster. Be careful not to confuse the two.

title: Is it possible for VolumeSnapshot to take backup of node disk in RHOCP 4 ?
issue: - Is it possible for `VolumeSnapshot` to take backup of node disk in RHOCP 4?- Node disks are mounted through the `local storage operator`(LSO). Does it support `VolumeSnapshot`?
resolution: - `VolumeSnapshot` in OpenShift cannot directly take a backup of a node disk.- Kubernetes/RHOCP does not have functionality to snapshot or back up the entire node disk, as it's not a resource managed directly by Kubernetes/RHOCP.- Node disks are local disks attached to the nodes that contain local storage, but unless the storage is specifically provisioned as a`PersistentVolumes`(PV) and attached to a pod, RHOCP does not treat these as PV.- `VolumeSnapshot` is designed to work with `PersistentVolumes`, which are separate from the node disk. A node disk typically contains system files, logs, and other local data. The `VolumeSnapshot` is specifically designed to take snapshots of `PersistentVolumes` that are linked to RHOCP workloads, such as databases or application data.- `VolumeSnapshot` will not work even If in case the node disks are mounted through the `local storage operator`(LSO), because, As of now the support for `VolumeSnapshot` is only for `CSI`. It's default working of kubernetes.
root_cause: - Node disks are local disks attached to the nodes that contain local storage, but unless the storage is specifically provisioned as a PV and attached to a pod, RHOCP does not treat these as `PersistentVolumes`.- `VolumeSnapshot` applies specifically to `PersistentVolumes`, which are abstractions that represent storage managed by Kubernetes/RHOCP, typically backed by external/cloud storage services.

title: Elasticsearch in OpenShift Service Mesh has yellow status due to shard allocation failure in RHOCP 4
issue: - Elasticsearch in `OpenShift Service Mesh` has yellow status.- Elasticesearch pod has below log message reporting a shard allocation failure. ~~~ shard has exceeded the maximum number of retries [5] on failed allocation attempts- manually call [/_cluster/reroute?retry_failed=true] to retry, [unassigned_info[[reason=ALLOCATION_FAILED], failed_attempts[5], delayed=false, details[failed shard on node [2eWoWRKwQcmfsVrh_dthuQ]: failed to create shard, failure IllegalStateException[environment is not locked]; nested: AccessDeniedException[/elasticsearch/persistent/elasticsearch/data/nodes/0/node.lock];], allocation_status[no_attempt]]]" ~~~- The log says Elasticsearch has stopped trying to allocate this shard automatically.
resolution: - Force the retry of shard allocation using steps below: 1. Login to the `elasticsearch-cdm ` pod: ~~~ $ oc rsh ~~~ 2. Run below command inside `elasticsearch-cdm `pod to force the retry of shard allocation: ~~~ $ es_util POST /_cluster/reroute?retry_failed=true ~~~- After this scale down the `elasticsearch-cdm` pods and then scale up: ~~~ $ oc scale deploy--replicas=0 ~~~ ~~~ $ oc scale deploy--replicas=1 ~~~

title: Inability to use structured.message as search filter on External Elasticsearch in RHOCP 4
issue: - Why structured.message doesn't work as a search filter on External Elasticsearch?
resolution: To overcome the issue where `structured.message` cannot be used as a search filter in Elasticsearch due to its treatment as a text field, follow these best practices.- Avoid using `reserved/logging` fields like message, log for `structured JSON` instead use names as details, logdata etc.- Verify indexing in Elasticsearch using mappings to ensure `nested fields` are treated as object or keyword not text.
root_cause: `structured.message` can not be used as a search filter in Elasticsearch this is because Elasticsearch treats certain fields like message as text fields, and text fields are:- Not analyzed for `structured JSON`.- Not indexed in a way that allows nested filtering.

title: oc-mirror plugin fails with " tls: failed to parse certificate from server: x509: negative serial number" in RHOCP 4

resolution: At the time of writing this article, a feature enhancement request has been submitted to the Red Hat Engineering team and is being tracked under [RFE-7924](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/RFE-7924). According to the latest update Red Hat Engineering team is investigating and analyzing the x509: negative serial number issue and working on their code base accordingly. **Workaround:** Set/export below environment variable on the node where oc-mirror is running: GODEBUG=x509negativeserial=1 **NOTE:** The environment variable `GODEBUG=x509negativeserial=1` is used to allow Go programs to accept X.509 certificates that have negative serial numbers.

title: MCP in Degraded State due to etcdserver: request is too large during cluster upgrade.
issue: Master MachineConfigPool(MCP) is in degraded state during OpenShift Container Platform upgrade between minor version (e.g., 4.14 to 4.16) due to the `machineconfig` size is exceeding the etcd limit of 1.5MB.

Machine Config Operator stuck into degraded state with following message: ~~~ message: 'Failed to resync 4.15.50 because: error during syncRequiredMachineConfigPools: [context deadline exceeded, failed to update clusteroperator: [client rate limiter Wait returned an error: context deadline exceeded, error MachineConfigPool master is not ready, retrying. Status: (pool degraded: true total: 3, ready 3, updated: 3, unavailable: 0)]]' reason: RequiredPoolsFailed status: "True" type: Degraded ~~~

MCP stuck into degraded state with the following error message: ~~~ message: 'Failed to render configuration for pool master: etcdserver: request is too large' reason: "" status: "True" type: RenderDegraded ~~~
resolution: This issue has been reported to Red Hat Engineering and is tracked in [OCPBUGS-62619](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPBUGS-62619). For more information, please open a [new support case](https://access.redhat.com/support/cases/#/case/new/) with Red Hat Support. #### Workaround Review the machineconfigs and their content that are bigger in size to relate with the objects these machineconfig relates to and try reducing the size ensuring that not hitting the etcd limit of 1.5 MB.
root_cause: The rendered `machineconfig` has been grown to a size that exceeds the default limit of 1.5 MiB for the etcd object, resulting in errors when attempting to store large objects in etcd (e.g., ConfigMaps, Secrets, Custom Resources) as describes in KCS Solution [Requests to etcd are rejected due to exceeding `--max-request-bytes` (1.5 MiB) limit in RHOCP 4](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7070199)

title: Vector collector pods crashing because of unknown severity in RHOCP 4
issue: - After creating / modifying `ClusterLogForwarder`, all the `vector` collector pods start to crash with with below error: ~~~ $ oc get pods-n openshift-logging NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE cluster-logging-operator-785c8d9d4b-w2w9p 1/1 Running 0 5d collector-2rkfc 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 283 23h collector-6f94m 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 283 23h collector-9pkm9 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 282 23h collector-9tz6c 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 283 23h collector-fm9kk 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 283 23h collector-ht2mq 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 283 23h ======== $ oc logs-n openshift-logging 2025-10-08T10:07:11.464307501Z Creating the directory used for persisting Vector state /var/lib/vector 2025-10-08T10:07:11.470178915Z Starting Vector process... 2025-10-08T10:07:11.488776291Z 2025-10-08T10:07:11.488723Z ERROR vector::cli: Configuration error. error=invalid value: integer `8`, expected unknown severity 2025-10-08T10:07:11.488776291Z in `sinks.abc_syslog` ~~~
resolution: - Edit `ClusterLogForwarder` and correct the severity as per `syslog` standards: ~~~ $ oc edit clusterlogforwarder-n openshift-logging------ Output Omitted------ outputs:- name: sbc-syslog syslog: facility: local0 rfc: RFC5424 severity: info < <====== Replace info with informational type: syslog url: udp://10.0.0.1:514------ Output Omitted------ ~~~- Save the changes, it will trigger restart of `vector` collector pods. The newly created pods will get into running state.
root_cause: This happens because `syslog` severity config follow a particular standard where `informational` is the correct keyword and using `info` is incorrect.

title: Limitation of Azure IPI Installer: Using StandardSSD in Azure Storage account for OpenShift Image Registry instead of PremiumSSD
issue: Openshift clusters on Azure Cloud using IPI install method fails to create `Premium storage`.
Image registry is of `StandardSSD` type resulting in slow performance.
Azure storage account created default `StandardSSD` instead of `PremiumSSDv2` during IPI.
resolution: Red Hat is aware of this issue and we have raise [RFE](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/RFE-8118) with the Engineering team. Alternate to IPI, you can:- Use the `User Provisioned Infrastructure` (UPI) approach instead of IPI.- With a `User Provisioned Infrastructure` (UPI) approach, you can fully control the image registry storage setup from **Day 1**, including using `Premium SSD v2`. As of now, there is no official support in the `IPI` installer to customize the `storage account SKU` for the image registry. It is likely to be implemented in OpenShift 4.21, based on the current roadmap and discussions.
root_cause: * The OpenShift IPI for Azure has `hardcoded logic` to create the image registry’s backing storage using a `Standard_LRS` storage account. * The installer currently does not expose any variables or parameters to customize the `storage SKU` or class used for the image registry at deployment time. * This design choice is made to optimize for `cost-efficiency` and broad compatibility, especially for general-purpose use cases. * As a result, we cannot directly configure the image registry to use `Premium SSD v2` through the IPI workflow.

title: Query traces from TempoStack using cli in RHOCP 4
issue: - Is it possible to query traces from TempoStack using cli?- How to query traces from TempoStack using cli?
resolution: This solution is only applicable for **Multitenant TempoStack.** 1. Create `TempoStack` custom resource and required RBAC using [this documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.17/html/distributed_tracing/distr-tracing-tempo-installing#installing-a-tempostack-instance_distr-tracing-tempo-installing). 2. Create a serviceaccount to setup authentication: ~~~ $ oc create sa tempo-test-n ~~~ 3. Provide authorization for the serviceaccount using tempostack-traces-reader ClusterRole (created in step 1): ~~~ $ oc adm policy add-cluster-role-to-user tempostack-traces-reader-z tempo-test ~~~ 4. Create a token using below command: ~~~ $ oc create token tempo-test-n ~~~ 5. Identify the gateway route generated by creation of TempoStack: ~~~ $ oc get route-n NAME HOST/PORT PATH SERVICES PORT TERMINATION WILDCARD tempo-simplest-gateway tempo-simplest-gateway-tracing-system.apps.example.com tempo-simplest-gateway public reencrypt None ~~~ 6. Curl the route using below syntax and it will retrieve the traces: ~~~ $ token=$(oc create token tempo-test-n) $ curl-G-kv-H "Authorization: Bearer $token" https:// /api/traces/v1/dev/api/traces--data-urlencode "service= " ~~~ 7. Replace with the actual FQDN of tempo-gateway and replace with name of service resource from where the traces needs to be queried. 8. If the TempoStack is a Service Mesh member, then ingress connection needs to be allowed using below NetworkPolicy: ~~~ apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: allow-from-openshift-ingress namespace: spec: ingress:- from:- namespaceSelector: matchLabels: network.openshift.io/policy-group: ingress podSelector: {} policyTypes:- Ingress ~~~ 9. To create a long lived serviceaccount token in step 4 or 6, refer [this knowledge base](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7025261).

title: Expose API and Ingress using MetalLB in a baremetal cluster
issue: - Need to expose the **OpenShift API*
and **Ingress*
in a secondary network to allow the connections to the cluster from a different network than the default one.
resolution: In order to expose the API and Ingress services in a secondary network using MetalLB, we just need to create two services, one for API and one for Ingress, as described below. For this example, we are going to refer to the secondary network as OAM (Operations, Administration and Management), because it is a common use case to use a different network to allow the administrators to access the cluster and services exposed by the workloads running in the cluster. #### Expose API- To expose the API in a secondary interface using MetalLB, we need to create a service within the `openshift-kube-apiserver` namespace, pointing to the Pods with label `apiserver: true`. The service needs to expose the port **TCP/6443** of those Pods. We also need to ad the required MetalLB annotations (shown in the example below), taking in account that in those annotations we refer to the `ipAddressPool` called `oam`, this must be configured previously: ~~~ apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: annotations: metallb.io/ip-allocated-from-pool: oam metallb.universe.tf/address-pool: oam metallb.universe.tf/allow-shared-ip: oam metallb.universe.tf/ip-address-pool: oam name: api-metallb-oam namespace: openshift-kube-apiserver spec: externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster ipFamilies:- IPv4 ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack ports:- name: https port: 6443 protocol: TCP targetPort: 6443 selector: apiserver: "true" sessionAffinity: None type: LoadBalancer ~~~ #### Expose Ingress- To expose the Ingress service (`*.apps. *`), we need to create a `Service` within the `openshift-ingress` namespace, pointing to the Pods with the label `ingresscontroller.operator.openshift.io/deployment-ingresscontroller: default`. In this case the ports to be exposed are **80, 443 and 1936 TCP**. As in the API the MetalLB annotations are required as well. ~~~ apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: router-internal-default-metallb namespace: openshift-ingress annotations: metallb.universe.tf/ip-address-pool: oam metallb.universe.tf/allow-shared-ip: oam metallb.universe.tf/address-pool: oam spec: type: LoadBalancer externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster selector: ingresscontroller.operator.openshift.io/deployment-ingresscontroller: default ports:- name: http port: 80 protocol: TCP targetPort: http- name: https port: 443 protocol: TCP targetPort: https- name: metrics port: 1936 protocol: TCP targetPort: metrics ~~~ #### DNS requirements In order to access the OpenShift API and Ingress published in the secondary network with a MetalLB service, using a new ip address, it is necessary to update the DNS resolution for these endpoints on the network or host that is going to use those. Let’s take as an example the subdomain for the API is `api.ocp.mydomain.lab`, and the DNS is configured pointing this to the ip address `192.168.0.1`, which is connected to the baremetal network. We have configured the MetalLB services to use an `ipAddressPool` with the ip `10.110.2.1`. We can update the **/etc/hosts** file on the machine that is going to make the requests to the OpenShift API with something like this: ~~~ 10.110.2.1 api.ocp.mydomain.lab ~~~ Or also you can **update the zone in the DNS server** used by the host that is going to run the requests, pointing the API subdomain to the MetalLB service ip. You can check it with a dig like below. ~~~ $ dig api.ocp.mydomain.lab; < <> > DiG 9.16.23-RH < <> > api.ocp.mydomain.lab;; global options: +cmd;; Got answer:;;-> > HEADER < <- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 18422;; flags: qr aa rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1;; OPT PSEUDOSECTION:; EDNS: version: 0, flags:; udp: 1232;; QUESTION SECTION:;api.ocp.mydomain.lab. IN A;; ANSWER SECTION: api.ocp.mydomain.lab. 0 IN A 10.110.2.1;; Query time: 0 msec ~~~ > **IMPORTANT** > The baremetal network DNS resolution should keep it as it is, because that is needed but the right operation of the cluster. #### TLS Certificates As the TLS connections are terminated in the pods (for the openshift-kube-apiserver and openshift-ingress), and the subdomain is not going to change, everything will work without any validation issues.

title: [RHACS] How to update Central's CA certificate?
product: Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security for Kubernetes
issue: - According to [the documentation](https://docs.openshift.com/acs/4.6/configuration/reissue-internal-certificates.html#reissue-internal-certificates-central_reissue-internal-certificates), the expiration date of Central's CA certificate is set to 5 years and is not automatically updated.- How to update Central's CA certificate?
resolution: **WARNING** Updating Central's CA certificate breaks the ACS installation. All Secured Clusters will have to be re-registered. **Do not perform this operation unless the internal CA expired or other emergency situations (e.g. leaked certificates)**- Follow the steps below to update Central's CA certificate:- Back up existing `central-tls` secret $ oc-n stackrox get secret/central-tls-o yaml > central_tls_backup.yaml- Delete `secret/central-tls` in the namespace where `Central` is deployed. $ oc-n stackrox delete secret/central-tls secret "central-tls" deleted- Verify that `secret/central-tls` has been re-created. $ oc-n stackrox get secret/central-tls NAME TYPE DATA AGE central-tls Opaque 5 2s- [Restart all Central services pods](https://docs.openshift.com/acs/4.6/configuration/reissue-internal-certificates.html#restart-central_reissue-internal-certificates) to load the new secret. $ oc-n stackrox delete pods-all- Create a new init bundle or Cluster Registration Secret- In all Secured Clusters connected to this ACS Central, delete all existing TLS secrets $ oc-n stackrox delete secrets sensor-tls collector-tls admission-control-tls- If using ACS 4.7 or newer, also delete the following secrets, if they exist: $ oc-n stackrox delete secret cluster-registration-secret $ oc-n stackrox delete secret \ tls-cert-sensor \ tls-cert-collector \ tls-cert-admission-control \ tls-cert-scanner \ tls-cert-scanner-db \ tls-cert-scanner-v4-indexer \ tls-cert-scanner-v4-db- Deploy the new init bundle (or CRS) to all Secured Clusters- Restart all pods of all Secured Clusters $ oc-n stackrox delete pods-all **Important** After a CA change, all ACS pods must be restarted, as described above (on both Central, and all Secured Clusters).
root_cause: - Central's CA certificate is stored in `secret/central-tls`.- If the expiration date needs to be changed, `secret/central-tls` must be manually re-created.

title: Empty namespace error on KServe after Openshift AI upgrade
issue: - My Openshift AI instance stopped working after upgrading it from v2.16 to v2.22.- The DSC is generating `empty namespace may not be set when a resource name is provided` error messages after upgrading from v2.16 to v2.22.
resolution: - While upgrading Openshift AI from older releases should consider several feature changes that might be reviewed in the [upgrading guide](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_ai_self-managed/2.22/html-single/upgrading_openshift_ai_self-managed/index#overview-of-upgrading-openshift-ai-self-managed_upgrade) before performing the upgrade process.- In cases when the **DataScienceCluster (DSC)** configuration defines the **KServe** component as **Managed** and the *reconcile* process fails, the generated **error** should be reviewed. For example, if after upgrading the OpenShift AI, gets the following **ReconcileError**: ~~~ Normal ReconcileError 1m datasciencecluster unable to patch object status... message:an empty namespace may not be set when a resource name is provided reason:Error status:False type:KserveReady] ~~~ That means that some component from the defined **KServe** is preventing the reconcile process. If the Openshift cluster has already created a `KNativeServing` resource, the Red Hat OpenShift AI Operator cannot install `KServe` and configure its dependencies, and the installation does not proceed. To fix that, the `knative-serving` from KServe definition in the `DSC` configuration file should be removed: ~~~ kserve: defaultDeploymentMode: RawDeployment managementState: Managed nim: managementState: Managed rawDeploymentServiceConfig: Headless serving: ingressGateway: certificate: type: SelfSigned managementState: Removed name: knative-serving <--- REMOVE THIS LINE ~~~
root_cause: - To configure a *Managed* KServe in OpenShift AI, should be reviewed in the Openshift cluster are not already installed `ServiceMeshControlPlane` or `KNativeServing` resources as described in the [Automated installation of KServe procedure](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_ai_self-managed/2.22/html-single/installing_and_uninstalling_openshift_ai_self-managed/index#configuring-automated-installation-of-kserve_component-install)

title: Loki ingester fails to flush stream because of SerializationError in RHOCP 4

title: OCP4: egressfirewall not denying dnsName entries
issue: - egressFirewall blocking traffic for some dnsName entries, but not all.
resolution: - Use A record and not CNAME record. ~~~ # getent hosts myrealdomain.foo 203.0.113.1 myrealdomain.foo.amazonaws.com myrealdomain.foo oc create-f- <
root_cause: - The matched dnsName entry was against the CNAME record and not the A record for the upstream nameserver.

title: Migration pre-check error: Unacceptable CPU info: CPU doesn't have compatibility.
product: Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift
issue: - Cold migration of instances is successful, but live migration fails in RHOSO 18 environments.- Cold migration of instances is successful, but live migration fails in RHOSP 17 environments.
resolution: **DISCLAIMER: The following information has been provided by Red Hat, but is outside the scope of the posted Service Level Agreements andsupport coverage. The information is provided as-is and any configuration settings or installed applications made from the information in this article could make the Operating System unsupported by Red Hat Global Support Services. The intent of this article is to provide information to accomplish the system's needs. Use of the information in this article at your own risk.** ### RHOSO 18- edit `nova.conf` with the following: ~~~ [workarounds] skip_cpu_compare_on_dest=true ~~~ ### RHOSP 17- edit `nova.conf` with the following: ``` crudini--set /var/lib/config-data/puppet-generated/nova_libvirt/etc/nova/nova.conf workarounds skip_cpu_compare_on_dest True systemctl restart $(systemctl list-units--no-legend tripleo_nova_compute*--all--plain | awk '{print $1}' | grep-v healthcheck | grep-v virt) ```
root_cause: For the live migration workflow in RHOSO 18 environments utilizing the `host-model` cpu mode in `Nova`, there have been issues determining CPU compatibility for some model of processors based off of the CPU flags. The nova live-migration workflow currently uses the output from `virsh capabilities`. `Libvirt` uses `virsh domcapabilities` The workaround will force `Nova` to defer to `libvirt` to evaluate CPU compatibility **But please aware, using this way to bypass the check only for testing purpose. It doesn't mean Red Hat support user for different CPU usage in one cluster. Any production purpose still remain the constraints from [here](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openstack_platform/17.1/html-single/configuring_the_compute_service_for_instance_creation/index#con_migration-constraints_migrating-instances)**

title: Cluster operator authentication is degraded with certificate error in logs
issue: - RouterCertsDegraded: secret/v4-0-config-system-router-certs.spec.data[apps.example.com]-n openshift-authentication: certificate could not validate route hostname oauth-openshift.apps.example.com: **x509: certificate signed by unknown authority*
(possibly because of "**crypto/rsa: verification error**" while trying to verify candidate authority certificate "**MyCorp Issuing CA**")
resolution: The bundle set in the proxy/cluster/trustedCA should include ALL trusted certificates. Please refer to the documentation [Enabling the cluster-wide proxy](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/latest/html/configuring_network_settings/enable-cluster-wide-proxy#nw-proxy-configure-object_config-cluster-wide-proxy) which describe how to set create the bundle in a configmap.
root_cause: Red Hat Openshift Container Platform (RHOCP) uses the proxy/cluster/trustedCA field to store the trusted certificates that it should rely on. This bundle is merged to the default node trusted bundle to ensure that all desired certificate can be trusted. So when using an intermediate certificate to trust domains, this intermediate certificate should also be added to the trust bundle in RHOCP, in addition to the related Root CA. Chain of Trust: **Domain Certificate** => **Intermediate CA** => **Root CA** The arrows point to whom is trusting the requester. When using an intermediate certificate, it's not possible to trust a domain directly from the Root CA: **Domain Certificate** => **Root CA**_This will not work if the Domain Certificate has been created from an intermediate certificate_ If the intermediate certificate **MyCorp Issuing CA** is used to trust the domain ***.apps.example.com**. This intermediate certificate **MyCorp Issuing CA** will be trusted by the company Root CA **MyCorp root CA** Looking at the error: ~~~ RouterCertsDegraded: secret/v4-0-config-system-router-certs.spec.data[apps.example.com]-n openshift-authentication: certificate could not validate route hostname oauth-openshift.apps.example.com: **x509: certificate signed by unknown authority** (possibly because of "**crypto/rsa: verification error**" while trying to verify candidate authority certificate "**MyCorp Issuing CA**") ~~~ The message describes that the domain **apps.example.com** has been **signed by unknown authority**, as there is an error while trying to verify candidate authority certificate "**MyCorp Issuing CA**" This means that the intermediate certificate has not been added to the **trustedCA** bundle.

title: How do I set the MTU for my network interface?
issue: How do I set the MTU for my network interface?
resolution: ## To temporarily change the MTU (not persistent on reboot)- The interface `eth0` has an MTU set to 1500 bytes. ``` # ip link show eth0 | grep mtu 2: eth0: mtu 1500 qdisc fq_codel state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000 ```- To change the setting **temporarily** (to 1200 in this example) issue the following command as root: ``` # ip link set dev eth0 mtu 1200 ```- Verify the changes: ``` # ip link show eth0 | grep mtu 2: eth0: mtu 1200 qdisc fq_codel state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000 ```--- ## To make the change persistent ### With NetworkManager:- The interface `eth0` has an MTU set to 1200 bytes.- To set MTU persistently to 1500 use `nmcli connection modify $YOUR_CONNECTION_PROFILE 802-3-ethernet.mtu 1500` command: ``` # ip link show eth0 | grep mtu 2: eth0: mtu 1200 qdisc fq_codel state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000 # nmcli connection show NAME UUID TYPE DEVICE eth0 c7f818a2-3a2c-462a-ba75-ba4964e00c90 ethernet eth0 # nmcli connection modify eth0 802-3-ethernet.mtu 1500 # nmcli connection up eth0 Connection successfully activated (D-Bus active path: /org/freedesktop/NetworkManager/ActiveConnection/8) # ip link show eth0 | grep mtu 2: eth0: mtu 1500 qdisc fq_codel state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000 ``` ### Without NetworkManager edit the network-script file:- The interface `eth0` has an MTU set to 1200 bytes.- To make the setting permanent for eth0, edit the configuration file `/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-eth0` and add the line `MTU=1500` as shown below: ~~~ # ip link show eth0 | grep mtu 3: eth0: mtu 1200 qdisc pfifo_fast state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000 # cat /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-eth0 | grep MTU MTU=1500 # ip link show eth0 | grep mtu 3: eth0: mtu 1500 qdisc pfifo_fast state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000 ~~~- Then, restart the network service: ~~~ # systemctl restart network ~~~ ### For Specific Interface Types- Bonding: [How to change MTU value for bonding interface](https://access.redhat.com/site/solutions/64136)- Loopback: [How do I manage the "lo" loopback interface using NetworkManager?](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/2108251)

title: rook-ceph-osd-X Pod Stuck in CrashLoopBackOff/init after Node Reboot/OCP Upgrade monclient(hunting) - OpenShift Data Foundation
issue: In situations where the Local Storage Operator (LSO) cannot use /dev/disk/by-id/ symlinks, users will sometimes incorrectly configure their localvolume/localvolumediscovery objects to use the non-persistent /dev/sdN or /dev/vdN device files. When this occurs, the path in the PV will reflect `/dev/sdX`/`dev/vdX`. This can cause issues when the device file names change (Ex. /dev/sda changes to /dev/sdb) during a node reboot or an OCP upgrade. After which the PV can no longer communicate with the proper symlink located in the `/mnt/local-storage/ /` directory on the node. If you are on vsphere and disk.EnableUUID is not set to `true`, running `$ ls-l /dev/disk/by-id` UUID will NOT display any UUIDs. When this is the case please refer to the KCS [How to check and set the disk.EnableUUID parameter from VM in vSphere for OpenShift Container Platform](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/4606201) ~~~ 2024-06-21T17:10:24.362235635Z debug 2024-06-21T17:10:24.361+0000 7fc951f22700-1 monclient(hunting): handle_auth_bad_method server allowed_methods [2] but i only support [2] ~~~ **Related Articles:*
[Disk device (/dev/sda- /dev/sdb- /dev/sdc- /dev/sdd) changes after each node rebooting and impact pods using Local Storage Operator](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7059585)
resolution: # Preface: It's important to understand that this is a workflow. Depending on the exact circumstances, there could be one OSD down, or many. If there are many OSDs down, a pod disruption budget or flags thrown by the rook-ceph-operator (nobackfill, norecover, etc.) have been instituted to safeguard data integrity. In this workflow, since each node will have to be shutdown one at a time (while monitoring Ceph) to edit the VM, it will be important to initially get the OSDs up and running, allowing for rebalance, and for Ceph to return `HEALTH_OK` all PGs `active+clean`, then finally fix the UUIDs/Symlinks on each node. **Warning: Work one node at a time, DO NOT proceed to the next node, until ALL OSDs on the previous node are up/running. Losing too many OSDs could jeopardize data integrity (data loss).** 1. With a notepad tool, run the following commands and capture the data/begin sorting OSD IDs, PVs, PVCs, hostnames, and paths of the devices. ~~~ $ oc get pod-n openshift-storage-o 'custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.labels.ceph-osd-id,PVCNAME:.spec.volumes[*].persistentVolumeClaim' | grep-v none ~~~ **Example:** ~~~ NAME PVCNAME 0 map[claimName:ocs-deviceset-0-data-089lnk] 1 map[claimName:ocs-deviceset-0-data-1sr5dx] 2 map[claimName:ocs-deviceset-1-data-0nk5m5] ~~~ ~~~ $ oc get pv-o 'custom-columns=HOST-NAME:.metadata.labels.kubernetes\.io/hostname,PVCNAME:.spec.claimRef.name,SYMLINK:.spec.local.path,DEV-NAME:.metadata.annotations.storage\.openshift\.com/device-name' | grep-v none ~~~ **Example:** ~~~ HOST-NAME PVCNAME SYMLINK DEV-NAME node.1.com ocs-deviceset-0-data-1sr5dx /mnt/local-storage/localblock/sdb sdb node.2.com ocs-deviceset-0-data-089lnk /mnt/local-storage/localblock/sdb sdb node.3.com ocs-deviceset-1-data-0nk5m5 /mnt/local-storage/localblock/sdb sdb ~~~ 2. Set up two CLI Terminal windows for commands and monitoring. **NOTE:** Depending on how many OSDs are provisioned on this node, this may be a trial/error task where a symlink command will be issued to correct the symlink followed by a pod deletion to test if the correct symlink is in place. It is also helpful to have three CLI terminal windows up (one in the current node, one to run oc commands, and one to monitor Ceph). To run Ceph commands, see the [Configuring the Rook-Ceph Toolbox in OpenShift Data Foundation 4.x](https://access.redhat.com/articles/4628891) solution article. **Commands to monitor Ceph once rsh'd into the rook-ceph-tools pod:** ~~~ $ ceph status # <------------- monitor PGs and OSDs $ ceph osd tree $ <------------ better look at the OSDs/hosts ~~~ **Note:** In a given scenario where some OSDs are up and some are down (shown in the outputs using the command above), we can determine that the OSDs that are up/in, have the CORRECT path in the PV! That device did not shift names. **Example of an OSD that is up/running:** ~~~ $ oc get pods-n openshift-storage | grep rook-ceph-osd | grep Running NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE rook-ceph-osd-0-567869c6c4-5b56t 2/2 Running 0 76m $ oc describe pod-n openshift-storage rook-ceph-osd-0-567869c6c4-5b56t | grep-i claim ClaimName: ocs-deviceset-0-data-089lnk $ oc get pv-n openshift-storage | grep ocs-deviceset-0-data-089lnk local-pv-9a68ad40 1TiB RWO Delete Bound openshift-storage/ocs-deviceset-0-data-089lnk localblock $ oc describe pv-n openshift-storage local-pv-9a68ad40 | grep-i path Path: /mnt/local-storage/localblock/sdc <--- WE CAN RULE THIS OUT. THE OSD IS UP/RUNNING. THE SYMLINK TO /dev/sdc IS CORRECT (DON'T TOUCH). ~~~ 3. Debug into the first node and correct the symlink(s) on the first node. ~~~ $ oc debug node/node.1.com $ chroot /host ~~~ 4. Depending on how many devices are on the host will make this easier/more difficult, however, a good command to run to at least start to distinguish the devices is `$ lsblk`. **Note:** OSD devices will likely be the devices with no underlying/nested partitions and will usually (not always) be larger devices such as 500GiB, 1TiB, 2TiB, etc. **Example:** ~~~ $ lsblk sda 259:5 0 1T 0 disk <------ device shifted from sdb to sda ~~~ 5. Once it's been determined where the device went/may have gone, navigate to the LSO symlink folder. ~~~ $ cd /mnt/local-storage/ / $ ls-ltr sh-5.1# ls-ltr lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 68 Apr 26 18:32 sdb-> /dev/sdb <------------- symlink ~~~ 6. Now that we have confirmed the device shifted to `/dev/sda` in our example above, attempt to correct the symlink. ~~~ $ cd /mnt/local-storage/ / $ ln-sf /dev/sda sdb ~~~ 7. Delete the pod. ~~~ $ oc delete pod-n openshift-storage rook-ceph-osd-X- ~~~ **NOTE:** If the pod comes up/running the symlink correction was successful. However, as discussed previously, if there are many OSDs on the host this may transition to a trial/error process. If this is the case repeat steps 4-7 until success is finally achieved. 8. Once all OSDs are up/running on the first node, proceed to the next node and repeat steps 3-7, and for the remaining nodes, only proceeding to the next node when all OSDs on the current node being worked are up/Running. 9. After all OSDs on all the Nodes are running, monitor the rebalance in Ceph and don't proceed to bring down the nodes to enable UUID until all PGs are `active+clean`. ~~~ $ oc rsh-n openshift-storage rook-ceph-tools- $ ceph status health: HEALTH_OK <------------------------------------- Needs to be before bringing down the first node services: mon: 3 daemons, quorum a,b,c (age 84m) mgr: b(active, since 84m), standbys: a mds: 1/1 daemons up, 1 hot standby osd: 6 osds: 6 up (since 84m), 6 in (since 84m) data: volumes: 1/1 healthy pools: 4 pools, 209 pgs objects: 99 objects, 154 MiB usage: 421 MiB used, 600 GiB / 600 GiB avail pgs: 209 active+clean <---------------------------- Needs to be before bringing down the first node io: client: 1.2 KiB/s rd, 2.7 KiB/s wr, 2 op/s rd, 0 op/s wr ~~~ 10. Once rebalancing is finished (Step 9), begin enabling `disk.EnableUUID=TRUE` and `uuid.action=keep` on each host, one at a time, and only proceed to the next node once Ceph reflects the example in Step 9. To gracefully bring down a storage node, follow the steps to scale down any mon/osd on the node being worked on. Additionally, delete any noobaa pod on that node once it's been cordoned. See [How to safely reboot an OCS/ODF 4 node](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/6495631) solution for more info. Lastly, DO NOT forget to scale up the mons/OSDs once the node has been uncordoned and in `Ready` status. 11. The following documentation will assist in this process (Since this is Infrastructure Specific, relevant VMWare docs will be provided, however it is up to the user to pursue the most up-to-date documentation regarding their virtual environment): [VMWare: Cannot find "disk.EnableUUID = "TRUE"" parameter in vmx file](https://kb.vmware.com/s/article/52815) [VMWare: Changing or keeping a UUID for a moved virtual machine](https://kb.vmware.com/s/article/1541) [How to check and set the disk.EnableUUID parameter from VM in vSphere for OpenShift Container Platform](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/4606201) [Use of VMware VMotion with OpenShift Container Storage / OpenShift Data Foundation](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/6444891) 12. Once UUIDs have been enabled ON THE FIRST NODE (devices may shift again), you can now run `$ ls-l /dev/disk/by-id` in the node and begin seeing UUIDs. Both scsi UUIDs and wwn UUIDs should be present. Although scsi IDs were used frequently in prior versions of LSO. The new UUIDs LSO defaults to are the new wwn UUIDs. Although either will work, when fixing symlinks use the wwn UUIDs. 13. To begin correcting the symlinks to the UUID, this may be a trial and error process again, however, a helpful command in Ceph that may reveal which UUID is associated with which OSD, is the following command: ~~~ $ oc rsh-n openshift-storage rook-ceph-tools- ~~~ **Example for osd.0. Change ID number based on desired OSD:** ~~~ $ ceph osd metadata 0 "device_ids": "wwn-0x6000c29a28e6d9e51bf43c386e40d6b9", <---- does this have a UUID? If not continue with trial/error (steps 3-7) ~~~ 14. Correct the symlink. **Example:** ~~~ $ oc debug node/node.1.com $ chroot /host $ lsblk $ ls-l /dev/disk/by-id $ cd /mnt/local-storage/ / ln-sf /dev/disk/by-id/wwn-0x6000c29a28e6d9e51bf43c386e40d6b9 sdb ~~~ 15. Delete the pod. ~~~ $ oc delete pod-n openshift-storage rook-ceph-osd-X- ~~~ **NOTE:** If the pod comes up/running the final symlink correction was successful. Once corrected on all OSDs, the node will finally be able to survive reboots. Repeat on remaining nodes while monitoring Ceph.
root_cause: Without UUID enabled in virtualized environment LSO defaults to using device IDs. For example `/dev/sdb`, `/dev/sdc/`, etc. which can shift upon node reboots.

title: CA Cert is not updated in application Secret by cert-manager when CA gets renewed.
