View the member list: etcdctl member list-w table * Example output ~~~ +------------------+---------+------------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+ | ID | STATUS | NAME | PEER ADDRS | CLIENT ADDRS | +------------------+---------+------------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+ | 6fc1e7c9db35841d | started | ip-10-0-131-183.ec2.internal | https://10.0.131.183:2380 | https://10.0.131.183:2379 | | 757b6793e2408b6c | started | ip-10-0-164-97.ec2.internal | https://10.0.164.97:2380 | https://10.0.164.97:2379 | | ca8c2990a0aa29d1 | started | ip-10-0-154-204.ec2.internal | https://10.0.154.204:2380 | https://10.0.154.204:2379 | +------------------+---------+------------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+ ~~~ * Take note of the ID and the name of the unhealthy etcd member, because these values are required later in the procedure. The etcdctl endpoint health command will list the removed member until the replacement procedure is completed and the new member is added. 4. Remove the unhealthy etcd member by providing the ID note above to the etcdctl member remove command: etcdctl member remove 6fc1e7c9db35841d (1) (1): Replace `6fc1e7c9db35841d` with the ID of the member on the unhealthy node * Example output ~~~ Member 6fc1e7c9db35841d removed from cluster b23536c33f2cdd1b ~~~ 5. View the member list again and verify that the member was removed: etcdctl member list-w table * Example output ~~~ +------------------+---------+------------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+ | ID | STATUS | NAME | PEER ADDRS | CLIENT ADDRS | +------------------+---------+------------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+ | 757b6793e2408b6c | started | ip-10-0-164-97.ec2.internal | https://10.0.164.97:2380 | https://10.0.164.97:2379 | | ca8c2990a0aa29d1 | started | ip-10-0-154-204.ec2.internal | https://10.0.154.204:2380 | https://10.0.154.204:2379 | +------------------+---------+------------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+ ~~~ **Important:** After you remove the member, the cluster might be unreachable for a short time while the remaining etcd instances reboot. 6. Exit the rsh session into the etcd pod exit #### Turn off etcd quorum guard [\[ocp\]](#ocp) {#ocp_step_2} 1. Run the following command to turn of the etcd quorum guard: oc patch etcd/cluster--type=merge-p '{"spec": {"unsupportedConfigOverrides": {"useUnsupportedUnsafeNonHANonProductionUnstableEtcd": true}}}' **Note:** The referenced [OpenShift documentation \[ocp\]](#ocp) includes a step to delete the node. However, as noted later in the documentation, removing the bmh and machine will cause the operator to remove the node. #### Remove the old secrets for the etcd member that was removed [\[ocp\]](#ocp) {#ocp_step_3} 1. List the secrets for the unhealthy etcd member that was removed. oc get secrets-n openshift-etcd | grep (1) (1): Replace ` ` with the name of the failed/off node (deleted in previous step) 2. There should be three secrets associated with the affected node whose names start with the following * etcd-peer- * etcd-serving-metrics- * etcd-serving- 3. Delete the secrets associated with the affected node that was removed. i. Delete the peer secret: oc delete secret-n openshift-etcd etcd-peer- (1) (1): Replace ` ` with the name of the affected node. ii. Delete the serving secret: oc delete secret-n openshift-etcd etcd-serving- (1) (1): Replace ` ` with the name of the affected node. iii. Delete the metrics secret: oc delete secret-n openshift-etcd etcd-serving-metrics- (1) (1): Replace ` ` with the name of the affected node. **Note:** For this type of installation there should be no ControlPlane machine set. #### Ensure that the BareMetal Operator is available [\[ocp\]](#ocp) {#ocp_step_5} 1. Ensure that the Bare Metal Operator is available by running the following command: oc get clusteroperator baremetal * Example output ~~~ NAME VERSION AVAILABLE PROGRESSING DEGRADED SINCE MESSAGE baremetal 4.18.0 True False False 3d15h ~~~ 2. Save the affected BareMetalHost object to a file for later use by running the following command oc get-n openshift-machine-api bmh-o yaml > bmh_affected.yaml (1) (1): Replace ` ` with the name of the affected node (which normally matches the associate bmh name). 3. Ensure the `yaml` content of the saved `BareMetalHost` is correct: cat bmh_affected.yaml #### Remove the affected BareMetalHost [\[ocp\]](#ocp) {#ocp_step_6} 1. Remove the affected BareMetalHost object by running the following command oc delete-n openshift-machine-api bmh (1) (1): Replace ` ` with the name of the affected node (which normally matches the associate bmh name). #### Obtain the machine for the affected node [\[ocp\]](#ocp) {#ocp_step_4} 1. Run the following command to identify the machine associated with the affected node oc get machines-n openshift-machine-api-o wide * Example Output ~~~ NAME PHASE TYPE REGION ZONE AGE NODE PROVIDERID STATE examplecluster-control-plane-0 Running 3h11m openshift-control-plane-0 baremetalhost:///openshift-machine-api/openshift-control-plane-0/da1ebe11-3ff2-41c5-b099-0aa41222964e externally provisioned examplecluster-control-plane-1 Running 3h11m openshift-control-plane-1 baremetalhost:///openshift-machine-api/openshift-control-plane-1/d9f9acbc-329c-475e-8d81-03b20280a3e1 externally provisioned examplecluster-control-plane-2 Running 3h11m openshift-control-plane-2 baremetalhost:///openshift-machine-api/openshift-control-plane-2/3354bdac-61d8-410f-be5b-6a395b056135 externally provisioned examplecluster-compute-0 Running 165m openshift-compute-0 baremetalhost:///openshift-machine-api/openshift-compute-0/3d685b81-7410-4bb3-80ec-13a31858241f provisioned examplecluster-compute-1 Running 165m openshift-compute-1 baremetalhost:///openshift-machine-api/openshift-compute-1/0fdae6eb-2066-4241-91dc-e7ea72ab13b9 provisioned ~~~ #### Delete the machine of the unhealthy member [\[ocp\]](#ocp) {#ocp_step_7} 1. Delete the machine of the unhealthy member by running the following command: oc delete machine-n openshift-machine-api (1) (1): Replace ` ` with the machine name found previously to be associated with the affected node. **Note:** After you remove the BareMetalHost and Machine objects, the Machine controller automatically deletes the Node object. a. If deletion of the machine is delayed for any reason or the command is obstructed and delayed, you can force deletion by removing the machine object finalizer field. ***Do not*** interrupt machine deletion by pressing `Ctrl+c`. You *must* allow the command to proceed to completion. Open a new terminal window to edit and delete the finalizer fields. #### Verify that the machine was deleted [\[ocp\]](#ocp) {#ocp_step_8} 1. Verify that the machine was deleted by running the following command: oc get machines-n openshift-machine-api-o wide #### Verify that the nodes has been deleted [\[ocp\]](#ocp) {#ocp_step_9} 1. Verify that the node has been deleted by running the following command: oc get nodes #### Wait for Cluster Operators [\[ocp\]](#ocp) {#ocp_step_9a} 1. Wait for all of the cluster operators to complete rolling out changes before proceeding to the next step * The following command can be used to monitor the progress: ~~~ watch oc get co ~~~ #### Create the new BareMetalHost [\[ocp\]](#ocp) {#ocp_step_10} 1. Edit the saved `bmh_affected.yaml` file from the earlier step i. Remove the following metadata items: a. creationTimestamp b. generation c. resourceVersion d. uid ii. Remove the status section iii. The resulting file should resemble the following: ~~~ apiVersion: metal3.io/v1alpha1 kind: BareMetalHost metadata: labels: installer.openshift.io/role: control-plane name: openshift-control-plane-2 namespace: openshift-machine-api spec: automatedCleaningMode: disabled bmc: address: credentialsName: disableCertificateVerification: true bootMACAddress: ab:cd:ef:ab:cd:ef bootMode: UEFI externallyProvisioned: true online: true rootDeviceHints: deviceName: /dev/disk/by-path/pci-0000:04:00.0-nvme-1 userData: name: master-user-data-managed namespace: openshift-machine-api ~~~ 2. Create the BareMetalHost oc create-f bmh_affected.yaml * The following warning is expected upon creation of the BareMetalHost ~~~ Warning: metadata.finalizers: "baremetalhost.metal3.io": prefer a domain-qualified finalizer name to avoid accidental conflicts with other finalizer writers ~~~ #### Create New ControlPlane Node [\[ocp\]](#ocp) {#ocp_step_11} 1. Extract the controlplane ignition secret using the following commands that include removal of the starting userData line. ~~~ oc extract secret/master-user-data-managed \-n openshift-machine-api \--keys=userData \--to=- \ | sed '/^userData/d' > new_controlplane.ign ~~~ 2. Create an nmstate file similar to the sample below for the new node’s network configuration. ~~~ interfaces:- name: eno1 type: ethernet state: up mac-address: "ab:cd:ef:01:02:03" ipv4: enabled: true address:- ip: 192.168.20.11 prefix-length: 24 dhcp: false ipv6: enabled: false dns-resolver: config: search:- iso.sterling.home server:- 192.168.20.8 routes: config:- destination: 0.0.0.0/0 metric: 100 next-hop-address: 192.168.20.1 next-hop-interface: eno1 table-id: 254 ~~~ **Note:** The failed node’s networkConfig section in the agent-config.yaml from the original cluster deployment can be used as a starting point for the new controlplane node’s nmstate file. The following illustrates extraction of that section for the first control plane node. ~~~ cat agent-config-iso.yaml | yq.hosts[0].networkConfig > new_controlplane_nmstate.yaml ~~~ 3. Create the customized Red Hat CoreOS live ISO with the following command ~~~ coreos-installer iso customize rhcos-live.86_64.iso \--dest-ignition new_controlplane.ign \--network-nmstate new_controlplane_nmstate.yaml \--dest-device /dev/disk/by-path/xxxxx \-f ~~~ 4. Boot the new ControlPlane node with the customized Red Hat CoreOS live ISO. 5. Approve the Certificate Signing Requests (CSR) to join the new node to the cluster. #### Link Node, BareMetalHost, and Machine (derived from [\[bmh\]](#bmh) {#bmh_link_host}) **Note:** This procedure is adapted from [Solution 6471021](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/6471021) 1. Generate the providerID lines for control plane nodes ~~~ oc get-n openshift-machine-api baremetalhost-l installer.openshift.io/role=control-plane-ojson | jq-r '.items[] | "baremetalhost:///openshift-machine-api/" +.metadata.name + "/" +.metadata.uid' ~~~ 2. Identify the cluster ~~~ oc get machine-n openshift-machine-api \-l machine.openshift.io/cluster-api-machine-role=master \-L machine.openshift.io/cluster-api-cluster ~~~ 3. Create a Machine for the new ContrlPlane Node (adjust the machine object name as required) ~~~ apiVersion: machine.openshift.io/v1beta1 kind: Machine metadata: annotations: metal3.io/BareMetalHost: openshift-machine-api/new-controleplane-machine (1) finalizers:- machine.machine.openshift.io labels: machine.openshift.io/cluster-api-cluster: bmtest-extpr-master-2 (2) machine.openshift.io/cluster-api-machine-role: master machine.openshift.io/cluster-api-machine-type: master name: new-controlplane-machine (1) namespace: openshift-machine-api spec: metadata: {} providerID: (3) providerSpec: value: apiVersion: baremetal.cluster.k8s.io/v1alpha1 hostSelector: {} image: checksum: "" url: "" kind: BareMetalMachineProviderSpec userData: name: master-user-data-managed ~~~ a. replace `new-controlplane-machine` with the name of the new machine (which can be the machine name deleted previously) b. replace `bmtest-extpr` with the `CLUSTER-API-CLUSTER` value shown in the previous step for the other control plane machines c. put the providerID value shown in the output of step 1 for the the new baremetal host here * The following warning is expected: ~~~ Warning: metadata.finalizers: "machine.machine.openshift.io": prefer a domain-qualified finalizer name to avoid accidental conflicts with other finalizer writers ~~~ 4. Link the new ControlPlane Node and Machine to the BareMetalHost by performing the following commands in a single bash shell session. i. Define the `NEW_NODE_NAME` variable ~~~ NEW_NODE_NAME=new-controlplane (1) ~~~ ii. Define the `NEW_MACHINE_NAME` variable ~~~ NEW_MACHINE_NAME=new-machine (2) ~~~ iii. Define the `BMH_UID` by using the following command to extract it from the new node’s bmh ~~~ BMH_UID=$(oc get-n openshift-machine-api bmh $NEW_NODE_NAME-ojson | jq-r.metadata.uid) echo $BMH_UID ~~~ iv. Patch consumerRef object into baremetal host ~~~ oc patch-n openshift-machine-api bmh $NEW_NODE_NAME--type merge--patch '{"spec":{"consumerRef":{"apiVersion":"machine.openshift.io/v1beta1","kind":"Machine","name":"'$NEW_MACHINE_NAME'","namespace":"openshift-machine-api"}}}' ~~~ v. Patch providerID into the new node ~~~ oc patch node $NEW_NODE_NAME--type merge--patch '{"spec":{"providerID":"baremetalhost:///openshift-machine-api/'$NEW_NODE_NAME'/'$BMH_UID'"}}' ~~~ vi. Review the providerIDs ~~~ oc get node-l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane-ojson | jq-r '.items[] |.metadata.name + " " +.spec.providerID' ~~~ 5. Set bmh poweredOn ~~~ oc patch-n openshift-machine-api bmh $NEW_NODE_NAME--subresource status--type json-p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/status/poweredOn","value":true}]' ~~~ 6. Review bmh poweredOn status ~~~ oc get bmh-n openshift-machine-api-ojson | jq-r '.items[] |.metadata.name + " PoweredOn:" + (.status.poweredOn | tostring)' ~~~ 7. Review the bmh provisioning state ~~~ oc get bmh-n openshift-machine-api-ojson | jq-r '.items[] |.metadata.name + " ProvsioningState:" +.status.provisioning.state' ~~~ 8. Change the provisioning (state if necessary) ~~~ oc patch-n openshift-machine-api bmh $NEW_NODE_NAME--subresource status--type json-p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/status/provisioning/state","value":"unmanaged"}]' ~~~ 9. Set the machine provisioned state ~~~ oc patch-n openshift-machine-api machines $NEW_MACHINE_NAME-n openshift-machine-api--subresource status--type json-p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/status/phase","value":"Provisioned"}]' ~~~ #### Add The New Etcd Member {#new_etcd} 1. Add the new etcd member to the etcd cluster by performing the following steps in a single bash shell session i. A later step requires the IP of new control plane node. Use the following command to find the IP of the new control plane node: ~~~ oc get nodes-owide-l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane ~~~ ii. List the etcd pods ~~~ oc get-n openshift-etcd pods-l k8s-app=etcd-o wide ~~~ iii. rsh into one of the Running etcd pods. The etcd pod on the new node should be CrashLoopBackOff. ~~~ oc rsh-n openshift-etcd (1) ~~~ (1): replace runningpod with the name of a running pod shown in the previous step iv. View the etcd member list: ~~~ etcdctl member list-w table ~~~ v. Add the new contrlplane etcd member ~~~ etcdctl member add--peer-urls="https://192.168.20.42:2380" (1) ~~~ (1): replace new-controlplane with the node name of the new node, and replace 192.168.20.42 the IP of the new node. vi. Exit the rsh shell ~~~ exit ~~~ #### Force Etcd redeployment [\[clp\]](#clp) {#clp_step_5} 1. Force etcd redeployment by entering the following command ~~~ oc patch etcd cluster-p='{"spec": {"forceRedeploymentReason": "single-master-recovery-'"$(date--rfc-3339=ns)"'"}}'--type=merge ~~~ #### Turn the quorum guard back on [\[clp\]](#clp) {#clp_step_6} 1. Turn the quorum guard back on by issuing the following command: ~~~ oc patch etcd/cluster--type=merge-p '{"spec": {"unsupportedConfigOverrides": null}}' ~~~ #### Wait for the Cluster Operators {#wait_cl_ops} 1. Use the following command to monitor the clusteroperator rollout: ~~~ watch oc get co ~~~ ### References {#refer} * [ocp] [Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform Documentation- Configure- Backup and Restore](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.19/html/backup_and_restore/control-plane-backup-and-restore#restore-replace-stopped-baremetal-etcd-member_replacing-unhealthy-etcd-member) {#ocp} * [clp] [Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform Documentation- Configure- Backup and Restore- Replacing an unhealthy etcd member whose etcd pod is crashlooping](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.19/html/backup_and_restore/control-plane-backup-and-restore#restore-replace-crashlooping-etcd-member_replacing-unhealthy-etcd-member) {#clp} * [bmh] [BareMetalHost reference is missing after adding a host to Openshift Assisted Installer cluster](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/6471021) {#bmh} * [rig] [How to retrieve Master or Worker Ignition Configuration from OpenShift Container Platform 4?](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/5504291)
root_cause: * The root cause identified is that the ABI method currently only supports adding worker nodes, and there is no direct support for adding or replacing control plane nodes using ABI. * Current [Red Hat documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.19/html/backup_and_restore/control-plane-backup-and-restore#backup-etcd) for “**Replacing Control Plane**” provides general steps applicable to OpenShift clusters but does not clarify whether these steps are supported for clusters originally installed using the **Agent-based Installer**. * This issue is being tracked on Jira ticket [OSDOCS-15865](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OSDOCS-15865), * A feature request for a simplified Day-2 control plane node replacement is being tracked by Jira ticket [RFE-6515](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/RFE-6515).

title: Explaination of AIDE Checks statuses in File Integrity operator
issue: - What's the meaning of AIDE Checks return statuses?
resolution: The status codes observed in the context of the File Integrity Operator with AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) typically indicate the outcome of the integrity check. In AIDE, the exit codes use a [bitmask](https://github.com/aide/aide/blob/bfb084864939471ede09f7c8432c576b6f3a6294/src/report.c#L975) system (0-7) where each bit represents a type of change: | Exit code | Binary | Meaning | |-----------|--------|---------------------------------| | 0 | 000 | No changes | | 1 | 001 | Only added files | | 2 | 010 | Only removed files | | 3 | 011 | Added + removed | | 4 | 100 | Only modified files | | 5 | 101 | Added + modified | | 6 | 110 | Removed + modified | | 7 | 111 | Added + removed + modified | Additionally, the following exit codes are defined for generic error conditions: ~~~ 14 Writing error 15 Invalid argument error 16 Unimplemented function error 17 Configuration error 18 IO error 19 Version mismatch error 20 EXEC error 21 File lock error 22 Memory allocation error 23 Thread error 24 Database error 25 received SIGINT, SIGTERM or SIGHUP ~~~ Please refer to the aide man page for more details: ~~~ $ man aide ~~~ Also find the man page online at: [https://linux.die.net/man/1/aide](https://linux.die.net/man/1/aide) **Disclaimer**: Links contained herein to external website(s) are provided for convenience only. Red Hat has not reviewed the links and is not responsible for the content or its availability. The inclusion of any link to an external website does not imply endorsement by Red Hat of the website or their entities, products or services. You agree that Red Hat is not responsible or liable for any loss or expenses that may result due to your use of (or reliance on) the external site or content. The File Integrity Operator uses these AIDE return codes to populate status fields in its resources like:- NodeStatus (e.g., Succeeded, Failed)- The integritylog ConfigMap contains the detailed scan output

title: [RHACS] Can we disable the Stackrox Scanner and only use Scanner V4
product: Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security for Kubernetes
issue: - After installing Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security for Kubernetes (RHACS), both the Stackrox Scanner and the Scanner V4 are active. Are both needed? According to the [documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_advanced_cluster_security_for_kubernetes/4.9/html-single/release_notes/index#deprecated-and-removed-features_release-notes-49), the Stackrox scanner is deprecated.- Can the StackRox scanner be removed or disabled?
resolution: - The StackRox Scanner (Scanner V2) has been deprecated since RHACS `4.6`. [Deprecated](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_advanced_cluster_security_for_kubernetes/4.9/html-single/release_notes/index#deprecated-and-removed-features_release-notes-49:~:text=DEP-,StackRox%20Scanner,-DEP) means it is included and supported, but not recommended for new deployments. Although the StackRox Scanner is deprecated, it still must be enabled on the cluster where Central is installed due to software dependencies.- Although it is deprecated, the StackRox Scanner is still included in `RHACS 4.9` to perform specific tasks, such as scanning nodes and platform components, while Scanner V4 handles container image scanning. Scanner V4 became the default scanner for new installations starting in `RHACS 4.8`.- Refer to the following documentation links for the main differences between the Stackrox Scanner and the Scanner V4:- [Layer compression formats](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_advanced_cluster_security_for_kubernetes/4.9/html-single/release_notes/index#deprecated-and-removed-features_release-notes-49)- [Supported Operating Systems](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_advanced_cluster_security_for_kubernetes/4.9/html/operating/examine-images-for-vulnerabilities#supported-operating-systems_examine-images-for-vulnerabilities)- Datasources for [ScannerV4](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_advanced_cluster_security_for_kubernetes/4.9/html-single/architecture/index#scanner-v4-vuln-sources)- Datasources for [Stackrox](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_advanced_cluster_security_for_kubernetes/4.9/html-single/architecture/index#stackrox-scanner-vuln-sources)

title: How to schedule Service Mesh 3 pods on infra nodes
issue: - Is it possible to schedule Red Hat Service Mesh (OSSM) 3 workload on Infra nodes?- Can nodeSelector or toleration be used to schedule OSSM 3 workload on specific nodes same as OSSM 2?
resolution: For the Istio CR, nodeSelector and tolerations can be used under the `spec.value.pilot` section: ~~~ spec: value: pilot: nodeSelector: node-role.kubernetes.io/infra: "" tolerations:- key: "node-role.kubernetes.io/infra" operator: "Exists" effect: "NoSchedule" ~~~
root_cause: By default, the OSSM 3 Operator has no nodeSelector or tolerations defined, so its pods can be scheduled on any available nodes.

title: MetalLB to replace keepalived operator
issue: What is the migration path from the keepalived operator to the MetalLB operator?

The goal is to safely transition existing Service objects from the Keepalived Operator's control to the MetalLB Operator's control one by one, allowing both systems to manage different subsets of external IPs concurrently until the migration is complete.
resolution: Please follow these steps to deploy MetalLB, configure its IP pools, and then iteratively migrate your services. ### Phase 1: Deploy MetalLB and Configure IP Pool This phase ensures MetalLB is operational and ready to accept new services. **Step 1: Install the MetalLB Operator** Install the MetalLB Operator via the OpenShift OperatorHub. Once the Operator is running, create the necessary MetalLB Custom Resource (CR) instance. ~~~ # Create the MetalLB custom resource cat <
root_cause: * MetalLB operating in layer2 mode provides support for failover by utilizing a mechanism similar to IP failover. However, instead of relying on the virtual router redundancy protocol (VRRP) and keepalived, MetalLB leverages a gossip-based protocol to identify instances of node failure. When a failover is detected, another node assumes the role of the leader node, and a gratuitous ARP message is dispatched to broadcast this change. * Using MetalLB instead of IP failover is preferable for ensuring high availability of pods and services. * MetalLB and IP failover are incompatible. Make sure they are not managing the same IPs. If you configured IP failover for your cluster, perform the steps to remove IP failover after uninstalling the keepalived Operator.

title: Configuring Egressip on secondary interface [RHOCP]
issue: When an `EgressIP` object is created on a node's secondary interface, traffic may fail to leave with the designated `EgressIP` address, as the necessary source network address translation (SNAT) does not occur, despite the `EgressIP` being correctly attached to the interface.
resolution: For `Egressip` configuration on secondary interface, refer to the product documentation-- [Considerations for using an egress IP on additional network interfaces](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.18/html/ovn-kubernetes_network_plugin/configuring-egress-ips-ovn#nw-egress-ips-multi-nic-considerations_configuring-egress-ips-ovn). In addition to the steps given in the product documentation, make sure the following configurations are present on the node for the secondary interface:- Configure a default gateway to the secondary interface with higher metric than the primary interface. ~~~ $ nmcli connection modify +ipv4.routes "0.0.0.0/0 " $ nmcli-f ipv4.route-metric,ipv4.routes con show bondx.12xx ipv4.route-metric:-1 ipv4.routes: {ip = 0.0.0.0/0, nh = 172.xxx.xx.1, mt = 300} ~~~---- It is possible that after assigning the default gateway, the secondary interface connection profile has not refreshed. If this is the case, follow the steps below: ~~~ $ nmcli con down $ nmcli con up ~~~- Verify that default gateway route is visible in main table for secondary Interface with higher metric value: ~~~ $ route-n ~~~- If the route is visible, then recreate the `EgressIP` object then verify the functionality. ### NMstate operator {#nmstate1}- Check the current metric from default route within RHOCP node via `SSH` access: ~~~ $ ip route | grep default default via dev br-ex proto dhcp src xxxxx metric 48 <----- ~~~- The same logic can be applied using `NMstate` operator, however the `default` `route` with higher metric is configured via `NNCP` policies. In case of IPv6, it is needed to adapt the configuration accordingly. See the example configuration: ~~~ apiVersion: nmstate.io/v1 kind: NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy metadata: name: egressip-secondary-network spec: desiredState: routes: config:- destination: 0.0.0.0/0 metric: 300 <---- Higher than 48 next-hop-address: next-hop-interface: nodeSelector:: " " ~~~- Confirm that `NNCP` and `NNCE` policies have been successfully applied into desired nodes: ~~~ $ oc get nncp,nnce | grep egressip nodenetworkconfigurationpolicy.nmstate.io/egressip-secondary-network Available SuccessfullyConfigured nodenetworkconfigurationenactment.nmstate.io/.egressip-secondary-network Available SuccessfullyConfigured ~~~- Confirm if the route is correctly available within `egressip` node via custom `routing` `table`: ~~~ $ ip route | grep default default via dev br-ex proto dhcp src xxxxx metric 48 <----- default via dev proto static metric 300 <--- New route with higher metric ~~~- It is recommended to reassign all `egressips` from this node to ensure that new route is configured: ~~~ $ oc label node/ k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable- $ oc label node/ k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable= ~~~ **NOTE:** ~~~~ The mentioned configuration can affect the node's traffic operation. It is recommended to run desired tests in TEST environment before configuring the same in PRODUCTION clusters. ~~~~
root_cause: The `default gateway` is missing from the secondary interface of the node where the `EgressIP` is created. To resolve this, a `default gateway` must be assigned to the secondary interface with a higher metric value (e.g., 300) than the primary default route.

title: Why do I get events of failed Pods after creating a monitoringStack?
issue: After the creation of a `monitoringStack` you can see `Events` of failed `Pods`.
resolution: Red Hat is aware of this issue and is tracking the resolution in the following Bug: [COO-1511](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/COO-1511).
root_cause: * There is a race condition which can lead to missing `RoleBinding` which is getting created after the Pod has been created. After the Pod fails one time the next startup will be successful.

title: How to calculate maximum number of pods, which we can set on each worker node in RHOCP 4.x
issue: - How many pods can I allocate per OpenShift node?- What parameter will affect the max number of pods per node?- How to calculate the max number of pods based on Host Prefix?
resolution: ####Parameter that affects the max number of pods per node- **podsPerCore**: The `podsPerCore` parameter limits the number of pods the node can run based on the number of processor cores on the node. For example, if podsPerCore is set to 10 on a node with 4 processor cores, the maximum number of pods allowed on the node is 40. This parameter is configured using [KubeletConfig CR](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.9/nodes/nodes/nodes-nodes-managing-max-pods.html#nodes-nodes-managing-max-pods-about_nodes-nodes-jobs)- **maxPods**: The `maxPods` parameter limits the number of pods the node can run to a fixed value, regardless of the properties of the node. This parameter is configured using [KubeletConfig CR](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.9/nodes/nodes/nodes-nodes-managing-max-pods.html#nodes-nodes-managing-max-pods-about_nodes-nodes-jobs)- **Host Prefix**: The Cluster Network CIDR and Host Prefix will also affect the max number of pods on each node. The Host Prefix will limit the max number of IPs available on each node for the pod. Starting with OpenShift 4.14, you can modify the `clusterNetwork` IP address range after installation. For earlier versions however, they must be set at the time of installation. Check the information about this in the document [link](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.14/html/networking/cluster-network-operator#nw-operator-cr_cluster-network-operator). ####Calculating the max number of pods based on Host Prefix- Check the current CIDR and Host Prefix for the cluster using the following command. ~~~ $ oc describe network.config/cluster | grep 'Cidr\|Host\ Prefix' | head-2 Cidr: 10.10.0.0/14 Host Prefix: 24 ~~~- Calculate the maximum number of hosts per network by referring to previous values. ~~~ $ ipcalc 10.10.0.0/24 | grep Hosts\/Net Hosts/Net: 254 ~~~- It is possible to run a max of 254 pods per node. Note: In all three parameters `podsPerCore`, `maxPods`, `Host Prefix`, whichever parameter is lower is considered as max pod limit for that node.
root_cause: - The max pods per node are dependent on `KubeletConfig` and `host network` configurations

title: Authentication methods supported by the collector to log forward in RHOCP 4
issue: Wishing to forward messages to a remote server over HTTPS using for the authentication a token
Unclear on how to configure authentication/secret for the `clusterLogForwarder`
What are the authentication methods supported in the collector?
Does the `clusterLogForwarder` support to use an API-Key or API token to authenticate?
resolution: Starting in Red Hat OpenShift Logging 6. It's possible to use different authentication methods. The methods supported for each output type and how to define them are visible in the API. For verifying the `authentication` options available for the different output types: 1. List the output types supported by the collector ~~~ $ oc explain obsclf.spec.outputs ~~~ 2. List the options for that specific type. The next example is for the output type HTTP ~~~ $ oc explain obsclf.spec.outputs.http.authentication GROUP: observability.openshift.io KIND: ClusterLogForwarder VERSION: v1 FIELD: authentication DESCRIPTION: Authentication sets credentials for authenticating the requests. FIELDS: password Password to use for authenticating requests. token Token specifies a bearer token to be used for authenticating requests. username Username to use for authenticating requests. $ oc explain obsclf.spec.outputs.http.authentication.token GROUP: observability.openshift.io KIND: ClusterLogForwarder VERSION: v1 FIELD: token DESCRIPTION: Token specifies a bearer token to be used for authenticating requests. FIELDS: from-required- From is the source from where to find the token secret Use Secret if the value should be sourced from a Secret in the same namespace. ~~~ For being able to log forward using an API-Key or API token. The API-Key can be set in the `clusterLogForwarder.spec.headers`. This configuration goes in clear text. Red Hat is aware of the feature request "[OBSDA-994- Header Api-tokens should be injected via secret in ClusterLogForwarder](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OBSDA-994#)" for being able to log forward using an API-Key being stored in a secret. If this feature is required, please open a [new support case](https://access.redhat.com/support/cases/#/case/new/). #### Example for output type HTTP using a bearer token 1. Create a secret containing the token ~~~ $ oc-n openshift-logging create secret generic http-secret--from-literal token= ~~~ 2. Configure the `clusterLogForwarder` HTTP output to use the secret containing the token ~~~ apiVersion: observability.openshift.io/v1 kind: ClusterLogForwarder metadata: name: namespace: openshift-logging [...] spec: managementState: Managed outputs:- name: type: http http: authentication: token: secretName: http-secret key: token [...] ~~~ #### Example for output type HTTP using a API-Key or API token `clusterLogforwarder` configuration for using an API-Key: ~~~ [...] outputs:- http: headers: Authorization: Api-Token Content-Type: application/json accept: application/json; charset=utf-8 method: POST name: http tls: insecureSkipVerify: false type: http url: 'https:// ' [...] ~~~

title: OCP UI Fails to Display Virtual Machines After Upgrade: "Something Went Wrong" Error.
issue: - After upgrade to 4.20.8 OCP UI is no longer able to display configuration of virtual machines.- When we try to open any virtual machine from Virtualization-> Virtual Machine-> VM Name opens error message: ~~~ Minified React error #130; visit https://reactjs.org/docs/error-decoder.html?invariant=130&args[]=undefined&args[]= for the full message or use the non-minified dev environment for full errors and additional helpful warnings. ~~~ [image=[src="images/image_70.png", title="Something wrong happened", alt="Something went wrong.", size="LG- Large", data-cp-size="50%", data-cp-align="center", caption="Something wrong happened", lightbox="true"]]
resolution: - Upgrade OpenShift Virtualization Operator to same as OpenShift Cluster version.
root_cause: - The OpenShift Virtualization Operator should ideally run on the exact same version as the OpenShift Cluster. While Red Hat tests a one-version lag during upgrades (n-1), it is not recommended. Having the Operator two or more versions behind the cluster (n-2) is neither supported nor tested by Red Hat.

title: Error in Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security for Kubernetes Sensor Component: Unable to Determine Collector Version
product: Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security for Kubernetes
issue: Error message in sensor pods: ~~~
``kubernetes/clusterhealth: Errors while getting collector info: [unable to determine collector version] ~~~
resolution: Make sure the collectionMethod is set to CORE_BPF, and once you apply this change this will restart the pod with all three containers included.
root_cause: As this error is frequently seen after an upgrade if the Sensor was updated but the Collector image is still an older version or Collector pods are stuck in a "CrashLoopBackOff" state, they might not be alive long enough for the system to read their version information.

title: Webhook violations could become a very large JSON body when using a Generic Webhook notifier for Integration to qRadar in RHACS
product: Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security for Kubernetes
issue: The large webhook payloads from the Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security (RHACS) QRadar integration and could cause confusion with customers and show truncation or dropped events.
resolution: To limit these large payloads for QRadar integration with RHACS customers can:- focusing on high-fidelity alerts and their security policies.You can do this by using policy criteria to focus only on Critical or High severity vulnerabilities or policy violations, dramatically reducing the volume of alerts being sent downstream.- Focus policies using criteria like network exposure (e.g., ports exposed to external clients) to target where the actual risk is highest, which reduces the total number of policy violations that generate notifications.- Use an external workaround such as trying an intermediary system like Kafka or Red Hat Fuse to receive the webhook, process the data (e.g., strip the embedded full policy definition if unneeded), transform the payload, and then forward the trimmed data.- Go into QRadar configurations itself since it has a default maximum TCP syslog payload size of 4096 bytes, which may be insufficient for these large RHACS payloads and is often recommended to be increased to at least 32000 bytes in the QRadar configuration to prevent truncation or dropped events.
root_cause: The large webhook payloads from the Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security (RHACS) QRadar integration are primarily due to the default behavior of RHACS alert notifications, which include grouping multiple events and embedding full policy definitions. This is by design RHACS groups related policy violations to minimize notification spam and provide a more comprehensive view of an issue at a given time. This aggregation naturally results in a larger payload than sending single, individual events. For each alert, the system includes the complete details of the policy that was violated and allows for understanding the full scope, criteria, and impact of the policy without needing to switch between systems or look up policy IDs. However, it also will significantly increases the size of the JSON payload sent via the webhook,as this data sent to QRadar is essentially the same data contained within the "alerts" objects in the API's Violations section.

title: Cluster Logging Operator referencing elasticsearch despite no ES deployment

title: Which image formats are supported in Red Hat OpenStack Platform & 	Red Hat Openstack Services on Openshift
issue: - Trying to upload qcow2 images to glance using cinder iscsi / ceph as backend fails.- Trying to create a volume from a qcow2 image using cinder iscsi / ceph as backend fails.
resolution: - This fails because **block-based storage backends** dont recognize the QCOW2 file format.- In Red Hat OpenStack Platform (RHOSP) 17.1 and Red Hat Openstack Services on Openshift (RHOSO) 18.0, block storage presents a "raw" disk to the operating system.- Trying to push a QCOW2 file onto a block device will cause the system to "see" the QCOW2 header as corrupted data or a non-bootable disk.- Using swift to store images in qcow2 while using any **block-based storage backend** for cinder will require for these files to be converted to raw which requires temp space and time.- This often causes failures to launch instances. ### Storage backends that require raw conversion- The following backends for Red Hat OpenStack Platform (RHOSP) 17.1 and Red Hat Openstack Services on Openshift (RHOSO) 18.0 require images to be in RAW format for proper functionality, performance, and volume-to-image operations: * **Red Hat Ceph Storage (RBD):** This is the most common backend. While it can technically store QCOW2 headers, it breaks the "Copy-on-Write" (CoW) cloning features and high-performance snapshotting that Ceph is known for. Red Hat strictly recommends RAW for RBD. * **Cinder iSCSI (Generic LVM):** Standard iSCSI drivers using Linux LVM create raw logical volumes. They cannot interpret the metadata inside a QCOW2 file. * **Cinder iSCSI and FC (Dell PowerStore / PowerMax):** These hardware drivers require the RAW format to utilize hardware-assisted cloning and to ensure the LUN is bootable by Nova. * **Cinder iSCSI and FC (NetApp ONTAP Block):** When using ONTAP via iSCSI or Fibre Channel, the "Copy Offload" and deduplication features are optimized for RAW block data. * **Cinder iSCSI and FC (Pure Storage FlashArray):** Pure's Purity OS handles data reduction at the block level. Using QCOW2 on these volumes interferes with the array's ability to manage the data efficiently and often leads to boot failures. * **Cinder Fibre Channel (Generic):** Like iSCSI, generic FC drivers provide a raw block interface that does not support file-level formats like QCOW2. * **Local LVM Storage:** If your Cinder nodes use local disks managed by LVM, these are presented as raw block devices. ### When is QCOW2 Supported? You should only keep images in QCOW2 format if you are using a **file-based** backend where the storage system sees a filesystem, such as: * **NFS** * **Swift (Object Storage)** * **S3-compatible storage**

title: Configuring outbound SSL connection from Quarkus deployed on Openshift
issue: - When trying to make outbound SSL connection from Quarkus we are getting below error: ~~~ javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException: sun.security.validator.ValidatorException: PKIX path building failed: sun.security.provider.certpath.SunCertPathBuilderException: unable to find valid certification path to requested target ~~~- We have configured `quarkus.http.ssl.certificate.trust-store-file` to trust server certificate but still we are getting below error: ~~~ javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException: sun.security.validator.ValidatorException: PKIX path building failed: sun.security.provider.certpath.SunCertPathBuilderException: unable to find valid certification path to requested target ~~~- Unable to make outbound SSL connection from the java application deployed in Openshift. Below error is observed in the logs: ~~~ javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException: sun.security.validator.ValidatorException: PKIX path building failed: sun.security.provider.certpath.SunCertPathBuilderException: unable to find valid certification path to requested target ~~~
resolution: To enable outbound SSL connection(where the external endpoint has privately signed certificate) we need to mount truststore in the java application deployed over Openshift. In case adding the CA certificate during the build time(using Dockerfile/Containerfile- [Option 2. Add a CA certification when building a container- Build time option](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/6999986)) is not an option, then use below steps to mount the truststore: **Step1**: Import the server's certificate into a truststore. ~~~ keytool-import-trustcacerts-alias server_cert-file server.cert-keystore truststore.jks ~~~ **Step2:** Create a secret from truststore.jks file created in previous step. ~~~ oc create secret generic truststore-n REPLACE_WITH_CURRENT_NAMESPACE--from-file=truststore=/path/to/your/truststore.jks ~~~ **Step3:** Add the secret and secret mount path in `application.properties` like following: ~~~ quarkus.openshift.mounts.my-volume.path=/mnt quarkus.openshift.secret-volumes.my-volume.secret-name=truststore ~~~ Or mount the secret directly in the application Deployment using following command: ~~~ $ oc set volume deployment/--add--name=truststore-volume-m /mnt-t secret--secret-name=truststore--default-mode='0755' ~~~ **Step4:** [Deploy](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_build_of_quarkus/quarkus-3.2/guide/85e494b4-4e47-4831-8294-212c4c838c7b#_5aa3db0f-2cca-4983-9f1c-f1a4043ea971) the RHBQ application to Openshift. **Step5:** Pass the truststore JVM argument to the Deployment Config(of application deployed in previous step) ~~~ oc set env dc/ JAVA_OPTS_APPEND="-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=/mnt/truststore-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=password_of_your_truststore" ~~~
root_cause: Outbound SSL connection use Java system properties to configure their truststore certificates.

title: Restarting the Bare Metal Host results in deletion of the underlying node in RHOCP
issue: - Restarting the Bare Metal Host results in deletion of the underlying node from the cluster, upon successful reboot it gets added as a new node.
resolution: - Check for any existing *`MachineHealthCheck`* in your environment created for remediating unhealthy nodes. Remove the one which is deleting the nodes. ~~~ $ oc get mhc-A $ oc get mhc-n-o yaml <--- To check the specs of the *`MachineHealthCheck`* $ oc delete mhc-n ~~~- For hybrid environment including both VMs and BMHs, check if vSphere Cloud Provider Interface (CPI) operator is installed in the cluster and remove it.
root_cause: - The *`MachineHealthCheck`* monitors the node object for conditions like *`Ready=False`* or *`Ready=Unknown`* and once the timeout defined in the *`MachineHealthCheck`* config is reached, the Machine API deletes the Machine object.- The vShpere Cloud Provider Interface (CPI) operator handles the identity and lifecycle of nodes. It may affect the Bare Metal Host in hybrid infrastructure environment which includes both VMs and BMH.

title: Tracing UI is missing "trace:id" from the dropdown in the TraceQL query search bar
issue: - When constructing queries using the `TraceQL` query search bar located in the OpenShift console's *Observe > Traces

panel, the auto-completion feature for trace-level attributes (prefixed with trace:) incorrectly omits the critical `trace:id` attribute.- The dropdown only offers suggestions such as `trace:duration`, `trace:rootName`, `trace:rootService`, and `traceDuration`. This missing suggestion impairs the user experience, making it difficult to quickly search for a specific trace by ID.
resolution: - This can be resolved by upgrading `Cluster Observability Operator` (COO) to version 1.3.0 or later and `Red Hat OpenShift Distributed Tracing` (RHOSDT) platform version 3.8.- Further details on the status of the bug reported to Red Hat Engineering can be found at [the associated Jira ticket](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OU-1037).
root_cause: - This is a known defect within the Tracing UI plugin in which the list of auto-completion suggestions fails to include the `trace:id` attribute.- This bug has been reported to Red Hat Engineering and the issue can be tracked in [the associated Jira ticket](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OU-1037).

title: Prune Filter do not filter structured json logs.
issue: - Prune Filter do not filter structured json logs.- Structured JSON fields remain unaffected by the prune filter.- Pruning logic does not apply to structured JSON fields.
resolution: Pipelines control the log flow from inputs to outputs using specific references. Filters within a pipeline transform or drop messages sequentially. This order is critical because earlier filters can prevent logs from reaching later stages. Example: ~~~ pipelines:- filterRefs:- cluster-labels- application-filter- parse-json inputRefs:- application ~~~ Here, the application-filter attempt to prune data before json parsing occurred. Consequently, fields example structured.XXX were not removed/kept based on `application-filter`. Placing the application-filter after the parse-json filter ensures the data is properly structured before pruning logic is applied. Hence,parse-json filter should be listed before application-filter: ~~~ pipelines:- filterRefs:- parse-json <-- This should be listed first- cluster-labels- application-filter <-- This should be listed last inputRefs:- application ~~~

resolution: **NOTE: It's out of Red Hat's support scope, and may change without notice.** * In the `glibc` source code, `iconvdata/*.irreversible` define the table of these characters. ~~~ $ ls *irreversible ARMSCII-8.irreversible CP1258.irreversible EUC-KR.irreversible IBM1160.irreversible IBM856.irreversible SJIS.irreversible BIG5HKSCS.irreversible CP932.irreversible EUC-TW.irreversible IBM1161.irreversible IBM922.irreversible TSCII.irreversible BIG5.irreversible EUC-JP.irreversible IBM1132.irreversible IBM1163.irreversible ISIRI-3342.irreversible CP1255.irreversible EUC-JP-MS.irreversible IBM1133.irreversible IBM1164.irreversible SHIFT_JISX0213.irreversible ~~~ * These files can be found in [glibc src.rpm package](https://access.redhat.com/downloads/content/glibc/x86_64/package-latest) or [glibc upstream repository](https://sourceware.org/git/?p=glibc.git;a=tree;f=iconvdata;hb=HEAD)

title: Log forwarding not working in OpenShift due to invalid ClusterLogForwarder output reference in RHOCP 4
issue: - `Log forwarding` in an OCP cluster is not working as expected.- Logs are either not forwarded to the `external SIEM` system or the ClusterLogForwarder (CLF) resource reports an `Invalid status`.- Logs are not in the expected `JSON` format.
resolution: - The `ClusterLogForwarder configuration` was `invalid` due to a `mismatch` between the `pipelines.outputRefs` and the `defined outputs` in `.spec.outputs`: ``` $ oc get ClusterLogForwarder-n openshift-logging-o yaml... status: conditions:- lastTransitionTime: "2025-08-21T05:50:59Z" message: No valid inputs, outputs, or pipelines. Invalid CLF spec. <----------------- reason: Invalid status: "False" type: Ready... ```- In the `pipelines` section, listing a `single destination` to forward the logs to called `securonix-syslog` in the `outputRefs` section: ```... pipelines:- inputRefs:- audit labels: forwarded_by: openshift log_type: audit name: forward-audit-logs outputRefs:- securonix-syslog <----------- parse: json... ```- `securonix-syslog` defined anywhere as an `output` in the outputs section. So either need to changed the `outputRefs` in the `pipelines` section to use one of the outputs defined, or need to add a section for `securonix-syslog` with the configuration of where logs would be sent to it.

title: How can retrieve the serial number and hardware information  from the cluster nodes?
product: Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management for Kubernetes
issue: - We essentially want to get the hardware serial number and hostname for each nodes. We are trying to get the node serial number of all the nodes that are attached to cluster. IIn one of the environments we checked, the BareMetalHost (BMH) resource doesn’t show any node name or serial number. We’re trying to understand why there’s a deviation in the BMH output across different managed clusters.
resolution: If the cluster is unmanaged state then from ACM we don't have a control over it. The unmanaged state mean that for every node there is no credential configured to control anything. Please check for credential for baremetal clusters: 1.5.8 \"Creating a credential for an on-premises environment\", https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_advanced_cluster_management_for_kubernetes/2.13/html-single/clusters/index#creating-a-credential-for-an-on-premises-environment. Some clusters don't have HW details. (ABI clusters): BMH resources are created at install time for platform:baremetal clusters but not for platform:none clusters. Nodes added on day 2 with oc adm node-image create will not have BMHs. HardwareDetails information is collected by the agent at install time and written into the BMH. If no BMH was created at install time then the data isn't stored anywhere. BMH (BareMetalHost) belongs to Bare Metal Operator (BMO) used when deployed OCP on a bare-metal host, the BMO maintains an inventory of the physical hosts in the cluster by mapping each bare-metal host to an instance of the BareMetalHost custom resource definition. metal3 introduced the BareMetalHost resource that features hardware, software, and firmware details. [1] When you provision a bare-metal host to the cluster, please take a look at [3], you must define a BareMetalHost resource for that host. If the node would be deleted then BMH could be deleted as a part of it. 1: "4.5.2. About the BareMetalHost resource" https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.18/html/installing_on_bare_metal/bare-metal-postinstallation-configuration#bmo-about-the-baremetalhost-resource_bare-metal-postinstallation-configuration 2: "4.5.4. Editing a BareMetalHost resource" https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.18/html/installing_on_bare_metal/bare-metal-postinstallation-configuration#bmo-editing-a-baremetalhost-resource_bare-metal-postinstallation-configuration 3: "Chapter 5. Expanding the cluster" https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.18/html/installing_on_bare_metal/bare-metal-expanding-the-cluster

title: Audit logs in RHOCP 4 shows system:serviceaccount:openshift-logging:cluster-logging-operator  cannot list resource hostedcontrolplanes
issue: - Observed repeated 403 Forbidden errors in the OpenShift audit logs indicating that the cluster-logging-operator is failing to list hostedcontrolplanes resources. This generates excessive noise in the audit log.- The issue occurs when stale CRDs related to Hypershift Addon remain in the cluster after the add-on has been uninstalled, Sep 18 2025 15:03:33 Sep 18 2025 15:03:28 Sep 18 2025 15:03:33 1758200613771 Sep 18 2025 15:03:28 1758200613727 CEjRN14huCAE8grqp/uh0g==:201:42457:80594 403 list ResponseComplete "[""system:serviceaccounts"",""system:serviceaccounts:openshift-logging"",""system:authenticated""]" Red Hat user1 Openshift " <134> 1 2025-09-18T13:03:28.235Z node1.ocp.example.com vector--- {""@timestamp"":""2025-09-18T13:03:28.235639788Z"",""annotations"":{""authorization.k8s.io/decision"":""forbid"",""authorization.k8s.io/reason"":""""},""apiVersion"":""audit.k8s.io/v1"",""auditID"":""9ada7a7c-614c-473f-ab4f-025b1f86ab72"",""file"":""/var/log/kube-apiserver/audit.log"",""hostname"":""node1.ocp.example.com"",""k8s_audit_level"":""Metadata"",""kind"":""Event"",""level"":""Metadata"",""log_type"":""audit"",""objectRef"":{""apiGroup"":""hypershift.openshift.io"",""apiVersion"":""v1beta1"",""namespace"":""openshift-logging"",""resource"":""hostedcontrolplanes""},""openshift"":{""cluster_id"":""dd2e67a1-45b3-4e49-****-bd272d2eaa6d"",""sequence"":1758200608235919816},""requestReceivedTimestamp"":""2025-09-18T13:03:28.233039Z"",""requestURI"":""/apis/hypershift.openshift.io/v1beta1/namespaces/openshift-logging/hostedcontrolplanes"",""responseStatus"":{""code"":403,""details"":{""group"":""hypershift.openshift.io"",""kind"":""hostedcontrolplanes""},""message"":""hostedcontrolplanes.hypershift.openshift.io is forbidden: User \""system:serviceaccount:openshift-logging:cluster-logging-operator\"" cannot list resource \""hostedcontrolplanes\"" in API group \""hypershift.openshift.io\"" in the namespace \""openshift-logging\"""",""metadata"":{},""reason"":""Forbidden"",""status"":""Failure""},""sourceIPs""
resolution: **Note:** The following steps should only be performed if the Hypershift / Hosted Control Planes feature is NOT being used in your environment. If you are using Hypershift, do not delete these CRDs; instead, investigate the RBAC permissions for the logging operator.- Ensure the hypershift-addon is uninstalled and the Hosted Control Planes feature is disabled if it is not required.- Manually delete the remaining Hypershift CRDs found in the diagnostic steps, and repeat for any other stale hypershift CRDs found, oc delete crd hostedcontrolplanes.hypershift.openshift.io- Restart the cluster-logging-operator pod to force it to rediscover the available APIs. Once it realizes the Hypershift CRDs are gone, it will stop attempting to list those resources. oc delete pod-l name=cluster-logging-operator-n openshift-logging

However, because the feature is not fully active or configured, the operator service account lacks the specific permissions to access these stale API resources, resulting in authorization failures in the audit log.

resolution: - Ensure that your cluster can provision the required storage.- Verify you have a default StorageClass defined, or that the StorageClass requested by the PVC exists.- Check for issues with your storage provisioner and ensure there is sufficient capacity.- Once the underlying storage issue is resolved, the PVC will transition to a Bound state, and the result server pod will start correctly. title: Is Ansible Automation Platform supported or entitled to run on OpenShift infrastructure nodes?
issue: Question about running Ansible Automation Platform (AAP) on OpenShift infrastructure nodes

Whether Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform (AAP) can be deployed on OpenShift infrastructure nodes in order to consolidate workloads or reduce resource consumption.There is confusion around whether this deployment model is supported and compliant with Red Hat OpenShift subscription entitlements.
resolution: * Ansible Automation Platform is classified as a customer application workload, not a core OpenShift infrastructure component. * OpenShift infrastructure nodes are reserved exclusively for components essential to cluster operation and management (for example: ingress/routers, integrated registry, monitoring, logging, GitOps, and Service Mesh). * The OpenShift infrastructure node entitlement applies only when those nodes run entitled infrastructure components. * Deploying AAP on infrastructure nodes: * Is not covered by the infrastructure node entitlement. * Requires the nodes to be fully subscribed as worker nodes if AAP workloads are scheduled on them. * The supported and compliant deployment model is to run AAP on worker nodes. ## Recommended Action * Deploy Ansible Automation Platform on: * Standard worker nodes, or * Dedicated worker nodes labeled for AAP workloads (using nodeSelector and/or tolerations). * Ensure infrastructure nodes are used only for entitled OpenShift infrastructure components. * If additional capacity is required, scale or add worker nodes rather than scheduling application workloads on infrastructure nodes. ## Additional Information * While it may be technically possible to schedule AAP workloads on infrastructure nodes, this configuration is not recommended and may result in subscription non-compliance and support limitations. * [KCS article](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7040450), describes how to configure tolerations and scheduling, but does not address subscription entitlement or compliance considerations. * Always verify node roles, entitlements, and subscription counts when planning workload placement in OpenShift. ## References * [Infrastructure Nodes in OpenShift 4](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/5034771) * [OpenShift Self-Managed Subscription Guide](https://www.redhat.com/en/resources/self-managed-openshift-subscription-guide#section-4) lists the components allowed on Infrastructure nodes (such as Ingress, Registry, Monitoring, Logging, GitOps, and Service Mesh). AAP is not included in this list. * OpenShift Container Platform[infrastructure components](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.16/html/machine_management/creating-infrastructure-machinesets#infrastructure-components_creating-infrastructure-machinesets) lists the specific "Infrastructure Components" that are entitled to run on these nodes without consuming a worker subscription.

title: How to extend a manually created iSCSI PV?
issue: You need to expand an iSCSI Persistent Volume (PV) in OpenShift to a larger size. The PV was manually created (static provisioning).
resolution: 1. Backup your volume data first using OADP or `oc cp` 2. On the iSCSI storage provider side, increase the LUN to desired size 3. Resize the iSCSI device on the OpenShift node ``` # login to node which pod belongs to # Find the paths to the logical unit number (LUN) $ multipath-l # Resize the paths $ echo 1 > /sys/block/sdX/device/rescan $ echo 1 > /sys/block/sdY/device/rescan # Resize the multipath device $ multipathd resize map multipath_device # Resize the file system $ df-hT # If ext4 $ resize2fs /dev/mapper/mpatha # Or if type is xfs $ xfs_growfs /dev/mapper/mpatha # check size increased $ lsblk $ df-hT ``` 4. Modify PV/PVC storage size setting for the volume ``` $ oc edit pv spec: capacity: storage: 100Gi # update to desired size $ oc edit pvc spec: resources: requests: storage: 100Gi # update to desired size ``` Note: When expanding OpenShift Monitoring storage, PVC is created from volumeClaimTemplate. Perform steps 1-2 for both pods volumes and adjust the configmap volumeClaimTemplate request storage size for PVC size update. ``` $ oc-n openshift-monitoring edit configmap cluster-monitoring-config $ oc-n openshift-user-workload-monitoring edit configmap user-workload-monitoring-config data: config.yaml: | prometheusK8s: # check component to change volumeClaimTemplate: spec: resources: requests: storage: 100Gi # update to desired size ``` 5. Wait for the pod started and running ``` $ oc get pod ``` 6. check the pod volume size is expanded ``` $ oc rsh df-h ``` Reference:- [RHEL doc- Resizing an online multipath device](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/9/html/configuring_device_mapper_multipath/managing-multipathed-volumes_configuring-device-mapper-multipath#resizing-an-online-multipath-device_managing-multipathed-volumes)- [OpenShift doc- resize a persistent volume (PV) for monitoring components](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/9/html/configuring_device_mapper_multipath/managing-multipathed-volumes_configuring-device-mapper-multipath#resizing-an-online-multipath-device_managing-multipathed-volumes) Other available solution:- [Migrate prometheus data to larger persistent volume](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/6958231)

title: RHOCP ABI Installation fails with separate encrypted root and var partitions
issue: - While doing ABI installation the RHCOS nodes fails with the following error. ~~~ [57.527725] localhost ignition[2141]: disks: createLuks: op(17): executing: "cryptsetup" "isLuks" "/run/ignition/dev_aliases/dev/disk/by-partlabel/var" "--type" "luks2" [57.527741] localhost ignition[2141]: disks: createLuks: op(17): [finished] checking if /dev/disk/by-partlabel/var is a luks2 device [57.539957] localhost ignition[2141]: disks: createLuks: volume wipe was not requested and luks device "/dev/disk/by-partlabel/var" could not be reused: config must not specify clevis binding ~~~
resolution: - To resolve this issue, enable the disk wipe option within the custom machine configs. ~~~ $ cat 99-custom-var-partition-master-conf.yaml apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1 kind: MachineConfig metadata: labels: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: master name: 99-var-partition-master spec: config: ignition: version: 3.2.0 storage: disks:- device: /dev/disk/by-id/coreos-boot-disk wipeTable: false partitions:- label: root number: 4 resize: true sizeMiB: 51200- label: var number: 5 sizeMiB: 0 luks:- name: var device: /dev/disk/by-partlabel/var clevis: tpm2: true wipeVolume: true-------> Here filesystems:- device: /dev/mapper/var path: /var format: xfs label: var wipeFilesystem: true---------> Here systemd: units:- name: var.mount enabled: true contents: | [Unit] Before=local-fs.target [Mount] What=/dev/mapper/var Where=/var Options=defaults,prjquota [Install] WantedBy=local-fs.target ~~~- **Recommendation**- Make sure to use stable real path as disk names- `device: /dev/disk/by-id/coreos-boot-disk`.
root_cause: - During node boot, it was observed that disk encryption fails as the target volume is not successfully wiped.
