title: Issues setting up Gateway API CRD in OpenShift on non-cloud infrastructure providers
issue: - Official documentation on how to configure the new `Gateway API CRD` on OpenShift Container Platform seems incomplete as it doesn't show on the next steps to make ingress traffic work once `Gateway API` objects are created.- All `Gateway API` objects have been created and look fine, but nothing else is created to be able to allow traffic to the respective services.- Able to configure everything manually, however multiple issues happening and/or not working as expected.
resolution: At the moment of this writing the new `Gateway API` on OpenShift Container Platform is not fully supported on vSphere, bare metal and agnostic infrastructures (aka. on-premises installations). This feature as of the latest 4.21 version is only fully supported and integrate on cloud providers infrastructures, like AWS, GCP, etc, since on these platforms the additional ingress and `DNS` resources necessary are created automatically once the `Gateway API objects` are created. For on-premises clusters, it is recommended to avoid the usage of this new feature for production usage until it is fully supported. Check below for more information on the ongoing RFE. As workaround, manual configuration and integration with MetalLB based `LoadBalancer services` to fully have ingress connections setup for `Gateway API`. Infrastructure DNS servers must also be configured accordingly to allow the correct routing to the services created (this is outside of scope of this article, since it is user specific). Another possible workaround is to still use OpenShift routes using the default `ingressController` or any `sharded ingressController`, by pointing the subdomain created in gateway to the respective `ingressController` domain. In case this features is being used in Service Mesh, the recommended is to continue the usage of the long time supported and integrated way of `istio-ingressgateways` and OpenShift routes. Or in case of Service mesh Ambient Mode, because `Gateway API` is required for this mode, it is recommend to evaluate its usage in production clusters, since it might be preferred to have a mature and proven solution with `sidecars`, `ingressgateways` and OpenShift routes, until the `Gateway API` feature is fully supported.
root_cause: There are Jira tickets being worked on this issue, one being RFE to support integration of Gateway API in non-cloud infrastructures, which can be checked [here](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/NE-2010), and the second one to update our documentation on adding further steps once this integration is fully supported and this one can be followed [here](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSDOCS-18072).

title: How to use nested containers in OpenShift 4.20
issue: Documentation is unclear about how to use [Linux user namespaces](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.20/html/nodes/working-with-pods#nodes-pods-user-namespaces-configuring_nodes-pods-user-namespaces) in OpenShift 4.20 to start nested containers. Trying to start a pod with, e.g., image `registry.redhat.io/ubi10/podman` and UID `1000` does not start without setting `securityContext.privileged` to `true`, which should not be needed.
resolution: **Waiting on Engineering Cases:** These issues have been reported to Red Hat engineering. They are being tracked in the following Bugs: * [OCPBUGS-76952 (Incorrect specification of UID ranges in nested-container SCC)](https://issues.redhat.com//browse/OCPBUGS-76952) * [OCPBUGS-77039 (Misleading documentation about the requirements to run pods in Linux user namespaces)](https://issues.redhat.com//browse/OCPBUGS-77039) For more information, please open a [new support case](https://access.redhat.com/support/cases/#/case/new/) on the Red Hat Customer Portal referring to this solution. ### Requirements To make nested containers work with OpenShift Container Platform 4.20, the following requirements must be met: * A SecurityContextConstraint (SCC) that * allows UIDs in the range of 0 to 65534 * allows privilege escalation (namely the `SETUID` and `SETGID` capabilities) * sets the `container_engine_t` SELinux context * requires user namespaces (definition `userNamespaceLevel: RequirePodLevel`) * A pod definition that allows FUSE (annotation `io.kubernetes.cri-o.Devices: /dev/fuse`) ### Step-by-step guide The following steps demonstrate how to make nested containers work with UID `1000` and container image `registry.redhat.io/ubi10/podman`: * Create a namespace: ``` oc new-project user-namespace-test ``` * Create the following SCC named `nested-container-fixed`: ``` oc apply-f- < < EOF allowHostDirVolumePlugin: false allowHostIPC: false allowHostNetwork: false allowHostPID: false allowHostPorts: false allowPrivilegeEscalation: true allowPrivilegedContainer: false allowedCapabilities:- SETUID- SETGID apiVersion: security.openshift.io/v1 defaultAddCapabilities: null fsGroup: ranges:- max: 65534 type: MustRunAs groups: [] kind: SecurityContextConstraints metadata: annotations: include.release.openshift.io/ibm-cloud-managed: "true" include.release.openshift.io/self-managed-high-availability: "true" include.release.openshift.io/single-node-developer: "true" kubernetes.io/description: 'nested-container is specially tailored for running nested containers. It balances a tight security profile, while remaining loose enough to be useful to run nested containers in. In addition to requiring pods run with a user namespace, it allows SETUID and SETGID capabilities, requires the "container_engine_t" SELinux type, allows any users within the range of 0-65534, allows privilege escalation (to allow a container engine to run new{uid/gid}map), and allows any seccomp profile. Since any pods running within this SCC must use a user namespace ("hostUsers: false"), their actual UID/GID on the host will be allocated by the kubelet to be unprivileged, and any capabilities the pod is granted will not apply outside of the pods user namespace.' name: nested-container-fixed priority: null readOnlyRootFilesystem: false requiredDropCapabilities: null runAsUser: type: MustRunAsRange uidRangeMin: 0 uidRangeMax: 65534 seLinuxContext: seLinuxOptions: type: container_engine_t type: MustRunAs seccompProfiles:- '*' supplementalGroups: ranges:- max: 65534 type: MustRunAs userNamespaceLevel: RequirePodLevel users: [] volumes:- configMap- csi- downwardAPI- emptyDir- ephemeral- persistentVolumeClaim- projected- secret EOF ``` **NOTE:** Above SCC resource should be deleted when OpenShift's own SCC `nested-container` has been fixed in OpenShift 4.20. * Create the following ClusterRole named `system:openshift:scc:nested-container-fixed`: ``` oc apply-f- < < EOF apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: ClusterRole metadata: name: system:openshift:scc:nested-container-fixed rules:- apiGroups:- security.openshift.io resourceNames:- nested-container-fixed resources:- securitycontextconstraints verbs:- use EOF ``` **NOTE:** Above ClusterRole resource should be deleted when OpenShift's own SCC `nested-container` has been fixed in OpenShift 4.20. * Create a role binding for the service account used to run the pod, here `default`. Please replace the two `FIXME` placeholders with the appropriate namespace before executing the command: ``` oc-n FIXME apply-f- < < EOF apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: system:openshift:scc:nested-container-fixed roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: ClusterRole name: system:openshift:scc:nested-container-fixed subjects:- kind: ServiceAccount name: default namespace: FIXME EOF ``` **NOTE:** Above RoleBinding resource should be changed to reference ClusterRole `system:openshift:scc:nested-container` when OpenShift's own SCC `nested-container` has been fixed in OpenShift 4.20. * Create the following deployment. Please replace the `FIXME` placeholder with the appropriate namespace before executing the command: ``` oc-n FIXME apply-f- < < EOF apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: nested-containers annotations: openshift.io/required-scc: nested-container-fixed spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: nested-containers template: metadata: labels: app: nested-containers annotations: io.kubernetes.cri-o.Devices: /dev/fuse openshift.io/required-scc: nested-container-fixed spec: hostUsers: false containers:- name: podman image: registry.redhat.io/ubi10/podman:10.1 command:- sleep- infinity securityContext: capabilities: add:- "SETUID"- "SETGID" runAsUser: 1000 EOF ``` **NOTE:** The relevant parts in above Deployment definition are the `io.kubernetes.cri-o.Devices: /dev/fuse` annotation, the `hostUsers: false` as well as `runAsUser: 1000` definitions. The `openshift.io/required-scc: nested-container-fixed` annotations can be optionally set to make sure that this specific SCC is used. **NOTE:** Above Deployment resource should be changed to reference SCC `nested-container` in annotations `openshift.io/required-scc` when OpenShift's own SCC `nested-container` has been fixed in OpenShift 4.20. * Wait for the pod to successfully run, then open a remote shell to run a nested container. Please replace the `FIXME` placeholder with the appropriate namespace before executing the command: ``` oc-n FIXME rsh $(oc-n FIXME get pods--selector app=nested-containers-o name) sh-5.2$ podman run registry.access.redhat.com/ubi10-minimal echo hello from nested container Trying to pull registry.access.redhat.com/ubi10-minimal:latest... Getting image source signatures Checking if image destination supports signatures Copying blob 819501e18c85 done | Copying config c441290048 done | Writing manifest to image destination Storing signatures hello from nested container ```
root_cause: SCC `nested-container` is incorrectly specifying UID ranges: ``` runAsUser: type: MustRunAsRange ranges:- min: 0 max: 65534 ``` The correct specification looks as follows: ``` runAsUser: type: MustRunAsRange uidRangeMin: 0 uidRangeMax: 65534 ```

title: RHACS Central DB pod fails with Init:CreateContainerError and permission denied after rescheduling due to volume attachment issues
product: Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security for Kubernetes
issue: In Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security (RHACS), the `central-db` pod fails to start and remains in: Init:CreateContainerError The following errors are observed during the init container phase: Error: relabel failed... lsetxattr... permission denied Examples:- /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata/base/1: permission denied- /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata/PG_VERSION: permission denied Additional observations:- The PVC contains existing PostgreSQL data- The issue occurs after pod restart or rescheduling- The pod is running under `nonroot-v2` SCC- Volume may still be attached to a previous node- Multi-Attach behavior may be observed Impact:- Central DB is unavailable- RHACS Central UI and functionality are impacted
resolution: This issue occurs when the underlying ODF / Ceph cluster reaches the full threshold (~85%), causing the cluster to enter a read-only state. To resolve: 1. Temporarily increase the Ceph full ratio: oc exec-it $(oc get pod-n openshift-storage-l app=rook-ceph-operator-o name) \-n openshift-storage-- \ ceph osd set-full-ratio 0.88-c /var/lib/rook/openshift-storage/openshift-storage.config 2. Reclaim space on the nodes using fstrim: for i in $(oc get node-l '!node-role.kubernetes.io/master'-o name); do oc debug $i-- chroot /host fstrim-av; done 3. Verify Ceph cluster health: ceph-s ceph df ceph osd df tree 4. Once storage pressure is relieved, restart the affected workload: oc-n stackrox scale deploy/central-db--replicas=1 Expected result:- Ceph exits read-only state- central-db pod starts successfully- Applications recover
root_cause: The ODF / Ceph cluster reached its full threshold (~85% utilization), which triggered a read-only state. This prevented write operations to the persistent volume, causing PostgreSQL initialization to fail with permission denied and relabel errors.

title: Keystone fails to create trust for federated user as a trustor and Heat user as a trustee
product: Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift
issue: - Keystone fails to create trust for federated user as a trustor and Heat user as a trustee because role assignments through groups are overlooked
resolution: `keystone` section of `OpenStackControlPlane` resource should be modified, `[federation]/default_authorization_ttl = 480` definition should be added: spec.keystone.template: customServiceConfig: | [federation] default_authorization_ttl = 480 Documentation bug: [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSPRH-28545](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSPRH-28545)
root_cause: During trust creation, Keystone re-validates the trustor’s project roles from backend effective role assignments rather than relying only on the current token. For federated users, group memberships coming from mapping are token-lifetime only by default unless membership persistence is enabled via `[federation]/default_authorization_ttl` in `keystone.conf` or `authorization_ttl` on the IdP’s side. By default this value is 0, so it’s disabled.

title: How to use iotop command to troubleshoot the processes causing high I/O wait time on the OCP4
issue: - How to use iotop command on the OCP4?- How to troubheshoot the processes causing high I/O wait time on the OCP4?
resolution: Solution 1: Use `oc debug node` command- Run `oc debug node/node_name`, It will run a debug pods for node and drop you in the shell(TTY) of this pod. ```bash # oc debug node/ sh-5.1# whereis iotop iotop: /usr/sbin/iotop /usr/share/man/man8/iotop.8.gz ``` Solution 2: Running a daemon ```bash # oc new-project metrics-debug # oc adm policy add-scc-to-user privileged-z default/ cat < < EOF > ds.yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: DaemonSet metadata: name: metrics-daemonset labels: app: metrics-daemonset spec: selector: matchLabels: app: metrics-daemonset template: metadata: labels: app: metrics-daemonset spec: nodeName: ocp-tnkfb-worker-2 ## Select nodes that you want to troubleshoot hostPID: true hostIPC: true hostNetwork: true containers:- name: metrics-daemonset image: quay.io/openshift-release-dev/ocp-v4.0-art-dev@sha256:651732e89586140ee9fd7ca8772e0adbf9606fff461759235dbbd42af5636eae command:- bash--c- "sleep infinity " imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent securityContext: runAsUser: 0 runAsGroup: 0 privileged: true EOF oc create-f ds.yaml # oc get po NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE metrics-daemonset-b6zgd 1/1 Running 0 2m59s # oc rsh metrics-daemonset-b6zgd sh-5.1# whereis iotop iotop: /usr/sbin/iotop /usr/share/man/man8/iotop.8.gz ```

title: How to collect specific performance metrics using `sar` on OpenShift Container Platform nodes
issue: When we attempt to run `sar` to check on things like memory, CPU load, or context switching, to troubleshoot slowness or performance crunches on OpenShift nodes, we get a `command not found` error.
resolution: On RHCOS, many standard debugging tools aren't part of the default path. However, you can still pull these metrics by using `oc debug`. This creates a temporary pod with the right permissions and tools to peek into the node's performance. To get the data you need, run the following commands. Note that **1 100** means the command will sample data every **1 second**, repeating **100 times**. Feel free to tweak those numbers if you need a longer or shorter window. 1. **Average Load:** `oc debug node/-- sudo sar-q 1 100` 2. **Memory Usage:** `oc debug node/-- sudo sar-r 1 100` 3. **Device I/O:** `oc debug node/-- sudo sar-d 1 100` 4. **Disk Stats (`iostat` style):** `oc debug node/-- sudo iostat 1 100` 5. **CPU Usage (Total):** `oc debug node/-- sudo sar-u 1 100` 6. **CPU Usage (Per Core):** `oc debug node/-- sudo sar-P ALL 1 100` 7. **Context Switching:** `oc debug node/-- sudo sar-w 1 100` > **Note:** If you want to save this to a file on your local machine for analysis, you can redirect the output like this: > `oc debug node/-- sudo sar-q 1 100 > load_report.txt`
root_cause: OpenShift nodes typically run on **Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS)**, which is a "minimalist" operating system. It's designed to be lean and secure, so it doesn't include the `sysstat` package (which provides the `sar` command) in the standard user path. The `oc debug` command is the intended way to access these low-level system metrics without cluttering the host OS.

title: The Kube API Server pods can't rollout to a new revision while a control plane node is not ready, causing authentication issues
issue: A control plane is in `NotReady` state for too long and can't be brought back at the moment (e.g., waiting for a hardware part), hence causing some issues cluster-wide overtime.
`oc login` fails with the below error message: ~~~ Login failed (401 Unauthorized) ~~~
resolution: * Before proceeding, check whether the [KCS solution](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7124336) resolution steps can mitigate the issue. * While the node is in `NotReady` status, remove its `node-role.kubernetes.io/master` label: ~~~ $ oc label node node-role.kubernetes.io/master- ~~~ * Then, wait for the new revision `installer` pods to get completed on the remaining healthy nodes, and for those nodes new `kube-apiserver` pods to get up (`5/5 Running`) showing the updated revision. You can monitor the progress with the below command: ~~~ $ watch-c 'oc get po--show-labels | grep-E "apiserver=true|app=installer"' ~~~ * After the rollout is finished, add the label back to the failed node while it is still in `NotReady` state: ~~~ $ oc label node node-role.kubernetes.io/master= ~~~
root_cause: The installer controller priority flow can be checked in the `nodeToStartRevisionWith` function in the [source code](https://github.com/openshift/cluster-kube-apiserver-operator/blob/e9bc90906c726823f154c78d3e568c98ff77b6a5/vendor/github.com/openshift/library-go/pkg/operator/staticpod/controller/installer/installer_controller.go#L329): ~~~ 1. Already upgrading nodes- If any node has TargetRevision!= 0, it's chosen first installer_controller.go:334-340 2. Nodes with failed revisions- Nodes with LastFailedRevision > mostCurrent are next 3. Not ready nodes- The oldest node that's not in staticPodStateReady state installer_controller.go:354-379 4. Wrong revision nodes- The oldest node with a revision different from CurrentRevision 5. Oldest current revision- The node with the lowest CurrentRevision value ~~~

title: OCP4: Machine Config continually updating /etc/mco/proxy.env without changes to the proxy/cluster object
issue: - On OpenShift 4, you are observing that your nodes are continually rolling out new machine-config revisions.- Inspecting these changes between `rendered-worker- ` machine-configs reveals that the file /etc/mco/proxy.env is continually being refreshed, as is `resolv-prepender` script.- Cluster proxy is NOT being manually changed and is statically defined and rollout has completed successfully.- Expecting platform to be stable but observe frequent rollouts and updated rendered configs.
resolution: - Review your created NetworkAttachmentDefinitions, especially those of type `whereabouts`.- Ensure that your NOPROXY configuration includes the cidr ranges of any specified subnet in whereabouts. $ oc edit proxy/cluster ~~~ spec: httpProxy: http://your-target-proxy:80 httpsProxy: http://your-target-proxy:80 noProxy:.custom-domain.com,.alternative-custom-domain.com,10.0.0.0/24,11.0.0.0/24,64:ff9b:1::/48, ## <--- update trustedCA: name: custom-ca status: noProxy: ## <--- disregard, will update automatically when spec line is changed. ~~~
root_cause: `Resolv-prepender` is always updated when the `proxy` is updated because it injects the proxy variables explicitly into the script to be referenced by the execution. [So when the proxy changes, so does the resolv-prepender.](https://github.com/openshift/machine-config-operator/blob/259e93240c73f8cf3e33d79bb7569b50567439db/templates/common/on-prem/files/resolv-prepender.yaml#L8-L19) ~~~ {{if.Proxy-}} {{if.Proxy.HTTPProxy-}} export HTTP_PROXY={{.Proxy.HTTPProxy}} {{end-}} {{if.Proxy.HTTPSProxy-}} export HTTPS_PROXY={{.Proxy.HTTPSProxy}} {{end-}} {{if.Proxy.NoProxy-}} export NO_PROXY={{.Proxy.NoProxy}} {{end-}} {{end-}} ~~~ As a result- we see two files changed, but the origin for both is `proxy updates.` Network Operator handling of whereabouts networks must ensure all IPs used in the cluster are observed by noProxy if a proxy is defined to ensure traffic flows properly. Because you are using WHEREABOUTS, you are applying a new IP address from a pool of IPs. When a new pod comes online, a new IP is selected, which is then added to the `noProxy` ruleset to ensure we do not conflict/route these packets incorrectly. The existing/default proxy config **does not include a cidr range for this custom range**, so in order to ensure traffic flows as expected, every time an IP is applied from the range, MCO injects a new update to the proxy's `status.noProxy` field to include this specific new IP to prevent conflict. This triggers a rollout. Because the proxy hasn't stipulated a NOPROXY entry for the whole cidr, the CNO has to update the proxy every time the pods re-allocate from this pool, which is highly disruptive. It is therefore necessary to ensure that `spec.noProxy` specifies the full cidr range that whereabouts network-attachment-definitions can draw from so that new IP allocations do not trigger a node configuration update.

title: Operation cannot be fulfilled on pipelineruns.tekton.dev "pipeline": the object has been modified; please apply your changes to the latest version and try again
issue: - `PipelineRun` are stuck in ` PipelineRunTimeout` status, but no ` TaskRun` pods are scheduled.- The PipelineRun status or OpenShift events show the following error: ~~~ Operation cannot be fulfilled on pipelineruns.tekton.dev "...": the object has been modified; please apply your changes to the latest version and try again ~~~
resolution: ` ClusterTasks ` are deprecated resources from OpenShift Pipelines 1.17. To resolve this, migrate the Pipeline definition to use [` Resolvers`](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_pipelines/1.13/html/creating_cicd_pipelines/remote-pipelines-tasks-resolvers "https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_pipelines/1.13/html/creating_cicd_pipelines/remote-pipelines-tasks-resolvers"). 1. Make sure to that the ` enable-api-fields ` is set to ` beta ` in the ` TektonConfig` (this is the default from 1.12+, but verify if[migration failed](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7054083 "https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7054083")): ~~~ apiVersion: operator.tekton.dev/v1alpha1 kind: TektonConfig metadata: name: config spec: [...] pipeline: [...] enable-api-fields: beta [...] ~~~ 2. Update Pipeline Reference: Replace the ` taskRef` using ` kind: ClusterTask` with a resolver. Example whn using the Cluster Resolve to reference a task from the `openshift-piplines` namespace: ~~~ spec: tasks:- name: testTask taskRef: resolver: cluster # Replaces 'kind: ClusterTask' params:- name: name value: testTask- name: kind value: task- name: namespace value: openshift-pipelines ~~~
root_cause: ClusterTaks resources are deprecated since OpenShift Pipelines 1.17+.

title: OpenShift Virtualization: preventing asymmetric routing across VLAN interfaces
issue: - Why API server's reply traffic use the secondary interface instead of the primary interface when having multiple VLAN Interfaces?
resolution: - Implementing `Policy-Based Routing` on `Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization` nodes can help prevent asymmetric routing issues on Virtual Machines.- This approach involves configuring traffic originating from the subnet associated with the `primary interface (br-ex)` to use a dedicated routing table (e.g., table 100).- To maintain consistency and avoid asymmetric routing and misrouting conditions, all routes from the primary routing table will be replicated into a new routing table (e.g., table 100), excluding those associated with the `secondary interfaces (e.g.: br-sec-11, br-sec-12, etc. etc.)`.- In this direction, the implementation of a `systemd service` in the `Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization` nodes based on the `ip monitor` capability could enhance real-time synchronization from the main routing table to the new dedicated routing table (e.g.: table 100).- The following steps outline the necessary actions to implement this resolution: 1. Create the `sync-rt-table.sh` script incorporating the following content: ``` #!/bin/bash # ============================================================================= # # route-sync.sh- version 2.0- Mar 9, 2026 #- IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN support for multiple bridge interfaces. #- ip rule defined with priority 32700 # # ============================================================================= # ============================================================================== # route-sync.sh configuration # ============================================================================== # The pattern below handles exact names and partial prefixes. # Example: "br-list" will ignore "br-list1", "br-list2", "br-list-extra", etc. # Pipe is used as separator between bridge interfaces. # Add \b before ad after the bridge name to exactly match a bridge name as in this example: "\bbr-pippo\b|\bbr-active\b" IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN="br-sec|br-test|br-pippo|br-pluto|br-list|br-active" # Modifying the following two parameters may affect other OpenShift routing and functionalities. # Please ensure to test any changes in a controlled environment before applying them to production. PRIORITY=32700 TARGET_TABLE=100 # ============================================================================== # Sanity Checks & Protection # ============================================================================== # PROTECTION: Prevent br-ex from being filtered even if included in the pattern if [["$IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN" =~ "br-ex"]]; then # Removes br-ex and cleans up leading/trailing/double pipes IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN=$(echo "$IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN" | sed-E 's/\|?br-ex\|?//g; s/^\|//; s/\|$//; s/\|\|/|/g') logger-t route-sync "WARNING: 'br-ex' was removed from IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN to protect connectivity." # Fallback if pattern becomes empty if [-z "$IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN"]; then IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN="^$" # Matches nothing fi fi # ============================================================================== # Functions # ============================================================================== log_msg() {logger-t route-sync "$1"} setup_policy_rule() {log_msg "Verifying Policy Routing setup with priority $PRIORITY..." # Identify the default interface and its global IP INTERFACE=$(ip route show default | awk '/default/ {print $5; exit}') SOURCE_IP=$(ip-o-4 addr show $INTERFACE | grep-vE "169.254|global vip" | awk '/scope global/ {print $4; exit}' | cut-d/-f1) # Identify the br-ex subnet SUBNET=$(ip route show dev br-ex | grep "proto kernel" | grep "$SOURCE_IP" | grep-Ev 'local|broadcast' | awk '{print $1}' | uniq) if [-z "$SUBNET"]; then log_msg "ERROR: Could not determine SUBNET for $INTERFACE. Rule setup skipped." else # Check if the specific rule with the specific priority already exists if! ip rule show | grep-q "^$PRIORITY:.*from $SUBNET lookup $TARGET_TABLE"; then log_msg "Adding ip rule: from $SUBNET lookup $TARGET_TABLE priority $PRIORITY" # Remove existing rule for this subnet if it exists under a different priority to avoid duplicates ip rule del from "$SUBNET" lookup "$TARGET_TABLE" 2> /dev/null # Add the rule with the explicit priority ip rule add from "$SUBNET" lookup "$TARGET_TABLE" priority "$PRIORITY" else log_msg "Policy rule for $SUBNET with priority $PRIORITY already exists." fi fi} reconcile_tables() {log_msg "Starting full reconciliation for Table $TARGET_TABLE..." # 1. Sync from Main to Target (excluding ignored patterns) ip route show table main | grep-vE "dev ($IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN)" | while read-r route; do # We use 'replace' to be idempotent ip route replace $route table $TARGET_TABLE 2> /dev/null done # 2. Cleanup stale routes in Target ip route show table $TARGET_TABLE | while read-r route; do clean_comp=$(echo "$route" | sed 's/scope link//g' | xargs) if! ip route show table main | grep-Fq "$route" && \! ip route show table main | sed 's/scope link//g' | grep-Fq "$clean_comp"; then ip route del $route table $TARGET_TABLE 2> /dev/null log_msg "Removed stale: $route" fi done} # ============================================================================== # Execution flow # ============================================================================== #--- Initial Setup--- setup_policy_rule reconcile_tables #--- Start Monitoring--- log_msg "Monitoring routes/links (Ignoring: $IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN)..." ip monitor route link | while read-r line; do # Case 1: An interface comes UP if [["$line" == *": <"*",UP,"*]]; then dev_name=$(echo "$line" | awk-F': ' '{print $2}' | awk '{print $1}') # Ignore if matches pattern or virtual container interfaces (@if2) if [["$dev_name" =~ $IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN]] || [["$dev_name" == *@if2]]; then continue fi log_msg "Link $dev_name is UP. Triggering reconciliation..." setup_policy_rule reconcile_tables continue fi # Case 2: Route deleted (STRICT MODE) if [["$line" == "Deleted "*]]; then # Check if the route involves an ignored device if [["$line" =~ dev\ ([^[:space:]]*)($IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN)]]; then continue fi clean_route=$(echo "$line" | sed 's/^Deleted //') if ip route del $clean_route table $TARGET_TABLE 2> /dev/null; then log_msg "STRICT DELETE: Removed $clean_route from Table $TARGET_TABLE" fi continue fi # Case 3: Route Added/Replaced if [["$line" =~ ^([0-9]|add|replace|default)]]; then # Skip ignored devices if [["$line" =~ dev\ ([^[:space:]]*)($IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN)]]; then continue fi # Skip routes that already specify a table (avoid loops) [["$line" == *"table"*]] && continue clean_route=$(echo "$line" | sed 's/^add //;s/^replace //') if ip route replace $clean_route table $TARGET_TABLE 2> /dev/null; then log_msg "Synced to Table $TARGET_TABLE: $clean_route" else ip route add $clean_route table $TARGET_TABLE 2> /dev/null && \ log_msg "Added to Table $TARGET_TABLE: $clean_route" fi fi done ``` 2. Adapt the `IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN` parameter in the `sync-rt-table.sh` to your environment: ``` IGNORE_DEV_PATTERN="br-sec|br-test|br-pippo|br-pluto|br-list|br-active" # This pattern is used to filter routes associated with secondary bridge interfaces. # Example: "br-list" will ignore "br-list1", "br-list2", "br-list-extra", etc. # Multiple patterns are separated by the pipe "|" character. # To match exact bridge names, include word boundaries (\b) before and after # the name, e.g.: "\bbr-pippo\b|\bbr-active\b" Point Of Attention: # Modifying the following two parameters may affect other OpenShift # Virtualization's routing and functionalities. # Please ensure to test any changes in a controlled environment before applying # them to production. PRIORITY=32700 TARGET_TABLE=100 ``` 3. Define a `MachineConfig` to create the `sync-rt-table.service` to be applied to the `Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization` nodes: 1. Convert the content of `sync-rt-table.sh` to `base64` single row (`wrap` disabled as effect of `-w0`) as in the example below: ``` # cat sync-rt-table.sh | base64-w0; echo  ``` 2. root_cause: - In an infrastructure environment configured as follows:- Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization deployed on a three-node cluster.- Customer workloads (virtual machines) operating on the same nodes as the `OpenShift API pods`.- The Virtualization cluster is configured with `ipForwarding: Global` and `routingViaHost: true`.- It has been noted that API server response traffic is being directed through the secondary network interface (br-sec) of the Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization nodes, where Virtual Machines are also connected, rather than through the primary interface (br-ex) that handled the initial request.- This behavior results in asymmetric routing and may lead to potential packet drops due to strict Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) checks on the Customer Virtual Machines' side.

title: Pod Fails with TopologyAffinityError on a NUMA Node
issue: Pod deployment fails with TopologyAffinityError on a NUMA (Non Uniform Memory Access) topology node
The issue occurs when trying to deploy a pod on a node with specific SRIOV (Single Root I/O Virtualization) and NUMA policy configurations.

The scheduler repeatedly attempts to allocate the pod to a worker node with insufficient NUMA node resources and fails with below error. ~~~ 25s Warning TopologyAffinityError pod/pod_name Resources cannot be allocated with Topology locality ~~~
resolution: * NUMA Resources Operator should be used to manage the NUMA-aware workloads effectively. * Check the pods NodeSelector and Affinity rules if no NUMA Resources Operator is used
root_cause: Here the pod was assigned to NUMA node without enough resource because the workload was using default-scheduler which do not check the numa resources before allocating the pod to the node. That means If a node have 2 NUMA node with CPU 32 each and a pod already allocated on NUMA node 0. On allocating a new pod with NUMA 0 specification. The default scheduler just check the nodes available resource which is NUMA0 + NUMA1, it dosesn't know about the NUMA topology constraint. Only when using NUMa-scheduler it will check if enough resource available on the NUMA0 node and assign the pod correctly. Refer to the [RHOCP 4.16- Scheduling NUMA-aware workloads](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.16/html/scalability_and_performance/cnf-numa-aware-scheduling#cnf-troubleshooting-numa-aware-workloads_numa-aware) documentation for more details.

title: Migrating Ceph Object Storage Daemons (OSDs) / Disks in OpenShift Data Foundation (ODF) - Using the Same Storageclass (Migrating Device Size/Type)
issue: In some instances, it may be necessary to migrate to different Ceph Object Storage Daemons (OSDs). OSDs are the backing devices (disks) Ceph pools/storageclasses use to store data. Common reasons for this operation are as follows: 1. Datastore is getting full/moving to a new datastore. If this scenario aligns with the planned migration, please use the [Migrating Ceph Object Storage Daemons (OSDs) / Disks in OpenShift Data Foundation (ODF) to a New Storageclass (Migrating Datastore/Local Storage Backing Devices)](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7134647) solution. 2. Migrating to a differently sized/type of OSD, or simply executing an expedited redeployment. If this scenario aligns with the planned migration of your environment, this is the correct solution. 3. Expanding on [2], each OSD, regardless of size, uses 2 CPU and 5GiB of memory in most deployments. Reference [7.3. Resource requirements](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_data_foundation/4.20/html-single/planning_your_deployment/index#resource-requirements_rhodf) of the Product Documentation for more information. Many small devices can become costly/inefficient when disks can be consolidated to a bigger device, eliminating the need to consume unnecessary resources for the same amount of storage space. 4. Redeploying many OSDs. For example, if older OSDs were ID’d following step 5 of the [OpenShift Data Foundations Upgrade Pre-Checks](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7009011) solution and found to be writing in 64K blocks instead of the 4K blocks needed for modern Ceph releases. This is a serious bug, shown in the [ODF OSD goes into CrashLoopBackOff due to the following error: "bluefs enospc"](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/6999849) article, has been known to cause data loss, and the migration process can expedite the OSD redeployment by bringing in healthy devices immediately before removing the older/affected devices. **WARNING: This process, if followed correctly, is fairly straightforward and safe. However, take extra precautions during the removal of the older OSDs. OSDs should ONLY be removed one at a time, allowing for rebalancing between removals. Ceph should be allowed to progress to a state of HEALTH_OK, all PGs active+clean (scrubbing is OK) before removing the next OSD, and so on. Failure to do so and executing the rapid removal of OSDs before rebalancing is allowed to finish can result in complete data loss!!!!**
resolution: **Note:** This process was introduced in ODF v4.16 as General Available. If you're on a supported platform, deployed dynamically **(NOT LOCAL STORAGE)**, and accept resizing the OSD PV/PVC as opposed to migrating, you can bypass this resolution and use the Product Documentation: [3.1.2. Scaling up storage capacity on an AWS cluster by resizing existing OSDs](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_data_foundation/4.16/html-single/scaling_storage/index#proc_scaling-up-storage-capacity-on-an-aws-cluster-by-resizing-existing-osds_aws) [5.1.2. Scaling up storage capacity on VMware a cluster by resizing existing OSDs](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_data_foundation/4.16/html-single/scaling_storage/index#proc_scaling-up-storage-capacity-on-a-vmware-cluster-by-resizing-existing-osds_vmware) [6.1.2. Scaling up storage capacity on a Microsoft Azure cluster by resizing existing OSDs](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_data_foundation/4.16/html-single/scaling_storage/index#proc_scaling-up-storage-capacity-on-a-cluster-by-resizing-existing-osds_azure) # Migrating Using the Same Storageclass ONLY: 1. If using Local Storage devices via the Local Storage Operator (LSO), it may be helpful to edit the LSO configuration with a `minSize` and `maxSize` to hone in on the new device size. This will result in Persistent Volumes (PVs) no longer being provisioned with the old size and only the newer device sizes will have PVs provisioned. In the LocalVolume or LocalVolumeSet Custom Resource CR), add the following spec: **Example if upgrading from 512GiB to 2TiB, 512GB will no longer be provisioned as PVs:** ~~~ spec: deviceInclusionSpec: minSize: 1.8Ti maxSize: 2.2Ti ~~~ Once complete, add the new storage devices to the hosts. 2. **Skip this step if new hosts are not applicable**. If new nodes/hosts are being brought in, ensure they have the correct labels. Reference the [Install Red Hat OpenShift Data Foundation 4.X: Step 2: Preparing Nodes](https://access.redhat.com/articles/5692201#step-2-preparing-nodes-3) article for more information. 3. Take a backup of the storagecluster.yaml: ~~~ $ oc get storagecluster-n openshift-storage ocs-storagecluster-o yaml > storagecluster.yaml ~~~ 4. Edit the `storagecluster.yaml` and adjust the count to the value needed to bring in the exact number of new devices desired. **Be sure to describe your nodes** to validate you have the CPU and memory needed for the extra devices (2 CPU / 5GiB memory per device). See the examples below: ~~~ $ oc edit storagecluster-n openshift-storage ocs-storagecluster ~~~ **NOTE:** Count x Replica = Total # of devices; however, topology differs. **WARNING: DO NOT EDIT THE REPLICA, ONLY THE COUNT.** Validate the `failureDomain` in the `storagecluster.yaml` status section, for example: **failureDomain: rack** or **failureDomain: zone:** ~~~ storageDeviceSets:- config: {} count: 1 <---- increasing this to 2 will bring in 3 new devices (one device per rack/zone) storageClassName: localblock replica: 3 <--- This will be dictated by the # of racks/zones, one OSD per rack/zone failureDomain: rack ~~~ **failureDomain: host:** ~~~ storageDeviceSets:- config: {} count: 3 <---- increasing this from 3 to 6 will bring in 3 new devices (one device per host) storageClassName: localblock replica: 1 <---- replica will always be 1, only one OSD per host multiplied by the count failureDomain: host ~~~ 5. After the `storagecluster.yaml` has been edited, the new `rook-ceph-osd` devices will be deployed, and **Ceph must be allowed to rebalance.** ~~~ $ oc exec-it $(oc get pod-n openshift-storage-l app=rook-ceph-operator-o name)-n openshift-storage-- ceph status-c /var/lib/rook/openshift-storage/openshift-storage.config health: HEALTH_WARN <-----------------------------------------------NEEDS TO BE HEALTH_OK PRIOR TO OSD REMOVAL services: osd: 6 osds: 6 up (since 3m), 5 in (since 4m); 171 remapped pgs pgs: 59392/205137 objects degraded (28.952%) 65904/205137 objects misplaced (32.127%) 159 active+undersized+degraded+remapped+backfill_wait <--DO NOT PROCEED 62 active+clean <-------------------------------------- ALL PGs MUST BE "active+clean" PRIOR TO OSD REMOVAL 11 active+remapped+backfill_wait <--------------------- DO NOT PROCEED 1 active+undersized+degraded+remapped+backfilling <----DO NOT PROCEED ~~~ 6. Once all desired OSDs are up/in and provisioned, scale the rook-ceph-operator down: ~~~ $ oc scale deployment-n openshift-storage rook-ceph-operator--replicas=0 ~~~ 7. After Ceph has been validated to be `HEALTH_OK` and all PGs are `active+clean`, scrubbing is ok; we can start with the first OSD removal ONLY. Derived from the [Replacing devices](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_data_foundation/4.20/html/replacing_devices/index) product documentation, the example below is for rook-ceph-osd-1: ~~~ $ oc delete jobs-n openshift-storage--all $ osd_id_to_remove=1 $ oc scale-n openshift-storage deployment rook-ceph-osd-${osd_id_to_remove}--replicas=0 $ oc process-n openshift-storage ocs-osd-removal-p FAILED_OSD_IDS=${osd_id_to_remove} FORCE_OSD_REMOVAL=false |oc create-n openshift-storage-f- ~~~ 8. The OSD removal job can be tracked with the `$ oc get jobs-n openshift-storage` command. Once the output shows `1/1` the job is complete and you should no longer have the OSD deployment. Additionally, the OSD will be removed from Ceph/the Ceph tree: ~~~ $ oc get deployment-n openshift-storage $ oc exec-it $(oc get pod-n openshift-storage-l app=rook-ceph-operator-o name)-n openshift-storage-- ceph osd tree-c /var/lib/rook/openshift-storage/openshift-storage.config $ oc exec-it $(oc get pod-n openshift-storage-l app=rook-ceph-operator-o name)-n openshift-storage-- ceph status-c /var/lib/rook/openshift-storage/openshift-storage.config health: HEALTH_WARN <-----------------------------------------------NEEDS TO BE HEALTH_OK BEFORE NEXT REMOVAL services: osd: 5 osds: 5 up (since 3m), 5 in (since 4m); 171 remapped pgs pgs: 59392/205137 objects degraded (28.952%) 65904/205137 objects misplaced (32.127%) 159 active+undersized+degraded+remapped+backfill_wait <--DO NOT PROCEED 62 active+clean <-------------------------------------- ALL PGs MUST BE "active+clean" PRIOR TO OSD REMOVAL 11 active+remapped+backfill_wait <----------------------DO NOT PROCEED 1 active+undersized+degraded+remapped+backfilling <----DO NOT PROCEED ~~~ 9. Once Ceph is validated to be `HEALTH_OK` and all PGs `active+clean`, repeat steps 7-8 until all undesired OSDs are removed. **Example of What is Needed for Next Removal:** ~~~ health: HEALTH_OK <-----------------------------------------------NEEDS TO BE HEALTH_OK BEFORE NEXT REMOVAL services: osd: 5 osds: 5 up (since 3m), 5 in (since 4m); pgs: 233 active+clean <-------------------------------------- ALL PGs MUST BE "active+clean" ~~~ **Example Once all Undesired OSDs have been Removed:** ~~~ health: HEALTH_OK <----------------------------------------------- NEEDS TO BE HEALTH_OK BEFORE NEXT REMOVAL services: osd: 3 osds: 3 up (since 3m), 5 in (since 4m); <------------------ Desired OSDs achieved pgs: 233 active+clean <-------------------------------------- ALL PGs MUST BE "active+clean" ~~~ 10. Once all undesired Ceph OSDs are removed and Ceph's health is validated, edit the storagecluster back to the desired count, see step 4 for examples. 11. Once the count is correct in the `storagecluster.yaml`, scale up the rook-ceph-operator. You should not see any OSD prepare pods/jobs, this means the count is set correctly and the migration is complete. ~~~ $ oc scale deployment-n openshift-storage rook-ceph-operator--replicas=1 ~~~

title: Enabling Root and Data Disk Encryption on RHOSO 18.0 with Customer-Managed Keys
product: Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift
issue: - Enabling Root and/or Data disks encryption on Customer VMs with customer-owned encryption keys- Configuring Red Hat Openstack Services on Openshift for customer-managed encryption keys
resolution: - add creator role to the user for the project: ~~~ $ openstack role add--user--project creator ~~~ These are the steps for enabling Root & Data Disk Encryption:- add keys to barbican: ~~~ $ openstack secret order create--name customer_disk_key \--algorithm aes--mode ctr--bit-length 256 \--payload-content-type=application/octet-stream key ~~~- use the keys to encrypt volumes: $ openstack volume type create--encryption-provider nova.volume.encryptors.luks.LuksEncryptor--encryption-cipher aes-xts-plain64--encryption-key-size 256--encryption-control-location front-end LuksEncryptor-Template-256 ~~~- In RHOSO Barbican is enabled by default so no need to add this service like in past OSP deployments. source: https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openstack_services_on_openshift/18.0/html-single/performing_security_operations/index#proc-generating-symmetric-key_managing-secrets-keys https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openstack_services_on_openshift/18.0/html-single/performing_security_operations/index#proc_encrypting-block-storage-volumes_encrypting-and-validating-storage-services
root_cause: N/A

title: All authenticated basic users can view project openshift-virtualization-os-images in RHOCP 4
issue: - A basic user can able to view project `openshift-virtualization-os-images`.
resolution: - This is expected behavior as the Boot Source images are stored in the `openshift-virtualization-os-images` project namespace and are called a specific name.- The role-binding `os-images.kubevirt.io:view` is the one that is giving the access to all users who are able to authenticate successfully.- Authenticated users with `os-images.kubevirt.io:view` can only perform `get, list, watch` operations in the namespace to list OS images. However, only a user with ClusterRole `os-images.kubevirt.io:edit` or as an administrator can modify images.- For a more information, see [Creating Default OS Images to Auto-Clone in OpenShift Virtualization](https://cloud.redhat.com/blog/creating-default-os-images-to-auto-clone-in-openshift-virtualization).

title: Image creation through Horizon fails when the 'direct' upload method is set
issue: Since Red Hat Openstack Services on Openshift 18.0.14 the **direct*
upload method is the default upload method in the Dashboard service (Horizon).

When trying to create an OpenStack image through Dashboard service it fails returning the following error messages: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'data') Error: Unable to create the image

The Network panel at the Web browser developer tools shows it's failing due to invalid Certificate Authority: "request": {"method": "PUT", "url": "https://glance-default-public-openstack.apps.. /v2/images/ /file",... "response": {... "redirectURL": "", "headersSize":-1, "bodySize":-1, "_transferSize": 0, "_error": "net::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID", "_fetchedViaServiceWorker": false},...}
resolution: ### Option 1 (recommended): Add your own Certificate Authority * You can add your own Certificate Authority to replace the default generated certificate. * Please follow the procedure described in [Configuring Security service](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openstack_services_on_openshift/18.0/html/configuring_security_services/custom-tls-certificates_security-services) guide of Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift 18.0 documentation. ### Option 2 (workaround): Using the legacy upload method. * Set back the **legacy** upload method. This was the default upload method previous to 18.0.14 release. * Update the configuration within the OpenStackControlPlane CustomResource as follows: spec: horizon: template: customServiceConfig: | HORIZON_IMAGES_UPLOAD_MODE = 'legacy' * The Horizon Pod(s) will restart after the change.
root_cause: The RHOSO public endpoints have been deployed with self-signed Certificate Authority (**rootca-public**) managed by cert-manager operator. When a client tries to create an image through Horizon, the Web browser does not recognise the CA as trusted when reaching the Glance's public endpoint to upload the file.

title: How to delete operator or images using oc-mirror --v2 that were mirrored using oc-mirror --v1
issue: - How to delete operator or images using oc-mirror--v2 that were mirrored using oc-mirror--v1
resolution: 1. Confirm which operators or images were mirrored using `oc-mirror--v1`, then create `ImageSetConfiguration` object for `oc-mirror--v2` to `Mirror to Disk`. ```bash # cat imageset-v2.yaml apiVersion: mirror.openshift.io/v2alpha1 kind: ImageSetConfiguration mirror: operators:- catalog: registry.redhat.io/redhat/redhat-operator-index:v4.20 targetTag: v4.20 packages:- name: dns-operator defaultChannel: stable channels:- name: stable minVersion: '1.3.0' maxVersion: '1.3.0' additionalImages:- name: registry.redhat.io/rhtas-tech-preview/redis-trillian-rhel9@sha256:914089e0e8407420ce07f44dad49da75d34c88eac6314ea8d6e45ff0745e4b42- name: registry.redhat.io/rhceph/snmp-notifier-rhel9@sha256:37e1ba0708b3bd4297295bd0f1b12d6493b0515b607d442c5121231963b803a6- name: registry.redhat.io/rhceph/oauth2-proxy-rhel9@sha256:d5dad759381869449e8dcc34a397664130952fa9f0364059b5375e6ae04c26e7 # oc-mirror-c imageset-v2.yaml file://$(dir)--v2 ``` 2. Create `DeleteImageSetConfiguration` object, and generate `delete-images.yaml` using `oc-mirror--v2` ```bash # cat delete.yaml apiVersion: mirror.openshift.io/v2alpha1 kind: DeleteImageSetConfiguration delete: operators:- catalog: registry.redhat.io/redhat/redhat-operator-index:v4.20 targetTag: v4.20 packages:- name: dns-operator defaultChannel: stable channels:- name: stable minVersion: '1.3.0' maxVersion: '1.3.0' additionalImages:- name: registry.redhat.io/rhtas-tech-preview/redis-trillian-rhel9@sha256:914089e0e8407420ce07f44dad49da75d34c88eac6314ea8d6e45ff0745e4b42- name: registry.redhat.io/rhceph/snmp-notifier-rhel9@sha256:37e1ba0708b3bd4297295bd0f1b12d6493b0515b607d442c5121231963b803a6- name: registry.redhat.io/rhceph/oauth2-proxy-rhel9@sha256:d5dad759381869449e8dcc34a397664130952fa9f0364059b5375e6ae04c26e7 # oc-mirror delete--config delete.yaml--workspace file://$(dir)--v2--generate docker://$(privateregistry)--delete-v1-images 2026/03/20 01:42:27 [INFO]: $(dir)/working-dir/delete file created ``` 3. Delete operator or image using `oc-mirror--v2` ```bash # oc-mirror delete--v2--delete-yaml-file $(dir)/working-dir/delete/delete-image.yaml docker://$(privateregistry) ``` For more information, please open a [new support case](https://access.redhat.com/support/cases/#/case/new/) with Red Hat Support.

title: How to get the resource ID of an ARO cluster?
issue: - How to check if an OpenShift cluster is ARO?- How to differentiate if a cluster is a Red Hat managed ARO cluster or a self-managed OCP cluster on Azure platform.- How to check if an OpenShift cluster is an ARO cluster by examining its Azure Resource ID?
resolution: An ARO cluster will have an Azure `Resource ID` that contains `Microsoft.RedHatOpenShift` on it, which looks like: ~~~ /subscriptions/$sub_id/resourceGroups/$rg/providers/Microsoft.RedHatOpenShift/openShiftClusters/$cluster_name ~~~ It is possible to get the `Resource ID` with the `az` CLI command: ~~~ $ az aro show-n [cluster_name]-g [rg_name]--query 'id' ~~~ #### Additional Information in the cluster for ARO clusters only There is also some information in the cluster to check if it's an ARO cluster or not:- Existence of the ARO `Custom Resource Definition` (CRD) and getting the `Resource ID` from it (this resource is **not collected by must-gather**, so it's only available when checking the cluster): ~~~ $ oc get cluster.aro.openshift.io cluster-o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,RESOURCE_ID:.spec.resourceId NAME RESOURCE_ID cluster /subscriptions/$sub_id/resourceGroups/$rg/providers/Microsoft.RedHatOpenShift/openShiftClusters/$cluster_name ~~~- The `configmap` `cluster-config-v1` in namespace `kube-system` show if the cluster is ARO (it can be shown in a must-gather): ~~~ $ oc get cm cluster-config-v1-n kube-system-o yaml [...] platform: azure: aro: true [...] image: offer: aro4 publisher: azureopenshift sku: aro_48 [...] ~~~ > **Note:** The steps below are valid for clusters that were initially installed at version 4.7 or later:- The `configmap: openshift-install-manifests` in namespace `openshift-config` has **ARO** in the `invoker` field (it can be shown in a must-gather): ~~~ $ oc get cm openshift-install-manifests-n openshift-config-o yaml apiVersion: v1 data: invoker: ARO [...] ~~~
root_cause: An ARO cluster has an Azure `Resource ID` and also some resources indicating that the cluster is ARO.

title: How do I clear the preset java options in JBoss EAP 8 OpenShift?
product: Red Hat JBoss Enterprise Application Platform
issue: - How can I set the same value for the minimum and maximum heap sizes (e.g.-Xms2g-Xmx2g) and increase the interval between GC cycles in JBoss EAP 8 for OpenShift?- How can I clear the default java startup options `-XX:MinHeapFreeRatio=10`, `-XX:MaxHeapFreeRatio=20`, `-XX:GCTimeRatio=4`, and `-XX:AdaptiveSizePolicyWeight=90` are set in the JBoss EAP 8 for OpenShift image?- In `ubi9/openjdk-21-runtime`, setting `JAVA_OPTS` environment variable gives us full control over the default Java startup parameters as [documented](https://github.com/rh-openjdk/redhat-openjdk-containers/blob/ubi9-openjdk-containers-1.24/modules/jvm/module.yaml#L22-L25). However, in JBoss EAP 8 for OpenShift, even if `JAVA_OPTS` is set, the default java startup options are not removed.
resolution: Enhancement request [JBEAP-32580 [OpenShift] Setting JAVA_OPTS should disable default JVM options](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/JBEAP-32580) has been filed. Currently, there is no way to disable the default java startup options using environment variables. As a workaround, replace the container script `/opt/jboss/container/java/jvm/java-default-options` with an empty implementation to override the default java options: ~~~ $ cat > java-default-options < <'EOF' #!/bin/sh jvm_specific_diagnostics() {:} return 0 EOF oc create configmap disable-java-default-options--from-file=java-default-options oc set volume deployment/--add--name=disable-java-default-options--mount-path=/opt/jboss/container/java/jvm/java-default-options--sub-path=java-default-options--configmap-name=disable-java-default-options--default-mode=0774 oc set env deployment/ JAVA_OPTS="-XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50.0-XX:MaxHeapFreeRatio=100-XX:MetaspaceSize=256m-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError-Xlog:gc*::time,uptimemillis" ~~~ The following demonstrates that the default Java startup options `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=80.0`, `-XX:+UseParallelGC`, `-XX:MinHeapFreeRatio=10`, `-XX:MaxHeapFreeRatio=20`, `-XX:GCTimeRatio=4`, `-XX:AdaptiveSizePolicyWeight=90` and `-XX:MetaspaceSize=96m` are now disabled: ~~~ $ oc exec-- jps-lvm | grep jboss-modules.jar 489 /opt/server/jboss-modules.jar-mp /opt/server/modules org.jboss.as.standalone-Djboss.home.dir=/opt/server-Djboss.server.base.dir=/opt/server/standalone-c standalone.xml...-XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50.0-XX:MaxHeapFreeRatio=100-XX:MetaspaceSize=256m-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError-Xlog:gc*::time,uptimemillis-Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/./urandom-Djava.net.preferIPv4Stack=true-Djboss.modules.system.pkgs=jdk.nashorn.api,com.sun.crypto.provider... ~~~

title: Windows virtual machines in OpenShift Virtualization show only Video Controller (VGA Compatible) and do not support installing graphics drivers
issue: - Windows virtual machines in OpenShift Virtualization display a Video Controller (VGA Compatible) in Device Manager with an **unknown driver**.- No graphics driver can be installed.
resolution: - The **unknown driver** in Windows can be ignored.- This behavior is by design under current OpenShift Virtualization versions.- The default graphics interface provided for VMs is a VGA / bochs-compatible framebuffer (i.e. basic VGA).- There is no Windows driver shipped or supported for the bochs or VGA display device under KubeVirt / OCP.- Consequently, Windows falls back to using its built-in Microsoft Basic Display Adapter, and no additional graphics driver can be installed.- This limitation is inherent to the virtualization stack, it is not a misconfiguration of the guest. **An RFE** [CNV-48281](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/CNV-48281) has been opened to request changing the default video device from bochs/VGA to virtio-video for modern operating systems (Windows 10+)
root_cause: - OpenShift Virtualization uses `bochs-display` as the default video device. **References**: [list of supported drivers and instructions](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/host-devices/) [Virtual Hardware – Video & Graphics Device](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/virtual_hardware/)

title: What does swappiness do and how does it affect swap_tendency?
issue: - What does swappiness do and how does it affect swap_tendency?
resolution: **Note:**_The swapping algorithm is overhauled in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6 and up to consider active and inactive memory for both file-backed and anonymous (non-file-backed) memory. While swappiness still exerts a considerable shift in behaviour on swap activity on a system, swappiness no longer uses the algorithm described below. As such, `swap_tendency`, `distress`, and `mapped_ratio` no longer exist in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6 and above._- Swappiness is a property for the Linux kernel that changes the balance between swapping out runtime memory, as opposed to dropping pages from the system page cache. Swappiness can be set to values between 0 and 100, inclusive. A low value means the kernel will try to avoid swapping as much as possible where a higher value instead will make the kernel aggressively try to use swap space.- As this parameter sets the kernel's balance between reclaiming pages from the page cache and reclaiming pages by swapping out process memory, a discussion of page reclaim overall is warranted. The reclaim code works (in a very simplified way) by calculating a few numbers:- The `distress` value is a measure of how much trouble the kernel is having freeing memory. The first time the kernel decides it needs to start reclaiming pages, distress will be zero; if more attempts are required, that value goes up, approaching a max value of 100.- The `mapped_ratio` value is an approximate percentage of how much of the system's total memory is mapped (i.e. is part of a process's address space) within a given memory zone.- And `vm_swappiness` is the swappiness parameter, set to 60 by default. With these numbers in hand, the kernel calculates its "swap tendency": ~~~ swap_tendency = mapped_ratio/2 + distress + vm_swappiness; ~~~- If swap_tendency is below 100, the kernel will only reclaim page cache pages. Once it goes above that value, however, pages which are part of some process's address space will also be considered for reclaim. So, if the system's distress value is low and swappiness is set to 60, the system will not swap process memory until 80% of the total RAM in the system is allocated. Users who would like to never see application memory swapped out can set swappiness to a low value, say 5 or 10, causing the kernel to ignore process memory until the distress value gets quite high.- Overall, increasing this value will make the system more inclined to utilize swap space, leaving more memory free for caches. Decreasing this value will make the system less inclined to swap, and may improve application responsiveness.- Tuning `vm.swappiness` incorrectly may hurt performance or may have a different impact between light and heavy workloads. Changes to this parameter should be made in small increments and should be tested under the same conditions that the system normally operates.

title: kernel crash while running NIC NVM update Intel E825-C NIC
issue: - Observed the kernel crash while running nvmupdate64e NIC NVM update from OS...- We even saw the NULL pointer dereference in the Kernel crash
resolution: - Do not perform firmware updates during production.- Or before flash NVM, remove all sriov networks resource pool so that there are no VFs in `ip addr`.- Red Hat have submitted this patch upstream that fixes the issue: ~~~ [iwl-net] ice: fix NULL pointer dereference in ice_reset_all_vfs() ~~~ The patch will be backported to Red Hat Enterprise Linux and Red Hat Openshift Container Platform when it is accepted by upstream.
root_cause: - The ice driver crashes due to txq_map and rxq_map NULL pointers because VSI structures are changing due to the firmware update.
